input: A 38-year-old man presented to the First Department of Orthopaedics at the University of Athens in June, 2013, with a 4-year history of an enlarging left shoulder mass. He reported minor recurrent injury during athletic activity. Medical and family history were unremarkable. Clinical examination showed a firm, painless mass. Radiography showed calcifications posterior to the left scapula (figure, A). CT scan showed multiple calcified nodules, without scapular erosion (figure, B). MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity (figure, C). Serum calcium, phosphate, vitamin D, and amounts of parathyroid hormone were within normal limits. Differential diagnosis included tumoral calcinosis, myositis ossificans, synovial chondromatosis, and synovial sarcoma. Tumoral calcinosis consists of lobulated, well-demarked calcifications, generally at the extensor surfaces of large joints. Myositis ossificans consists of bone and cartilage formation within muscle; rapid evolution and absence of lobular morphology are typical features. Synovial chondromatosis consists of intrasynovial proliferation of cartilage, with typical rings-and-arcs calcifications and intra-articular location. Synovial sarcomas are poorly defined and infiltrative, with punctuate calcifications occurring sporadically. Because of the absence of family history of tumoral calcinosis and biochemical abnormalities in this patient, and to avoid potential diagnostic pitfalls, a needle biopsy was done. Histology was consistent with tumoral calcinosis showing amorphous calcium nodules surrounded by histiocytic and giant cell reaction. The lesion was completely surgically excised, without any recurrence at the 3-year follow-up in September, 2016. Follow-up is ongoing.

A 61-year-old man presented with bilateral, asymptomatic, indurated non-pitting verrucous plaques and nodules on his extremities and buttocks. He was diagnosed with Graves' disease 20 years ago. The patient developed hypothyroidism secondary to radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid 4 years prior to presenting to us and received levothyroxine replacement therapy, after which he attained a sustained euthyroid state. However, he developed an asymptomatic rash over his extremities and buttock, which worsened gradually. On physical examination, several plaques that were leathery in texture and nodules were observed on his extremities and buttock (figure A每D). The results of thyroid-function tests were normal (free tri-iodothyronine [T3] 3﹞83 pg/mL, local reference 1﹞80每4﹞10; free thyroxine [T4] 1﹞23 ng/dL, local reference 0﹞81每1﹞89) except for a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 0﹞094 米IU/mL (local reference 0﹞38每4﹞34) and thyrotrophin receptor antibody concentration of 280﹞51 IU/L (local reference <13). Results of liver and kidney function tests were normal, and concentrations of calcium, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D3, parathyroid hormone, urinary calcium, and urine phosphorus were within normal limits. On histological examination of skin lesion biopsy specimens stained with haematoxylin and eosin and alcian blue, abundant deposition of mucin was seen in the dermis (figure E, F). The final diagnosis according to the pathology report was myxedema. Despite application of potent topical corticosteroids, occlusive or compressive therapy, and multipoint subcutaneous injection of long-acting glucocorticoid, the skin lesions showed no obvious signs of remission after 6 months of treatment.Myxedema results from the accumulation in the dermis of glycosaminoglycan secreted by fibroblasts. The pathogenesis of the extrathyroidal manifestations of myxedema involves fibroblast activation and increased glycosaminoglycan production. Some studies postulate that the destruction of the thyroid gland by therapeutic drugs (especially iodine-131) results in the release of an antigen from thyroid cells that then stimulates the production of the thyrotrophin receptor antibody. The fibroblast in the orbital area and pretibial dermis share antigenic sites that underlie the autoimmune process that causes Graves' disease. Thereby crossreaction contributes to the development of myxedema occurring long after euthyroid status is achieved through treatment. Although myxedema does not seem to be related to the concentrations of T3 and T4, only four cases of euthyroid patients being diagnosed with myxedema have been reported in the literature.

A 55-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with fistulising ileocolonic Crohn's disease 5 years ago presented with pain and swelling at the right hip for 2 months. For the past 3 years before presentation, the patient had not attended previous outpatient clinic appointments and had stopped using medication prescribed for Crohn's disease. On examination, the patient looked ill and cachectic. She was not able to walk without support, had a fever (38～C), her conjunctivas were pale, and she had multiple fistulas on her right inguinal region and right flank. The right inguinal fistula was active with visible faecal discharge. Her right hip was swollen, warm, and had decreased range of motion. Laboratory investigations identified iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 9﹞8 g/dL, haematocrit 30%, mean corpuscular volume 77 fL) and leukocytosis (neutrophil count 8730 cells per mm3), elevated C-reactive protein (96 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (31 mm/h), and decreased albumin (1﹞5 g/dL).The patient's clinical features, including fever, monoarthritis of a large joint, short duration of presentation, and extensive intestinal involvement with a penetrating disease phenotype, suggested an alternative diagnosis to inflammatory arthritis. Furthermore, a CT of the abdomen showed effusion and narrowing of the right coxofemoral joint space adjacent to the diseased ileal segment that was consistent with septic arthritis. To investigate the fistula route, a fistulogram was obtained by injecting contrast through the orifice of the right inguinal fistula, which showed that the tract was extending from the terminal ileum to the right hip joint and right pararenal space (figure). Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were commenced for septic arthritis. The patient improved clinically with resolution of fever within the first 2 weeks of antibiotic therapy and nutritional support. A follow-up CT showed reduced inflammation at the right hip; however, the patient had fever after 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy. Surgical management was decided by the multidisciplinary team due to fever and the active fistula. During surgery, an enteroenteric fistula located 15 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve was detected, which necessitated an ileocaecal resection and diverting ileostomy. After surgery, the patient received 2 more weeks of intravenous antibiotics for septic arthritis (total 6 weeks). We treated the patient with infliximab plus immunomodulator therapy after the antibiotic therapy, which achieved clinical remission at 12 weeks of treatment and endoscopic remission at 24 weeks.
Patients with Crohn's disease can develop intestinal and extraintestinal complications. Although inflammatory arthritis is a common extraintestinal manifestation of Crohn's disease, septic arthritis should be considered in patients with a penetrating disease phenotype and requires a tailored approach to management.
output: Enteroarticular fistula from terminal ileum causing septic arthritis of the right hip in Crohn＊s disease

A 60-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve and dilatation of the ascending aorta had surgical bioprosthesis implantation with aortic repair. 6 weeks after the sternotomy scar had completely healed, several soft nodules appeared progressively along the scar without pus or grains (figure, A). He had no fever, pain, or erythema on the sternal area. Laboratory tests showed normal leucocytosis, and C-reactive protein was 190﹞48 nmol/L. Cultures of cutaneous swabs and biopsy samples grew meticillin-sensitive?Staphylococcus aureus?(MSSA). Mycobacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Investigation of skin biopsy samples showed a dermal polymorphic infiltrate with epithelioid and giant cell granulomas without necrosis or grains (figure, B). Periodic-acid Schiff, Gram, Grocott, and Zielh stains were negative. Thoracic CT revealed a sternum osteolysis with periosteal reaction and bone disjunction (figure, C). Sternum osteitis was confirmed by surgical findings and cultures of bone sample, positive for MSSA. The treatment combined surgical drainage and antibiotic therapy with 1 week of intravenous cefamandole followed by oral ofloxacine and rifampicin for 3 months. The patient did not relapse during more than 15 months of follow-up.Botryomycosis is a rare, chronic, and granulomatous cutaneous bacterial infection mostly due to Staphylococcus aureus, presenting as nodules typically characterised by the formation of grains. However, lesions can be atypical, similar to pyogenic granulomas. Cutaneous lesions usually reveal underlying, chronic soft tissue, muscle, or bone staphylococcal infection, as in our case. Pathophysiology of botryomycosis involves a balance between a low virulence of the bacteria and host resistance.
When presented with such lesions, clinicians should look for an underlying bone or soft tissue staphylococcal infection, especially in patients who have had recent surgery.
output: Botryomycosis with sternal osteomyelitis due to methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus

A 27-year-old Asian man presented with erythematous, violaceous, and photosensitive lesions on the face, upper chest, and scalp, which had developed over 6 months (figure A). The patient had previously consulted a private practitioner for malar and heliotrope rash with photosensitivity and periorbital puffiness, who prescribed him methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine. However, the lesions progressed with ulceration over bilateral malar areas and the left mandibular angle (figure B每C), associated with non-scarring alopecia, oral ulcers, and violaceous papules on the dorsal aspect of metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints (Gottron's papules). There were no other comorbidities. On examination, the patient's blood pressure was 146/96 mm Hg and he had facial ulcers, as described (figure B每C). Investigations revealed he had mild elevation of alanine aminotransferase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, both elevated up to 2?℅ the upper limit of normal.
Based on the patient's history and symptoms, a number of differential diagnoses were considered, including dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus vulgaris (tuberculosis), granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and sarcoidosis. Buruli ulcer, which might also have a similar presentation, has yet to be reported in India. He had no clinical, radiological, or laboratory evidence of myositis, interstitial lung disease, neuropathy, nephritis, or arthritis. Serum creatine kinase, nerve conduction study results, and urine analysis were within normal limits and a high-resolution chest CT showed no abnormalities. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy sample from the ulcer edge from the left mandibular angle revealed perivascular and periadnexal lymphoid infiltrates, vacuolar interface dermatitis, and basement membrane zone thickening (figure D). Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgA, IgG, IgM, C1q, and C3. Ziehl每Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacillus, and there was no evidence of malignancy. Serology for antinuclear antibody (Hep-2 cell by indirect immunofluorescence assay) was negative; although, an immunoblot was strongly positive for anti-MDA5. A diagnosis of anti-MDA5 amyopathic dermatomyositis was made.
Treatment with a combination of oral prednisolone (30 mg per day for 2 weeks, tapered over 2 months), mycophenolate mofetil (2 g per day), and topical tacrolimus healed his facial ulcers completely and dramatically reduced facial erythema, oral ulcers, heliotrope rash, and Gottron's papules over 7 months (figure E每F). The patient was followed up initially on a monthly basis for 3 months and then once every 3 months subsequently. Residual post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was noted at 1 year after starting mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone (figure E每F). The patient also remained hypertensive during the first 2 months of treatment, which was managed and controlled with lifestyle modifications alone. The patient has been under follow-up for 18 months with no additional symptoms, and continues to be treated with mycophenolate mofetil.
Anti-MDA5, a myositis-specific antibody, is typically associated with ulcers on the digits and extensor surfaces and facial ulcerations have not been reported previously. Progressive facial ulcers without accompanying myositis make for a diagnostic challenge.

A 96-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of pleuritic chest pain 4 days after a single-chamber transvenous pacemaker had been implanted. A chest radiograph and computed tomographic scan of the chest showed the tip of the right ventricular lead in the left pleural space. What rhythm does the electrocardiogram show?
output:
Based on the clinical history of a recent pacemaker implantation followed by pleuritic chest pain, and the imaging findings (CXR and CT) showing the pacemaker lead tip perforating the right ventricle and residing in the left pleural space, the pacemaker lead is not in contact with the myocardium. Consequently, the electrical stimuli (pacing spikes) generated by the pacemaker are unable to depolarize the heart muscle.

The electrocardiogram displays distinct vertical pacing spikes occurring at a regular interval, but most of these spikes are not followed by a QRS complex. This indicates that the electrical impulse is failing to initiate a heartbeat. This rhythm disturbance is known as failure to capture.

A 61-year-old Japanese man with a history of cord-blood transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia 15 years previously, and chronic graft-versus-host disease of the skin, was admitted for bleeding due to a duodenal ulcer. A maintenance dose of 5 mg prednisone was administered daily. The patient was successfully treated with a combination of endoscopic clipping and proton-pump inhibitor. 7 days after the episode of gastrointestinal bleeding, the patient underwent repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopies, which showed multiple, newly developed, shallow ulcers in the oesophagus. Some of the lesions were circumscribed and discrete (figure).An oesophageal biopsy of the lesions was done, and histopathology of the oesophagus showed ballooning degeneration and multinucleated epithelial giant cells with eosinophilic intracellular inclusion bodies (figure). The biopsy samples showed neither malignancy nor graft-versus-host disease. Immunohistochemical staining of the specimens was also positive for herpes simplex virus, but negative for cytomegalovirus. On the basis of the gross and histopathological findings, herpes simplex oesophagitis was diagnosed. After the patient completed a 10 day course of intravenous aciclovir, repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopies showed no abnormalities.
Herpes simplex virus is one of the most common pathogens causing infective oesophagitis. Herpes simplex oesophagitis is commonly seen in patients with immunosuppressive status, including after bone marrow transplantation, but has also been reported in immunocompetent individuals. In some patients, oesophagitis due to other pathogens such as cytomegalovirus or Candidia spp has been reported. Diagnosis is often confirmed by a combination of the gross oesophagogastroduodenoscopy findings, a histopathological examination, and an immunohistochemical stain of the biopsied specimen. Oesophageal herpes simplex lesions detected by oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are typically referred to as volcano ulcers, and appear as discrete, diffusely scattered shallow ulcers. The Cowdry type-A inclusion body is a classic histopathological finding in biopsy specimens of herpes simplex oesopohagitis as seen in this case, and is observed in up to 70% of biopsy specimens.

Our 17-year-old male patient, with a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS), presented to the UK Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome National Diagnostic Service for specialist advice and support, following the sudden death of his brother, who was also affected by vEDS. The patient and his brother were heterozygous for the familial COL3A1 (c.547G>A p.[Gly183Ser]) variant, identified following predictive testing in childhood. Despite having a molecular diagnosis in childhood (done locally), the patient only presented to our specialist service after the death of his brother.
Our patient had easy bruising and translucent skin with prominent superficial veins, particularly around the chest and forehead, and subtle facial features consistent with vEDS (figure). He had an initial left, then subsequent right, recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax requiring pleurodesis (figure). He is now receiving magnetic resonance angiography screening locally and has recently commenced losartan, in order to reduce vascular events.
His brother's medical history comprised an intra-abdominal bleed following a fall from a skateboard, (managed conservatively), and bypass surgery for a ruptured right subclavian artery aneurysm at age 19 years (figure). At age 20 years, he presented to hospital with loss of sensation in the right arm and severe, acute-onset chest pain. He deteriorated quickly and went into cardiac arrest, with no response to resuscitation efforts. Post-mortem examination confirmed the cause of death was aortic dissection. Magnetic resonance angiography screening was planned following his initial vascular event, but did not occur before death. He was not on medical therapy.
This diagnosis was first identified in the father of our patient, who suffered an intestinal arterial rupture at age 16 years, had previous joint dislocations (thumb and shoulder), and early-onset varicose veins (figure), which prompted the genetic testing in the two children when they were young to screen for vEDS. He was also referred to our specialist service following the death of his son. He had also been managed elsewhere (locally), but was not on treatment.
vEDS is a rare type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and accounts for less than 5% of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnoses, with an estimated prevalence of between 1 in 50?000 to 1 in 200?000. This autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder is characterised by fragile connective tissues due to altered type III collagen. Potentially fatal consequences include blood vessel dissection and rupture, tension pneumothorax, and hollow organ rupture (primarily sigmoid colon). Musculoskeletal manifestations, in addition to those described in this family, can include small-joint hypermobility and distal contractures (including talipes).
In an emergency, the diagnosis of vEDS must be considered to guide medical care or intervention due to increased tissue fragility and the risk of bleeding. Longitudinal management comprises regular vascular screening, although vessel dissection can occur spontaneously. 汕 blockers, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and lifestyle modifications have been shown to reduce vascular events. Multidisciplinary involvement is recommended for planned procedures.

A 30-month-old girl attended our clinic for exploration of optic nerve atrophy after she initially presented with respiratory difficulties at 20 months of age. The patient, who had been born at 39 weeks of gestation, also had feeding difficulties, nasal obstruction, and a reduced ability to open her mouth; she had developed progressive macrocephaly in the first few months of life (appendix).
On examination, she had dysmorphic facial features〞a bulging forehead, a wide nasal bridge, and hypertelorism; she also had macroglossia, divergent strabismus, nasal obstruction, reduced mouth opening, and mastication and swallowing difficulties. Additionally, the patient had mixed hearing loss due to blockage of the ossicular chain with ossification of the petrous bone and cochlear nerve compression. output:
Based on the clinical presentation of a 31-year-old man from El Salvador with HIV/AIDS presenting with neurological symptoms (headache, confusion, gait instability, fever) and brain MRI showing a large mass with Trypanosoma cruzi identified on brain aspirate, the diagnosis is **Chagas disease** (American trypanosomiasis) with cerebral involvement.

The vector responsible for transmission of *Trypanosoma cruzi* is:

**Triatomine bug (Reduviid bug/Kissing bug)**

These blood-sucking insects of the family Reduviidae (particularly species in genera *Triatoma*, *Rhodnius*, and *Panstrongylus*) transmit the parasite through their feces during feeding. The bugs typically bite around the mouth and eyes at night, hence the common name "kissing bugs." The parasite enters through the bite wound or mucous membranes when the victim rubs the infected feces into the site.

In immunocompromised patients like those with HIV/AIDS, *Trypanosoma cruzi* can cause severe reactivation disease, including meningoencephalitis with brain abscess formation (chagoma), as seen in this case.

Our 17-year-old male patient, with a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (vEDS), presented to the UK Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome National Diagnostic Service for specialist advice and support, following the sudden death of his brother, who was also affected by vEDS. The patient and his brother were heterozygous for the familial COL3A1 (c.547G>A p.[Gly183Ser]) variant, identified following predictive testing in childhood. Despite having a molecular diagnosis in childhood (done locally), the patient only presented to our specialist service after the death of his brother.
Our patient had easy bruising and translucent skin with prominent superficial veins, particularly around the chest and forehead, and subtle facial features consistent with vEDS (figure). He had an initial left, then subsequent right, recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax requiring pleurodesis (figure). He is now receiving magnetic resonance angiography screening locally and has recently commenced losartan, in order to reduce vascular events.
His brother's medical history comprised an intra-abdominal bleed following a fall from a skateboard, (managed conservatively), and bypass surgery for a ruptured right subclavian artery aneurysm at age 19 years (figure). At age 20 years, he presented to hospital with loss of sensation in the right arm and severe, acute-onset chest pain. He deteriorated quickly and went into cardiac arrest, with no response to resuscitation efforts. Post-mortem examination confirmed the cause of death was aortic dissection. Magnetic resonance angiography screening was planned following his initial vascular event, but did not occur before death. He was not on medical therapy.
This diagnosis was first identified in the father of our patient, who suffered an intestinal arterial rupture at age 16 years, had previous joint dislocations (thumb and shoulder), and early-onset varicose veins (figure), which prompted the genetic testing in the two children when they were young to screen for vEDS. He was also referred to our specialist service following the death of his son. He had also been managed elsewhere (locally), but was not on treatment.
vEDS is a rare type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and accounts for less than 5% of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome diagnoses, with an estimated prevalence of between 1 in 50?000 to 1 in 200?000. This autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder is characterised by fragile connective tissues due to altered type III collagen. Potentially fatal consequences include blood vessel dissection and rupture, tension pneumothorax, and hollow organ rupture (primarily sigmoid colon). Musculoskeletal manifestations, in addition to those described in this family, can include small-joint hypermobility and distal contractures (including talipes).
In an emergency, the diagnosis of vEDS must be considered to guide medical care or intervention due to increased tissue fragility and the risk of bleeding. Longitudinal management comprises regular vascular screening, although vessel dissection can occur spontaneously. 汕 blockers, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and lifestyle modifications have been shown to reduce vascular events. Multidisciplinary involvement is recommended for planned procedures.

A 44-year-old man attended our hospital reporting reduced vision in his left eye. 10 days earlier he had been started on treatment with supplemental oxygen, intravenous antibiotics, and corticosteroids because of a moderately severe pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2. The patient explained that a blackish patch〞extending from just below his left eye to the left side of his face to the level of his mouth〞had also developed 2 days earlier (figure).The patient was a known diabetic; he had no history of malignancy.
On examination his temperature was 37～C, pulse was 84 beats per min, blood pressure was 118/82 mm Hg, and respiratory rate was 16 breaths per min; pulse oximetry showed an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. The patient had exophthalmos, ophthalmoplegia, and chemosis of his left eye. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in his right eye, but he reported no perception of light in his left eye.
Laboratory investigations showed a random blood sugar concentration of 298 mg/dL (normal 140 or below), glycated haemoglobin A1c of 9﹞8% (normal 4每5﹞6), arterial blood pH 7﹞4 (normal 7﹞35每7﹞45), serum bicarbonate concentration 24 mEq/L (normal 23每30), and a mild neutropenia (1510 neutrophils per 米L; normal 1800每6300).
Examination of a potassium hydroxide mount of nasal scrapings showed broad, pauci-septate hyphae; and Sabouraud dextrose agar culture and lactophenol cotton blue mount were suggestive of Rhizopus arrhizus (figure).
Contrast-enhanced MRI showed non-enhancement of the bilateral middle and inferior turbinate: the characteristic so-called black turbinate sign (figure). Contiguous extension of non-enhancing soft tissue into the left middle and ethmoidal air cells, with a breach in the cribriform plate to involve the basal frontal region was noted (figure). T2-hyperintense diffuse inflammatory changes were seen in the soft tissues of the left orbital region〞involving the pre-septal, post-septal, and intraconal and extraconal compartments with orbital fat stranding (figure). Heterogeneously enhancing soft-tissue inflammatory changes were noted on the left side of the face involving the premaxillary region, buccal fat pad, and infra-temporal fossa (figure). Together〞the clinical picture and the radiological findings〞indicated mucormycosis.
The patient was started on intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a dose of 5 mg/kg per day; an insulin infusion was also continued because of persistent hyperglycaemia. Extensive debridement, a left total maxillectomy, and orbital exenteration were done under a general anaesthetic; however, the patient died 6 days later.
During the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in India, an unprecedented surge in cases of mucormycosis was observed: immune dysregulation caused by the SARS-CoV-2 and the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and corticosteroids〞particularly in patients with poorly controlled diabetes with ketoacidosis〞is likely to have contributed to the rise.
COVID-19 followed by mucormycosis carries a very high mortality rate and timely detection, antifungal therapy, and aggressive surgical debridement remain key factors in the management (video).

Based on the patient's origin (Eritrea), the clinical history of long-term intermittent fevers (suggestive of a relapsing form of malaria due to liver hypnozoites), and the blood smear finding of a ring-form trophozoite inside a red blood cell that is noticeably enlarged and pale compared to the surrounding cells, the diagnosis is infection with *Plasmodium vivax*. The enlargement of the infected red blood cell is a key morphological feature distinguishing *Plasmodium vivax* (and *P. ovale*) from *Plasmodium falciparum* and *Plasmodium malariae*. *Plasmodium vivax* is the most common cause of malaria in the Horn of Africa (Eritrea/Ethiopia).

A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab〞a PD-1 inhibitor〞and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32～C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10?518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8每10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0﹞52 g/L; typical level <0﹞4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50每70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control〞despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

input: A 3-week-old male newborn was brought to the pediatrician with three large scalp lesions, which had appeared in the first week of life. The lesions were annular with raised papular and pustular borders and flat, hyperkeratotic central areas. The baby＊s mother, who was originally from Somalia, had similar skin lesions on her upper trunk. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Tinea capitis (dermatophytosis/ringworm of the scalp)

The clinical presentation shows classic annular lesions with raised, scaly/pustular borders and central clearing - the characteristic appearance of dermatophyte infection (tinea). The fact that the mother has similar lesions on her trunk suggests tinea corporis, indicating likely transmission of the dermatophyte infection from mother to infant.

In neonates, tinea capitis can present early if there is direct contact with an infected caregiver. The geographic origin (Somalia) is relevant as certain dermatophyte species are more prevalent in different regions.

A 2-year-old boy presented to our unit with swelling of the left side of his face and mouth. He had been investigated before we saw him, and imaging was consistent with recurrence of a giant cell tumour in the left maxilla. 2 months earlier, the patient had a subtotal resection of the mass; he had initially presented aged 1 year and 11 months with a painless swelling of the left side of his mouth. On examination the patient was generally well; he had a 2 cm?℅?2 cm reddish purple bulging lesion on the left palate.A CT scan, with contrast, of the maxillofacial region showed that the tumour had invaded the left nasal cavity, maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and raised the floor of the left orbit.
We started the patient on high-dose denosumab〞 1﹞7 mg/kg given subcutaneously every 4 weeks〞which was continued after he had been allowed home. The size of the tumour reduced substantially.
After 7 months of treatment, the boy developed pain in his left knee; an x-ray showed dense sclerosis about the distal femoral, proximal tibial, and fibular metaphyses along with two atypical stress fractures (figure). An x-ray of his left hand showed diffuse sclerosis with an asymptomatic atypical stress fracture of the metaphysis of the distal ulna (figure).
Because of propitious response seen on the tumour by the treatment, together with the observed metaphyseal sclerosis and concern for atypical stress fractures, we decided to stop the denosumab and do a further surgical resection of the lesion.
Follow-up will involve the patient being seen every 3 months with serial imaging to monitor for tumour recurrence.
Giant cell tumours are rare benign primary bone neoplasms composed of neoplastic primitive mesenchymal stromal cells that overexpress receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa 汕 ligand (RANKL) which promotes formation of osteoclast-like giant cells that create osteolytic lesions. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that suppresses osteoclastogenesis and inhibits bone resorption. In neoplastic disorders such as giant cell tumours of bone, denosumab may also promote osteoblastic differentiation resulting in mineralisation of the lesion. Sclerotic bands are a manifestation of antiresorptive therapy in children before closure of the epiphyseal growth plates, and result from disruption in osteoclastic resorption of growth plate cartilage. The extent of sclerosis varies depending on the patient's age, growth rate, and antiresorptive regimen. Denosumab has potent anti-osteoclastic effects, and oncologic doses may result in bone turnover suppression〞particularly in young children with rapid skeletal growth〞which may result in stress fractures, as seen in our patient. Children treated with denosumab should undergo clinical monitoring for potential adverse metaphyseal effects. Radiographic assessment may be helpful in evaluating metaphyseal changes and should be done in any patient presenting with bone pain (video).
output: Denosumab-induced metaphyseal sclerosis with atypical stress fractures

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 6.5 g per deciliter (reference range, 12.0 to 16.0), and normal renal function. Chest and abdominal radiographs were obtained. output:
Based on the radiographic findings showing extensive metallic opacities distributed throughout the lungs and abdomen (consistent with mercury deposition), combined with the clinical history of:
- Folk remedy administration for tinea cruris
- 3-month history of fatigue, nausea, and dry cough
- Severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL)

**Diagnosis: Mercury poisoning (elemental mercury toxicity)**

The appropriate treatment for this condition is **chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA/Succimer) or dimercaptopropane sulfonate (DMPS)**, along with supportive care including blood transfusion for severe anemia.

A 61-year-old woman with a 4-day history of asthenia, fever, and a rash was seen by our team in the hospital intensive care unit.
The patient had clear cell renal cell carcinoma with tumoral thrombosis of the right renal vein and inferior vena cava. She was being treated with a checkpoint inhibitor, pembrolizumab〞a PD-1 inhibitor〞and the endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGF-R) tyrosine kinase inhibitor, axitinib, before re-assessment for surgery, in the oncology day hospital unit. 3 days after the third infusion of pembrolizumab, the patient had been admitted to the intensive care unit because she had become haemodynamically unstable; she had developed heart failure, and purpura fulminans (figure; appendix) over her arms and legs, which had initially appeared as livedo racemose a few hours before. She had also been found to have an ascending sensory motor deficit of her lower limbs.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell; her blood pressure was 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 30 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 100% on 15 L/min oxygen, and temperature was 32～C. She was confused, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 (eye opening response 2, verbal response 2, and motor response 4). She needed both noradrenaline and dobutamine because of her cardiac failure. Additionally, the patient was being treated with meropenem and amikacin; axitinib had been stopped at the point of admission to the intensive care unit.
Laboratory investigations showed high concentrations of N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (10?518 pg/mL; typical level <125 in people younger than 75 years) and troponin (109 ng/L; typical level <14). Concentrations of liver enzymes and thyroid-stimulating hormone were elevated; C-reactive protein concentration was 36 mg/L (typical range 8每10). Analysis of a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed an elevated protein concentration (0﹞52 g/L; typical level <0﹞4) and a normal white blood cell count; cultures of blood, CSF, urine, and skin showed no abnormalities.
PCR skin swab testing was negative for Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae, resulting in the cessation of antibiotics treatment.
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed diffuse thickening of the wall of the colon; echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% (normal range 50每70). MRIs of brain and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. An electromyogram showed severe sensory-motor neurogenic damage compatible with axonal length-dependent processes without demyelination.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a skin biopsy showed thrombosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis, which, considering the patient's presentation, investigations, and history in the round, led us to conclude she had developed an immune-induced myocarditis, acute motor and sensory axonal polyneuropathy, colitis, hypothyroidism, hepatitis, and purpura fulminans.
The patient was commenced on pulse methylprednisolone (1 g per day for 5 days) and intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g per kg over 4 days), which resulted in the improvement of her general condition. She had three separate plasma exchanges to clear the pembrolizumab and surgery of the deepest wounds with skin grafts.
The corticosteroids were gradually tapered down over the next 4 months, and at follow-up 6 months later the skin lesions had completely healed. The patient's neoplastic disease was under control〞despite discontinuation of the pembrolizumab and axitinib.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have become established treatments for several cancers including malignant melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. Such developments have, in some patients resulted, in treatment-related adverse effects of variable severity. Immune-related purpura fulminans associated with pembrolizumab has been reported previously in a patient treated for lung carcinoma.

A 68-year-old woman with a 20-day history of exertional dyspnoea, acrocyanosis, and critical ischaemia〞dry gangrene〞of her fingers, presented to our rheumatology clinic (figure); she also reported the recent onset of pain in the small joints of her hands and wrists, Raynaud's phenomenon in her fingers and toes, and a feeling of general fatigue. The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36﹞0～C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased〞including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1﹞7 mg/dL (normal level <0﹞3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2?℅?1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0﹞8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost〞as a vasodilator〞to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints〞as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.
output: Antisynthetase syndrome with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease and critical digital ischaemia (dry gangrene)

A 46-year-old woman attended our emergency department reporting a 3-month history of dyspnoea and, in the last 2 weeks, lower limb oedema. The patient had a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which had been diagnosed 13 years before, and had been treated with oral hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day. 1 year earlier, she had presented with syncope; an electrocardiogram (ECG) had showed paroxysmal third-degree atrioventricular block, and a dual-chamber pacemaker had been fitted. An echocardiogram had shown normal biventricular systolic function and mild to moderate left ventricular hypertrophy with an interventricular septum diameter of 13 mm (normal range 6每9); no further investigations were done.
On examination, at our hospital, the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 80/40 mm Hg, she had peripheral oedema, jugular venous distension, pulmonary crackles, and cold extremities. An ECG showed atrial fibrillation with ventricular pacing at 69 beats per min (appendix). Laboratory tests showed a significantly raised N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentration of 31?255 ng/L (normal range 0每86) and high-sensitivity cardiac troponin concentration of 543 ng/L (normal range 0每14); and signs of hepatic injury with alanine aminotransferase concentration of 126 U/L (normal range 3每45), aspartate aminotransferase concentration of 92 U/L (normal range 0每40), total bilirubin concentration of 2﹞51 mg/dL (normal range 0﹞25每1). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction〞left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%〞and a restrictive filling pattern. Severe concentric hypertrophy was evident with an interventricular septum diameter of 17 mm and heterogeneous myocardial texture (figure).
The differential diagnoses we considered included inflammatory and infiltrative cardiomyopathies〞specifically reactive systemic (AA) amyloidosis related to the long-lasting autoimmune disorder〞or a hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy.
Inotropic support was immediately started, the hydroxychloroquine was discontinued, and the patient was admitted to our intensive care unit. Despite all these measures, 3 days after admission, the patient developed cardiogenic shock and required haemodynamic support with venous-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
An endomyocardial biopsy was done with the patient on temporary mechanical support; we hoped the results would inform ongoing treatment. Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at biopsy showed vacuolisation of multiple cardiomyocytes with no inflammatory infiltrate; no amyloid was found (figure). Transmission electron microscopy showed lamellar lysosomal structures〞myeloid bodies〞and curvilinear inclusions consistent with drug-induced myocardial toxicity. Considering these classic findings, a diagnosis of hydroxychloroquine-induced cardiomyopathy was made.
8 days after admission, despite maximal pharmacological and mechanical support, the patient died due to refractory cardiogenic shock while heart transplantation screening was ongoing. The results of metabolic testing, available after the patient's death, showed no evidence of lysosomal storage disorders〞including Fabry's disease and mucopolysaccharidoses. Additionally, the heart post-mortem showed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy: septal thickness 16 mm (normal value 13﹞6 mm [SD 2﹞0 mm]) and an increased thickness of the right ventricle free wall of 8 mm (normal value 3﹞8 mm [SD 0﹞9 mm]). The cardiac mass was also increased (weight 500 g; typical range 190每360; figure).
Chronic use of hydroxychloroquine can result in a drug-induced cardiomyopathy characterised by concentric hypertrophy and conduction abnormalities. Early clinical suspicion is essential, since the condition is potentially reversible. Delay in discontinuation of the drug may not improve the pathology, especially in patients〞as in this case〞with advanced heart failure.

The patient, a farmer, had been unable to carry out her daily tasks for the past 1 month. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension treated with nebivolol; she had never smoked cigarettes.
On examination, the patient was distressed and tachypnoeic; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 92% on 21% fraction of inspired oxygen; respiratory rate was 25 breaths per min. Her temperature was 36﹞0～C. Inspiratory crackles were heard on auscultation of the chest; neurological examination showed no abnormalities and proximal muscle strength of her arms and legs was within typical limits.
Laboratory investigations found antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a speckled pattern. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies were positive and anti-Ro52 antibodies were strongly positive (range from negative to borderline to positive, and strongly positive) identified through immunoblotting. Anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Acute phase proteins were increased〞including concentration of C-reactive protein, which was 1﹞7 mg/dL (normal level <0﹞3).
Chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure). Additionally, ulnar artery pulses were clinically absent with severely diminished blood flow observed during doppler ultrasound; CT angiography showed occlusion of the ulnar arteries bilaterally.
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, we diagnosed rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease due to antisynthetase syndrome complicated by critical ischaemia in her fingers. She was treated with three doses of pulse methylprednisolone (500 mg) followed by high dose intravenous prednisolone (1 mg/kg) and rituximab (2?℅?1 g intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days). The patient was also anticoagulated with subcutaneous enoxaparin 8000 IU/0﹞8 mL twice daily and aspirin 100 mg daily; intravenous iloprost〞as a vasodilator〞to counteract the ischaemia and to aid reperfusion was started.
The patient's condition stabilised with no further deterioration of the ischaemia in her fingers or her pulmonary function, and she was allowed home 42 days after her initial presentation. She was prescribed supplemental oxygen to use at home at a flow rate of 2 L/min.
At her last follow-up, 3 months after her initial presentation, the patient reported some progression of the digital ischaemia with gangrene up to the distal interphalangeal joints; her lung function had not changed, and a follow-up vascular ultrasound showed improved blood blow of the previously diminished pulses. The patient reported no fatigue but nevertheless still required home oxygen therapy.
Antisynthetase syndrome is one of a group of immune-mediated idiopathic inflammatory myopathies which primarily affect skeletal muscle but may also involve other organs such as the lungs, skin, and joints〞as in our patient. Multimodality immunosuppressive therapy may be required to control both the muscle and pulmonary manifestations of the disease; more recently CAR T-cell treatment has been used. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment improve outcomes.

A 37-year-old man attended our hospital with a 1-week history of fever, chills, headaches, sore throat, generalised malaise, and a rash on his arms, legs, trunk, and in his groin. The patient also reported significant pain and discomfort in his rectum when defecating. He had a history of HIV and metastatic Kaposi sarcoma; secondary syphilis, which had been treated; and hypertension. He was prescribed the following medications: emtricitabine-tenofovir, doravarine, darunavir-cobicistat, and hydrochlorothiazide.The patient reported no recent travel or contact with human or animal with a similar rash or illnesses. He reported no history of varicella zoster virus infection as a child and said he had received all childhood vaccinations. The patient reported no sexual activity for the past 6 months.
On examination, the patient was afebrile: temperature 37﹞3～C. He appeared uncomfortable and had several scattered, pink, umbilicated papules, vesicles, and pustules on the trunk, upper and lower extremities, groin, and peri-anal region (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12﹞7 g/dL (normal 13﹞3每16﹞3), CD4+ T-helper cell count of 262 cells per mcL (normal 490每1740), HIV-1 RNA PCR less than 20 copies per mL, and an absolute lymphocyte count of 3﹞01 per uL (normal 1﹞1每2﹞7). Serology was negative for Bartonella henselae, Aspergillus spp, hepatitis A, B, and C, cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), and (1↙3)-汕-D-glucan.
Immunohistochemical analysis of a biopsy sample of one of the truncal papules was negative for HSV-1, HSV-2, and Treponema pallidum. Warthin-Starry staining was negative for spirochetes and periodic-acid-Schiff staining was negative for fungal organisms. Histopathological analysis of the biopsy sample showed focal epidermal necrosis with underlying acute inflammation in the superficial dermis and individually necrotic keratinocytes at the periphery. A Dacron swab of one of the truncal lesions was positive for human monkeypox virus.
Considering our patient's history of immunosuppression, we prescribed doxycycline, ceftriaxone, and valacyclovir; we subsequently gave him a 2-week course of 600 mg of tecovirimat twice a day. He reported no significant adverse effects and the skin lesions healed rapidly. At follow-up one month later, the patient reported areas of hyperpigmentation at the sites of the healed lesions and said he was doing well.
Monkeypox is caused by the monkeypox virus, a member of the Poxviridae family and Orthopoxvirus genus. The virus is transmitted via large respiratory droplets, direct or indirect contact with bodily fluids or lesion material, or contact with fomites〞including bedding or towels. Malaise, lymphadenopathy, headache, myalgia, and cutaneous symptoms can occur within 1每3 days of the onset of fever. Lesions may initially appear as macules progressing to papules, vesicles, and pustules that dry up and fall off. The development of skin lesions, in addition to viral prodromal symptoms, in immunocompromised patients should raise the possibility of other diagnosis, such as primary or secondary infection with varicella zoster virus or other organisms such as Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, or Bartonella henselae; we considered this unlikely in our patient given his presentation. Molluscum contagiosum also presents with umbilicated papules, but usually without systemic symptoms. Notably, proctitis has recently been recognised as being associated with a human monkeypox infection. Tecovirimat is approved for treating human smallpox disease. Treatment in cases of human monkeypox should be considered in severe cases, immunocompromised patients, paediatric populations, pregnant or breastfeeding women, and people with concurrent disease or other comorbidities.

According to the patient, her swelling had increased in size over a few months before presentation. The pain was confined to the medial aspect of the proximal leg. On examination, she did not have any skin changes, but had a tender palpable mass measuring approximately 8﹞0 cm. She neither had any restriction in her range of motion nor neurovascular compromise. input: A 32-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of tingling in his arms and legs and a 2-week history of inability to walk. A positive Romberg test, sensory ataxia, impaired proprioception and vibratory sensation, and preserved nociception were noted. Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine showed hyperintensity in the posterior spinal cord from C1 to T12 and hyperintense lesions in the dorsal column on T2-weighted images. A vitamin B12 level was 107 pg per ml (reference value, >231) without macrocytic anemia. Toxicity of which of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?
output:
Nitrous oxide (N2O) toxicity

The clinical presentation and imaging findings are classic for subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord due to vitamin B12 deficiency. In a young patient (32 years old) without macrocytic anemia but with low B12 levels, nitrous oxide abuse is the most likely etiology.

Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidizes the cobalt ion in vitamin B12, inactivating it and causing functional B12 deficiency that leads to demyelination of the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord.

A 70-year-old man presented to our clinic in April, 2014, with a 4 month history of painful, pruritic rash involving the scalp, face, chest, and back. He had a history of colon cancer and deep venous thrombosis. A biopsy sample of the rash had been interpreted as eczema, but he had had only minimum improvement with short courses of both topical and systemic corticosteroids and antibiotics. Examination showed a healthy-looking man with erythematous papules and plaques displaying cornflake-like scale in a seborrheic distribution (figure). Oral and ocular mucosae were normal. Previous serological studies, including antinuclear antibody (ANA), complement, and serum protein electrophoresis, were normal. We did lesional punch biopsy for routine histology (appendix) and perilesional punch biopsy for direct immunofluorescence (figure). Clinicopathological findings were diagnostic of pemphigus foliaceus.Pemphigus foliaceus is a rare autoimmune bullous disease characterised by pathogenic autoantibodies against desmoglein-1 (a desmosomal protein) that cause disruption of intercellular adhesion between keratinocytes in the epidermal granular layer (acantholysis). This results in fragile bullae that rupture easily to form erosions with characteristic scale crust. Pemphigus foliaceus often begins on the upper body in a seborrheic distribution, but progresses to widespread involvement or erythroderma if not appropriately treated. Pruritus and burning are common and can be exacerbated by UV exposure. Unlike pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus is rarely associated with mucosal involvement. Diagnosis is made with biopsies for routine histology and direct immunofluorescence. Pemphigus foliaceus typically arises in middle age and can be drug-induced, such as by penicillamine and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. An endemic form, Fogo Sevelagem (※wild fire§), occurs in South America and has been linked with exposure to black flies.
Before effective treatment was available pemphigus foliaceus fatality reached 60% due to dehydration and sepsis. Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, has recently gained favour as treatment of choice for pemphigus foliaceus and other autoimmune bullous diseases because of relatively high rates of induced remission compared with classic treatments. We prescribed 30 mg prednisolone daily and rituximab (375 mg/m2 intravenously once weekly for 4 weeks) for our patient, and triamcinolone 0﹞1% cream twice daily. At follow-up 2 months after treatment with rituximab most skin lesions were healed and we could reduce prednisolone to 20 mg daily (appendix). He will be followed up every 3 months until prednisolone is tapered off completely.

input: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of dyspnea. He required intubation and ventilation when he was found to be in hypercapnic respiratory failure. Five days after admission to the ICU, his urine became green. Which of the following medications caused this?
output:
Propofol

The green discoloration of urine in this intubated ICU patient is a classic side effect of **propofol**, a sedative-hypnotic agent commonly used for sedation in mechanically ventilated patients.

Propofol is metabolized in the liver, and its phenolic metabolites are excreted in the urine. These metabolites can impart a green color to the urine, typically appearing after several days of continuous propofol infusion. This phenomenon is benign and reversible upon discontinuation of the medication.

A 23-year-old man presented to our centre with a 1-day history of non-exertional shortness of breath. The patient stated that he woke up in the morning with wheezing; he reported no fever, chills, nasal congestions, or productive cough.
The patient had been diagnosed with asthma when he was a child; he had previously needed a hospital admission which required him to be intubated, due to an exacerbation of his illness. Notably, he had never been seen by a respiratory physician, but had previously been treated for pneumonia both as an inpatient and an outpatient. He reported using an inhaler of albuterol daily.
On examination, the patient was initially tachypnoeic on bilevel positive airway pressure with increased respiratory effort and oxygen saturation of 89%; his lungs were clear on auscultation bilaterally with minimal wheezing heard. A chest x-ray showed bilateral opacities and he was admitted for empirical treatment of asthma exacerbation. A CT scan of the patient's chest was requested primarily to assess for parenchymal lung disease; however, it showed an H-type tracheooesophageal fistula at the T3 level, which we concluded was most likely to have been congenital in origin (figure).Upon further questioning, the patient reported no symptoms of dysphagia, frank aspiration, or gastro-oesophageal reflux. Additionally, he had none of the other clinical features of either VACTERL association〞specifically vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, renal anomalies, and limb abnormalities〞or CHARGE syndrome〞specifically coloboma, cranial nerve abnormalities, choanal atresia, and so-called CHARGE ear (middle and inner ear abnormalities, which can contribute to hearing problems, and atypically shaped external ears). An echocardiogram, MRI of the spine, anorectal examination, and renal ultrasounds were all within usual range.
On discussion with the patient, we decided to operate. Bronchoscopy confirmed a fistula (figure) through which a stiff catheter was passed into the oesophagus; the end of the catheter was retrieved via oesophagoscopy and brought back out through the mouth to allow for retraction and identification of the fistula by fluoroscopy (figure). The fistula was divided〞closing the tracheal and oesophageal defects〞via a right cervical approach. A sternocleidomastoid rotational flap was then interposed between the trachea and oesophagus; intraoperative monitoring of the recurrent laryngeal nerve confirmed that it was undamaged. A postoperative oesophagram showed no fistula recurrence or leak; the patient retained a normal swallowing mechanism, and his voice was unaffected after surgery.
At follow-up 4 months after the operation, the patient was well; he reported no dysphagia or respiratory difficulties. He said he had used his inhaler on one occasion since discharge from hospital.
Congenital tracheooesophageal fistulae are a rare developmental anomaly that may present soon after birth, in infancy, in childhood, or in adulthood〞as in our patient. The diagnosis should be considered in patients of any age with unexplained chronic, recurrent respiratory symptoms or cases of suspected gastro-oesophageal reflux.

A 29-year-old woman presented with a 23-year history of multiple joint swelling and intermittent pain. Physical examination showed large, soft, and fluctuant soft tissue swelling of the hands, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles, bilaterally (figure A; appendix p 2). Symmetric tense knee effusions restricted her range of motion. She had previously had multiple recurrences of panuveitis, cataract, and secondary glaucoma in both eyes for 7 years, with retinal detachment leading to blindness in her left eye. 9 years earlier, she had undergone knee synovectomy, and histopathological examination showed extensive infiltration of mature adipose tissue, consistent with lipoma arborescens. Noncaseating granulomas were also observed at higher magnification (figure B). MRI of the knee at that time showed diffuse villous and frond-like intra-articular fatty masses in the suprapatellar bursa, with associated marked joint effusion (appendix p 3). Her father had displayed almost identical symptoms and had died 19 years previously, at the age of 34 years.
Immunological tests showed no abnormalities. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was slightly elevated, at 34 mm/h. MRI of the right hand revealed multiple lobulations along the tendons, with joint effusions (figures C and D, appendix p 4); the signal intensity of the frond-like lobules was high on T1-weighted images (figure C) and very low on fat-saturated T2-weighted images (figure D), indicating their fatty composition. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a novel heterozygous missense frameshift mutation in NOD2 (1066G>C [Glu356Gln]), which was predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis (appendix p 5). The patient recalled having scaly erythematous lesions in childhood. A diagnosis of Blau syndrome was made. Genetic analysis could not be done on the father, but, given his medical history, it is highly probable that he had a severe form of Blau syndrome.
Blau syndrome is an autoinflammatory granulomatosis disease resulting from mutations in NOD2 and characterised by skin, joint, and eye disorders. Joint manifestations are chronic and symmetrical polyarthritis, which usually start within the first decade of life, with marked soft-tissue swelling, especially in the wrists and ankles, due to synovial granulomatous inflammation. Ocular involvement usually occurs later than other symptoms but accounts for the highest morbidity.
Lipoma arborescens is a rare disorder that results in the growth of fatty tissue within the joint linings, often leading to swelling, pain, and restricted movement, primarily affecting the knee, although it can involve multiple joints. Hand involvement, early childhood onset, and familial inheritance in lipoma arborescens are very rare, suggesting a possible misdiagnosis. Joint involvement in Blau syndrome presenting as lipoma arborescens has only been documented once but cases might be underestimated due to the lack of genetic confirmation. Hence, Blau syndrome should be looked for in lipoma arborescens cases with uveitis, familial history, hand joint involvement, or early onset.
If the condition had been identified sooner, blindness might have been averted in the patient, highlighting the importance of early recognition and treatment. In this case, the patient was treated with glucocorticoids and thalidomide, resulting in pain relief and stabilisation. Glucocorticoids were tapered gradually, with the addition of tofacitinib.

A 40-year-old man attended our ophthalmology department reporting a gradual worsening of vision in both eyes over the previous few months.The patient had a history of sensorineural hearing loss and he had received a kidney transplant at age 19 years; he had previously been diagnosed with X-linked Alport syndrome. Genetic testing, at the time, showed a mutation in the COL4A5 gene. The kidney was donated by the patient's healthy father; the patient has one healthy brother and no children. His mother was identified as the carrier and she was also affected by the disease. The patient was prescribed sirolimus 3 mg daily and prednisolone 5 mg daily.
On general examination, he was well. Regarding his eyes, a slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed a clear crystalline lens with an anterior lenticonus〞a subtle protrusion of the anterior surface〞in both eyes (figure); the protrusion was clearly visible on anterior segment swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT; figure) and was also detected as an oil-droplet sign with retro-illumination (figure).
Additionally, the patient showed the typical retinal findings of Alport syndrome: central fleck retinopathy〞seen as scattered pigmentation irregularities around the macula, which were more obvious on red free images (figure)〞temporal retinal thinning on retinal OCT (figure), and peripheral retinopathy. His best corrected vision was reduced to 20/40 (typical 20/20) in both eyes.
We implanted a toric intraocular lens with extended depth of focus in both eyes after lens removal, which improved his vision to 20/25 bilaterally. At 3 months follow-up, the patient had a full corrected distance visual acuity of 20/20.
Alport syndrome is a rare, progressive, hereditary glomerular disease characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, and progressive impairment of kidney function caused by mutations in the COL4A5, usually inherited as X-linked〞as in our patient〞and COL4A3 and COL4A4 genes, which are transmitted in either an autosomal recessive or dominant pattern. The mutations disrupt collagen type IV synthesis, which is a crucial component of the basal membrane in the renal glomerulus, cochlea, cornea, lens capsule, retina, and skin.
Visual impairment is mostly caused by anterior lenticonus〞even if there is no cataract present; it is diagnostic for Alport syndrome, seen in 50% of patients, and can be treated effectively with lens replacement. Central and peripheral retinopathy is seen in 70% and 80% of patients, respectively, and usually does not affect vision. Lenticonus and central retinopathy are predictive for sensorineural hearing loss and renal failure before the age of 30 years. Therefore, in young men with hearing loss and haematuria, an eye examination can give helpful information in confirming the diagnosis of Alport syndrome.
output: Alport syndrome with anterior lenticonus and central fleck retinopathy

input: A 44-year-old man with diabetes and end-stage kidney disease presented with a 2-week history of pain and blurry vision in his left eye, fevers, and back pain. An ophthalmologic examination was notable for conjunctival injection and corneal clouding in the left eye. Visual acuity was 20/60 in the right eye and was reduced to minimal light perception in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination revealed a hazy, edematous cornea and a small hypopyon in the left eye. Cultures of vitreous fluid and blood grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the best next step in management in addition to systemic antimicrobial treatment?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and image showing:
- Left eye with corneal clouding/edema
- Conjunctival injection
- Hypopyon on slit-lamp examination
- Positive vitreous and blood cultures for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus
- Severely reduced vision (light perception only)
- Associated fevers and back pain suggesting systemic infection

**Endogenous Bacterial Endophthalmitis (left eye) secondary to Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia**

The best next step in management in addition to systemic antimicrobial treatment is:

**Intravitreal antibiotic injection with consideration for pars plana vitrectomy**

This is a case of endogenous endophthalmitis from hematogenous spread, and intravitreal antibiotics (typically vancomycin and ceftazidime) are essential for adequate intraocular drug levels, as systemic antibiotics alone have poor penetration into the vitreous cavity. Given the severity of presentation with only light perception vision, early vitrectomy may also be indicated.

A 54-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of rapidly worsening difficulty with her walking, tremor, a weak voice, and trouble swallowing.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome with positive anticardiolipin antibodies, which had been diagnosed more than 30 years earlier.
She had been treated with acenocoumarol, azathioprine, denosumab, and prednisolone.
On examination, the patient was distressed but her vital signs were normal. She had hypophonia, hypomimia, bilateral saccadic horizontal eye movements, and supranuclear upward gaze palsy. She had symmetrical brisk reflexes in all limbs with normal plantar reflexes; rigidity was found in both arms and legs with her right side affected more than her left. She had symmetrical bradykinesia in all limbs, and a resting and postural tremor bilaterally, that was more severe on her right side. The patient had a festinated gait and she needed support with walking; she had no arm swing, and episodically, experienced freezing (video).
T2 weighted MRI of the patient's brain showed hyperintense confluent lesions of the basal ganglia and thalami with multiple foci of restricted diffusion located in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions; bilateral peripheral microbleeds were seen on susceptibility weighted images (figure). The lesions showed no contrast enhancement and MRI of vessel walls showed no signs of vasculitis.
Transthoracic echocardiography findings were inconclusive〞specifically, we were unable to rule out the presence of valvular vegetations. Weighing up the pros and cons of carrying out an invasive procedure and further therapeutic interventions, we decided against a transoesophageal echocardiogram.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a normal leukocyte count of 2 cells per 米L (normal <4) and protein concentration of 445 mg/L (normal range 215每720); a slightly elevated glucose concentration of 4﹞7 mmol/L (normal range 3﹞0每4﹞0), with a low glucose CSF to serum ratio of 0﹞45 (normal range 0﹞51每0﹞81); and a slightly elevated L-lactate concentration of 2﹞33 米mol/L (normal range 1﹞42每2﹞22). Identical oligoclonal IgG bands were present in the CSF and serum.
Repeated blood and CSF cultures remained negative. We considered the probable diagnosis to be a flare-up of the patient's SLE with striatal encephalitis and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome.
Despite early aggressive immunosuppressive therapy, which included corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, plasmapheresis, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin, and anticoagulant treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin, the patient developed multiorgan failure and died 2 months after admission.
At autopsy, a Libman-Sachs endocarditis of the aortic and mitral valves, with signs of recent and semi-recent ischaemia in multiple organs caused by microthrombi, including the brain, kidneys, coronary arteries, and lungs were seen; histopathological analysis of a specimen of the brain showed central nuclei with foci of ischaemic alterations with foamy macrophages (appendix). Additionally, sporadic perivascular lymphocytic infiltration of the basal ganglia was seen; however, as this may be secondary to the presence of thrombi, we were unable to conclusively diagnose either encephalitis or vasculitis. No abnormalities were seen in the substantia nigra. Therefore, the cause of death was multiorgan failure due to microthrombi resulting from Libman-Sachs endocarditis and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. We assumed the extensive hyperintense lesions of the basal ganglia were related to an SLE-mediated striatal encephalitis, since they did not correspond to the brain regions showing multifocal ischaemia.
SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome both have very varied clinical presentations. Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome, while uncommon in SLE, is often fatal. Severe disease flares in SLE and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome require prompt, extensive treatment by a multidisciplinary team.
output: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome with Libman-Sachs endocarditis and SLE-mediated striatal encephalitis
target: Multiorgan ischaemia due to microthrombi caused by catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome  and Libman-Sachs endocarditis

input: An 81-year-old man with hypertension presented with pain and swelling of the left thigh and lower leg that had developed during the previous several hours. He had no history of recent surgery or trauma and no known personal or family history of clotting disorders. The left lower leg was tender, cold, and swollen, and the dorsalis pedis pulse was not palpable. What is the diagnosis?
output: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (acute iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis)
