A 54-year-old woman attended our hospital with a 2-week history of rapidly worsening difficulty with her walking, tremor, a weak voice, and trouble swallowing.The patient had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome with positive anticardiolipin antibodies, which had been diagnosed more than 30 years earlier.
She had been treated with acenocoumarol, azathioprine, denosumab, and prednisolone.
On examination, the patient was distressed but her vital signs were normal. She had hypophonia, hypomimia, bilateral saccadic horizontal eye movements, and supranuclear upward gaze palsy. She had symmetrical brisk reflexes in all limbs with normal plantar reflexes; rigidity was found in both arms and legs with her right side affected more than her left. She had symmetrical bradykinesia in all limbs, and a resting and postural tremor bilaterally, that was more severe on her right side. The patient had a festinated gait and she needed support with walking; she had no arm swing, and episodically, experienced freezing (video).
T2 weighted MRI of the patient's brain showed hyperintense confluent lesions of the basal ganglia and thalami with multiple foci of restricted diffusion located in both supratentorial and infratentorial regions; bilateral peripheral microbleeds were seen on susceptibility weighted images (figure). The lesions showed no contrast enhancement and MRI of vessel walls showed no signs of vasculitis.
Transthoracic echocardiography findings were inconclusive〞specifically, we were unable to rule out the presence of valvular vegetations. Weighing up the pros and cons of carrying out an invasive procedure and further therapeutic interventions, we decided against a transoesophageal echocardiogram.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a normal leukocyte count of 2 cells per 米L (normal <4) and protein concentration of 445 mg/L (normal range 215每720); a slightly elevated glucose concentration of 4﹞7 mmol/L (normal range 3﹞0每4﹞0), with a low glucose CSF to serum ratio of 0﹞45 (normal range 0﹞51每0﹞81); and a slightly elevated L-lactate concentration of 2﹞33 米mol/L (normal range 1﹞42每2﹞22). Identical oligoclonal IgG bands were present in the CSF and serum.
Repeated blood and CSF cultures remained negative. We considered the probable diagnosis to be a flare-up of the patient's SLE with striatal encephalitis and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome.
Despite early aggressive immunosuppressive therapy, which included corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, plasmapheresis, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin, and anticoagulant treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin, the patient developed multiorgan failure and died 2 months after admission.
At autopsy, a Libman-Sachs endocarditis of the aortic and mitral valves, with signs of recent and semi-recent ischaemia in multiple organs caused by microthrombi, including the brain, kidneys, coronary arteries, and lungs were seen; histopathological analysis of a specimen of the brain showed central nuclei with foci of ischaemic alterations with foamy macrophages (appendix). Additionally, sporadic perivascular lymphocytic infiltration of the basal ganglia was seen; however, as this may be secondary to the presence of thrombi, we were unable to conclusively diagnose either encephalitis or vasculitis. No abnormalities were seen in the substantia nigra. Therefore, the cause of death was multiorgan failure due to microthrombi resulting from Libman-Sachs endocarditis and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. We assumed the extensive hyperintense lesions of the basal ganglia were related to an SLE-mediated striatal encephalitis, since they did not correspond to the brain regions showing multifocal ischaemia.
SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome both have very varied clinical presentations. Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome, while uncommon in SLE, is often fatal. Severe disease flares in SLE and catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome require prompt, extensive treatment by a multidisciplinary team.

input: After 8 years of levothyroxine therapy, a male patient who underwent thyroidectomy at the age of 47 years for Graves' disease developed a 3 cm mass on his left hallux. The lesion was removed and diagnosed as localised myxoedema. Two years later, at the age of 57 years, the patient presented to our sarcoma service with a local recurrence. On physical examination, he had orbitopathy and no sign of pretibial myxoedema; the recurrence presented as a soft, mobile lump of the dorsal aspect of the hallux (figure). MRI showed a suprafascial mass with hyperintense T2-weighted signal and poorly defined margins (figure). To confirm the dermopathy and to exclude a soft tissue neoplasm, tissue slides of the previous surgery were reviewed. Haematoxylin and eosin stain showed a diffuse widening of the reticular dermis by a faintly basophilic acellular material, associated with isolated lymphocytes, that was dissecting collagen fibres and diffusing in perivascular and periadnexal spaces (figure). These microscopic features were consistent with an extracellular mucopolysaccharides deposit (ie, myxoedema). The original diagnosis was thus confirmed, the present lesion considered a recurrence, and the patient referred for conservative management.Graves' disease manifests with infiltrative orbitopathy in around 25% of patients, and with thyroid dermopathy in less than 5% of patients. Although usually located on the anterolateral aspect of the lower leg (pretibial myxoedema), it can occur elsewhere, especially after trauma. Dermopathy and orbitopathy can also occur after thyroid surgery, radioiodine therapy, or in clinically euthyroid patients. Myxoedema usually does not require treatment, and surgical excision is not advised due to recurrence (as in this patient). In case of cosmetic issues or interference with shoe fitting, topical glucocorticoids under occlusive dressing might be beneficial. Localised nodular myxoedema is a rare form of Graves' dermopathy, and although this mass-forming condition might cause concern about a soft tissue neoplasm, clinical presentation and histology warrant a conservative approach.

A 25-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent vomiting, abdominal distension, and weight loss.
4 months earlier, she had presented to the local district hospital because her work colleagues had thought she looked pale. The patient had been found to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 4﹞7 g/dL and a peripheral blood smear suggestive of a hypochromic microcytic anaemia. She had no other medical history. She was transfused 2 units of blood; she was investigated at the outpatient clinic but was not referred for endoscopic assessment.
On examination, we found the patient to be pale and cachectic. Her blood pressure was 122/74 mm Hg, heart rate was 100 beats per min, temperature was 37﹞0～C, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. On palpation of her abdomen, we felt a discernible, non-tender right upper quadrant mass; she had no other abnormal findings.
Investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8﹞1 g/dL, platelet count of 565?℅?109 per L (normal 150每400), and white cell count of 10﹞5?℅?109 per L; the mean corpuscular volume was 77﹞2 fL (normal 80每94) and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin was 23﹞1 pg per cell〞suggestive of iron deficiency anaemia. The patient's renal and liver function tests were unremarkable.
An abdominal CT scan showed〞on axial view〞a target-like lesion (figure) and〞on coronal view〞a sausage-shaped lesion at the third part of duodenum; the stomach appeared distended. An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a grossly elongated stomach with external compression at the second part of the duodenum.
We carried out an exploratory laparotomy and found a duodenojejunal intussusception. We were unable to manually reduce the lesion, and so carried out a segmental resection of third part of the duodenum and proximal jejunum with a side-to-side duodenojejunal anastomosis at the second part of the duodenum. Analysis of the excised lesion showed a 6 cm?℅?5 cm well-encapsulated and pedunculated tumour of the third part of the duodenum which acted as the intussusceptum telescoping into the proximal jejunum〞the intussuscipiens (appendix). Histological analysis of samples of the tumour showed a poorly differentiated extra-skeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum. Immunohistochemistry stains demonstrated strong and diffuse nuclear immunoreactivity to NKX2-2 and ERG, with membranous immunoreactivity to CD99, and an absence of nuclear immunoreactivity to FLI1: supporting a possible fusion of the EWSRI gene on chromosome 22q12 with the gene encoding the transcription factor ERG (appendix). The tumour cells exhibited no immunoreactivity to cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD20, CD3, LCA, TdT, synaptophysin, chromogranin, desmin, myogenin, S100, and 汐-smooth muscle actin.
Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged after a week. One month later, she returned reporting persistent abdominal and lower back pain. An abdominal CT showed enlarged coeliac, para-caval, and para-aortic lymph nodes with no lung metastases in the lower half of the thorax. Skeletal x-rays of the axial and cortical bones displayed no osteolytic bone lesions. The patient was urgently transferred to the oncology clinic but died before treatment was commenced.
Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the small intestine is an extremely rare tumour with poor prognosis. However, if detected early, it may be successfully treated with surgical resection and adjuvant chemotherapy. Young adults presenting with recurrent vomiting, weight loss, an abdominal mass, and anaemia should raise the suspicion of an aggressive malignancy (video).
output: Extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma of the duodenum with duodenojejunal intussusception
target: Fluid resuscitation followed by immediate laparotomy and bowel resection

The physical examination was notable for nonulcerated white plaques that formed a butterfly shape across the posterior oropharynx, upper uvula, and tonsils. No lymphadenopathy or skin or genital lesions were present. Testing for the human immunodeficiency virus was negative. A biopsy of the plaques showed dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. Which of the following tests is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?

A 5-year-old girl presented to her primary care physician with swellings on both sides of her neck. She was referred directly to the Center for Oncology, in Minsk, because she had been living 70 miles away from the Chernobyl Power Plant at the time of the accident, in the Gomel District of Belarus. An ultrasound scan of the area showed a suspicious nodule of more than 2 cm in diameter in her thyroid gland as well as multiple bilaterally enlarged lymph nodes in the neck. She had a thyroidectomy and bilateral lymphadenectomy. Histology showed an invasive papillary thyroid cancer over 2 cm in diameter and bilateral lymph node metastases (pathological stage T4N1bM0). The girl was given levothyroxine postoperatively to prevent hypothyroidism and to suppress TSH. However, because of the low quality of the drug available at that time, TSH suppression was not permanent and 2 years later, tumour recurred in a lymph node on the right side of the girl's neck and was removed during a unilateral dissection. She was then given a course of radioiodine therapy (RIT). A scan done after treatment showed intense uptake of iodine-131 (131I) in both lungs; a chest x-ray was normal. The RIT was repeated three times at intervals of 4每6 months (cumulative activity 5﹞3 GBq of 131I). However, because no change occurred in the level of 131I uptake in the lungs, it was thought that the metastases were not responding to the RIT, and five courses of chemotherapy with bleomycin were given, again without any clear metastatic response.The patient's clinical course and the small amounts of poor-quality〞selenium-75-contaminated〞131I available in Belarus resulted in her being selected for treatment at the University of Essen, Germany, where she had her fifth course of 3 GBq of 131I, given in hypothyroidism〞to ensure a high uptake of 131I〞with a raised TSH concentration (>80 mU/L). The patient's parathormone and serum calcium concentrations were both low, leading us to treat her for postoperative hypoparathyroidism. A post-therapy scan showed intense 131I uptake in the lungs (figure) and a correspondingly high serum concentration of the thyroid-specific tumour marker thyroglobulin of 3750 ng/mL, which should be undetectable after thyroidectomy if all benign or malignant thyroid tissue is removed.
The RIT was repeated five more times and 131I uptake in the lung metastases finally disappeared (figure). At her last follow-up examination, in the Gomel District, in September, 2019, no scintigraphic or radiological remnants of pulmonary metastases were seen. The patient's thyroglobulin concentration had decreased considerably to 17 ng/mL (classed as a stable partial response), mild pulmonary fibrosis was seen on a lung CT, and pulmonary function was reduced. A 42-year-old woman was reviewed by our team after a right femoral artery endarterectomy for acute ischaemia of her leg which developed following coronary angiography using femoral access. The patient had a history of type 1 diabetes〞managed by insulin pump therapy〞and diabetic-hypertensive kidney disease which had required maintenance haemodialysis for the previous 9 months.
Post-surgery, the patient's blood glucose concentration had increased to 21﹞7 mmol/L (typical range 3﹞9每5﹞6) or 391 mg/dL (typical range 70每100); capillary blood ketones were so high that they were unmeasurable (>8 mmol/L; typical level <0﹞6). An arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH at 7﹞26 (typical range 7﹞35?7﹞45), pCO2 23﹞8 mm Hg (typical range 35?45), bicarbonates 10﹞05 mmol/L (typical range 22?26), lactate 2﹞55 mmol/L (typical range <2), and an anion gap of 28﹞1 mmol/L (typical range 5?12). The insulin pump was functioning well. We concluded the findings compatible with a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
Haemodialysis and intravenous insulin, plus glucose supplementation, were started with careful monitoring of potassium and glucose levels; ketone levels reduced within 24 h.
A review of data from the patient's continuous glucose monitoring system showed chronically elevated monthly mean blood glucose concentrations, between 13﹞95?17﹞25 mmol/L (251每311 mg/dL); with low glycaemic levels and frequent hypoglycaemias on days the patient had dialysis and elevated glycaemic levels on days she did not have dialysis (figure; appendix). Additionally, we noticed a surprisingly high level of bicarbonate on the routine protocol of chronic haemodialysis; it had progressively increased from 30 mmol/L to 38 mmol/L over the previous 9 months to maintain a normal (>22 mmol/L) pre-dialysis serum bicarbonate concentration, as recommended by the latest guidelines (appendix).
Furthermore, we found the anion gap to be surprisingly high, which we thought unlikely to be caused by chronic kidney disease alone. Therefore, given the high level of ketones before and after dialysis, we concluded that the excessive need for bicarbonates was due to the DKA.
We excluded lactic acidosis since the lactate was only slightly increased at 2﹞55 mmol/L (typical level ≒2). And based on clinical history, we also ruled out salicylate intoxication, ingestion of toxic substances, and small intestine bacterial overgrowth.
The duration of the DKA was indicated by the progressive increase in bicarbonate in the dialysate, which, combined with the high glucose clearance during haemodialysis, had been responsible for maintaining metabolic stability without marked acidosis (appendix). However, ketones had increased to high levels because of limited clearance during successive haemodialysis sessions.
In conclusion then, the high ketonaemia with an exceptionally high anion gap〞despite partial clearance〞together with relatively moderate decreases in bicarbonate and pH, in a patient with end-stage kidney disease, suggested chronic DKA partially masked by alkalinisation of the dialysis baths.
In cases of high anion gap metabolic acidosis with end-stage kidney disease, necessitating bicarbonate-enriched dialysate, physicians must search for a cause of metabolic acidosis. In diabetic patients, the diagnosis of DKA should be considered first, especially with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes under pump therapy.Diagnosing DKA in dialysis patients is challenging. Relying solely on glycated haemoglobin or blood glucose levels during dialysis is insufficient to assess glucose control. As patients with end-stage kidney disease present with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, both the anion gap and the bicarbonate may not be the most reliable diagnostic parameters for DKA; therefore, the measurement of plasma 汕-hydroxybutyrate is key.
Although the optimal concentration of bicarbonate in dialysate for haemodialysis is uncertain, the presence of a high dialysate bicarbonate concentration (≡38 mmol/L) has been reported to be associated with poorer outcomes: all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalisation (appendix).
Regarding glucose variation in patients having dialysis, the lowest glycaemic level〞on days of dialysis〞is due to glucose loss to the dialysate and diffusion of glucose into erythrocytes. After dialysis, a paradoxical rebound hyperglycaemia occurs due to increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones〞specifically glucagon, adrenocorticotropic hormone, and cortisol〞and partial clearance of negligible amounts of insulin during dialysis, even though the insulin resistance is diminished after dialysis (appendix). The lack of glucose clearance then maintains hyperglycaemia on days between dialysis.

A 55-year-old man with a history of aortic valve replacement was admitted because of pelvic pain. He had been treated with antibiotics over the past 4 weeks for a presumed lower urinary tract infection with fever. Treatment had been unsuccessful. Both urine and blood cultures grew?Enterobacter cloacae. Abdominal radiography showed a thin line of air within the bladder wall, outlining its perimeter (figure). A bacteraemic emphysematous cystitis complicated by prosthetic valve endocarditis was diagnosed, and effective antibiotic treatment was initiated. Emphysematous cystitis is a potentially life-threatening condition caused by gas-producing pathogens. This rare form of urinary tract infection typically occurs in middle-aged diabetic women. Contrary to radiological findings, clinical features are non-specific (irritative bladder symptoms, pyuria, haematuria, and, rarely, pneumaturia). Plain abdominal radiography, as well as ultrasonography, may lead to the diagnosis but CT scan is regarded as the procedure of choice, particularly to rule out a vesicocolic fistula. Early diagnosis and management consists of antibiotic therapy, bladder drainage, and sometimes surgery.

The patient's main tasks had been in the blending process: mixing sand and soda ash, cutting, polishing, and repairing flat glass and fibreglass. He worked 9-h days in a poorly ventilated workspace and used personal protection equipment for less than 30 min per h. The patient had smoked one to two cigarettes daily for the past 26 years and stopped 4 months before his current presentation.
On examination he was well looking and not distressed; he had bilateral effusions in his wrist, metacarpophalangeal, and knee joints. Crackles were audible at the apex of his right lung.
Laboratory investigations showed positive antinuclear antibodies〞at a titre of 1:320, homogeneous pattern〞and raised anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies (ACPAs; 37 UI/ml; reference value <5). Rheumatoid factor was negative.

A 34-year-old man, from sub-Saharan Africa, was referred to our hospital for short stature, when he came to France, as an actor, to play the part of a child. The patient reported that at birth he required incubator support and that his growth was blunted from early childhood.At our first evaluation, his height was 137 cm, weight was 26﹞4 kg, and body-mass index 14 kg/m2. He had long extremities compared to his trunk and he had signs of hypogonadism〞including small intrascrotal testes (0﹞5 mL; typical 12每30 in adult males), absent pubic and axillary hair, micro-penis (2 cm), and a high-pitched voice.
Hormone assays showed combined pituitary hormone deficiencies with low serum morning cortisol and undetectable dehydroepiandrosterone-sulphate with low adrenocorticotropin; low thyroxine and triiodothyronine; undetectable testosterone and oestradiol; low inhibin B and low gonadotrophins; low prolactin; and growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 were both below detectable limits (appendix).
Brain MRI showed marked pituitary gland hypoplasia, absence of pituitary stalk and ectopic posterior hypophysis, and no extra-pituitary abnormalities.
The patient's bone age was 13 years, and knee MRI showed persistent growth plates at the distal femoral or proximal tibial epiphysis. Genetic testing did not identify pathogenic variants in any of the genes responsible for congenital hypopituitarism.
We commenced treatment with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, and recombinant human growth hormone replacement for 2 months before the patient had to return to his country as his visa had expired; he was provided with growth hormone cartridges for an additional 3 months.
Figure Congenital hypopituitarism treated in adulthood
Show full caption
Figure viewer
The patient returned to France 3 years later; his height was 142 cm, but otherwise, his clinical state was unchanged. We commenced stepwise replacement with hydrocortisone, levothyroxine, growth hormone, and gonadotropins for the next 4 years. His height increased to 161 cm〞an increase of 24 cm〞and he achieved normal pubertal development (appendix). During the increase in height, the patient developed scoliosis which necessitated surgical correction and an arthrodesis at T2-L1 (appendix).
At baseline, cardiac MRI showed a small heart〞but well-proportioned to the patient's body size〞with normal contractile function; hormone treatment resulted in linear, uniform growth of the heart with a progressive increase in ventricular mass and volume. Concomitant decrease in the extracellular space indicated that the cardiac growth resulted from cardiomyocyte correction of hypotrophy; the initial rapid decrease in extracellular space, after levothyroxine and hydrocortisone were started, was mostly attributed to resorption of myxoedematous infiltration, and possibly due to inflammation.
Growth hormone〞given prior to puberty induction〞transiently increased ventricular contractility to supraphysiologic values, with the ejection fraction reaching 78%; it normalised during gonadotrophin therapy. Left ventricular stroke volume increased proportionally compared to end-diastolic volume, reflecting the heart's ability to enhance its contractile strength in response to increased venous return〞Frank-Starling law.
We further observed a uniform increase of the cross-sectional area of the patient's femoral muscles during treatment accompanied by a progressive decrease of intramuscular fat fraction. Growth hormone induced transient glucose intolerance, which resolved during further therapy.
Congenital hypopituitarism is usually diagnosed and treated during childhood or adolescence to correct blunted growth and lack of pubertal development. Rarely is hormone replacement initiated in adulthood, and results of such cases are limited. Regarding the heart, the capacity to generate cardiomyocytes during adult life has been the subject of much debate; cardiomyogenesis is minimal in healthy humans after birth. Metachronous heart growth〞as seen in our patient〞from size of a child to a normal adult, has not previously been reported. In conclusion, hormone replacement, administered gradually, in an adult patient with congenital hypopituitarism can safely induce heart growth normalisation proportionate to linear growth (video).
output: Congenital hypopituitarism with pituitary stalk interruption syndrome (combined pituitary hormone deficiency)

Based on the clinical presentation and images showing:

- Palatal petechiae, buccal mucosal ulcerations, and pharyngeal erythema
- History of condomless sex 2 weeks prior

**HIV RNA viral load (plasma HIV RNA/nucleic acid amplification test)**

This is the first marker to become detectable, typically within 10-14 days of infection, followed by p24 antigen (approximately 2-3 weeks), then HIV antibodies (3-4 weeks for 4th generation tests, longer for older antibody-only tests).

A 26-year-old woman with a 2-year history of swelling of her eyelids and reduced vision was referred to our clinic by an ophthalmologist because of increased myopia, decreased visual acuity, scattered pale dots of the maculae, and suspected angioedema.
The patient had been diagnosed with attention deficit disorder and had been prescribed methylphenidate since adolescence. 5 years before we saw her, she reported having occasional episodes of dizziness thought to be caused by anaemia〞investigations at that stage had found an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR; 134 mm/h; typical rate 0每20) and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 9﹞5 g/dL; typical range 11﹞7每15﹞5). The patient had been found to have hepatitis C genotype 3 but was temporarily lost to follow-up.
On examination, we found the patient to be generally well but lethargic; she was thin with a BMI of 13﹞9 kg/m2 (typical range 18﹞5每25﹞0). She had bilateral upper and lower palpebral oedema (figure 1) and diminished visual acuity. Oedema was noted also in the face and lips; but despite slight distal lower extremity hyperalgesia and uncertainty of balance and side steps in tandem walk, there were no other abnormalities found.Fundoscopic examination showed abundant pale dots around the maculae and peripherally in the retinae (figure 2) indicating a crystal retinopathy; optical coherence tomography confirmed the diagnosis showing numerous retinal white dots, oedema of both fovea, and submacular cysts (figure 2).Laboratory investigations found that both the anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 8﹞2 g/dL) and the elevated ESR (129 mm/h) persisted. A comprehensive metabolic panel〞which included tests for plasma C-reactive protein concentration, sodium concentration, potassium concentration, creatinine concentration, calcium concentration, glucose concentration, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, thromboplastin time, amylase, cortisol, free thyroxine, thyroid stimulating hormone, angiotensin converting enzyme, and immunoglobulin subclass analysis〞and urinalysis found no abnormalities. Tests for infectious mononucleosis and HIV were negative; plasma albumin was 31 g/L (normal range 36每48) and prealbumin 0﹞13 g/L (normal range 0﹞23每0﹞37).
18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the whole body showed no signs of systemic disease, infection, or cancer. An electrocardiogram showed inverted T waves in the anterior leads; an echocardiogram showed mild enlargement of the right heart with a small pericardial effusion. Systolic flattening of the interventricular septum was present. Trace tricuspid regurgitation was seen. Right heart catheterisation confirmed precapillary pulmonary hypertension.
Histopathological analysis of a sample of a bone marrow biopsy showed abundant foamy macrophage infiltration characterised by clear cytoplasm (figure 2); additionally, histiocytes in the bone marrow contained dark pigmented fragments〞consistent with titanium deposits that can be associated with intravenous substance use. Furthermore, serum chitotriosidase activity was elevated (1036 nmol/h per mL; typical range 0每195), indicating possible increased macrophage activity or any of several lysosomal storage disorders. Neuropsychiatric assessment showed the patient had impairments of both short-term memory and executive functioning.
Brain MRI with contrast showed diffuse dural thickening and enhancement without any focal pathology of the brain (figure 2). Histopathologic examination of a sample obtained from dural biopsy indicated clusters of CD68-positive macrophages (figure 2); analyses of samples of biopsies from the skin and of biopsies obtained during a gastroscopy were normal.
At this stage our working diagnoses included chronic hepatitis C, severe protein energy malnutrition, secondary pulmonary hypertension, talc retinopathy, secondary histiocytosis, pachymeningitis, amyloidosis, and IgG4 disease.
Whole exome sequencing ruled out inherited causes of primary or secondary histiocytosis. On closer questioning, the patient said she had been intravenously injecting methylphenidate hydrochloride by dissolving the core of the tablets in water. Methylphenidate tablets contain titanium and high molecular weight polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as an adjuvant〞a substance associated with histiocytosis when used parenterally. A diagnosis of PVP histiocytosis was made. The patient was counselled and informed of the diagnosis and advised to avoid intravenous substance use. At follow-up 1 year later, she was more alert than before, and her appetite had improved; ESR had decreased ranging from 26 mm/h to 38 mm/h suggesting discontinuation of active intravenous substance use.
Bilateral swelling of the eyelids or periorbital oedema can be caused by nephrotic syndrome, thyroid eye disease, systemic infections such as mononucleosis, atopic or allergic swelling, sarcoidosis, dermatomyositis, lymphoma, IgG4 disease, and various histiocytoses. PVP is widely used in prescription drugs. Moderate and high molecular weight PVP is only used in oral preparations; when used intravenously patients may have renal insufficiency, anaemia, pathological fractures, and abdominal complaints. PVP can be deposited in most organs leading to severe dysfunction. Earlier intravenous abuse of oral PVP containing buprenorphine and methadone preparations, for maintenance therapy for opioid dependence, has been reported to cause severe, and even lethal PVP histiocytosis.

input: A 28-year-old woman came to our clinic saying she had blurred vision in her right eye. 22 h earlier, she had noticed areas of darkness in the lower half of her right visual field. Her medical history was unremarkable apart from her reporting that she had recurrent tonsillitis as a child. Corrected visual acuity was 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp examination of the anterior segment showed no abnormalities, with normal pupillary reactions. However, slit lamp biomicroscopy and fundus examination in the right eye showed intra-retinal oedema with retinal whitening in the superior area (figure). Fluorescein angiography showed an arterial filling defect along the superotemporal arcade (figure). A diagnosis of right eye superotemporal branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) was made. A cardiology review was sought as part of the mandatory systemic investigations required in such cases. Our cardiology colleagues reported that the patient's electrocardiogram was normal but that her echocardiogram showed moderate mitral stenosis. An analysis of her urine found no abnormalities. Her fasting blood glucose, blood cholesterol, and serum triglyceride concentrations were normal, and a full blood count showed values within the normal range. Also, both her erythrocyte sedimentation rate and serum C-reactive protein concentration were normal. The patient was treated with acetyl salicylate 75 mg once a day and spironolactone 25 mg once a day. She was seen again 12 months later, and her visual fields had improved and she had no further problems.The incidence of retinal arterial obstruction in patients under the age of 30 years has been estimated at less than one in 50?000 outpatients. Valvular heart disease〞originating from rheumatic fever〞remains an important cause of BRAO that should be borne in mind, although rates are declining in developed countries.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4每5 red blood cells per high power field).

Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac每mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. Considering the characteristic angiographic findings, multisystem presentation (fever, myalgia, hypertension, and central nervous system, gastrointestinal, and renal involvement) and laboratory features of inflammation, the patient was diagnosed with childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa. Clinical exome sequencing excluded inherited deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2 mutation).
Therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (30 mg/kg per day for 3 days) was followed by oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg per day for 4 weeks, gradually tapered to 5 mg/day over the next 16 weeks. The day after finishing the three methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses (500 mg/m2 per dose) were started once a month for 6 months. Vasculitis-induced ischemia resulted in generalised myalgia, anuric acute kidney injury requiring maintenance haemodialysis, stage 2 hypertension that was controlled on concomitant therapy with five oral antihypertensive medications (amlodipine, 0﹞6 mg/kg per day; prazocin, 0﹞6 mg/kg per day; enalapril, 0﹞6 mg/kg per day; metoprolol, 3﹞0 mg/kg per day; and clonidine, 5﹞0 mcg/kg per day), and nervous system involvement with seizures requiring two oral antiseizure medications (initially phenytoin, 5﹞0 mg/kg per day; which was changed to levetiracetam, 20﹞0 mg/kg per day). Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal〞primarily choreatic〞movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia〞particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4每36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8每33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12﹞1 g/dL (normal 11﹞0每14﹞0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1?344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26每192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100每240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease〞previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis〞is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease〞also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.
In Africa, choreatic movement disorders〞seen in our patient, which we believe is the first genetically confirmed case of VPS13A disease in a black patient from sub-Saharan Africa〞are often underdiagnosed; many cases are referred to traditional healers and customary medicine.

A 13-year-old boy presented to the paediatrics outpatient department with recurrent fever and abdominal pain that started 8 months before presentation. He was admitted to the paediatric nephrology unit for evaluation following a generalised seizure, persistent stage 2 hypertension, and melaena for one week requiring packed red cell transfusion. Significant examination findings included severe thinness (BMI-for-age 每5﹞2 standard deviation score), stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 136/110 mm Hg), pallor, and generalised muscle tenderness. Investigations identified normocytic normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 85 g/L), acute kidney injury (serum creatinine 353﹞6 米mol/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (serum ferritin 3312 pmol/L, serum C-reactive protein 146 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50 mm/h). Urinalysis revealed proteinuria (2+ on dipstick) and haematuria (4每5 red blood cells per high power field).

Serum hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and HIV antibodies were also absent. A non-reactive tuberculin skin test excluded tuberculosis infection. Malignant lesions were excluded after a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen. Worsening gastrointestinal bleeding prompted a CT angiogram. The beaded appearance of medium-sized arteries, alternating stenosis and dilatation, and microaneurysms, particularly along the coeliac每mesenteric axis, was consistent with polyarteritis nodosa (figure 1A, B, C). MRI with angiography showed similar abnormalities in intracranial vessels (figure 1D). Vasculitis-induced end-organ ischaemia was evident in both scans. During treatment initiation with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and the first cyclophosphamide pulse, mesenteric ischaemia deteriorated into gut perforation, requiring bowel resection and re-anastomosis. Post-operative peritonitis and septicaemia required intravenous broad-spectrum antimicrobials (renal-modified doses; piperacillin每tazobactam, 210 mg/kg per day; teicoplanin, 5 mg/kg per day; metronidazole, 30 mg/kg per day; and caspofungin, 50 mg/m2 per day) and intravenous vasopressors (adrenaline and noradrenaline, titrated to 1 米g/kg per min). Childhood-onset polyarteritis nodosa is a rare, severe condition that requires prompt recognition and management. Patients with Factor-Five Scores exceeding 2 have a fulminant course of polyarteritis nodosa with a high risk of mortality and long-term morbidities. This case illustrates the role of early diagnosis and treatment in preventing mortality and improving outcomes.

A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of progressively worsening difficulties in walking, eating and swallowing, presented to our department. Additionally, the patient's sister reported observing unusual behaviours over the past 6 months: she said her sister had been taking her meals to eat alone in the bathroom and had crafted a doll from leaves gathered from local trees, referring to it as her son (figure). The patient had no previous medical history or family history of similar difficulties.
On examination, the patient was cachectic, drooling her saliva, and had multiple injuries and scars on her tongue, lower lips, and arms caused by self-biting (figure); she had abnormal〞primarily choreatic〞movements of her trunk and oromandibular region, involuntary vocalisations, and vocal tics (video 1). She also had involuntary jaw opening and dystonia〞particularly during feeding (video 2). Limb examination showed mild bradykinesia, hypotonia, mild motor weakness, and reduced reflexes in all extremities.
Laboratory investigations found urea and electrolyte levels within normal range; liver enzymes were slightly elevated with alanine aminotransferase at 43 U/L (normal range 4每36 U/L) and aspartate aminotransferase at 74 U/L (normal range 8每33 U/L). Thyroid function was normal. Haemoglobin concentration was within the normal range at 12﹞1 g/dL (normal 11﹞0每14﹞0). The serum creatinine kinase level was elevated at 1?344 U/L (normal range for a woman is 26每192), and lactate dehydrogenase was raised at 269 UI/L (normal range for a woman is 100每240 UI/L). A blood smear showed that 15% of the red blood cells were acanthocytes (normal < 3%) (figure).
An MRI brain showed bilateral atrophy in the caudate nucleus and cortical atrophy in the frontal-parietal and occipital regions (figure). Nerve conduction studies showed axonal neuropathy affecting both sensory and motor neurons. Whole exome sequencing showed the patient to be a compound heterozygous carrier of two novel pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the VPS13A gene, namely: NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.2425C>T (p. Gln809*) and NM_033305.3(VPS13A): c.5072delA (p.Asp1691fs). No other pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants were found in any genes previously associated with adult-onset dystonia, chorea, or related movement disorders. Considering the findings together, we diagnosed VPS13A disease. Initially, we prescribed oral haloperidol with no response; she was switched to oral risperidone and tetrabenazine resulting in some improvement in both psychiatric and motor symptoms.
After 1 month, the patient was allowed home and followed up every 4 weeks as an outpatient. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate, with significant weight loss and worsening of both motor and psychiatric symptoms. At last review, she was receiving palliative care.
VPS13A disease〞previously known as Chorea-acanthocytosis〞is an autosomal recessive condition resulting from mutations in the VPS13A gene, which encodes a lipid transfer protein. Patients typically have progressive symptoms of chorea, oromandibular dyskinesia, Parkinsonism, neuropsychiatric issues, diminished or absent tendon deep reflexes and seizures. Symptoms usually begin around 30 years of age. Prognosis is poor, and the disease is ultimately fatal. Additional features indicative of VSP13A disease include elevated creatinine kinase levels, transaminitis, acanthocytocytosis, and caudate atrophy. The differential diagnoses include XK disease〞also known as McLeod syndrome. Both VSP13A and XK disease fall under the umbrella of neuroacanthocytosis syndrome: XK disease is an X-linked disorder predominantly affecting middle-aged men.
Huntington's disease, Huntington's disease-like 2, Wilson's disease, and other rare adult-onset choreatic disorders, including neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia, and c9orf72-related disorders, should also be considered as other possible differential diagnoses.
In Africa, choreatic movement disorders〞seen in our patient, which we believe is the first genetically confirmed case of VPS13A disease in a black patient from sub-Saharan Africa〞are often underdiagnosed; many cases are referred to traditional healers and customary medicine.

A baby girl delivered vaginally at full-term at a local hospital was found to have a global decrease in tone which was predominately in her arms. She had been born after an induction of labour because of decreased movements and oligohydramnios seen at 39 weeks of gestation on ultrasound.An ultrasound of the baby's head soon after birth demonstrated no obvious abnormalities. However, a T1-gadolinium enhanced MRI of the brain and spine showed an enhancing, intramedullary lesion extending from the medulla down to the upper thoracic spinal cord〞indicating a possible high-grade neoplasm (figure). The patient was transferred to our quaternary referral hospital and comprehensive cancer centre.
On examination, the baby was awake and alert, with a flat fontanelle, normal head circumference, and global hypotonia. Over the next 2 weeks, her quadriparesis became progressively worse〞the cervical spine showed signs of compression because of the expansile tumour in the spinal canal. We decompressed the cervical spine by doing a laminoplasty; we used electrostimulation, neuromonitoring, and intraoperative ultrasound to locate a safe midline entry point to obtain a biopsy and partially debulk the tumour. Histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample confirmed the suspected diagnosis of congenital spinal cord glioblastoma WHO grade IV.
Next generation sequencing showed a gene fusion involving the neurotrophin tropomyosin receptor kinase (NTRK) 1 gene: an inversion on chromosome 1q. No other pathogenic mutations, amplifications, deletions, or rearrangements were identified. Additionally, the tumour showed diffuse tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) positivity; she was treated with induction chemotherapy and the oral TRK inhibitor, larotrectinib, starting at a 50% dose of 50 mg/m2 twice a day for the first week to monitor for possible signs of toxicity because of the concurrent chemotherapy. The full dose of 100 mg/m2 twice a day was started in week 2 and continued. The patient tolerated the treatment well, and following cycle 1 of only conventional chemotherapy, a small reduction in size of the spinal cord tumour was seen.
2 weeks after the addition of larotrectinib, we observed a significant decrease in the size and enhancement on MRI of the lesion, with improvement in the patient's quadriparesis.
8 weeks into treatment with the oral TRK inhibitor and 4 cycles of carboplatin and etoposide, the tumour had completely regressed and was no longer visible with imaging (figure). 17 months after starting treatment, the patient was crawling and progressing toward walking; she continues treatment on the oral TRK inhibitor only, and there was no evidence of recurrence of the tumour.
The NTRK genes〞NTRK1, NTRK2, and NTRK3 which produce TRK proteins〞are affected by oncogenic fusions leading to a wide range of both paediatric and adult neoplasms. Small molecule TRK inhibitors have shown efficacy in treating a diverse array of TRK-positive tumours. In clinical trials of TRK inhibitors for tumours〞in both adult and paediatric patients with a variety of different primary tumour types with NTRK gene fusions〞response rates ranged from 75每93%. The first generation TRK inhibitors appear, on the whole, to be well tolerated in terms of adverse events: most are low grade〞including neurotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, anaemia and neutropenia, and nausea and vomiting.
Aided by histopathological examination findings, next generation sequencing can uncover NTRK fusions that may change the clinical course for patients with many primary tumours. While we could not entirely rule out a response to chemotherapy alone resulting in the improvement seen in our patient, the prognosis for congenital glioblastomas treated with chemotherapy alone remains very poor (video).
output: High grade, primary tumours of the brain and spine in infants do not harbour druggable oncogenic targets.

A 25-year-old man presented to our department with a 5-year history of an insidious, progressive weakness in his right hand. Despite being right-handed, he had recently become reliant on his left hand to carry out tasks needing manual dexterity. Clinical examination showed muscular atrophy without fasciculations of the first dorsal interosseous muscle and weakness of both the thenar and hypothenar muscles of the right hand; he also had atrophy but no fasciculation of the lumbrical and interosseous muscles. He complained of bilateral, electric shock-like sensations throughout his body when we examined the range of movements of his neck〞Lhermitte's sign. Laboratory investigations showed a serum B12 concentration of 648 pg/mL (normal range 174每878) and the serum panel for heavy metal toxicity〞including arsenic, mercury, and lead〞was negative. The association of the patient's electric shock-like sensations prompted us to do a dynamic cervical spine MRI study with the neck in positions of flexion and extension: MRI showed that the spinal cord was being compressed〞most noticeably at the level of the fifth cervical vertebral body〞and that the dorsal epidural space was abnormally expanding while in a flexed position (figure). A further dynamic cervical spine MRI done 6 weeks after the operation showed that the spinal cord was no longer being compressed when the patient flexed his neck (figure). input: In June, 2014, a 37-year-old man with known end-stage renal disease and chronic uraemic pericardial effusion presented to our institution with gradually worsening dyspnoea and orthopnoea, 4 days after a nephrectomy to control hypertension. He had been having regular haemodialysis three-times per week for the preceding 9 years after rejection of a transplanted kidney. On examination he was severely dyspnoeic at rest, and had a pulse rate of 102 beats per min, respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, and blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg with 25 mm Hg paradoxical changes. Lung auscultation showed left basilar bronchial breath sounds. Chest radiography indicated cardiomegaly with an air每fluid level at the level of the heart (figure). Chest CT showed hydropneumopericardium (figure). Echocardiography showed a massive pericardial effusion causing more than 25% respiratory variation of mitral inflow, consistent with tamponade physiology. We made a pericardial window and drained about 1 L of serosangiunous fluid. Pericardial fluid culture was negative and pericardial biopsy analysis showed acute and chronic inflammation and fibrosis. The patient had an uneventful hospital course after therapeutic drainage. 2 weeks later, follow-up echocardiography showed only mild pericardial effusion. In December, 2014, the patient was well, with echocardiography showing only mild pericardial effusion. In March, 2015, the patient was in a generally good condition but remained on the haemodialysis ward at the Namazi teaching hospital.Pneumopericardium usually happens after blunt or penetrating chest trauma, but is occasionally seen after intubation and mechanical ventilation. Except for recent intubation for nephrectomy, we could not find any risk factors in our patient. Rarely, pneumopericardium can superimpose on pre-existing pericardial effusion and lead to tension hydropneumopericardium, as in our patient. The plain radiographic imaging can resemble a large hiatal hernia or gastric torsion; a delineated heart border within an air每fluid level is helpful to exclude these differential diagnoses.

A 36-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-week history of palpitations in the context of 3 months of a dry cough, weight loss, and night sweats.The patient had no medical history, no recent foreign travel, and no contact with anyone who was unwell or who had been exposed to tuberculosis. He had no notable family history; he was born in Ghana and had moved to the UK 12 years earlier.
On examination, he was not distressed; his heart rate was 120 beats per min. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response; a chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly and CT angiography showed no signs of a pulmonary embolism but indicated a soft tissue mass surrounding the ascending aorta, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and a pericardial effusion. A CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed no abnormalities or extra-thoracic lymphadenopathy. Laboratory investigations showed a raised high-sensitive cardiac troponin-I (hs-TNI) concentration (60﹞6 ng/L; normal range 2﹞0每19﹞9), brain natriuretic peptide concentration (380; normal range 0每100), and C-reactive protein concentration (55 mg/l; normal 0每0﹞5).
Viral serology ruled out recent viral infection; HIV serology, serum angiotensin-converting-enzyme, autoimmune screen, and TB ELISpot were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography and cardiovascular MRI (CMRI) confirmed a global pericardial effusion with thickened basal〞mid-inferior and inferior-lateral〞left ventricular walls and mild biventricular dysfunction. A heterogeneous mass, involving the visceral pericardium and invading the left ventricular myocardium, with evidence of oedema and inflammation on T2-weighed MRI, and patchy fibrosis on late gadolinium enhancement in the thickened segments (figure), were also seen.
18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed increased activity in the pericardium〞the so-called ring-of-fire sign〞and the left ventricular wall; in the subcarinal, paratracheal, thoracic inlet, gastrohepatic, ileocolic, and right inguinal lymph nodes; and in lytic bone lesions in the seventh and ninth left ribs and fifth lumbar vertebra (figure). We did a bone marrow trephine and video-assisted thoracoscopy-guided pericardial window; and a pericardial and right lower lobe, and thoracic lymph node biopsy. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry ruled out lymphoma, malignant histiocytosis, and amyloidosis; Ziehl-Neelsen stains were negative for mycobacteria.
Our working diagnosis was initially sarcoidosis: histology showed a lung granuloma. However, the atypical cardiac features prompted us to seek further tissue samples prior to starting a glucocorticoid: a biopsy of the right inguinal lymph node showed necrotising granulomatous inflammation, and PCR showed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Based on the serum hs-TNI, the extensive pericardial and myocardial inflammation on PET and CMRI, and confirmation with PCR, we revised the diagnosis to tuberculous perimyocarditis. Quadruple anti-tuberculous therapy was given for 12 months with tapering glucocorticoid cover. Echocardiography, CMRI, and CT, 3 months after initiating the anti-tuberculous treatment, confirmed the full resolution of the left ventricular wall mass with no re-accumulation of the pericardial effusion (appendix); there was regression of the mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and the lytic bone lesions. Differentiating tuberculosis and sarcoidosis can be challenging as there is considerable overlap in their clinical, radiological, and histopathological presentations. Regarding cardiac tuberculosis, multimodal investigations and multidisciplinary management are essential for timely diagnosis and treatment (video).

A 52-year-old builder with a 6-year history of neck pain and dysphagia was referred to our rheumatology unit by a spinal neurosurgeon who was concerned the patient might have axial spondyloarthritis.
A review of the patient's history found that at age 45 years, he had been referred to the spinal surgeons; an x-ray and CT scan of the cervical spine showed osteophytosis at C5-C7 (figure). The radiologist had noted elongation of the styloid processes and calcification of the stylohyoid ligaments, suggestive of Eagle's syndrome.
Aged 47 years, new osteophytosis within mid and lower cervical spine were noted after the patient had a work-related injury.
Aged 50 years, the patient had been referred to both the neurosurgeons due to persistent neck symptoms, and to the Ear, Nose, and Throat (ENT) department because of ongoing dysphagia. We were able to teach the patient and his family to communicate using a smartphone voice-to-text translator.
3 months later, a repeat MRI showed that the mass had reduced in size and enhancement. Pure tones used in audiometry are simple sounds without the complex structure of speech, which has rapid, unpredictable fluctuations in frequency, amplitude, and timing. The auditory pathway processes sound timing and frequency extracting features that indicate what and where the sound is. The inferior colliculi begin to integrate the features that create an auditory object: the assignment of a sound to a specific source.
A general inability to perceive and identify the nature of any sounds is called auditory agnosia; although patients can hear pure tones, all complex sounds lose meaning, such that they cannot recognise or understand speech, music, or environmental sounds. The usual cause is bilateral temporal lobe lesions. A specific inability to understand speech, despite intact hearing of pure tones and intact language comprehension, is called verbal auditory agnosia (or word deafness); only speech sounds lose meaning, probably due to impaired processing of their rapidly changing acoustic content. The usual cause is bilateral lesions of the superior temporal gyrus or their projections, or〞like our case〞a single brainstem lesion of the inferior colliculi.

A 26-year-old woman with a 2-month history of postcoital bleeding〞which she described as very heavy loss and lasting 2 days〞attended our unit.
The patient used a progesterone implant for contraception. She had a history of two caesarean sections, aged 20 and 23 years; during both pregnancies she had been admitted to hospital for heavy antepartum bleeding in the first and third trimester respectively. Additionally, following a medical termination of pregnancy aged 25 years, the patient had prolonged vaginal bleeding lasting 2 months. She had no history of cervical surgery. She was prescribed sertraline for depression.
On examination she was generally fit and healthy-looking, and of typical range BMI. She had no abnormal cutaneous lesions.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 127﹞0 g/L (typical range 120﹞0每165﹞0), platelet count 201?℅?109 per L (typical range 150每400), white blood cell count 6﹞89?℅?109 per L (typical range 3﹞7每11﹞0), prothrombin time 10﹞1 s (typical range 20﹞0每30﹞0), C-reactive protein concentration 5﹞0 mg/L (typical level <5).
Colposcopic examination showed a smooth, well-defined, erythematous and vascular abnormality on the ectocervix (figure; appendix). A cervical punch biopsy was done resulting in profuse bleeding. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample obtained by cervical punch biopsy showed dilated and congested thin-walled blood vessels in the cervical stroma with erythrocytes within their lumen which was positive for CD31〞confirming the diagnosis of a benign capillary haemangioma (figure; appendix).
Pelvic ultrasound showed a normal cervix. A pelvic MRI found the haemangioma involved over two-thirds of the ectocervix causing expansion of the myometrial layer and reaching the external cervical os (figure; appendix).
Considering the patient's age and the size of the haemangioma, we decided on consultation with the patient that it was best to keep her under observation. At follow-up 6 months later, a repeat MRI and colposcopy showed the lesions to be stable.
Haemangiomas are common benign vascular lesions mostly found in the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and solid abdominal organs.
Haemangiomas located in the female genital tract are less common; in the cervix uteri they are extremely rare. Most cervical haemangiomas are of the cavernous subtype. Often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, clinical manifestations can include intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding, dyspareunia, fertility and obstetrical issues. Whilst many cervical haemangiomas will spontaneously regress, some can result in〞sometimes life-threatening〞haemorrhage during pregnancy and labour. Management of cervical haemangiomas includes surveillance or local excision; hysterectomy is usually reserved for rare cases where conservative and other surgical interventions have been unsuccessful. Uterine artery embolisation may be considered in cases of intractable cervical bleeding and cervical cerclage may be necessary to control bleeding〞especially in cases of extensive blood loss after local excision.
Differential diagnoses include invasive cancer and cervical ulcers, endothelial malignancies〞such as angiosarcoma〞and low-grade vascular neoplasms. Venous malformations are also important differentials in patients presenting with cervical masses and vaginal bleeding.

input: A 70-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with postprandial epigastric pain. He was prescribed antacids, which were ineffective; his weight then decreased by 11 kg in 3 months. Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy showed a mass in the antrum; histopathological analysis of a biopsy sample established that the mass was a signet-ring adenocarcinoma. The left supraclavicular lymph node is near the junction of the thoracic duct and the left subclavian vein, where the lymph from much of the body drains into the systemic circulation. An enlarged node can be the first sign of gastric cancer〞and is often called Virchow's node, because the association between left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and gastric cancer was first described by the German pathologist Rudolf Virchow (1821每1902). Virchow lectured and practised at the Charit谷 Medical School of the Humboldt University of Berlin, where he discovered several facts fundamental to modern medicine.
output: Gastric adenocarcinoma with Virchow's node metastasis

A 66-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 5-year history of recurrent episodes of epigastric burning pain, bloating, and constipation. In the past 3 months, the patient reported that his symptoms had resulted in him losing 4﹞5 kg in weight.He had a medical history of hypertension, but reported he was not taking any medications〞specifically aspirin or any non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
On examination the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 147/91 mm Hg, and his pulse rate was 95 beats per min. The patient had mild epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal distention; hypoactive bowel sounds were heard in the right upper quadrant region.
Laboratory investigations found a positive test for Helicobacter pylori using the 13C-urea breath test.
CT of the patient's abdomen showed gastric dilation above the junction between the gastric antrum and the duodenum where the calibre of the gastric antrum reduced substantially in diameter (figure).
The patient initially underwent gastric decompression using a nasogastric tube; he was then prescribed a 14-day course of H pylori triple therapy〞consisting of a proton pump inhibitor (pantoprazole), and the antibiotics clarithromycin and amoxicillin.
An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, done for further diagnostic evaluation, showed gastric stenosis and chronic gastritis. Immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue section confirmed the presence of H pylori with no evidence of gastric dysplasia.
The patient's symptoms were alleviated within 2 days, and after a successful oral food challenge with a regular diet, he was allowed home.
At 3-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic; a repeat upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed stenotic gastric regions〞without any visible obstruction〞and chronic inactive gastritis; further immunohistopathological examination of a sample of biopsied tissue was negative for H pylori, indicating successful eradication. The patient will be followed up episodically for the foreseeable future primarily to monitor for signs of gastric outlet obstruction recurrence.
Gastric outlet obstruction occurs in both acute and chronic peptic ulcer disease. Repeated episodes of acute peptic ulcer disease can cause progressive stenosis of the gastric antrum〞as probably occurred in our patient〞and subsequent gastric outlet obstruction.
Risk factors for peptic ulcer disease include poor diet and hygiene, reduced physical activity, use of NSAIDs and infection with H pylori. Notably, recurrent rates of obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease are variable; and interestingly, rates appear reduced in cases associated with H pylori. Endoscopic balloon dilation of the pylorus or more invasive surgical intervention is reserved for cases of gastric outlet obstruction that are not resolved with medical treatments.
Gastric outlet obstruction is a rare, but important, complication of peptic ulcer disease and identification of any risk factors〞specifically infection with H pylori〞aids diagnosis and treatment regimens.
output:
Based on the patient's history of recurrent epigastric pain, weight loss, and *Helicobacter pylori* infection, combined with the CT findings of significant gastric dilation and pyloric stenosis (narrowing), and the confirmation of chronic gastritis without dysplasia on biopsy, the diagnosis is gastric outlet obstruction resulting from chronic peptic ulcer disease.

**Gastric outlet obstruction due to peptic ulcer disease**

A 53-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer receiving 3-week cycles of vinorelbine (30 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8) plus capecitabine 2000 mg/m2 (days 1每14) at the All India Institute of Medical Science (New Delhi, India) developed a large erythematous lesion at the chemotherapy port site on her left chest after day 4 of vinorelbine therapy (figure). The lesion was slowly progressive with ulceration and bullae formation. A dye study showed that the catheter was intact and it was in position. She was managed with antibiotics (oral amoxicillin每clavulanic acid 625 mg three-times daily for 7 days), subcutaneous injection of hyaluronidase 900 IU, and warm compression and showed signs of recovery. A 13-year-old boy with a past medical history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and obesity was admitted with massive haematemesis, melaena, and severe epigastric pain. He had developed non-autoimmune diabetes (glutamate decarboxylase antibodies, islet tyrosine phosphatase 2 antibodies, insulin autoantibodies, and Zinc Transporter 8 antibodies were absent); HbA1c 14﹞5% at the age of 10 years, having multiple paternal inheritance. Although known to have a bulimic behaviour, his medical history was negative for gastrointestinal disorders and for gastrointestinal toxic drugs or caustic consumption.At admission, he had very poor metabolic control (glycaemia 840 mg/dL, HbA1c higher than 13%) because he had voluntarily withdrawn insulin and refused metformin. He complained of polyuria and polydipsia for several days before admission, had an altered mental status, and extreme dehydration of both skin and mucous membranes with a prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec). The initial blood count was 6?130?000 red cells per mL, haemoglobin 18﹞8 g/dL, haematocrit 54﹞5%, and 555?000 platelets per mL. Blood biochemistry analyses showed ketoacidosis (pH 7﹞07, HCO3 9﹞7 mmol/L, and blood ketones >7 mg/dL) and stage 3 prerenal acute kidney injury. Inflammatory indexes and blood toxicology screening were negative. His clinical condition was rapidly deteriorating and he was extremely dehydrated, in shock, tachycardic, unresponsive to verbal stimuli, and developed Kussmaul breathing. Soon after massive haematemesis episodes, blood tests showed severe normochromic anaemia (haemoglobin 7﹞4 g/dL [reference 13每16 g/dL]).
The endoscopic examination after removal of abundant blood residues showed circumferential black oesophagus appearance, sparing only the first proximal 3每4 cm (figure A). The stomach was filled with blood material and several mobile clots. After thorough cleansing, no sources of active or recent bleeding were found in the stomach or the duodenum. No biopsy samples were collected to avoid the risk of perforation. A CT angiogram showed oesophageal wall thickening and millimetric gaseous microareolas in pneumomediastinum (gas bubbles smaller than 1 cm, indicating esophageal microperforation).
The patient was treated with exclusive parenteral nutrition with continuous insulin infusion and monitoring of glycaemia, proton-pump inhibitors infusion, oral sucralfate, intravenous fluconazole, and broad antibiotic intravenous coverage. Within 4 weeks, the epigastric pain had resolved and the patient was able to feed orally safely. A repeated oesophagogastroduodenoscopy 1 month after admission showed complete recovery of the oesophageal mucosa, except for the presence of mild circumferential scar striae (figure B; green arrow). Findings on CT angiogram of the chest and abdomen were normal.
Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity of unknown cause that has been reported in the setting of multiorgan dysfunction, sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, thromboembolic disorders, alcohol intoxication, gastric volvulus, and cancer. Men are four times more affected than women and the peak incidence occurs at an average age of 67 years. A mortality rate of 7% has been reported, mainly linked to underlying diseases. To the best of our knowledge, this case is the first instance of so-called black oesophagus in paediatric age, perhaps an intriguing complication of childhood-onset diabetes. From the possible comorbidities, our patient had only diabetic ketoacidosis. Therefore, we hypothesise that blood hypo〞perfusion due to the extreme dehydration linked with ketoacidosis was the main factor leading to oesophageal ischaemia. Paediatricians addressing haematemesis in children with the aforementioned underlying conditions should be aware of oesophageal ischaemia as a possible differential diagnosis.
target: Black oesophagus by acute necrosis in an adolescent with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes

An 86-year-old woman with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis〞reporting progressive dyspnoea, rated as Class II on the New York Heart Association Functional Classification, for the previous few months〞had a transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in our unit. The patient's valve was replaced with an aortic valve bio prosthesis (Evolut PRO/PRO+ 29 mm [Medtronic Evolut?]).
Immediately after the valve had been replaced, continuous electrocardiogram monitoring showed ST-segment elevation in all antero-septal leads. A coronary angiogram showed complete occlusion of the distal part of the left anterior descending artery (figure 1).We then did a mechanical embolectomy〞using a stent retriever (enVast 4﹞5?℅?37 mm [enVast?]) combined with vacuum-assisted aspiration〞which resulted in the immediate restoration of blood flow in the blocked artery; no residual material was seen in the vessel on repeat angiography (figure 1).
The extracted material was amber-coloured, calcified, and 2 mm in size; histopathological examination showed that it was mostly composed of collagen, proteoglycans, and extracellular matrix〞compatible with a fragment of a leaflet from the patient's original aortic valve (figure 2). Additionally, substrates appeared non-birefringent under polarised light, confirming the absence of polymer-coated device fragments.The patient's chest pain promptly resolved; concentration of high-sensitivity troponin peaked at 24 h (202 ng/L; normal value <14). The patient remained asymptomatic for 1 day after the operation.
On day 2 postoperatively, she developed severe abdominal pain; an abdominal CT scan showed patency of both the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries with radiological signs of intestinal ischaemia. The patient had abdominal surgery which was complicated by multiple-organ failure; she died 4 days after the index TAVR.
Embolisation of aortic valve debris is a feared complication during TAVR, typically resulting in cerebrovascular accidents, and mesenteric or peripheral ischaemia. Histological analysis of captured material from cerebral protective devices has previously been done.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report showing that embolisation of aortic valve debris〞confirmed by histological examination〞into coronary circulation can be extracted with a stent retriever. Coronary embolisation during TAVR is unpredictable and no effective preventive measures exist; conventional angioplasty is often unsuccessful because of the presence of the calcified, non-friable material inside the vessel.

output: Coronary artery embolization of aortic valve debris following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR)

A well demarcated, erythematous, indurated, mildly tender plaque was present, extending from the dorsum of the right hand to the elbow (figure). He had a white blood cell count of 8﹞4?℅?109 cells per L, haemoglobin concentration of 11﹞5 g/dL, platelet count of 146?℅?109 per L, sodium concentration of 141 mmol/L, potassium concentration of 4﹞4 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration of 246 米mol/L.

A skin biopsy was done and a mucinous substance was observed. Histological results showed encapsulated yeast forms that stained positive with periodic acid-Schiff stain and Gomori methenamine silver stains, and mucoid capsules staining strongly with mucicarmine and Alcian blue (figure). Fungal cultures were positive for Cryptococcus gattii.

An 80-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with chest pain and shortness of breath.The patient had a long medical history of diabetes, ischaemic heart disease, and end-stage kidney disease requiring regular haemodialysis.
On examination we found him to be in acute distress, with bilateral ankle oedema, and basal lung crackles. An electrocardiogram showed ST segment depression over leads V2-V6 and a Q wave in lead III. Laboratory investigations showed a serum cardiac troponin T concentration of 1297 ng/L (normal <14) with an unaffected creatinine phosphate kinase level.
We made a diagnosis of an acute non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
1 day after a percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stent insertion into the right coronary artery and mid-left anterior descending artery, he began to repeatedly vomit; he also developed a low-grade fever with a temperature of 37﹞8～C. An urgent chest x-ray (figure) showed a radio-opaque nodule〞not seen in previous x-rays〞in the right lower lung field. We initially wondered whether the patient had aspirated his denture but on review of the lesion we were unconvinced. However, on closer inspection using magnification, we found the radio-opaque object had a complex internal structure consisting of a microchip, a battery, and an electronic circuit (figure). Before the film was sent for reporting, our physician examined the patient and found a subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) transmitter device (FreeStyle Libre Flash Glucose Monitoring System, Abbott Laboratories, Chicago, IL) which had been displaced from deltoid muscle to the patient's back. We treated the patient as if he had a diagnosis of a nosocomial infection and his condition improved with intravenous piperacillin and tazobactam.
He was allowed home after 14 days and at follow-up 2 weeks later the patient was well with no angina or chest symptoms. However, the patient died 6 months later with a recurrent myocardial infarction.
In patients with a history of heart disease, unidentified electronic gadgets seen on chest x-ray might well be cardiac related〞specifically pacemakers. Although CGM devices are typically located on the upper arm, they may slip〞especially in semiconscious patients and those requiring frequent transfers〞to other body parts. CGM devices may look like unexpected foreign objects on limited resolution x-rays. As CGM gains in popularity, health-care professionals should be able to identify CGM devices and be aware of their potential to move to unexpected positions where they may cause consternation on x-ray interpretation. Using appropriate magnification of x-rays may be necessary for recognising CGM devices.
output: Displaced subcutaneous continuous glucose monitoring device
