A 48-year-old Chinese man with a 12-month history of increasing shortness of breath on exertion was admitted to our hospital. He was a heavy smoker and had been diagnosed with Child-Pugh class C alcoholic cirrhosis 5 years earlier, which was complicated by oesophageal varices that haemorrhaged 1 month before this admission; he had an urgent gastroscopy and the varices were banded.On physical examination, he was asymptomatic while lying supine but dyspnoeic while sitting up. He had clubbing of his fingers (figure), clear lung fields, and pitting ankle oedema. An arterial blood gas while supine and breathing room air showed a partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 57 mm Hg with a widened alveolar每arterial oxygen gradient (Grad[A每a] O2) of 66 mm Hg (normal gradient for a 40-year-old man is less than 14 mm Hg). However, when the PaO2 was retaken while the patient was sitting upright, it dropped to 43 mm Hg. His chest x-ray was unremarkable.
Looking at these clinical features in the round, we suspected that our patient had hepatopulmonary syndrome. To confirm the diagnosis and to investigate the patient's pathophysiology further, we did a contrast-enhanced transthoracic echocardiography, which, with saline bubbles appearing in the left side of the heart, indicated intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting (figure). An intravenous injection of agitated saline in a healthy person will only show bubbles in the right side of the heart because they would be trapped by the pulmonary capillaries as they travel through the lung.
Hepatopulmonary syndrome is an important diagnostic consideration in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension who present with respiratory symptoms and digital clubbing. The pathogenesis is poorly understood but leads to pulmonary vascular angiogenesis and intrapulmonary vascular dilatation: this causes a ventilation每perfusion mismatch, reduced oxygen diffusion, and intrapulmonary shunting. The symptoms of a gravity-dependent hypoxaemia〞namely, dyspnoea, platypnoea (dyspnoea in an upright position), and orthodeoxia〞are characteristic but not pathognomonic. A consensus group has defined a clinically relevant Grad(A每a) O2 in patients with the disease as at least 15 mm Hg (>20 mm Hg in those older than 64 years of age). The additional presence of digital clubbing and cyanosis would strongly suggest a diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome. Additional investigations〞including respiratory function tests and a chest CT〞are non-specific but useful to exclude other causes of dyspnoea such as a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. A technetium-99m-labelled macroaggregated albumin scan〞where radioactively labelled particles are usually prevented from passing through the pulmonary veins〞may help in the diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome. However, the test also shows positive results in patients with intracardiac shunts. Long-term oxygen therapy provides symptomatic relief for patients with hepatopulmonary syndrome, but liver transplantation is the only definitive cure. Our patient was discharged home with continuous oxygen therapy at 4 L per min and is awaiting orthotopic liver transplantation.

A 51-year-old woman with a 3-year history of painful hips presented to our mineral metabolism service having been referred by her general practitioner. The pain was present at rest and made worse by more vigorous movement; she used crutches to walk.Regarding her medical history, the patient had transfusion-dependent 汕-thalassaemia intermedia and had been having regular red blood cell transfusions since she was 40 days old; she had a splenectomy aged 29 years. She reported that she was currently receiving two units of filtered red blood cells every 15 days; her mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin concentration for the past 12 months was between 9﹞5 and 10﹞0 g/dL. Genotypically, she had compound heterozygous mutations: intervening segments (IVS)-I每110 (G>A) and IVS-I每6 (T>C). Additionally, she had diabetes mellitus. Both the patient's parents had microcytic anaemia. She was being prescribed deferasirox, cholecalciferol, proton pump inhibitors, and ultralong acting insulin.
On examination we found her to be generally well; she had pain on flexion, internal rotation, and adduction of both hips that limited her range of movements.
Laboratory investigations done prior to our consultation showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9﹞5 g/dL, haematocrit 27﹞5%, red blood cell count 3﹞26?℅?1012 per L, serum iron concentration 208 米g/dL (normal range 60每170), and ferritin concentration 590 米g/L (normal range 24每336).
An x-ray of the patient's hips showed flattening of both the femoral heads〞particularly apparent on the left hip〞and a T2-weighted MRI showed heterogeneous signal intensity with geodic cavities and marrow oedema, findings indicative of bilateral avascular necrosis of both hips. We recommended the patient have bilateral hip replacement but she did not want to have any surgical intervention. The patient continues to manage her pain with analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories.
Several skeletal abnormalities have been documented in 汕-thalassaemia and avascular necrosis of the head of the femur is quite rare. It is more commonly seen in patients with sickle cell disease〞where the prevalence may be up to 22%. Even rarer is the finding〞as seen in our patient〞of bilateral osteonecrosis. Multiple microfractures, local hypoxia, and medullary expansion with possible arterial compression represent the most important pathophysiological mechanisms underlying skeletal necrosis.

A 60-year-old man was brought to our emergency room after he collapsed while working out in a gym. He was unable to speak to his personal trainer or move his right side after he fell. He had a history of uncontrolled hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and a previous left occipital stroke. When we saw him, his blood pressure was 205/115 mm Hg, which we controlled with intravenous nicardipine. He was not on any anticoagulation or antiplatelet medication. Physical examination showed the man had a profound right-sided hemiplegia, expressive aphasia, and leftward gaze deviation. A non-contrast CT scan (figure) of the man's head showed a 44 mL intracerebral haemorrhage in the left basal ganglia without intraventricular extension. CT angiography of the head showed a fusiform aneurysm characterised by a 1 cm dilatation of the left supraclinoid internal carotid artery distant from the haemorrhage site and no evidence of vascular malformation. A repeat non-contrast head CT, performed 6 h after the first, found that the clot had not increased in size. MRI of the patient's brain showed scattered small cerebellar and occipital infarcts, diffuse white matter disease, and subcortical small vessel disease.The following day, 36﹞5 h after symptom onset, we performed a left frontal minimally invasive endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation with the Artemis aspiration device (Penumbra, Alameda, CA, USA) in our angiography suite. A non-contrast CT scan (figure) of the patient's head, performed on postoperative day 1, demonstrated that the haemorrhage had almost completely been evacuated, with just 1 mL remaining, and a small cavity in the place where the haematoma had been. After 2 weeks in the neurosurgical intensive care unit, the patient was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility, where he regained movement in his right side and the ability to speak short phrases. 1 year after his haemorrhage, he was living independently with home nursing care and he was able to walk with a walker for assistance. A CT scan at that time showed a residual haematoma cavity (figure).
Minimally invasive intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation is an increasingly common surgical technique used to treat spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage. A study in The Lancet, evaluating a different minimally invasive evacuation technique〞stereotactic catheter placement with aspiration and thrombolysis〞showed that the intervention did not improve functional outcome in patients with intracerebral haemorrhage. However, the results did show that in a prespecified secondary analysis〞when no more than 15 mL of haematoma remained at the end of the treatment〞patients had improved functional outcome at 1 year compared to medically managed controls. Endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation, as we have shown here, is an alternative type of minimally invasive evacuation technique, with some evidence suggesting that it can reliably meet established surgical goals.
Even though endoscopic intracerebral haemorrhage evacuation may be achievable in patients〞as in our case〞they may still be left with functional impairment. Further, it is worth noting that although minimally invasive evacuation can be technically successful, several other factors impact long-term clinical outcome in intracerebral haemorrhage, including baseline functional status, patient age, the presence or absence of intraventricular haemorrhage, severity of white matter disease, subsequent hospital complications, and other confounders: the true effect of this procedure remains unknown.

input: A 60-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital because of an abnormal endoscopic finding in the oesophagus at a regular health check. He reported receiving no medication and had no history of alcohol misuse. The patient was a former smoker and reported sometimes feeling heartburn. Laboratory data revealed no pronounced abnormalities. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed short segment Barrett's oesophagus and a whitish elevated lesion adjacent to the Barrett's oesophagus lesion (figure, A). Vessel structures could not be seen by magnified narrow band imaging, because of a whitish plaque (figure, B). Chromoendoscopy with Lugol's iodine solution showed decreased staining of the lesion (figure, C). A biopsy was done, and histology confirmed cell proliferation of the squamous epithelium. Although cellular atypicality was mild, we considered the lesion to be potentially malignant. Therefore, an endoscopic submucosal dissection was done for an en-bloc complete resection and diagnosis. Histology showed papillary growth and nests of well differentiated squamous epithelium pushing into the underlying stroma, which is typical of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma (figure, D). Pathological examination revealed tumour depth invasion into the lamina propria mucosa (stage T1a) without lymphovascular invasion. The patient was monitored closely and no recurrence had occurred at 3 months after the endoscopic submucosal dissection.Oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is a very rare malignancy. Although, the cause of such lesions is debated, it has been suggested that oesophageal verrucous carcinoma is associated with achalasia, acid reflux, and alcohol and nicotine misuse. The common endoscopic appearance of most oesophageal verrucous carcinomas is an elevated whitish plaque that is clearly circumscribed. Oesophageal verrucous carcinomas are difficult to diagnose before surgical resection. Accurate diagnosis is often delayed because the endoscopic finding of a whitish plaque is similar to a Candida infection and squamous cell papilloma. In addition, superficial biopsies are frequently false negative for malignancy because of highly differentiated histology. Endoscopic resection can be curative for oesophageal verrucous carcinoma restricted to the epithelium and the lamina propria mucosa. A lack of recognition of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma leads to a delay in diagnosis and progression of the disease. To improve the chance of curative treatment, endoscopists need to recognise the macroscopic findings and frequent difficulties associated with diagnosis of oesophageal verrucous carcinoma.

A 55-year-old man presented with 10 years of progressive handwriting impairment and rapid, slurred speech. In his thirties, he had worked as a welder without access to personal protective equipment. Neurologic examination was notable for reduced facial expression, blepharospasm, and cluttered, dysarthric speech. Postural reflexes were mildly impaired. MRI imaging of the head showed a nonenhancing, T1-weighted, hyperintense signal in the basal ganglia on both sides. Ceruloplasmin and iron levels were normal. What treatment should be administered?
output:
Chelation therapy (e.g., disodium edetate/EDTA or succimer)

The clinical presentation and imaging findings are consistent with **manganism** (manganese-induced parkinsonism) resulting from chronic occupational manganese exposure during welding without proper protective equipment.

Key diagnostic features:
- History of welding without PPE (significant manganese exposure source)
- Progressive parkinsonism with dystonia (blepharospasm)
- Characteristic T1-weighted hyperintensity in bilateral basal ganglia (particularly globus pallidus) due to manganese accumulation
- Normal ceruloplasmin (excludes Wilson disease)
- Normal iron levels (excludes other causes of basal ganglia T1 hyperintensity)

The treatment is **chelation therapy** to reduce manganese body burden.

input: A 37-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of pain and swelling in the left upper arm that had started after blunt trauma during soccer practice. The heart rate was 120 beats per minute, the blood pressure 96/54 mm Hg, and the body temperature 37.9～C. Examination of the left upper arm was notable for swelling, tenderness, and crepitus. The overlying skin was red and warm to the touch. An initial radiograph is shown. Which of the following factors is most associated with increased mortality in this diagnosis?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and radiograph showing gas within the soft tissues of the upper arm (evidenced by the lucent areas within the soft tissue), along with the clinical findings of:
- Rapid progression following minor trauma
- Systemic signs (tachycardia, hypotension, fever)
- Local signs (swelling, tenderness, crepitus, erythema, warmth)

The diagnosis is **Gas gangrene (Clostridial myonecrosis/Necrotizing soft tissue infection)**

The factor most associated with increased mortality in this diagnosis is **delay in surgical debridement/time to surgery**.

Other significant mortality factors include:
- Truncal involvement
- Hypotension/shock at presentation
- Clostridial species involvement
- Advanced age
- Underlying immunocompromise

However, the single most critical modifiable factor affecting mortality is the delay in surgical intervention, as prompt aggressive surgical debridement is the cornerstone of treatment for necrotizing soft tissue infections.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 米g/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35﹞0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects〞known as blueberry spots〞ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32每35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and m邦llerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

A 62-year-old man with a parastomal hernia at the site of a urinary conduit and symptoms of urinary obstruction lasting several months presented to our hospital.
The patient previously had a radical cysto-prostatectomy with formation of an ileal conduit ileostomy〞involving the interposition of a segment of small bowel between the distal end of the ureters and the skin resulting in urine being collected in a stoma bag〞because of a high grade transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder 7 years earlier.
Additionally, he had a history of Child-Pugh A cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C, which had been successfully treated, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; he used tiotropium bromide and fluticasone inhalers and was prescribed methadone.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 135/77 mm Hg, pulse was 87 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Some deformity and asymmetry were seen on inspection of his abdomen: a bulge was visible inferior and lateral to the conduit; overall the abdomen was soft with some mild tenderness noted at the stoma site. Bowel sounds were normal. The conduit ileostomy was pink and warm. The patient reported that only a small amount of urine had been collected in the past few days and we noted little urine output. Regarding the hernia, we found that it was partially reducible with some incarceration, and we concluded that the ileal conduit had obstructed acutely secondary to a parastomal hernia.
Laboratory investigations found an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1﹞73 m2 (normal >90) and creatinine concentration of 223 米mol/L (normal 61﹞9每114﹞9); C-reactive protein concentration was 132 mg/L (normal <5).
Percutaneous nephrostomies〞urinary drains placed directly in the lumbar region connecting the renal calices to drainage bags which allow alternative urine drainage from the kidneys〞were inserted under CT imaging guidance and urine began flowing normally. Ureteric stents were then passed through the percutaneous nephrostomies with proximal ends in the renal calyces and distal ends in the deep end of the conduit.
The patient was then taken to theatre and had a parastomal hernia repair using the Pauli technique which involved tunnelling the stoma through the retro-muscular space and offsetting the trephine in the peritoneum and the anterior sheath. Notably〞as always occurs with this technique〞the procedure resulted in the bowel changing direction as it traversed the abdominal wall (figures 1, 2). Postoperatively, the patient was well; the urinary obstruction was resolved and urine flowed, as expected, through the conduit. The nephrostomy tubes were capped, and renal function remained normal.
2 weeks later, endoscopic removal of the stents was attempted but it had to be abandoned due to, what was thought to be, a stricture in the conduit caused by the surgery at the time of the hernia repair; the result was a micro perforation of the stoma at the anterior sheath where the bowel changed direction.
The patient was treated conservatively and the perforation healed, and he was allowed home. At follow-up 2 weeks later, the stoma was patent; the ureteric stents were removed via the nephrostomy tubes which were then also removed.
Parastomal hernias are a common and challenging surgical problem; patients present with chronic pain, bowel obstruction and ischaemia, and difficulties in keeping stoma appliances adequately sited.
Recurrence rates are high and there are risks of surgical site complications. The Pauli technique of parastomal hernia repair is increasingly being adopted by specialists because of improved outcomes; key has been the use of synthetic mesh in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane.
Crucially, patients who have had a parastomal hernia repaired using a Pauli technique have a stomal course through the abdominal wall that may be unexpected; it is similar to a Sugarbaker repair, but in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane. Essentially, the bowel lumen changes direction twice〞firstly at the deep peritoneal position it travels anteriorly at a right angle to the abdominal wall, then in the intramural retro-muscular position it is parallel to the abdominal wall, and finally at the superficial anterior sheet it moves through the abdominal wall anteriorly through the skin to end in the stoma (figures 1, 2). Furthermore, the segment of bowel contained within the abdominal wall is unusually long and looks different on imaging; other common parastomal hernia repair techniques〞including direct suture, mesh keyhole, or cruciate repairs〞do not have these specific anatomical changes. Enhanced clinician awareness of these anatomical aspects will minimise the risk of complications during instrumentation of the stoma and avoid unnecessary concerns over successfully repaired hernias.

input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C每E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology每European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I每K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

A 62-year-old man with a parastomal hernia at the site of a urinary conduit and symptoms of urinary obstruction lasting several months presented to our hospital.
The patient previously had a radical cysto-prostatectomy with formation of an ileal conduit ileostomy〞involving the interposition of a segment of small bowel between the distal end of the ureters and the skin resulting in urine being collected in a stoma bag〞because of a high grade transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder 7 years earlier.
Additionally, he had a history of Child-Pugh A cirrhosis secondary to hepatitis C, which had been successfully treated, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; he used tiotropium bromide and fluticasone inhalers and was prescribed methadone.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his blood pressure was 135/77 mm Hg, pulse was 87 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. Some deformity and asymmetry were seen on inspection of his abdomen: a bulge was visible inferior and lateral to the conduit; overall the abdomen was soft with some mild tenderness noted at the stoma site. Bowel sounds were normal. The conduit ileostomy was pink and warm. The patient reported that only a small amount of urine had been collected in the past few days and we noted little urine output. Regarding the hernia, we found that it was partially reducible with some incarceration, and we concluded that the ileal conduit had obstructed acutely secondary to a parastomal hernia.
Laboratory investigations found an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1﹞73 m2 (normal >90) and creatinine concentration of 223 米mol/L (normal 61﹞9每114﹞9); C-reactive protein concentration was 132 mg/L (normal <5).

Ureteric stents were then passed through the percutaneous nephrostomies with proximal ends in the renal calyces and distal ends in the deep end of the conduit.
The patient was then taken to theatre and had a parastomal hernia repair using the Pauli technique which involved tunnelling the stoma through the retro-muscular space and offsetting the trephine in the peritoneum and the anterior sheath. Notably〞as always occurs with this technique〞the procedure resulted in the bowel changing direction as it traversed the abdominal wall (figures 1, 2). The patient was treated conservatively and the perforation healed, and he was allowed home. At follow-up 2 weeks later, the stoma was patent; the ureteric stents were removed via the nephrostomy tubes which were then also removed.
Parastomal hernias are a common and challenging surgical problem; patients present with chronic pain, bowel obstruction and ischaemia, and difficulties in keeping stoma appliances adequately sited.
Recurrence rates are high and there are risks of surgical site complications. The Pauli technique of parastomal hernia repair is increasingly being adopted by specialists because of improved outcomes; key has been the use of synthetic mesh in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane.
Crucially, patients who have had a parastomal hernia repaired using a Pauli technique have a stomal course through the abdominal wall that may be unexpected; it is similar to a Sugarbaker repair, but in the retro-muscular or preperitoneal plane. Essentially, the bowel lumen changes direction twice〞firstly at the deep peritoneal position it travels anteriorly at a right angle to the abdominal wall, then in the intramural retro-muscular position it is parallel to the abdominal wall, and finally at the superficial anterior sheet it moves through the abdominal wall anteriorly through the skin to end in the stoma (figures 1, 2). input: A 26-year-old man was referred to our orthopaedics department with left thigh pain. Radiography and CT revealed a cortical mass unilaterally on the medial side of the distal femoral diaphysis (figure A, B). The lesion extended with osteoblastic and osteolytic changes that accompany a periosteal reaction. MRI revealed a contrast-enhanced soft tissue mass surrounding the cortical lesion (figure C每E). No major blood vessel or bone marrow infiltration was observed. Our primary differential diagnosis was malignancy, particularly periosteal osteosarcoma, followed by fracture, osteomyelitis, or periostitis. A periosteal biopsy did not show malignancy but did reveal neutrophilic inflammation (figure F, G). Additional testing showed elevated inflammatory markers and arterial wall thickening in the aortic arch and its common branches (figure H) but not in the left femoral artery. At follow-up 2 months after the first visit, the patient reported general fatigue. Carotid bruits and blood pressure differences between the arms were observed. The patient was diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis based on the American College of Rheumatology每European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology classification criteria. Treatment of Takayasu arteritis was initiated using daily oral prednisolone (initial dose of 80 mg followed by decreasing dose thereafter) followed by subcutaneous tocilizumab (162 mg/week), after which the left thigh pain disappeared and periostitis subsided on imaging (figure I每K). The patient's Indian Takayasu Clinical Activity Score decreased from 6 to 2. We concluded that the femoral lesions were associated with Takayasu arteritis. Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that presents with non-specific symptoms and signs, but periostitis is a rare manifestation. Isolated bone lesions incline the diagnosis more towards malignancy than systemic disease; however, several previous reports have shown isolated Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis. Local inflammation of the periosteum might create a malignancy-like mass and periosteal osteosarcoma is suspected when the mass affects the femoral diaphysis in young adults. As patient presentation and imaging findings of Takayasu arteritis-associated periostitis might mimic periosteal osteosarcoma, it is imperative to rule out malignancy and maintain a broad differential diagnosis.

A 32-year-old right-handed woman presented to our neurology clinic with a 3-month history of intermittent blurriness of her vision and left-sided paraesthesia in her arm and leg. The patient said the problems began shortly after she gave birth to her first child and gradually became worse over the following 12 weeks.She had no significant medical history and was prescribed no medications.
On examination she was fit and well; she had no retinal hemangiomas, her hearing was normal, and we found no neurofibromas. A full neurological review found no abnormalities: specifically, her visual acuity was unaffected; a sensory system and cerebellar examination were within normal limits. Notably, the patient's left-sided paraesthesia did not follow a dermatomal distribution.
All laboratory investigations〞including the haematocrit〞were normal. We did not carry out any genetic testing.
An MRI of the patient's brain showed a 3 mm lesion within the inferior aspect of the posterior lobe of the left cerebellum; the lesion demonstrated contrast enhancement on T1 weighted imaging (figure), suggesting vascularity. A digital subtraction angiogram showed no evidence of a shunting vascular malformation. We were unable to make a clear diagnosis at that time because the MRI findings did not correlate with the patient's symptoms. We therefore decided to observe the lesion with repeated imaging over an extended period of follow-up. At the time, our list of initial differential diagnoses included vascular lesions, such as arteriovenous malformations, metastatic tumour, and primary cerebellar tumour.
2 years later, the abnormality had grown to 5 mm at its widest part (figure) and was surrounded by a small amount of oedema. Importantly, the patient reported no change in her symptomatology and had no abnormalities on neurological examination. We decided to continue watching and waiting: monitoring the lesion with radiographic imaging and follow-up appointments. The possibility of resection was discussed with the patient but she decided to continue with the plan to keep the situation under observation and review.
4 years after initial presentation, an expansile intraparenchymal fluid collection had developed around the lesion, which now had the characteristic appearance of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma (figure); the pathognomonic findings included a T2 hyperintense cyst with a non-enhancing wall and a strongly enhancing mural nodule.
The patient elected to have a suboccipital craniotomy in order to remove the lesion; intraoperative findings were consistent with a hemangioblastoma and the procedure was completed without any complications. She recovered fully from the operation and at follow-up 2 years later, she was neurologically intact and reported resolution of her initial presenting symptoms.
The relationship between pregnancy and its potentiation of cerebellar hemangioblastoma formation continues to cause controversy. Our case〞where the patient presented shortly after giving birth without a clear association between her presenting symptoms and the initial MRI findings〞unfortunately prevented us from adding any significant insights into the debate.
In addition, while the majority of cerebellar hemangioblastomas are associated with Von Hippel每Lindau disease, some, like our patient, lack the other characteristic features of the syndrome: angiomatosis including retinal capillary hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts and tumours, and endolymphatic sac tumours (video).

input: A 73-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of left flank pain. Findings from a physical examination were normal. Laboratory testing was notable for a platelet count of 652,000 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 150,000 to 400,000) with an otherwise normal complete blood count. No previous platelet count was available. Computed tomography of the abdomen with intravenous contrast material showed a filling defect in the left renal artery and a perfusion defect in the left renal cortex, consistent with an occlusive thrombosis of the left renal artery and associated renal infarction. Further testing revealed no evidence of cardioembolic disease, renal artery injury, or inherited thrombophilia. Genetic testing was positive for a genetic variant. Which of the following variants is most likely to be associated with the above findings?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation of:
- Left renal artery thrombosis with renal infarction
- Elevated platelet count (652,000/mm3) - thrombocytosis
- No evidence of cardioembolic disease, renal artery injury, or inherited thrombophilia
- Age 73 years

The combination of **arterial thrombosis** and **thrombocytosis** in an elderly patient without other identifiable causes is highly suggestive of a **myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)**.

**JAK2 V617F mutation**

This mutation is found in approximately 95% of patients with polycythemia vera and 50-60% of patients with essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. JAK2-positive MPNs are associated with an increased risk of both arterial and venous thrombotic events, including renal artery thrombosis. The unexplained thrombocytosis combined with arterial thrombosis in this clinical scenario strongly points to this diagnosis.

A 41-year-old woman presented to our hospital complaining of breathlessness and pain in the right side of her chest. She said that the problem was not new and that it happened every time she had her period: she had begun menstruating 24 h earlier.On examination she had reduced breath sounds and dullness to percussion on the right side of her chest. In her medical history, it was noted that she had been diagnosed with catamenial pneumothorax 9 years earlier for which she was treated with the gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist buserelin 1200 米g/day; she stopped taking it after 6 months.
A CT scan of her chest showed a moderately sized pneumothorax on the right side. A blood test showed a serum concentration of the tumour marker cancer antigen 125 of 2219 U/mL (normal level <35﹞0 U/mL). Considering the history and the current presentation, we concluded that our patient had again had a catamenial pneumothorax. We therefore decided to do a thoracoscopy, during which a red lesion was seen in the pleura of the superior segment of the right lower lobe (figure) and two black lesions were seen in the pleura of the right middle lobe: the lesions were resected. Additionally, several small defects〞known as blueberry spots〞ranging between 2-3 mm in diameter, were seen on the right side of the diaphragm (figure), through which the liver was visible. Histopathological examination of both the diaphragmatic and the pulmonary lesions showed endometrial stroma, which was oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive and CD10 positive.
The lesions were cut out and resected areas were covered with sheets of polyglycolic acid and fibrin glue. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and no further lesions were identified; however, 72 days after the surgery, she had a further pneumothorax. She was re-started on buserelin.
Catamenial pneumothorax is a rare condition and has a mean age of onset of 32每35 years. The pneumothorax usually occurs within 72 h before or after the start of menstruation. The lesions are classically on the right side and endometriosis might also be present. The actual cause is unknown, but three theories have been proposed as underlying mechanisms: retrograde regurgitation of endometrial cells through the ovarian duct into the pelvis and then into the diaphragm; metastatic spread of endometrial cells through lymphatic or venous dissemination; and m邦llerian cell metaplasia of the coelomic epithelium.
Menstruation has a clear association with the worsening of several other diseases including migraine, epilepsy, and some psychological disorders. Questions about the relationship of any symptoms to the menstrual cycle can sometimes provide an important clue to the precise diagnosis.

input: A 35-year-old man presented to our department with palpitations and mild shortness of breath. He was of Haitian origin and had emigrated to the USA when he was 24 years old. A physical examination, an electrocardiogram (ECG), a full blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic profile showed no abnormalities. However, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 3 cm?℅?2 cm echolucent lesion in the apex of the left ventricle (figure; video 1). The patient did not report having a fever or any other systemic problems, but he had been to Haiti 5 months earlier. A cardiac MRI showed a solitary, avascular lesion located in the anterior wall of the left ventricle (figure; video 2); this lesion had no communication with the left ventricular cavity and was non-fatty and cystic. No pericardial or valvular abnormalities were seen. A CT scan of the heart confirmed the lesion was cystic and without any calcification; the coronary arteries were normal and, importantly, were not compressed by the mass. CT scans and MRIs of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no further cysts in any other organs. Serum serology by western blot testing for antibodies against specific IgG glycoproteins was negative for Echinococcus granulosus and Trypanosoma cruzi but positive for Taenia solium. The patient was then treated for 2 weeks with oral albendazole 400 mg twice a day. He reported no further symptoms and the lesion was no longer visible on a further transthoracic echocardiogram (figure; video 3) repeated 1 week after completing the treatment; a repeat cardiac MRI showed that the lesion had decreased considerably in size. Cysticercosis is endemic in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The disease can develop after consuming foods contaminated with faeces that contain T solium eggs shed from a human carrier. The brain, skeletal muscle, and subcutaneous tissue are involved most frequently; isolated cardiac cysticercosis is rare. The need for concomitant treatment with steroids〞particularly in neurocysticercosis〞has been much debated because of concerns about seizures and worsening neurological symptoms on the initiation of anthelmintic therapy. In cases of isolated cardiac cysticercosis, there is no consensus for the routine use of steroids. In our patient, given that there was only mild oedema around the solitary lesion, the ECG was normal, and because he was on a cardiac monitor in hospital when albendazole was started, we were able to keep him under observation. Furthermore, it is of note that in other inflammatory cardiac conditions〞such as pericarditis〞steroids have been linked to increased relapse and recurrence. The rapid response to anthelmintic therapy in this case〞reassuringly confirmed on repeat imaging〞shows that in select cases, such as this one, albendazole may be used without steroids, with close clinical and cardiac monitoring and serial imaging.

Abdominal and thoracic imaging showed numerous hepatic masses, abdominal and thoracic lymphadenopathy, and vertebral sclerotic osseous disease. output:
Uveal melanoma with metastatic disease

The MRI shows a mass within the right globe (note the abnormal appearance of the right eye compared to the normal left eye with its homogeneous vitreous signal). In a patient who has been blind in that eye for years, presenting with pain and inflammation, combined with the imaging findings of hepatic masses, lymphadenopathy, and sclerotic bone lesions, this is consistent with uveal melanoma with widespread metastases.

Uveal melanoma has a predilection for metastasizing to the liver, and the constellation of findings including the intraocular mass and pattern of metastatic disease supports this diagnosis.

input: A 52-year-old man visited our hospital to have a general checkup. Routine gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a twisted lumen with a corkscrew appearance in the distal oesophagus. No other abnormality was identified (figure A). Our patient did not have any symptoms of dysphagia or retrosternal pain. A single-contrast barium examination of his oesophagus confirmed a spiral staircase peristalsis and an absence of peristalsis in the oesophageal body. CT of the mediastinum was done, and virtual endoscopy of the oesophagus showed the typical features of corkscrew oesophagus (figure B). Although manometry might be necessary to diagnose corkscrew oesophagus, we did not recommend this to our patient because his corkscrew oesophagus had been diagnosed, without any previous symptoms. In the future, our patient will need to be treated with drugs such as muscle relaxants and anxiolytic agents, in conjunction with either antireflux therapy or surgical myotomy. Currently, we only advise him not to consume cold fluids to prevent the development of symptoms.

A 35-year-old man presented to our department with palpitations and mild shortness of breath. He was of Haitian origin and had emigrated to the USA when he was 24 years old. A physical examination, an electrocardiogram (ECG), a full blood count, and a comprehensive metabolic profile showed no abnormalities. However, a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 3 cm?℅?2 cm echolucent lesion in the apex of the left ventricle (figure; video 1). The patient did not report having a fever or any other systemic problems, but he had been to Haiti 5 months earlier. A cardiac MRI showed a solitary, avascular lesion located in the anterior wall of the left ventricle (figure; video 2); this lesion had no communication with the left ventricular cavity and was non-fatty and cystic. No pericardial or valvular abnormalities were seen. A CT scan of the heart confirmed the lesion was cystic and without any calcification; the coronary arteries were normal and, importantly, were not compressed by the mass. CT scans and MRIs of the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no further cysts in any other organs. Serum serology by western blot testing for antibodies against specific IgG glycoproteins was negative for Echinococcus granulosus and Trypanosoma cruzi but positive for Taenia solium. The patient was then treated for 2 weeks with oral albendazole 400 mg twice a day. He reported no further symptoms and the lesion was no longer visible on a further transthoracic echocardiogram (figure; video 3) repeated 1 week after completing the treatment; a repeat cardiac MRI showed that the lesion had decreased considerably in size. Cysticercosis is endemic in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa and Asia. The disease can develop after consuming foods contaminated with faeces that contain T solium eggs shed from a human carrier. The brain, skeletal muscle, and subcutaneous tissue are involved most frequently; isolated cardiac cysticercosis is rare. The need for concomitant treatment with steroids〞particularly in neurocysticercosis〞has been much debated because of concerns about seizures and worsening neurological symptoms on the initiation of anthelmintic therapy. In cases of isolated cardiac cysticercosis, there is no consensus for the routine use of steroids. In our patient, given that there was only mild oedema around the solitary lesion, the ECG was normal, and because he was on a cardiac monitor in hospital when albendazole was started, we were able to keep him under observation. Furthermore, it is of note that in other inflammatory cardiac conditions〞such as pericarditis〞steroids have been linked to increased relapse and recurrence. The rapid response to anthelmintic therapy in this case〞reassuringly confirmed on repeat imaging〞shows that in select cases, such as this one, albendazole may be used without steroids, with close clinical and cardiac monitoring and serial imaging.

A 31-year-old woman reporting a headache and epigastric pain for the past 12 h attended our unit. She had a history of gestational hypertension and 5 days earlier had a caesarean section at term; there had been no post-partum haemorrhage and she had been allowed home. The patient's haemoglobin concentration had been 11﹞7 g/dL (normal >10 post partum), and the serum creatinine concentration 48 米mol/L (normal <90); she was normotensive and on no medication.On examination, we found the patient to be lethargic: her blood pressure was 193/102 mm Hg, and she had hyper-reflexia and bilateral clonus. A spot urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio was 57 mg/mol (normal <30), her haemoglobin concentration was 9﹞5 g/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 764 mIU/L (normal <600), alanine transaminase 127 IU/L (normal <70), and the serum creatinine concentration 115﹞0 米mol/L were raised: indicating possible post-partum pre-eclampsia with partial HELLP〞Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets〞syndrome and acute kidney injury.
We started the patient on fluids, and intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulphate. Over the next 24 h, she passed 10﹞9 L of clear urine despite a total fluid intake of 3﹞7 L. Laboratory investigations for polyuria (appendix) excluded osmotic diuresis and post-partum hypopituitarism; however, her urine osmolality was 228 mOsmol/kg (normal >600), suggestive of diabetes insipidus causing pure-water loss.
A water deprivation test showed an inability to concentrate urine fully: the plasma osmolality reached 301 mOsmol/kg〞maximum endogenous antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release occurs above the threshold of 295 mOsmol/kg〞and her urine osmolality failed to rise sufficiently (figure). A desmopressin test with a vasopressinase-resistant ADH analogue found urine osmolality increased by 13% to 426 mOsmol/kg (figure). We did not assess plasma ADH or copeptin levels because the polyuria resolved when liver function recovered. She was allowed home 4 days later; her blood pressure and urine were normal.
Taken together, the findings suggested a partial central diabetes insipidus (DI) due to a transient deficiency in ADH caused by an excess of vasopressinase resulting from impaired liver function because of the HELLP syndrome. The polyuria abated when the transaminitis resolved. Further, we believe the increase in urine concentration after desmopressin was small because of wash-out of the renal medullary concentrating gradient from water diuresis.
DI is characterised by a failure of the kidneys to conserve water due either to ADH deficiency (central DI) or resistance (nephrogenic DI) resulting in hypotonic polyuria. In pregnancy, DI occurs when the breakdown of ADH by placental vasopressinase is enhanced because of either increased production in multiple pregnancy or〞as in our patient〞decreased hepatic catabolism. Gestational DI commonly occurs in the third trimester, coinciding with peak placental vasopressinase synthesis, and rarely in the early post-partum period.
Given pre-eclampsia〞the most frequent cause of acute kidney injury in pregnancy〞typically results in oliguria, a good urine output in such patients may be falsely reassuring: if the urine output is above 3L per day and urine osmolality is less than 300 mOsmol/kg, gestational DI should be considered.
Finally, if gestational DI is missed, patients are at high risk of severe hypernatraemia resulting from the standard pre-eclampsia management of fluid restriction, and seizures, as the magnesium sulphate will be rapidly excreted. Therefore, in the context of polyuria, it might be necessary to increase fluids; the magnesium sulphate infusion rate might also need to be increased and levels monitored for toxicity (video).
output: Transient gestational diabetes insipidus secondary to HELLP syndrome

A 25-year-old woman came to the accident and emergency department with a 12-h history of sudden onset regurgitation and complete dysphagia. She had had gastric banding in 2008, for morbid obesity. A plain chest radiograph showed an abnormal appearance of the gastric band (figure). Normally, a gastric band appears as a single radio-opaque bar lying diagonally, at 40每50 degrees to the vertebral column. When a gastric band slips, part of the gastric fundus herniates through the band, initially causing the left side of the band to move caudally and subsequently forcing the anterior part of the band further caudally; an annular appearance of the band results (figure). On the basis of the history and this radiographic finding, the band was deflated in the emergency department, and the patient was given urgent laparoscopic band removal. With the increase in obesity surgery it is important to highlight such complications, as emergency deflation and band removal is necessary to prevent necrosis of the herniated stomach.

A 34-year-old woman who collapsed during a mountain trek in northern Spain was initially assessed at an emergency rescue centre. She was unresponsive, asystolic, and pulseless, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a tympanic temperature of 18～C. Advanced life support was started, and the woman was transferred to our hospital. She arrived 2 h and 25 min after the first evaluation〞she was still in asystole, had unreactive dilated pupils, and had a core temperature of 20﹞2～C. An arterial blood sample showed a pH of 6﹞81, a lactate concentration of 10﹞3 mmol/L (normal 0﹞5每1), and a potassium concentration of 4﹞4 mmol/L (normal 3﹞5每5). Peripheral venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) support was started and a fine ventricular fibrillation rhythm was immediately seen on an electrocardiogram (ECG). The patient also started gasping, ventilator asynchronies appeared, and a burst suppression pattern was seen on a bispectral index monitor; these difficulties disappeared after she was given sedatives.During the first few hours of extracorporeal support, the patient had coagulopathy, bleeding, lung oedema (figure), and a highly variable ECMO flow. However, once the woman was stable, her body temperature was progressively increased at a rate of 3～C per h. The patient regained pupillary reactivity after 3 h of extracorporeal support. When her temperature reached 30～C, coarse ventricular fibrillation was observed. She was then defibrillated, which resulted in a posterior effective rhythm〞meaning that 6 h and 10 min after the initial assessment there was return of spontaneous circulation. In 2012, an 84-year-old Chinese man presented with progressive, chronic left atraumatic knee pain and swelling. His medical history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis treated in China in 1951 and rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed in 2006. His joint pain progressed despite use of disease modifying drugs and steroid injections. Antitumor necrosis factor inhibitors were not used because of concerns of tuberculosis reactivation. Clinical examination showed he had antalgic gait, knee effusion, stiffness, and joint-line tenderness. Laboratory results included erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h and C-reactive protein of 205 mg/L. Radiographs showed severe tri-compartmental degenerative arthritis (figure A).The patient underwent total knee arthroplasty in August, 2012 (figure B). Extensive synovitis was noted and pathological examination showed granulomatous inflammation (figure C). Staining of synovial tissue for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis PCR were negative. The patient's knee symptoms initially improved, but 5 months after total knee arthroplasty he developed a draining sinus from the knee incision. He underwent irrigation and debridement of the knee with exchange of the polyethylene tibial insert. Initial synovial tissue fluid cultures were negative, but subsequent acid-fast bacilli cultures from synovial tissue and joint fluid grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Sputum cultures were negative for pulmonary tuberculosis. He started a course of antituberculosis therapy including rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for treatment of tuberculosis prosthetic joint infection in February, 2013. He was advised to undergo a two-stage resection-revision arthroplasty but declined further surgery and thus an implant retention strategy was pursued. The patient completed 12 months of antituberculosis therapy in February, 2014. He has since continued rifampicin and isoniazid treatment with a plan for long-term suppressive therapy in the setting of retained prosthesis. At his latest follow-up, 2 years after initial diagnosis of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection, the incision had healed without clinical sign of infection and his knee has a pain-free range of motion from 0每95～.
Tuberculous arthritis accounts for 1每5% of people with tuberculosis. Scarce data are available for optimum management of tuberculous prosthetic joint infection. This case illustrates an unusual reactivation of tuberculosis in an isolated extra-pulmonary site after joint replacement surgery. Prompt initiation of antituberculosis therapy might enable implant retention, although continuation of suppressive therapy might be needed. In the setting of globalisation and the increasing use of immunomodulatory therapies and joint replacement surgeries, this case illustrates the need for tuberculosis to be thought about early in the differential diagnosis for culture-negative prosthetic joint infection in patients with previous exposures or epidemiological risk factors.

A 25-year-old woman came to the accident and emergency department with a 12-h history of sudden onset regurgitation and complete dysphagia. She had had gastric banding in 2008, for morbid obesity. A plain chest radiograph showed an abnormal appearance of the gastric band (figure). Normally, a gastric band appears as a single radio-opaque bar lying diagonally, at 40每50 degrees to the vertebral column. When a gastric band slips, part of the gastric fundus herniates through the band, initially causing the left side of the band to move caudally and subsequently forcing the anterior part of the band further caudally; an annular appearance of the band results (figure). On the basis of the history and this radiographic finding, the band was deflated in the emergency department, and the patient was given urgent laparoscopic band removal. With the increase in obesity surgery it is important to highlight such complications, as emergency deflation and band removal is necessary to prevent necrosis of the herniated stomach.
output: Slipped gastric band (gastric band prolapse with herniation of the gastric fundus)

A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Investigations done before the operation showed total bilirubin was 6﹞4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 39 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 312 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 426 IU/L. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8﹞36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1?280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies〞namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver每kidney microsome antibodies〞were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes〞approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10每140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2﹞0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.
Sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis are mani-festations of IgG4-related disease, characterised by an abundance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in affected tissues. Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may〞as in our case〞have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

All pulses were palpable, and a sensory examination was normal; the lower part of her leg had a mottled, dusky appearance and a prolonged capillary refill time, and was cold to the touch.A full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12﹞9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 10﹞8?℅?109 per L, and a thrombocyte count of 235?℅?109 per L. Her international normalised ratio (INR) was 1﹞0, activated partial thromboplastin time was 25 s (normal 23每36), and fibrinogen concentration was 4﹞54 g/L (normal 2﹞0每4﹞3). A 68-year-old Polish man was admitted to our hospital because of continued, painless, and worsening jaundice, and malaise. 2 months earlier he had a Whipple's pancreaticoduodenectomy for suspected carcinoma of the pancreas. He initially presented with mild weight loss and pain in the epigastric area. He did not use alcohol above recommended limits and had not travelled abroad recently. On examination his skin and sclera were jaundiced, and he had excoriations on all four limbs and his torso. There was no ascites, oedema, lymphadenopathy, or orbitopathy. Investigations done before the operation showed total bilirubin was 6﹞4 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 62 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 39 IU/L, gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) 312 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) 426 IU/L. Serum tumour markers were within normal limits, and tests for hepatitis B and C were negative. A CT scan showed a mass in the head of the pancreas, normal liver parenchyma, and dilated extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and pancreatic duct proximally to the pancreatic head, and stricture of the pancreatic part of the common bile duct. Lymph nodes and abdominal vessels were normal.When we saw the patient, his total bilirubin (8﹞36 mg/dL), AST (89 IU/L), ALT (51 IU/L), GGT (443 IU/L), and ALP (712 IU/L) were increased. Antinuclear antibodies were detected at a titre of 1:1?280, with grainy fluorescence, but other antibodies〞namely, antimitochondrial antibodies, smooth muscle antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, or liver每kidney microsome antibodies〞were not found. An abdominal ultrasound scan showed dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, and stricture of the common bile duct. Magnetic resonance cholangio-pancreatography (MRCP) showed multiple strictures of the patient's bile ducts (figure). A percutaneous liver biopsy specimen showed mixed inflammatory infiltration surrounding neocholangioles, with IgG4 in plasmocytes〞approximately 60 per large field view, an IgG4:IgG ratio of more than 40%, mild fibrosis (grade 2 on the Batts-Ludwig scale), and cholestasis. The patient's serum IgG4 concentration was elevated at 380 mg/dL (normal 10每140). Looking at the presentation and the results in the round, we made a diagnosis of IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis.
We therefore started treatment with prednisone 40 mg once daily for 2 months, followed by azathioprine 2﹞0 mg/kg once a day. After 2 months, a repeat MRCP showed that the stenosis of the bile ducts had reduced (figure). Also, the patient's total bilirubin concentration and liver enzyme levels normalised, and his malaise improved.
A post-factum analysis of the head of the pancreas removed at the initial operation stained positively for IgG4, and a mixed inflammatory infiltration with IgG4 plasmocytes was seen.
Sclerosing cholangitis and pancreatitis are mani-festations of IgG4-related disease, characterised by an abundance of IgG4-positive plasma cells in affected tissues. Patients with IgG4-related disease are often misdiagnosed as having a malignancy because of the non-specific signs and pseudotumour-like lesions; they may〞as in our case〞have unnecessary surgical procedures and investigations. A full clinical assessment of any patient presenting with jaundice and a pancreatic mass must include measurement of IgG4 concentrations and a biopsy before surgeons put knife to skin.

A 27-year-old woman came to our hospital with increasing diffuse pain around the joints of her shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. She was well known to us because of her long history of problems due to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1〞with a mutation in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene.We first met her when she was 18 years old, after she was referred by her paediatrician for severe hypoparathyroidism, which was treated with alfacalcidol and calcium carbonate. The treatment resulted in the development of nephrocalcinosis at the age of 15 years. When she was 22 years old, she returned with a 3-month history of worsening dysphagia and vomiting because of achalasia and oesophageal candidiasis: she was unable to take her medication orally. She had also lost a substantial amount of weight〞at its nadir her body mass index was 15 kg/m2. She was admitted as an emergency with a total serum calcium concentration of 1﹞44 mmol/L (normal range 2﹞20每2﹞55) and prolonged QTc on her electrocardiogram. We started her on replacement therapy with subcutaneous recombinant human parathyroid hormone (rhPTH; 1每34) and colecalciferol. The dose of rhPTH (1每34) varied from 20 米g once to twice a day and hypocalcaemia was adequately controlled over 5﹞5 years〞mean albumin-adjusted serum calcium was 2﹞11 mmol/L.
The pain, she came to see us with, had developed after 3 years of treatment with the rhPTH (1每34) and had increased progressively. We first ruled out any inflammatory and autoimmune causes of the arthritis. Additional investigations showed that she had a low bone density of the distal radius (Z score SD ?3﹞0, normal score SD ?2) and increased markers of bone formation: alkaline phosphatase was 271 IU/L (normal range 42每98), osteocalcin was 87 ng/mL (normal range 2每12). A bone scan with whole-body early images showed precocious, intense bone uptake in the peripheral joints and in the axial skeleton, with no activity in the heart, kidneys, or bladder (figure). The images suggested that bone cells were being overstimulated by the rhPTH (1每34)〞appearing like so-called super bone scans seen in patients with hyperparathyroidism. The rhPTH (1每34) was discontinued and within 48 h the patient's joint pain stopped. However, she then developed a transient hypocalcaemia requiring high doses of intravenous and oral calcium with alfacalcidol; she had concomitantly low urinary calcium excretion, indicative of hungry bone syndrome. The bone scintigraphy returned to normal 1 year after the rhPTH (1每34) was stopped (figure).
In patients with hypoparathyroidism refractory to conventional treatment, rhPTH (1每34) therapy can effectively control hypocalcaemia, but whether it is safe in the long term is unclear. Further, abnormally increased metabolic activity of the bone may occur despite adequate calcaemic control, possibly due to the pharmacokinetics of the treatment. Bone scintigraphy〞including an early scan〞can be useful in detecting iatrogenic hyperparathyroidism in patients receiving either rhPTH (1每34) or rhPTH (1每84) treatment (video).

A 61-year-old woman came to our neurosurgery clinic complaining of spasms and episodic pain on the left side of her face; the spasms had been present for 20 years and the pain for 5 years. She said that initially the facial spasms affected only the corner of her left eye but over the years progressed to involve most of the muscles of the lower left side of her face. For the past 7 years, she had been given botulinum toxin injections twice per year, which had provided some relief. The pain, which developed alongside the spasms, was characterised by frequent episodes of excruciating, lancinating pain〞rated by the patient as very severe using a visual analogue pain scale〞along the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. The woman described several things〞including chewing, touching her face, and brushing her gums〞that clearly triggered the pain. Taking carbamazepine lessened the pain, but she stopped the drug because she could not tolerate the associated drowsiness. She never had any problems affecting the right side of her face. A neurological examination was normal, including intact corneal reflexes. She had no medical history of a stroke, transient ischaemic attack, or demyelinating disease.MRI of her brain showed a dolichoectatic left vertebral artery that indented and displaced both the facial and trigeminal nerves (figure). Considering the patient's symptoms and their development in the round, we made diagnoses of both hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia〞a combination known as painful tic convulsif. We carried out decompression of both nerves with a keyhole craniotomy, using a retrosigmoid approach (figure; appendix). Pleasingly, for both the patient and us, on waking up after the operation, she reported immediate and complete resolution of all her symptoms; at follow-up, 1 month later, she was still free of both the pain and the spasms.
Hemifacial spasm is a movement disorder affecting the muscles supplied by the facial nerve; in most cases it is caused by compression of the nerve root at the exit of the brainstem. In over 85% of patients, local injection with botulinum toxin results in easing of the symptoms. Trigeminal neuralgia is a rare, episodic facial pain that is unilateral. It may be mistaken for a dental problem because it usually affects the two lower branches of the trigeminal nerve: the maxillary and the mandibular. Microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve root is the most effective and long-lasting treatment.
Harvey Cushing first coined the phrase painful tic convulsif, in 1920, to describe the combination of the symptoms of hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia. The common source of our patient's two diagnoses shows that surgical microvascular decompression can be an effective and long-lasting treatment for either conditions〞presenting alone or together〞where medical treatments have failed.
output: Painful tic convulsif (combined hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia)

A 20-year-old man, who had a history of palpitations and syncope in early childhood〞from the age of 3 years to 7 years〞attended our clinic for a routine review. The patient had previously been seen by paediatric colleagues; he had a catheter ablation of an accessory atrioventricular pathway for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, aged 4 years. Over the intervening period of follow-up, a possible diagnosis of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy had been considered. Regarding his developmental history, the patient reported no difficulties; he had a good academic record and, at the time we saw him, was at university.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his height was 173 cm, weight 55 kg, heart rate 62 beats per min, blood pressure 115/74 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96%.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, with recurrence of ventricular pre-excitation, a PR interval of 90 ms (typical 120每200) and a delta wave. Laboratory investigations〞including high-sensitivity troponin T and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide〞were within typical range.
A cardiac MRI showed patches of intramyocardial fat which co-localised to areas with late gadolinium enhancement (figure 1). Furthermore, although more prominent in the left ventricle, fat was also detected in right ventricular para-septal structures and moderator band. Ventricular sizes, wall thickness, and systolic function were preserved, with no regional wall motion abnormalities even in the segments with abnormal tissue.
We reviewed the patient's paediatric records〞including previous cardiac MRIs. The first scan, aged 5 years, showed several ventricular masses suggestive of rhabdomyomas; scans over the next 15 years showed a progressive reduction in the size of the ventricular masses which co-localised to the regions detected by the late gadolinium enhancement, suggesting fibrofatty replacement (figure 2).
Sequencing of the TSC2 gene and TSC1-targeted analysis for deletions and duplications for suspected tuberous sclerosis complex found a variant of unknown significance in the TSC2 gene encoding for tuberin (c.2563+26G>A). Notably, the patient showed none of the extra-cardiac features of tuberous sclerosis complex〞including hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas, renal angiomylipomas, or brain tumours. However, the patient's father, who was found to have the same genetic variant as his son on the TSC2 gene, was noted to have hypomelanotic macules. Testing of the patient's DNA using an extensive genetic panel for both hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy was negative.
Considering the pattern and location of the fibrofatty replacement, and possible tuberous sclerosis complex, we concluded that the cardiac MRI findings were likely related to involuting rhabdomyomas. We explained the findings to the patient and advised treatment with 汕 blockers and continued follow-up with regular cardiac imaging.
Causes of myocardial fat include arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, chronic myocardial infarction, certain non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies〞such as dystrophinopathies, and rarely, inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy〞and tumours including lipomas and liposarcomas. Rhabdomyomas are the most common cardiac tumours in childhood, usually occurring in association with tuberous sclerosis complex; they may regress or even disappear or〞as we believe has occurred and is illustrated by the images in our patient〞present with intramyocardial fat foci in adults.

On examination, the left leg〞from the hip to the calf〞was markedly swollen, painful, and cyanotic, consistent with a diagnosis of phlegmasia cerulea dolens. All pulses were palpable, and a sensory examination was normal; the lower part of her leg had a mottled, dusky appearance and a prolonged capillary refill time, and was cold to the touch.A full blood count showed a haemoglobin concentration of 12﹞9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 10﹞8?℅?109 per L, and a thrombocyte count of 235?℅?109 per L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 32 mm/h (normal 0每27). The patient's C-reactive protein concentration was 29 mg/L (normal 0每1) and D-dimer concentration was 4﹞13 米g/mL (normal <0﹞5). Her international normalised ratio (INR) was 1﹞0, activated partial thromboplastin time was 25 s (normal 23每36), and fibrinogen concentration was 4﹞54 g/L (normal 2﹞0每4﹞3). Her serum electrolyte, urea, creatinine, and creatine kinase concentrations were all within the normal range.
An ultrasound scan of the patient's pelvis and upper leg showed deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the left common iliac vein that extended into the left common femoral vein. Other investigations including anti-thrombin, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, prothrombin variant, and factor V Leiden were negative.
Using catheter-directed thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator the DVT was dissolved. However, conventional angiography to confirm that the clot had dissolved showed a persistent narrowing of the left common iliac vein at the level of the right common iliac artery (figure). We decided against stenting the stenotic iliac vein because her signs and symptoms had resolved and there was angiographic evidence of good collateral venous circulation (figure). The patient was started on warfarin with a target INR of 2﹞0每3﹞0.
Some degree of compression of the left common iliac vein between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the right common iliac artery is found in 22% of cadavers. Rarely〞as may have happened in our patient〞engorged epidural veins, acting as collaterals, can cause low lumbar nerve root compression and back pain. Interestingly, the compressed left common iliac vein forms a barrier against clot passage, thereby affording the patient some protection against pulmonary embolism. Risk of a DVT is further increased by conditions that raise intra-abdominal or thoracic pressures, pregnancy, pelvic obstruction, right heart failure, prolonged periods of bed rest, standing or sitting, hypercoagulable states, injection of irritating drugs via a left leg cannula, and the presence of a foreign body (eg, a left femoral vein catheter).
