A 79-year-old man presented with symptoms and signs of upper respiratory tract infection; he had a history of permanent pacemaker implantation. An upright postero-anterior chest radiograph showed a raised right hemidiaphragm delineated by subdiaphragmatic air. Unlike free air, which forms an uninterrupted crescent-shaped subdiaphragmatic radiolucency, this radiograph showed a haustral pattern of subdiaphragmatic lucency (figure), overlapping the upper border of the liver shadow. On examination, clinical findings suggesting acute abdomen from rupture of a hollow viscus were absent and there was no recent history of abdominal surgery to account for the presence of subdiaphragmatic air. The visualisation of a gas filled transverse colon lumen interpositioned between the right hemidiaphragm and the liver on a chest film is called Chilaiditi's sign. A CT scan may confirm these anatomical relations. In our patient's radiograph, the haustral pattern of air was indicative of colonic origin, and the continuity of the subdiaphragmatic air was broken up by the shadow of the vertical plicae semilunares of the colon. Chilaiditi's sign was first described in 1910 by Demetrious Chilaiditi and it is an incidental radiographic finding. This sign can be mistaken for pneumoperitoneum and can lead to needless surgical intervention. Our patient was treated only for his upper respiratory tract infection.

A 61-year-old woman came to our neurosurgery clinic complaining of spasms and episodic pain on the left side of her face; the spasms had been present for 20 years and the pain for 5 years. She said that initially the facial spasms affected only the corner of her left eye but over the years progressed to involve most of the muscles of the lower left side of her face. For the past 7 years, she had been given botulinum toxin injections twice per year, which had provided some relief. The pain, which developed alongside the spasms, was characterised by frequent episodes of excruciating, lancinating pain〞rated by the patient as very severe using a visual analogue pain scale〞along the ophthalmic and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve. The woman described several things〞including chewing, touching her face, and brushing her gums〞that clearly triggered the pain. Taking carbamazepine lessened the pain, but she stopped the drug because she could not tolerate the associated drowsiness. She never had any problems affecting the right side of her face. A neurological examination was normal, including intact corneal reflexes. She had no medical history of a stroke, transient ischaemic attack, or demyelinating disease.MRI of her brain showed a dolichoectatic left vertebral artery that indented and displaced both the facial and trigeminal nerves (figure). Considering the patient's symptoms and their development in the round, we made diagnoses of both hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia〞a combination known as painful tic convulsif. We carried out decompression of both nerves with a keyhole craniotomy, using a retrosigmoid approach (figure; appendix). Pleasingly, for both the patient and us, on waking up after the operation, she reported immediate and complete resolution of all her symptoms; at follow-up, 1 month later, she was still free of both the pain and the spasms.
Hemifacial spasm is a movement disorder affecting the muscles supplied by the facial nerve; in most cases it is caused by compression of the nerve root at the exit of the brainstem. In over 85% of patients, local injection with botulinum toxin results in easing of the symptoms. Trigeminal neuralgia is a rare, episodic facial pain that is unilateral. It may be mistaken for a dental problem because it usually affects the two lower branches of the trigeminal nerve: the maxillary and the mandibular. Microvascular decompression of the trigeminal nerve root is the most effective and long-lasting treatment.
Harvey Cushing first coined the phrase painful tic convulsif, in 1920, to describe the combination of the symptoms of hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia. The common source of our patient's two diagnoses shows that surgical microvascular decompression can be an effective and long-lasting treatment for either conditions〞presenting alone or together〞where medical treatments have failed.
output: Painful tic convulsif (coexistent trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm due to vertebral artery compression)

A 20-year-old man, who had a history of palpitations and syncope in early childhood〞from the age of 3 years to 7 years〞attended our clinic for a routine review. The patient had previously been seen by paediatric colleagues; he had a catheter ablation of an accessory atrioventricular pathway for Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, aged 4 years. Over the intervening period of follow-up, a possible diagnosis of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy had been considered. Regarding his developmental history, the patient reported no difficulties; he had a good academic record and, at the time we saw him, was at university.
On examination, the patient was generally well; his height was 173 cm, weight 55 kg, heart rate 62 beats per min, blood pressure 115/74 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 96%.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, with recurrence of ventricular pre-excitation, a PR interval of 90 ms (typical 120每200) and a delta wave. Laboratory investigations〞including high-sensitivity troponin T and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide〞were within typical range.
A cardiac MRI showed patches of intramyocardial fat which co-localised to areas with late gadolinium enhancement (figure 1). Furthermore, although more prominent in the left ventricle, fat was also detected in right ventricular para-septal structures and moderator band. Ventricular sizes, wall thickness, and systolic function were preserved, with no regional wall motion abnormalities even in the segments with abnormal tissue.
We reviewed the patient's paediatric records〞including previous cardiac MRIs. The first scan, aged 5 years, showed several ventricular masses suggestive of rhabdomyomas; scans over the next 15 years showed a progressive reduction in the size of the ventricular masses which co-localised to the regions detected by the late gadolinium enhancement, suggesting fibrofatty replacement (figure 2).
Sequencing of the TSC2 gene and TSC1-targeted analysis for deletions and duplications for suspected tuberous sclerosis complex found a variant of unknown significance in the TSC2 gene encoding for tuberin (c.2563+26G>A). Notably, the patient showed none of the extra-cardiac features of tuberous sclerosis complex〞including hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas, renal angiomylipomas, or brain tumours. However, the patient's father, who was found to have the same genetic variant as his son on the TSC2 gene, was noted to have hypomelanotic macules. Testing of the patient's DNA using an extensive genetic panel for both hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy was negative.
Considering the pattern and location of the fibrofatty replacement, and possible tuberous sclerosis complex, we concluded that the cardiac MRI findings were likely related to involuting rhabdomyomas. We explained the findings to the patient and advised treatment with 汕 blockers and continued follow-up with regular cardiac imaging.
Causes of myocardial fat include arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, chronic myocardial infarction, certain non-ischaemic cardiomyopathies〞such as dystrophinopathies, and rarely, inflammatory dilated cardiomyopathy〞and tumours including lipomas and liposarcomas. Rhabdomyomas are the most common cardiac tumours in childhood, usually occurring in association with tuberous sclerosis complex; they may regress or even disappear or〞as we believe has occurred and is illustrated by the images in our patient〞present with intramyocardial fat foci in adults.

output: Involuting cardiac rhabdomyomas (tuberous sclerosis complex每associated) with fibrofatty replacement

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon〞who had not been involved in the original operation〞who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them〞suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure〞in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30每40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP〞as with our patient〞or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether〞in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology〞including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix〞in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

input: In March, 2010, a 53-year-old woman developed a black discolouration of her tongue. 4 weeks before developing the discolouration, she had had elective gynaecological surgery, from which she was recovering as an inpatient under our care. She did not smoke, but had a high intake of caffeinated drinks, including six cups of tea and two cups of coffee each day. During the course of her hospital stay she completed a 3-week course of amoxicillin clavulanate and metronidazole for a suspected postoperative pelvic infection. Tongue scrapings confirmed Candida infection, and we diagnosed our patient with lingua villosa nigra (black hairy tongue) caused by a Candida infection secondary to antibiotic use. Lingua villosa nigra is a condition that is often attributed to poor oral hygiene. It is characterised by hypertrophy and elongation of filiform papillae and lack of normal desquamation. The discolouration is thought to be due to secondary infection with porphyrin-producing chromogenic bacteria or yeast. It is more common in people chew tobacco, have caffeinated drinks, or have HIV infection. It is characteristically confined to the posterior two-thirds of the tongue, and generally causes no symptoms. Our patient was treated with a short course of fluconazole and her tongue returned to normal within 7 days.

A 37-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of recurrent episodes of flushing of the right side of her face after exercise and hot baths (figure). She explained that the flushing resolved after each episode following 1 h of rest. She reported no medical history.On examination, we found no abnormalities: specifically, the patient's nervous system〞including her cranial nerves〞was intact. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable〞including full blood count, liver and kidney function tests, electrolyte concentrations, thyroid function tests, tumour markers, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein concentration. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest, a carotid artery ultrasound, and enhanced MRIs of her head, neck, and cervical and thoracic spine, and cervicobrachial plexus were normal.
Considering the patient's symptoms and the absence of any pathology that might explain her presentation, we made a diagnosis of harlequin syndrome.
After an explanation of the diagnosis and reassurance of the patient, we decided not to offer her any treatment since she was not particularly troubled by the symptoms. At follow-up she reported that the flushing continued and that she was otherwise well.
Harlequin syndrome is characterised by unilateral facial flushing and sweating induced by exercise, heat, and emotion; most cases are idiopathic. However, a thorough examination and an extensive investigation are mandatory in order to rule out all known causes〞including a brainstem infarction, multiple sclerosis, syringomyelia, thyroid diseases, a superior mediastinum neurinoma, schwannoma at the lung apex, Pancoast tumour, and dissection of the internal carotid artery.
Unilateral disturbance of the sympathetic innervation of the face leading to an inability of the facial vasculature to dilate in response to normal stimuli is thought to be the cause of harlequin syndrome: a unilateral lack of flushing and sweating.
It should not be confused with Horner's syndrome〞a unilateral ptosis, reactive ipsilateral miosis, and hemifacial anhidrosis〞although they share similar lesion sites and some clinical manifestations. Most patients with harlequin syndrome〞as in our case〞do not require medical or surgical treatment unless, of course, there is an underlying disease (video).

Lingua villosa nigra is a condition that is often attributed to poor oral hygiene. It is characterised by hypertrophy and elongation of filiform papillae and lack of normal desquamation. It is more common in people chew tobacco, have caffeinated drinks, or have HIV infection. A 37-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of recurrent episodes of flushing of the right side of her face after exercise and hot baths (figure). She explained that the flushing resolved after each episode following 1 h of rest. She reported no medical history.On examination, we found no abnormalities: specifically, the patient's nervous system〞including her cranial nerves〞was intact. Routine laboratory investigations were unremarkable〞including full blood count, liver and kidney function tests, electrolyte concentrations, thyroid function tests, tumour markers, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein concentration. A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest, a carotid artery ultrasound, and enhanced MRIs of her head, neck, and cervical and thoracic spine, and cervicobrachial plexus were normal.
Considering the patient's symptoms and the absence of any pathology that might explain her presentation, we made a diagnosis of harlequin syndrome.
After an explanation of the diagnosis and reassurance of the patient, we decided not to offer her any treatment since she was not particularly troubled by the symptoms. At follow-up she reported that the flushing continued and that she was otherwise well.
Harlequin syndrome is characterised by unilateral facial flushing and sweating induced by exercise, heat, and emotion; most cases are idiopathic. However, a thorough examination and an extensive investigation are mandatory in order to rule out all known causes〞including a brainstem infarction, multiple sclerosis, syringomyelia, thyroid diseases, a superior mediastinum neurinoma, schwannoma at the lung apex, Pancoast tumour, and dissection of the internal carotid artery.
Unilateral disturbance of the sympathetic innervation of the face leading to an inability of the facial vasculature to dilate in response to normal stimuli is thought to be the cause of harlequin syndrome: a unilateral lack of flushing and sweating.
It should not be confused with Horner's syndrome〞a unilateral ptosis, reactive ipsilateral miosis, and hemifacial anhidrosis〞although they share similar lesion sites and some clinical manifestations. Most patients with harlequin syndrome〞as in our case〞do not require medical or surgical treatment unless, of course, there is an underlying disease (video).

A 51-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic complaining of repeated bouts of pain in his left groin. He said he had a lump that appeared intermittently in the area, and because of this, he regularly wore firm underwear. In his medical history, it was noted that 9 years earlier he had undergone an open flat mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. 14 months later, however, the problem had recurred; at this stage, he was managed by a different surgeon〞who had not been involved in the original operation〞who did a further open mesh repair. The second repair was also unsuccessful and the hernia recurred. 9 months later, the patient had another operation to repair the problem: this time, another surgeon did a laparoscopic total extraperitoneal (TEP) repair. Unfortunately, this too was unsuccessful, and the patient's problem recurred 3 months later. At this stage, the patient said he had lost hope in the possibility of his problem being resolved and he decided not to seek further help for some time.On clinical examination, two oblique scars were visible in the left groin area and there was also a palpable ridge above them〞suggestive of the mesh used in the previous laparoscopic inguinal repair. We found no evidence of a further hernia despite the patient repeatedly pointing out that the area of the medial groin below the scars was the source of his symptoms.
Given the rather complex history, we decided we needed to do an MRI of the groin while the patient was repeatedly putting the area under strain by increasing his intra-abdominal pressure〞in a similar way that coughing, bending over, or lifting a heavy object does. This showed a femoral hernia that contained omentum (figure). We decided to repair the hernia by using a prosthetic mesh plug through an infrainguinal approach to avoid the previously scarred areas. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient was free of symptoms and the problem had not recurred.
A femoral hernia is a protrusion of a peritoneal sac through the femoral ring or canal below the inguinal ligament. It is relatively uncommon in men but more frequent in women. About 5000 femoral hernia repairs are done in the UK each year; 30每40% of cases present acutely with an associated ten-fold increase in risk of mortality. By contrast with a femoral hernia, an inguinal hernia is essentially a defect due to weak connective tissue. As traditional sutured repairs are associated with high recurrence rates, the repair of both femoral and inguinal hernias is often augmented with synthetic prosthetic mesh by using either an open or laparoscopic (colloquially called a keyhole) technique. Laparoscopic approaches include a TEP〞as with our patient〞or a transabdominal preperitoneal repair. The ideal approach to a successful outcome is dependent on the patient's fitness, informed consent, and the surgeon's skill.
The key message here is that patients presenting with a history suggestive of an earlier recurrence of an inguinal hernia might actually have another problem altogether〞in our patient's case, a primary femoral hernia. We believe that ultrasound scans are unreliable in the assessment of such cases, especially when the groin area is disfigured. And we would suggest that an MRI, done with provocation or straining to increase pressure in the affected area during scanning, can be very useful. Furthermore, additional pathology〞including indurated lymph nodes, lobulated lipomas, and saphena varix〞in the absence of classic diagnostic clinical signs, may be detected.

A 14-year-old boy with early-onset guttate psoriasis vulgaris presented at our clinic with several reddish-purple, horizontal streaks on the distal part of his shins. Previously, he had been treated with narrow-band ultraviolet B, topical corticosteroids ranging from mild (hydrocortisone 17-butyrate cream 1 mg/g) to moderate (mometasone furoate cream 1 mg/g and betamethasone valerate ointment 1 mg/g), and tacrolimus ointment 1 mg/g〞but the response to treatment was not long lasting. The family consulted a licensed practitioner of traditional Chinese medicine who prescribed a so-called herbal cream (figure). The patient applied the cream topically on the psoriatic lesions twice a day. After 9 months of doing this, he developed a new rash on his shins that was later confirmed to be striae distensae (figure). We suspected that the cause was exposure to a corticosteroid〞but the patient had not been using a corticosteroid either topically or systemically during this time. The so-called herbal cream was suspected as a possible source; however, the content label only listed herbal ingredients including Chinese sumac, Sophora flavescens, Stemona tuberosa Lour. Nevertheless, the location of the striae was very unusual, and as a simple test, the herbal cream was applied on the upper arm of the senior physician; after 12 h, a strong vasoconstriction effect was seen (figure), which further raised our suspicion that the cream contained a corticosteroid. We therefore sent it for analysis at the Department of Official Medicines Control Laboratory, Swedish Medical Products Agency, Uppsala, Sweden. The laboratory used liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry and nuclear magnetic resonance, and reported that the cream contained both a potent corticosteroid (0﹞065% clobetasol propionate) and the antifungals ketoconazole and miconazole. We then reported this herbal product to the Danish Medicines Agency to ensure that it was dealt with appropriately.Prolonged exposure to traditional herbal creams or ointments resulting in cutaneous striae has previously been reported, and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has warned about a so-called natural Chinese herbal remedy〞Yiganerjing Cream〞containing the same ingredients as in our case. Furthermore, the hazards and adverse effects of herbal products are not confined to dermatology. The under-regulation of medicinal products is widespread, and the consequences of patients using such substances can be seen in clinics from all specialities. Patients who fail to respond adequately to conventional treatments often seek alternative treatment and as a result might expose themselves to potentially harmful agents. The importance of being vigilant when seeing patients taking and using herbal creams and remedies remains key to reaching the correct diagnosis. With such substances being freely available over the internet, the problem is likely to worsen.
output: Contact dermatitis and striae distensae secondary to undeclared corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate) in a traditional Chinese herbal cream

A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16﹞9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4每16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.
output: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome) with esophageal web

A 61-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 5-day history of sudden-onset, persistent myocloni in his left leg and the left side of his abdomen. Previously, the patient had been fit and well. He reported no recent fever, headache, or trauma.
14 months before admission, the patient had an allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for acute myeloid leukaemia with mutated nucleophosmin 1 which resulted in full remission.
On examination, we found the patient generally well; he had painless, rhythmic myocloni, with a frequency of 0﹞5每1﹞0 per s, of the proximal left leg and abdomen. The movements were continuous and would not be triggered or suppressed by any specific movements. The patient had no other atypical findings and cognitively was fully alert and conscious.
Laboratory investigations〞apart from a previously described macrocytosis〞were within typical range.
On day 1 after admission, an MRI of the patient's brain showed multiple cortico-subcortical fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery hyperintense lesions without diffusion restrictions or contrast-enhancement (figure).On day 2 after admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analyses showed normal cell and protein count; microbial multiplex PCR testing and cytology tests for malignancies were negative.
On day 3, a scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) showed no epileptiform discharges that correlated with the myocloni. Further investigations found no neoplasms.
On day 5, the myocloni extended to the proximal part of the left arm despite the patient being given multiple antiseizure medications.
On day 8 after admission, a biopsy of the brain was done and histopathological analysis of a sample of the biopsy showed T-cell-dominated perivascular lymphocyte infiltrates and endothelial proliferations without evidence of viral infection, demyelination, graft-versus-host disease, or neoplasia.
From day 9 after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated; he became disorientated and confused, then drowsy and stuporous; the myocloni continued.
Repeated MRIs, from days 5 to 12 after admission, showed progression of the multiple cortico-subcortical lesions (figure); the EEG showed right-hemispheric temporo-parietal focal slowing independent of the worsening of the patient's condition.
On day 15 after admission, he developed electroclinical super-refractory status epilepticus, which was finally terminated by continuous intravenous thiopental. At this stage autoimmune encephalitis was suspected and immunosuppressive treatment with prednisolone, plasmapheresis, intravenous immunoglobulins, and rituximab started; serum and CSF〞collected prior to initiation of the treatments〞was subsequently found to be positive for GABAA receptor antibodies (serum titre 1:320; normal <1:20; CSF titre 1:1), confirming the diagnosis of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis.
On day 33 and day 185, MRIs showed improvement (figure) with concomitant decreases in serum antibody titres (day 79, 1:20; day 186, <1:20) and serum neurofilament light chain concentrations〞day 34, 511﹞5 pg/mL (99﹞995 percentile); day 233, 25﹞4 pg/mL (97﹞20 percentile).
During the period of hospitalisation, the patient experienced multiple complications, including asystole, which required resuscitation, and critical-illness poly-neuromyopathy. After a prolonged stay in the intensive care unit, the patient was transferred to a neurorehabilitation unit.
At outpatient follow-up, the patient was ambulatory and had mild, residual paresis of his left leg (video); his neurological deficits continued to improve.
Autoantibodies against GABAA receptor cause an encephalitis characterised by seizures, cognitive impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and movement disorders. Underlying pathogenic mechanisms are, in most cases, unclear; associations between haematological malignancies and allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplants〞as in our case〞causing immune dysregulation may indicate possible aetiologies. Studies have reported a range of 9 to 43 months from completion of allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant to the development of GABAA receptor encephalitis.
Typical MRI changes, in conjunction with the patient's history and symptoms, should prompt consideration of anti-GABAA receptor encephalitis; confirmatory autoantibody results〞often available only after a significant length of time〞should not delay treatment initiation.

A 65-year-old man attended our hospital with a 15-day history of fever, fatigue, and anorexia. He had been seen at his local hospital before coming to us and had been given a variety of different anti-infective agents and antipyretic drugs to no avail. The patient was previously fit and well. He lived in the rural Henan province, China, and gave no history of recent travel.On examination, apart from an enlarged spleen〞measuring on ultrasound 70 mm thick and 175 mm long〞and a temperature of 39﹞6～C, we found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed decreased white blood cell count of 2﹞15?℅?109 per L (normal 3﹞5每9﹞5), red blood cell count of 3﹞75?℅?1012 per L (normal 4﹞3每5﹞8), haemoglobin concentration of 9﹞95 g/dL, platelet count of 78?℅?109 per L (normal 125每350), absolute neutrophil count of 1﹞57?℅?109 per L (normal 1﹞8每6﹞3), albumin concentration of 31﹞6 g/L (normal 35每55), and HDL concentration 0﹞55 mmol/L (normal >0﹞91). The patient's triglyceride (1﹞83 mmol/L; normal 1﹞7), D-dimer (37﹞58 mg/L; normal 0每0﹞55), procalcitonin (0﹞455 ng/mL; normal 0每0﹞046), ferritin (2508﹞5 ng/mL; normal 30每400), and 1,3-汕-D-glucan (166﹞50 pg/mL; normal 0每100) levels were raised.
The patient's globulin (27﹞0 g/L; normal 20每35), fibrinogen (2﹞75 g/L; normal 2每4), and aspergillus-antigen test for serum galactomannan (0﹞27 米g/L; normal 0每0﹞85) were in the normal ranges. The T-SPOT.TB (Oxford Immunotec, Oxford, UK) test was negative. Tests for HIV and tumour markers were negative; blood and bone marrow cultures were also both negative.
On day 2 of the admission, we did a bone marrow aspiration; marrow cytology showed an extremely low myelodysplasia and several haemophagocytic cells.
Our working diagnoses at this stage included malignant lymphoma, haemophagocytic syndrome, or an unidentified infectious disease. We decided to treat the patient with intravenous penciclovir, biapenem, and oral voriconazole, but his condition did not improve.
On day 5 of the admission, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS; Illumina NextSeq 550, San Diego, CA, USA) was done and 1791 sequence readings of both Leishmania infantum and Leishmania donovani were detected in peripheral blood within 24 h〞accounting for 0﹞671% of genome coverage. We then did a rK39 test (InBios International, Seattle, WA, USA) which was positive.
A second bone marrow aspiration showed the Leishmania spp amastigotes (figure)〞confirming the mNGS result. The patient was diagnosed as having visceral leishmaniasis and started on intravenous amphotericin B at a dose of 50 mg daily. After 8 days of treatment, the patient's fever had remitted; mNGS was repeated〞this time using peripheral blood〞showing 1226 sequence readings of L infantum and L donovani. After leaving hospital, he was further treated with sodium stibogluconate intramuscularly at a dose of 1﹞9 g daily for 10 days. At follow-up 1 month later, the fever, fatigue, and anorexia had fully resolved. As an emerging method of pathogen-detection, mNGS〞also known as shotgun sequencing〞is an unbiased and hypothesis-free way of diagnosing a variety of different organisms simultaneously and rapidly. It may be particularly useful when the organism is difficult to culture and where〞as in the case of leishmaniasis〞detection sensitivity depends upon the tissue (video).

A 27-year-old woman presented to our department for evaluation and treatment of dysphagia with recently diagnosed oesophageal stenosis. The patient had progressive difficulty in swallowing during the previous 2 years, first with solids then with liquids. The medical history showed that the patient was admitted to our clinic 5 months earlier for fatigue and she was diagnosed with severe iron deficiency anaemia. 2 months before presenting to our department, the patient underwent an oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), which revealed a 3-mm marked narrowing due to an eccentric oesophageal web 14 cm from the incisors preventing passage of either an adult or a paediatric endoscope (figure A). Biopsies taken from the oesophageal web showed that the mucosa had no substantial alterations. Physical examination showed that the patient was emaciated (BMI 16﹞9 kg/m2) and had bilateral angular cheilitis and koilonychia (ie, spoon-shaped nails). We completed the evaluation with a barium swallow (figure B) and a CT of the neck to assess the extent of the stenosis and to exclude extraluminal process. The examinations showed a focal stenosis in the upper oesophagus at the C6 level, without signs of malignancy. The EGD and the barium swallow findings with the history of severe iron deficiency anaemia led to a final diagnosis of an oesophageal web associated with Plummer-Vinson syndrome. The oesophageal web was managed by oesophageal dilation, which was done gradually multiple times over 6 weeks with a through-the-scope balloon to 18 mm in diameter (figure C). The patient reported complete resolution of dysphagia symptoms and is planned for regular surveillance of malignant transformation of the hypopharynx or the upper oesophagus with upper endoscopy.Plummer-Vinson syndrome, also known as Paterson-Brown Kelly syndrome, is a rare condition characterised by the triad of dysphagia, iron deficiency anaemia, and proximal oesophageal webs. The majority of reported cases (90%) are middle-aged female individuals. Although the exact pathogenesis of this condition is not fully understood, iron deficiency anaemia represents the most accepted hypothesis. Iron deficiency is postulated to especially affect the epithelial cells of the gastrointestinal tract due to their rapid turnover. Low iron concentrations lead to reduction in the activity of iron-dependent oxidative enzymes, which is speculated to cause mucosal atrophy and degeneration, eventually leading to the development of oesophageal webs after repeated injury. Although mucosal changes probably occur throughout the oesophagus, the postcricoid region incurs the most damage during the swallowing of solid food due to its restrictive skeletal surroundings, and is thus more susceptible to web formation. Barium swallow and EGD have high sensitivity to detect oesophageal webs. Many patients with mild dysphagia might have improved swallowing function through iron therapy alone, which restores impaired oesophageal contraction and the integrity of the oesophageal mucosa. However, long-standing dysphagia is unlikely to respond to iron therapy, necessitating the use of endoscopic oesophageal dilation. The recognition of this syndrome is crucial as it signifies a precancerous condition, with an estimated 4每16% increased risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the postcricoid pharynx and the upper oesophageal region. Annual EGD is recommended for the early detection of prematurely malignant transformation.

An ECG was obtained on arrival, at which time the patient reported no chest pain. Which of the following is the most likely site of the culprit lesion?
output:
Looking at these two ECGs, I can analyze the changes between the baseline state (left) and during/after ischemia (right).

The right ECG shows:
- Marked ST elevation in leads V1-V4 (anterior/septal leads)
- Deep, symmetric T wave inversions in the precordial leads
- ST depression in inferior leads

The left ECG (when patient was pain-free) shows:
- Deep symmetric T wave inversions in V1-V4 (Wellens' pattern - Type A/Type 2)
- These biphasic/deeply inverted T waves in the anterior leads during pain-free intervals are characteristic of critical stenosis

The pattern of ST elevation in V1-V4 during symptoms with Wellens' type T wave changes during pain-free intervals is highly specific for a critical stenosis of the **proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery**.

**Proximal left anterior descending coronary artery stenosis**

A 33-year-old homeless woman presented to the emergency room in September, 2012, with 2 days of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fever, and 1 week of pruritic rash. On examination she had a temperature of 41﹞0～C, blood pressure of 98/65 mm Hg, heart rate of 85 bpm, respiratory rate of 16 bpm, and O2 saturation of 47% on room air. She had a diffuse papular rash with vesicles of different ages with haemorrhagic crust affecting the trunk, extremities, face, and scalp, but sparing the palms and soles (figure). She had normal mental status, cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examination. Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral airspace opacities.
Within a few hours of presentation she suddenly became confused, with flaccid paralysis necessitating intubation and admission to the medical intensive care unit. Electroencephalogram showed non-convulsive status epilepticus. MRI brain showed multiple foci of punctate microhaemorrhages throughout the corpus callosum, both temporal lobes, and left posterior cingulate gyrus, consistent with infectious haemorrhagic encephalitis (figure). HIV testing was positive, with CD4 count 4 cells/米L (normal 348每1456 cells/米L), and viral load was 66?000 copies/mL (normal < 50 copies/mL). A skin biopsy sample stained positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV), but negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV).
Zoster-associated encephalitis from disseminated VZV can develop within days of the disseminated rash, and should be strongly suspected in immunosuppressed patients. Characteristic signs of zoster-associated encephalitis include acute delirium, typical signs of stroke such as headache with acute hemiplegia, aphasia, ataxia, hemisensory loss, or visual changes, dependent on the predominant location of the VZV vasculitis. Intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 h for 7每10 days should be started early if there is clinical suspicion of encephalitis.
Our patient was given intravenous aciclovir and multiple antiepileptic drugs to control her seizures. We treated her for VZV pneumonia, aspergillus pneumonia, propofol-induced pancreatitis, Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, and critical illness myopathy. After stabilisation in hospital she was started on antiretrovirals and pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis. After 2 months of rehabilitation she could walk independently and communicate without difficulty. At last follow-up in March, 2014, she had made a near full recovery in terms of her cognitive and motor function.
output: Disseminated varicella-zoster virus infection with hemorrhagic encephalitis (zoster-associated encephalitis) in advanced HIV/AIDS

A 33-year-old homeless woman presented to the emergency room in September, 2012, with 2 days of dry cough, dyspnoea, and fever, and 1 week of pruritic rash. She had a diffuse papular rash with vesicles of different ages with haemorrhagic crust affecting the trunk, extremities, face, and scalp, but sparing the palms and soles (figure). She had normal mental status, cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examination. Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral airspace opacities.

In March, 2020, a 59-year-old man presented to Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, Madrid, Spain, with a 15-day history of fever, headache, leg myalgia, and weight loss (4 kg). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. Initial diagnostic workup showed an increased concentration of C-reactive protein (16 mg/dL) and lymphopenia (700 lymphocytes per 米L). The patient was discharged and scheduled for a follow-up 3 weeks later. At 7 days after discharge, the fever and headache recurred. The patient was readmitted to the hospital and a PET scan was done, which showed an increase in metabolic activity on the vascular walls of small and medium vessels. A 38-year-old primigravid woman presented to our hospital at 31 weeks of gestation with severe abdominal pain. She had no uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or trauma. She was hypotensive, her abdomen was peritonitic and a fetal heart rate tracing showed fetal distress with bradycardia (60 beats per min [normal range 110每160 beats per min]). We performed a laparotomy within minutes of admission, which revealed that the uterus had split open along its entire length, as well as 1﹞5 L of haemoperitoneum. We delivered the baby, repaired the rupture, and transfused blood products to prevent consumptive coagulopathy in the mother. Unfortunately, the neonate's Apgar scores were 2 points at 1 min and 4 points at 5 mins, and blood gases within the umbilical cord showed severe metabolic acidosis (pH 6﹞84, bicarbonate 10﹞5 mmol/L, partial CO2 pressure 61﹞6 mm Hg, base excess ?23 mmol/L). He died despite resuscitation.As obstetricians, we were perturbed; a spontaneous uterine rupture before the onset of labour in women without a caesarean scar or myomectomy scar is extremely uncommon. However, when we examined our patient following the surgery, we noticed a unilateral Z thumb deformity of her left hand, which we confirmed on x-ray, and thin skin with multiple haemosiderin scars on her left foot (figure). We learned that she had a history of easy bruising in childhood and had sustained an open ankle fracture 6 years earlier while skipping, with rupture of the anterior talofibular ligament, peroneous tertius, and extensor digitorum brevis muscle tendons. Following orthopaedic surgery, she consulted three specialists, all of whom felt that the probability of a connective tissue disorder was low and that she did not require further investigation, given that she had no skin elasticity and her Beighton score was only 2 points.
However, considering the history of unprovoked uterine rupture, the low energy mechanism of the ankle injury, and our clinical findings, we reasoned that her a priori risk of connective tissue disorder was high. Therefore, with the patient's consent, we proceeded with genetic tests using next-generation sequencing of whole blood. The results confirmed a pathogenic, heterozygous variant (c.951+5G↙A [p.Gly300_Ala317del]) in the COL3A1 gene, consistent with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. This variant disrupts a splice donor site shown to cause exon skipping and in-frame deletion within the collagen helical domain. Subsequent echocardiography and whole-body magnetic resonance angiography of the patient excluded valvular disease, aortic root dilation, and vascular aneurysms (figure).
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder arising from deleterious missense, splicing, and haploinsufficiency variations in the COL3A1 gene, affects the synthesis of type III collagen, the foundation of the connective tissue in hollow viscera (eg, uterus), vessels, and skin. The physical features are subtle and the Beighton score (which includes the large joints in its calculation) can be misleadingly normal, given that large joint hypermobility and hyperextensibility of the skin〞characteristic of the more common forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome〞are unusual in the vascular form of the disease.
A history of recurrent, atraumatic bruising with haemosiderin pigmentation of the skin (as seen in our patient) suggests pathological soft-tissue fragility and should prompt genetic testing to avoid missing the diagnosis. Pregnant women are especially vulnerable, given that catastrophic complications from peripartum arterial and uterine rupture occur in 5% of women with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Adverse obstetric outcomes are potentially preventable through pre-pregnancy genetic counselling and targeted antenatal surveillance, but only if the syndrome is suspected sooner.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough〞her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3﹞8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4﹞5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced〞especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified〞notably vitamin E was 3 米mol/L (normal range 10每20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis〞cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders〞including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy〞where our patient was born〞screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.

A 38-year-old primigravid woman presented to our hospital at 31 weeks of gestation with severe abdominal pain. She had no uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or trauma. A 57-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease from type 2 diabetes was assessed at our specialist unit for a kidney transplant to be donated by his brother. The patient was unsensitised and blood group O; his 59-year-old brother was the same blood type and two-haplotype HLA-matched. Both the patient and his brother were enrolled into our immunological tolerance protocol, which combines a haematopoietic stem-cell transplant with a kidney transplant with the goal of inducing sustained mixed chimerism〞a state where the recipient's haematopoietic system has a mixture of both host and donor cells.Notably, the requirements for tacrolimus withdrawal include a stable mixed chimerism of greater than 5% of donor cells, no evidence of rejection on a series of renal biopsies, and no evidence of graft-versus-host disease.
Initially, the donor's haematopoietic stem cells were mobilised using granulocyte colony-stimulating factor. Peripheral blood apheresis was then done, and CD34+ and CD3+ cell products were isolated and cryopreserved.
On day 0, we did a left-sided donor nephrectomy and kidney transplant; the recipient was immediately started on tacrolimus and prednisone.
On day 1, the donor was allowed home and the recipient underwent conditioning with total lymphoid irradiation and an intravenous infusion of rabbit anti-thymocyte globulins.
On day 5, the recipient was allowed home; his urine output at that stage was 3﹞4 L per 24 h (normal >30每50 cc/kg per day) and his serum creatinine concentration was 0﹞89 mg/dL (normal 0﹞74每1﹞35).
On day 11, the prednisone tapering off was complete.
On day 12, donor CD34+ and CD3+ cell products and haematopoietic stem cells were infused, and mycophenolate mofetil was started and continued for one month.
At 3 months, repeated tests for levels of donor chimerism were sent to guide the tapering and withdrawal of the immunosuppression.
The tacrolimus tapering schedule continued until it was finally stopped at one year, at which point the recipient had a sustained mixed chimerism of 7% donor cells and stable renal function with a serum creatinine concentration of 0﹞87 mg/dL: we were able to pronounce the patient immunosuppression-free (figure; appendix).
2 months after stopping all immunosuppressive therapy, the patient was well and his kidney function remained stable.
Immune tolerance induction for patients undergoing kidney transplant offers the potential to mitigate the deleterious effects of long-term immunosuppression〞including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, diabetes, and nephrotoxicity〞for well selected patients. A 75-year-old man with suspected scleral thinning was referred to our ophthalmology clinic. The patient had visited his ophthalmologist in private practice reporting a 10-month history of bilateral, pigmented changes in his sclera.
The patient had a history of severe arthrosis involving several of his joints〞including both his shoulders, spine, and both knees and hips〞starting in his 60s; he had bilateral total knee endoprostheses of his left knee, aged 70 years, and aged 73 years of the right. He also had physiotherapy treatment. A report when the patient, aged 70 years, had the total knee replacement of his left knee described a deep black discolouration of the cartilage, menisci, and quadriceps tendon.
Additionally, he reported a previous Achilles tendon rupture, dilatative and obliterative arteriopathies〞including an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm, which was diagnosed incidentally, resulting in an infrarenal aortic prosthesis at aged 73 years. Also, aged 73 years, the patient was diagnosed with coronary artery sclerosis which did not require treatment; he was found to have peripheral arterial disease. Finally, the patient had prostate stones aged 73 years which were diagnosed after he reported difficulties with micturition; he had a transurethral resection of his prostate.
On examination, the patient was generally well; ophthalmology examination found nasal and temporal dark scleral discoloration on both eyes (figure), with full visual acuity, unremarkable anterior and posterior segments, and normal scleral thicknesses on ultrasound biomicroscopy anterior to the horizontal recti muscles (0﹞53 mm; typical range 0﹞4每0﹞6 equatorial). Coincidentally, we found that both the patient's ear cartilages appeared dark (figure).
Considering the patient's medical history and our findings in the clinic, we suspected a diagnosis of alkaptonuria and referred him to the hospital's clinic for metabolic diseases.
A 24-h urine sample was collected and analysed at the clinic for metabolic diseases; homogentisic acid urine concentration was 9350 mmol/mol creatinine (normal range <30 mmol/mol creatinine). The patient was informed about the diagnosis; his three sons and grandchildren, who have also reported difficulties with their joints, were recommended to have diagnostic testing for alkaptonuria.
The patient was advised to adhere to a low protein diet and was referred to nutritional specialists; he was also referred to the angiology department for reassessment of his peripheral arterial disease. Finally, cost approval for treatment with nitisinone was requested, approved, and started 5 months later.
Alkaptonuria is a rare, autosomal recessive protein metabolism disorder with deficient homogentisate 1,2 dioxygenase, an enzyme that breaks down tyrosine coded for by the HGD gene. Ochronosis describes the accumulation process of homogentisic acid as pigmented deposits in connective tissues; large joints, the cardiovascular system〞including heart valves and the intima of vessels; the urogenital system, the skin, and the eyes may be affected, leading to tissue or organ dysfunction and significantly impacting the quality of life. Treatment requires multidisciplinary collaboration, which comprises pain management, physiotherapy, and treating secondary complications such as osteoporosis or osteoarthrosis. Nitisinone, a triketone herbicide〞approved for the treatment of inborn errors of tyrosine metabolism, such as hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1〞has been shown to decrease urinary and serum homogentisic acid levels and thus may offer a biochemical cure for alkaptonuria; adverse effects of nitisinone include keratopathy or more severe systemic effects such as porphyria, leukocytopenia, or thrombocytopenia.

A 4-month-old girl presented to our emergency department with a low-grade fever and a persistent cough〞her parents reported a daily productive cough and said the child's stools had become greenish and greasy in recent weeks. The infant was the second child of non-consanguineous parents, born full-term after an unremarkable pregnancy; birthweight was 3﹞8 kg and meconium was passed on the first day of life.Examination showed insufficient weight gain: the child's weight (4﹞5 kg) was less than the third percentile on the normal growth curve. On chest auscultation, we heard bilateral crackles. The infant's social interactions and axial tone were good. However, she had a continuous large amplitude action tremor involving all limbs and head (video); the tremor increased at the beginning of the movement and was enhanced by sudden acoustic stimuli. Spontaneous movements were reduced〞especially in the lower limbs. Antigravity limb movements were reduced: she could move her arms towards an object in front of her but was unable to reach it.
Laboratory investigations showed normal electrolytes, glucose concentration, and liver enzymes. A depletion of the fat-soluble vitamins was identified〞notably vitamin E was 3 米mol/L (normal range 10每20). An x-ray showed bronchovascular markings.
We conducted a sweat test and diagnosed cystic fibrosis, confirmed by genetic analysis〞cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene homozygous F508del mutation. We started the patient on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and polyvitamin supplementation. 1 week later, the patient's motor function had improved: spontaneous movements had increased, and the tremor had almost disappeared (figure). She could play with her hands and feet and grasp objects. 1 month later, her vitamin E blood concentration was in normal range and neurological examination was normal (video).
Vitamin E deficiency is associated with movement disorders〞including ataxia and tremor; neurological symptoms develop after severe and prolonged deficiency. Monitoring and supplementation of vitamin E in patients with cystic fibrosis means that neurological symptoms are rare. In Italy〞where our patient was born〞screening has been mandatory since 1992. The patient did have expanded newborn screening, but results were negative for all screened diseases: blood concentration of immunoreactive trypsinogen was 49 ng/mL (cutoff value 62). False negatives, while rare, can occur in patients with the more severe class III mutations.
Finally, infants with a history of persistent coughing, unwellness, and a tremor should raise suspicions of having cystic fibrosis〞even if all newborn screening tests are negative.

A 15-year-old girl presented with short stature; her height was 1﹞42 m (3 cm below third percentile) and her bodyweight was 41﹞8 kg (around 50th percentile). She had a round face and several subcutaneous nodules over her forehead, hands, and knees. She had hypoplasia of her fourth and fifth metacarpals bilaterally (figure). Serum calcium and parathormone concentrations were normal. Genetic testing showed that she was heterozygous for a non-sense mutation affecting GNAS, confirming the diagnosis of pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism. GNAS encodes the 汐-chain of the heterotrimeric G-protein Gs, which couples receptors for many hormones and neurotransmitters to activation of adenylyl cyclase. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is indicative of genomic imprinting. Patients who inherit the mutation from the paternal allele develop pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, whereas inheritance from the maternal allele leads to pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism and renal resistance to parathormone and hypocalcaemia. Brachydactyly is due to premature closure of the epiphyses in the metacarpals.
output: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy without hormone resistance)

input: A 46-year-old woman, with no contributory history, presented with a 7 month growth in her right hallux. Initially, she had noticed a dark discolouration of the distal aspect of the toe, followed by a gradual non-tender swelling and subsequent effacement of the nail (figure). Results of an initial biopsy suggested that it could be a brown tumour, which prompted further biochemical tests, the results of which revealed a parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentration of 154 ng/L and a serum calcium concentration of 2﹞67 mmol/L in the setting of normal renal function and vitamin D sufficiency. Her 24 h urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio did not fit the criteria for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. Results of parathyroid scintigraphy showed a right inferior parathyroid adenoma. A dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan of the distal radius revealed a bone mineral density of 0﹞471 g/cm2 (T score ?3﹞7; Z score ?3﹞1). After a right inferior parathyroidectomy and a disarticulation of the distal hallux, PTH fell to 23 ng/L and serum calcium to 2﹞0 mmol/L. Pathology confirmed the presence of a parathyroid adenoma and a brown tumour of the hallux.
output: Subungual brown tumor secondary to primary hyperparathyroidism

A 21-year-old man presented for evaluation of Cushing's syndrome. His medical history was notable for an incidental diagnosis of acrogigantism at the age of 18 years, when he presented for an unrelated illness. At that time, investigations showed hypersecretion of growth hormone (somatotropin), normal serum cortisol, and a 1﹞6?℅?1﹞8?℅?2﹞0 cm sellar-suprasellar mass without parasellar extension (appendix p 1). He underwent transnasal transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary lesion, after which biochemical remission was reached at the cost of panhypopituitarism, including central diabetes insipidus. Histopathological examination showed a densely granulated somatomammotrophic adenoma with positive immunostaining for growth hormone and prolactin and negative staining for adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The patient was prescribed replacement therapy with levothyroxine, prednisolone, injectable testosterone ester, and oral desmopressin. Repeat imaging 3 months after surgery showed a partial empty sella and a thin rim of pituitary tissue, suggesting complete resection of the pituitary lesion (appendix p 1). 6 months after surgery, features of hypercortisolism were evident, including prominent weight gain (about 40 kg), extensive broad purple and dehiscent striae, severe proximal myopathy, tinea corporis, and repeated episodes of hypokalaemic periodic paresis. Glucocorticoid replacement was therefore discontinued (6 months before the patient presented to us).Our clinical examination of this man, height 2﹞12 m, weight 163 kg, and BMI 36﹞3 kg/m2, showed several catabolic features of Cushing's syndrome and residual features of previous growth hormone excess (figure). Biochemical evaluation showed ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome (post-low-dose dexamethasone suppression test: serum cortisol 604﹞1 nmol/L [reference: <50 nmol/L]; plasma ACTH 29﹞5 pmol/L [reference: 1﹞5每13﹞9 pmol/L]). Biochemical remission of acromegaly was confirmed by low serum IGF1 and random growth hormone concentrations. Functional imaging with 68Ga-DOTANOC PET-CT scan showed a large pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour (NET) and multiple liver metastases (appendix p 2) and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (appendix p 3). Biopsy of liver nodules was suggestive of a grade I NET, with negative immunostaining for ACTH. Growth hormone-releasing hormone plasma concentration was normal (9 pg/mL [reference: 5每18 pg/mL]). A diagnosis of pituitary acrogigantism and ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome (secondary to metastatic pancreatic NET) was considered. Exome sequencing showed no mutations in MEN1, CDKN1B, PRKAR1A, AIP, SDH, or MAX. Considering the metastatic nature of his disease, the patient was prescribed depot, long-acting release intramuscular injections of somatostatin analogue (octreotide 30 mg per month). He developed clinical and biochemical hypocortisolism (0800 h serum cortisol: <13﹞7 nmol/L; plasma ACTH: <1﹞0 pmol/L) and started physiological glucocorticoid replacement. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia was resolved on the follow-up 68Ga-DOTANOC PET-CT scan (appendix p 3).
This case highlights a rare presentation of multiple endocrine tumours in a young man. The patient had two of the three classic multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1-associated tumours (ie, pituitary and pancreatic), satisfying the clinical definition of the disease, even with a wild-type MEN1. About 10每30% of patients with clinical multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 have no mutations on gene sequencing, although they might have large coding-region deletions or duplications in MEN1.
A possibility of inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes should be considered in young patients who develop two or more NETs simultaneously or sequentially. Because an excess of growth hormone and IGF1 is known to accelerate cortisol metabolism, the presentation of Cushing's syndrome can be delayed, as was evident in this case.
output: Cushing's syndrome secondary to ectopic ACTH-secreting metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor in a patient with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 phenotype

A 4-year-old boy in a collision with a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road was referred to our hospital from a peripheral clinic. The child had injuries to his left leg, left arm, chest, and head; there was no history of loss of consciousness.
On examination, the patient was distressed and fractious; his blood pressure was 90/65 mm Hg, pulse was 142 beats per min, and oxygen saturation was 89%; his injured leg and arm had been splinted. He was in pain and had difficulty breathing; his respiratory rate was 43 breaths per min; an intercostal drain, which did not appear to be working, had been inserted for a suspected haemothorax at the clinic. High-pitched bowel sounds were audible all over the left side of the patient's chest and an inward concavity of the anterior abdominal wall〞known as a scaphoid abdomen〞was seen; no tenderness was found on palpation of the abdomen.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 9﹞9 g/dL (normal range 9﹞5每14); serum sodium concentration was 138﹞5 mmol/L (normal range 136﹞0每145﹞0) and potassium concentration was 3﹞7 mmol/L (normal range 3﹞5每5﹞2).
Chest x-rays showed an opacity of the left hemithorax, loss of normal contour of the left hemidiaphragm, a large intrathoracic air fluid level, and contralateral tracheal deviation indicating the presence of abdominal viscera in the chest (figure). We made a diagnosis of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia. And because the patient showed both respiratory and haemodynamic compromise, he was supported by 2 L per min oxygen therapy delivered by face mask. He was given fentanyl and paracetamol, both intravenously, because of pain before being intubated in the operating theatre. An emergency thoracotomy was done through a posterolateral approach, during which we found a herniated stomach, spleen, and small bowel, and a central diaphragmatic rupture close to the pericardium and extending anteriorly. Additionally, owing to viability of the visceral contents, reduction and primary repair of the diaphragmatic rupture was done using a non-absorbable suture; he was transfused 150 mL of packed red blood cells intraoperatively.
The patient made a good recovery after the operation and stayed on the ward for a further 6 weeks for management of the femoral shaft fractures. The fractures of the left femur and left humerus were managed using skin traction and sling and swathe, respectively.
At 6 weeks, the child's respiratory and cardiovascular symptoms had abated and skin traction was discontinued and a cast applied for management of the femoral shaft fracture; the patient was then allowed home.
Traumatic diaphragmatic hernia is a rare complication of thoracoabdominal injury that is commonly incorrectly diagnosed yet it carries high mortality. Blunt traumatic diaphragmatic hernia occurs because of a sudden rise in intrabdominal pressure that causes a tear in the diaphragm, leading to the migration of intrabdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity; patients have varying degrees of respiratory and cardiovascular compromise.
The Carter's scheme categorises traumatic diaphragmatic hernia into acute, latent, and obstructive phases. In the acute phase the diagnosis is usually missed in up to 66% of cases due to associated abdominal and musculoskeletal injuries〞as happened in our patient; the latent phase comprises non-specific respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms due to herniation of contents in the chest; and finally, the obstructive phase, which is associated with bowel obstruction that may proceed to ischaemia and strangulation.
A CT scan is the gold standard method for diagnosing traumatic diaphragmatic hernia but is not commonly available in many trauma centres in low-resource settings; a chest x-ray is more routinely done. While laparoscopic repair remains the recommended method of treating patients with traumatic diaphragmatic hernia, open surgical repair with or without a mesh is an option in haemodynamically unstable patients and in a low-resource setting where expertise and laparoscopic services are often unavailable. Clinicians assessing patients after traumatic injury should have a high index of suspicion for diaphragmatic hernia with attention paid to radiographic and chest auscultation findings to avoid complications of delayed diagnosis.
Road traffic crashes are the leading cause of death of children and young adults aged 5每29 years with an estimated 1﹞19 million deaths each year, according to a recent WHO report. About 92% of these road-related fatalities occur in low-income and middle-income countries, for which African countries take the greatest burden due to the young population. Resulting morbidities and disabilities lead to an average 4每5% loss of gross domestic product due to loss of productivity of those killed or disabled.
Uganda〞according to WHO〞ranks among those countries with the highest traffic death rates at 29 deaths per 100?000 people compared to 24﹞1 deaths per 100?000 in the African region and globally to 18﹞1 deaths per 100?000 people.
According to the Uganda police annual traffic report, mortality from road crashes was as high as 19﹞4% (4806 deaths of 24?728 casualties of road traffic accidents) in 2023. Collisions with pedestrians〞as in our patient〞constitute 20% of all traffic crashes and 37% of all those pedestrians die.

A 58-year-old man was hospitalised in our intensive care unit for severe, acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by an influenza virus infection. After 31 days, he was gradually weaned off mechanical ventilation. However, on the day after extubation, he had to be reintubated because of further respiratory distress. Emergency intubation was performed after rapid sequence induction using the short-acting anaesthetic agent etomidate, intravenously, at a dose of 0﹞3 mg/kg, and the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, intravenously, at a dose of 1 mg/kg. Orotracheal intubation was done without any difficulty. However, immediately after intubation, a change was noted on the electrocardiogram (ECG) (figure) and the patient became pulseless. The ECG showed ventricular tachycardia, which developed into ventricular fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated along with medical treatments to reduce his serum potassium concentration, which was 9﹞6 mmol/L; 1 h after the cardiac arrest, the serum potassium returned to within the normal range at 3﹞3 mmol/L. Of note, our patient had no contraindications to the use of succinylcholine before the reintubation〞specifically, his serum potassium concentration was 3﹞5 mmol/L and he had no neurological signs or muscle weakness.Closer examination of the ECG clearly showed the effects of hyperkalaemia on the heart during the incident: initially, the PR interval was prolonged and the T waves were tented (figure), next the P waves were lost, ST segment changes were seen, and the QRS complexes were prolonged (figure), and finally the QRS complex widened in a sine-wave configuration (figure). Succinylcholine is the first line neuromuscular blocking agent for rapid sequence induction because it is fast-acting. It causes depolarisation of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) located in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) leading to the efflux of intracellular potassium into the plasma. In cases of muscle denervation, including patients who have been in intensive care for a prolonged period, AChRs are upregulated in both the NMJ and throughout the muscle membrane; immature forms of AChRs are also released. These immature receptors are more sensitive to agonists with depolarisation occurring at lower concentrations and lasting for a longer time with no desensitisation. Succinylcholine in such situations can lead to a massive efflux of potassium from muscles to the plasma, with life-threatening consequences.
In cases of severe hyperkalaemia, treatment should include intravenous calcium salt〞chloride or gluconate〞to raise the threshold potential and to stabilise the myocardium, and drugs that promote cellular potassium reuptake〞eg, insulin, sodium bicarbonate, and 汕2 agonists. This case serves as a reminder that succinylcholine should be used with caution in patients who have been in the intensive care unit for a prolonged period even without so-called intensive care unit acquired weakness.
output: Succinylcholine-induced severe hyperkalaemia with cardiac arrest

A 36-year-old man with a 6-month history of asthenia, impotence, loss of libido, polyuria, and polydipsia attended our department; he also reported needing to wake up twice at night to urinate and Raynaud's phenomenon. The patient had a medical history of minor anxiety episodes and was prescribed prazepam.
On examination, his weight was 69 kg, height 1﹞79 m with a BMI of 24﹞1 kg/m2; the patient stated he had recently lost 5 kg. Significant muscle atrophy and a reduction of body hair was noted; his pulse was 72 beats per min, blood pressure 124/77 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97%. He had noticeable lymphadenopathy of cervical and inguinal nodes. Neurological examination was normal〞he had no disturbance of his vision.
Laboratory investigations showed total testosterone concentration of 0﹞12 ng/mL (normal level >1﹞65) with follicle-stimulating hormone concentration 1﹞4 IU/L (normal 1﹞4每18﹞1), and luteinising hormone concentration below 0﹞07 mIU/L (normal 1﹞5每9﹞3). Plasma cortisol concentration was 125 nmol/L (normal >140), and adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was 31﹞7 ng/L (10﹞3每48﹞3). Free T4 concentration was low at 4﹞98 ng/L (normal 7﹞0-14﹞8), with thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1﹞36 mIU/L (0﹞35每4﹞94). A 24-h water balance test showed marked polyuria and polydipsia: with a recorded water intake 5?500 mL and a urine output of 4?000 mL. The plasma osmolality was raised at 294 mOsm/L and the urinary osmolality was low at 246 mOsmol/L; the haematocrit was 51﹞1%.
A T1-weighted with gadolinium contrast MRI of the hypophysis showed a 6 mm thickening of the pituitary stalk at the optic chiasm level; T2-weighted MRI showed a bulging and plump appearance of the gland (figure). An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan of the brain showed hypermetabolic activity in the pituitary region (figure). A chest CT scan showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with associated pulmonary micronodules. Analysis of fluid obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage indicated lymphocytic alveolitis. Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of a superficial lymph node showed epithelioid cell granulomatous lymphadenitis without necrosis. All microbiological cultures were negative.
Considering the findings in the round: androgen deficiency; adrenal insufficiency; central hypothyroidism〞likely responsible for the Raynaud's phenomenon; and diabetes insipidus〞indicated by the elevated plasma osmolality with haemoconcentration, which excluded potomania, corroborated by the low urinary osmolality, we diagnosed sarcoidosis involving both the pituitary gland and stalk. The patient was initiated on intramuscular testosterone (250 mg every 3 weeks), hydrocortisone (20 mg daily with an emergency dose of injectable 100 mg), thyroxine 75 米g per day, combined with infliximab, the intravenously administered anti-TNF antibody.
At 6-month follow-up, the patient's overall clinical condition had improved. However, laboratory investigations indicated significant persistent endocrine insufficiency〞central hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and androgen insufficiency still requiring replacement therapy. Furthermore, attempts to extend intervals between desmopressin doses led to recurrence of polyuria and polydipsia: indicating ongoing anterior and posterior pituitary insufficiency. A repeat MRI showed that the pituitary stalk had reduced to a maximum thickness of 1 mm, the anterior pituitary flattened against the sella floor, and arachnoidocele; the posterior pituitary maintained a normal hyperintensity and morphology, as seen originally when the patient presented.
Sarcoidosis is a chronic infiltrative and inflammatory condition that may involve any organ, with predilection for the lungs and lymph nodes. Pituitary gland involvement, though less common, has long been recognised by physicians and should be considered. Additionally, it is important to note that endocrine insufficiency is, in most cases, unresponsive to anti-inflammatory treatments〞as occurred in our patient.
Differential diagnoses for infiltrative or inflammatory processes affecting the pituitary gland include primary〞craniopharyngiomas〞and secondary tumours, infections including tuberculosis, IgG-4-related disease, in children Langerhans＊ cell histiocytosis, autoimmune hypophysitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sheehan syndrome, and conditions of iron overload.
