A 25-year-old man attended his primary care physician reporting recurrent swellings on his hands and forearms. The patient said the lesions were itchy, but not painful, and had been appearing every week or so for the past few months.He had no significant medical history. On examination, the patient was apyrexial and physically well; an erythematous swelling was found on his right hand. Investigations found no abnormalities apart from a hypereosinophilia of 2﹞5?℅?109 per L (normal 0每0﹞5).
The patient was referred to the haematologists who found no cause for the eosinophilia but reviewed him every 6 months for the next 3 years.
6 years after his initial presentation, the patient attended a regional ophthalmology centre complaining of red, irritated right eye with a worm moving around in it. On examination he was systemically well but had a subconjunctival worm moving about in his right eye. The worm was removed under local anaesthetic with forceps. A random microfilaria count of the patient's serum was 1500 microfilaria per mL; the eosinophil count at that time was 2﹞0?℅?109 per L and he was referred to our tropical medicine hospital (figure; video). Exploration of his travel history found that, 7 years earlier, he had spent 3 months in Ilesa〞a state in the southwest of Nigeria. The patient said he lived alongside a local family in a traditional hut and visited forested national parks nearby.
We identified the worm as an adult female Loa loa worm and a sample of venous blood〞taken at midday〞showed a microfilaria count of 5230 microfilaria per mL. Filaria serology on ELISA was strongly positive for antibodies; it was weakly positive to Strongyloides spp〞probably due to cross-reactivity since stool analysis for ova, cysts, and parasites was negative〞and positive to Schistosoma spp but no ova were found in the patient's stools, urine, or semen.
To reduce the risk of meningoencephalitis, the patient was treated with a 21-day course of albendazole which lowered the microfilaria count to 950. He was then treated for a further 21 days with diethylcarbamazine; 1 month later the microfilaria count was zero.
He was seen 3 weeks later and found to be well with an eosinophil count of 1﹞1?℅?109 per L. 1 month later the eosinophil count was normal.
Eosinophilia can occur in a wide range of conditions: common causes include helminth parasitic infections, adverse reactions to medications, and atopic and allergic diseases.
L loa〞also known as the African eye worm〞is a filarial parasite endemic in central Africa and parts of southern Nigeria. It is transmitted by a bite from the deerfly Chrysops; migration of the adult worm may cause episodic angio-edema〞so-called Calabar swellings〞which we assume were the lesions initially reported by our patient. Diagnosis〞which may be made years after the patient first experiences symptoms〞is confirmed by detecting microfilaria in peripheral blood (video).

A 36-year-old man with a 6-month history of asthenia, impotence, loss of libido, polyuria, and polydipsia attended our department; he also reported needing to wake up twice at night to urinate and Raynaud's phenomenon. The patient had a medical history of minor anxiety episodes and was prescribed prazepam.
On examination, his weight was 69 kg, height 1﹞79 m with a BMI of 24﹞1 kg/m2; the patient stated he had recently lost 5 kg. Significant muscle atrophy and a reduction of body hair was noted; his pulse was 72 beats per min, blood pressure 124/77 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 97%. He had noticeable lymphadenopathy of cervical and inguinal nodes. Neurological examination was normal〞he had no disturbance of his vision.
Laboratory investigations showed total testosterone concentration of 0﹞12 ng/mL (normal level >1﹞65) with follicle-stimulating hormone concentration 1﹞4 IU/L (normal 1﹞4每18﹞1), and luteinising hormone concentration below 0﹞07 mIU/L (normal 1﹞5每9﹞3). Plasma cortisol concentration was 125 nmol/L (normal >140), and adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was 31﹞7 ng/L (10﹞3每48﹞3). Free T4 concentration was low at 4﹞98 ng/L (normal 7﹞0-14﹞8), with thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1﹞36 mIU/L (0﹞35每4﹞94). A 24-h water balance test showed marked polyuria and polydipsia: with a recorded water intake 5?500 mL and a urine output of 4?000 mL. The plasma osmolality was raised at 294 mOsm/L and the urinary osmolality was low at 246 mOsmol/L; the haematocrit was 51﹞1%.
A T1-weighted with gadolinium contrast MRI of the hypophysis showed a 6 mm thickening of the pituitary stalk at the optic chiasm level; T2-weighted MRI showed a bulging and plump appearance of the gland (figure). An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan of the brain showed hypermetabolic activity in the pituitary region (figure). A chest CT scan showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with associated pulmonary micronodules. Analysis of fluid obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage indicated lymphocytic alveolitis. Histopathological examination of a biopsy sample of a superficial lymph node showed epithelioid cell granulomatous lymphadenitis without necrosis. All microbiological cultures were negative.
Considering the findings in the round: androgen deficiency; adrenal insufficiency; central hypothyroidism〞likely responsible for the Raynaud's phenomenon; and diabetes insipidus〞indicated by the elevated plasma osmolality with haemoconcentration, which excluded potomania, corroborated by the low urinary osmolality, we diagnosed sarcoidosis involving both the pituitary gland and stalk. The patient was initiated on intramuscular testosterone (250 mg every 3 weeks), hydrocortisone (20 mg daily with an emergency dose of injectable 100 mg), thyroxine 75 米g per day, combined with infliximab, the intravenously administered anti-TNF antibody.
At 6-month follow-up, the patient's overall clinical condition had improved. However, laboratory investigations indicated significant persistent endocrine insufficiency〞central hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and androgen insufficiency still requiring replacement therapy. Furthermore, attempts to extend intervals between desmopressin doses led to recurrence of polyuria and polydipsia: indicating ongoing anterior and posterior pituitary insufficiency. A repeat MRI showed that the pituitary stalk had reduced to a maximum thickness of 1 mm, the anterior pituitary flattened against the sella floor, and arachnoidocele; the posterior pituitary maintained a normal hyperintensity and morphology, as seen originally when the patient presented.
Sarcoidosis is a chronic infiltrative and inflammatory condition that may involve any organ, with predilection for the lungs and lymph nodes. Pituitary gland involvement, though less common, has long been recognised by physicians and should be considered. Additionally, it is important to note that endocrine insufficiency is, in most cases, unresponsive to anti-inflammatory treatments〞as occurred in our patient.
Differential diagnoses for infiltrative or inflammatory processes affecting the pituitary gland include primary〞craniopharyngiomas〞and secondary tumours, infections including tuberculosis, IgG-4-related disease, in children Langerhans＊ cell histiocytosis, autoimmune hypophysitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Sheehan syndrome, and conditions of iron overload.

A 25-year-old man attended his primary care physician reporting recurrent swellings on his hands and forearms. The patient said the lesions were itchy, but not painful, and had been appearing every week or so for the past few months.He had no significant medical history. On examination, the patient was apyrexial and physically well; an erythematous swelling was found on his right hand. Investigations found no abnormalities apart from a hypereosinophilia of 2﹞5?℅?109 per L (normal 0每0﹞5).
The patient was referred to the haematologists who found no cause for the eosinophilia but reviewed him every 6 months for the next 3 years.
6 years after his initial presentation, the patient attended a regional ophthalmology centre complaining of red, irritated right eye with a worm moving around in it. On examination he was systemically well but had a subconjunctival worm moving about in his right eye. The worm was removed under local anaesthetic with forceps. A random microfilaria count of the patient's serum was 1500 microfilaria per mL; the eosinophil count at that time was 2﹞0?℅?109 per L and he was referred to our tropical medicine hospital (figure; video). Exploration of his travel history found that, 7 years earlier, he had spent 3 months in Ilesa〞a state in the southwest of Nigeria. The patient said he lived alongside a local family in a traditional hut and visited forested national parks nearby.
We identified the worm as an adult female Loa loa worm and a sample of venous blood〞taken at midday〞showed a microfilaria count of 5230 microfilaria per mL. Filaria serology on ELISA was strongly positive for antibodies; it was weakly positive to Strongyloides spp〞probably due to cross-reactivity since stool analysis for ova, cysts, and parasites was negative〞and positive to Schistosoma spp but no ova were found in the patient's stools, urine, or semen.
To reduce the risk of meningoencephalitis, the patient was treated with a 21-day course of albendazole which lowered the microfilaria count to 950. He was then treated for a further 21 days with diethylcarbamazine; 1 month later the microfilaria count was zero.
He was seen 3 weeks later and found to be well with an eosinophil count of 1﹞1?℅?109 per L. 1 month later the eosinophil count was normal.
Eosinophilia can occur in a wide range of conditions: common causes include helminth parasitic infections, adverse reactions to medications, and atopic and allergic diseases.
L loa〞also known as the African eye worm〞is a filarial parasite endemic in central Africa and parts of southern Nigeria. It is transmitted by a bite from the deerfly Chrysops; migration of the adult worm may cause episodic angio-edema〞so-called Calabar swellings〞which we assume were the lesions initially reported by our patient. Diagnosis〞which may be made years after the patient first experiences symptoms〞is confirmed by detecting microfilaria in peripheral blood (video).

A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery〞although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI〞caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture〞to a type 2 MI〞caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs〞type 1〞are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease〞including coronary embolism〞as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).
output: Coronary embolism causing type 2 myocardial infarction secondary to left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

A 19-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. He had no medical history. On examination his temperature was 38﹞8～C, he was dehydrated and tachycardic, and he had postural hypotension: his blood pressure was 110/40 mm Hg supine and 88/36 mm Hg standing. On palpation of his abdomen, the patient reported widespread pain with equivocal rebound tenderness. We also noted diffuse darkening of the mucous membranes and skin, which the patient said had gradually increased over the past 7 years. The hyperpigmentation was more pronounced on the skin over the patient's joints, hands and feet nail beds, gingivae, and the dorsum of the tongue (figure).Laboratory tests showed a sodium concentration of 116 mmol/L, a potassium concentration of 5﹞3 mmol/L, a low morning serum cortisol concentration of 63﹞4 nmol/L (normal range 172每496), and a high plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration of 440 pmol/L (normal range 1﹞5每13﹞9). We started the patient on an intravenous saline drip and gave him a bolus of 100 mg of hydrocortisone intravenously. After 24 h the patient's symptoms improved, and after 6 days his electrolytes normalised.
Further investigations found no HIV antibodies, no antibodies against 21-hydroxylase, no antibodies to Paracoccidioides brasiliensis (also known as South American blastomycosis), and a negative tuberculin test. However, the patient's serum concentration of hexacosanoic acid〞a very long chain fatty acid (VLCFA)〞was 2﹞82 米mol/L (normal range 0﹞22每0﹞88).

Additionally, when we repeated a neurological examination, we found the patient to have a previously unnoticed, slight left hemiparesis with preserved deep tendon reflexes, muscle tone, and normal sensation. Phenotypes range from a severe progressive cerebral form in boys to a myelopathy form in adults. AD may occur throughout the lifespan, independently of the neurological presentations; it is seen as an isolated manifestation in up to 10% of cases. X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy must be considered as a differential diagnosis of AD in young men〞even if neurological symptoms are not obvious at initial examination, as we found in our patient (video).

input: A 53-year-old woman presented with intensely itchy skin lesions and burning in her mouth. The following appearances are noted on examination of her wrist. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Lichen planus

The image shows the characteristic findings of lichen planus - violaceous (purple-tinged), flat-topped papules with fine white lines on the surface known as Wickham's striae (indicated by the arrow). The classic presentation includes the "6 Ps": Purple, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Pruritic Papules and Plaques.

The location on the flexor wrist is typical, and the combination of intensely itchy skin lesions with oral involvement (burning in mouth - suggesting oral lichen planus) strongly supports this diagnosis.

A 58-year-old man was hospitalised in our intensive care unit for severe, acute respiratory distress syndrome caused by an influenza virus infection. After 31 days, he was gradually weaned off mechanical ventilation. However, on the day after extubation, he had to be reintubated because of further respiratory distress. Emergency intubation was performed after rapid sequence induction using the short-acting anaesthetic agent etomidate, intravenously, at a dose of 0﹞3 mg/kg, and the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, intravenously, at a dose of 1 mg/kg. Orotracheal intubation was done without any difficulty. However, immediately after intubation, a change was noted on the electrocardiogram (ECG) (figure) and the patient became pulseless. The ECG showed ventricular tachycardia, which developed into ventricular fibrillation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated along with medical treatments to reduce his serum potassium concentration, which was 9﹞6 mmol/L; 1 h after the cardiac arrest, the serum potassium returned to within the normal range at 3﹞3 mmol/L. Of note, our patient had no contraindications to the use of succinylcholine before the reintubation〞specifically, his serum potassium concentration was 3﹞5 mmol/L and he had no neurological signs or muscle weakness.Closer examination of the ECG clearly showed the effects of hyperkalaemia on the heart during the incident: initially, the PR interval was prolonged and the T waves were tented (figure), next the P waves were lost, ST segment changes were seen, and the QRS complexes were prolonged (figure), and finally the QRS complex widened in a sine-wave configuration (figure). Succinylcholine is the first line neuromuscular blocking agent for rapid sequence induction because it is fast-acting. It causes depolarisation of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) located in the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) leading to the efflux of intracellular potassium into the plasma. In cases of muscle denervation, including patients who have been in intensive care for a prolonged period, AChRs are upregulated in both the NMJ and throughout the muscle membrane; immature forms of AChRs are also released. These immature receptors are more sensitive to agonists with depolarisation occurring at lower concentrations and lasting for a longer time with no desensitisation. Succinylcholine in such situations can lead to a massive efflux of potassium from muscles to the plasma, with life-threatening consequences.
In cases of severe hyperkalaemia, treatment should include intravenous calcium salt〞chloride or gluconate〞to raise the threshold potential and to stabilise the myocardium, and drugs that promote cellular potassium reuptake〞eg, insulin, sodium bicarbonate, and 汕2 agonists. This case serves as a reminder that succinylcholine should be used with caution in patients who have been in the intensive care unit for a prolonged period even without so-called intensive care unit acquired weakness.
output: Succinylcholine-induced severe hyperkalaemia causing ventricular fibrillation (hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest)

He had a medical history of obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), which was being treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). He had complained of snoring and a loss of concentration when he was first diagnosed with OSAS, in 2012.The referring pulmonologist said that the patient's Apnoea每Hypopnea Index had improved from 36 events per h to 0﹞3 events per h after the positive pressure was increased from 4 to 8 cm water (H2O), and for a short period there had been an improvement in the patient's problems, but then the CPAP seemed to make the situation worse〞his exercise tolerance decreased further, and he reported insomnia and pronounced morning fatigue.
When we examined the patient, his oxygen saturation was 94%. On auscultation of his chest, we heard a systolic murmur at the left, second intercostal space. An echocardiogram showed a large ostium secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) and an enlarged right ventricle with preserved systolic function (figure). The patient's mean pulmonary artery pressure was 18 mm Hg (normal <25) with no CPAP, indicating no pulmonary hypertension. However, there was evidence of shunting: the pulmonary to systemic output ratio was 2﹞8:1 (normal 1:1; greater than 1 indicates left-to-right shunting). We therefore concluded that the augmented CPAP had led to the development of his symptoms.

A 66-year-old man collapsed at home with chest pain. He was found by paramedics to be in ventricular fibrillation leading to a cardiac arrest. A post-resuscitation electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm and inferolateral ST-segment elevation. On arrival at our department he had an emergency invasive coronary angiogram which showed an occluded left circumflex artery, confirming myocardial infarction (MI). We opened the artery using a balloon, and following recanalisation, we identified a substantial filling defect indicative of a large thrombus (figure). Following stent implantation, normal coronary artery flow was restored and the patient made an uneventful recovery〞although brief paroxysms of atrial fibrillation were noted on cardiac monitoring in the ensuing 24 h.The patient enrolled in a research study (NCT03943966) of PET/CT angiography using a novel radiotracer, 18F-GP1, which binds to activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors and provides an assessment of thrombus formation. CT angiography confirmed a patent stent that co-localised with intense 18F-GP1 uptake on the PET/CT images, consistent with acute thrombus trapped behind the stent (figure).
Incomplete contrast opacification in the left atrial appendage made assessment on CT challenging. However, the presence of a separate and discrete filling defect raised the possibility of an in-situ appendage thrombus, which was confirmed on the 18F-GP1 PET/CT scan (figure). The clinical diagnosis was therefore changed from type 1 MI〞caused by an atherosclerotic plaque rupture〞to a type 2 MI〞caused by a coronary embolism arising from a left atrial appendage thrombus in the context of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation.
The patient was commenced on apixaban 5 mg twice a day, aspirin 75 mg daily, and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. The patient was allowed home after 2 days and made a full recovery.
Differentiation between type 1 and type 2 MIs is important because different therapeutic interventions are required to prevent recurrence. Most MIs〞type 1〞are due to acute coronary occlusion from a thrombus forming on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. In type 2, MIs are caused by a mismatch between the supply and demand of myocardial oxygen in the context of another disease〞including coronary embolism〞as seen in our patient. Adjunctive invasive or non-invasive imaging can often help clarify the clinical diagnosis and guide management (appendix; video).
output: Coronary embolic myocardial infarction secondary to left atrial appendage thrombus from paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (Type 2 MI)

A 59-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and haemodialysis since 2008 was admitted with painful, non-healing ulcerations on his legs. The lesions developed without known trauma 2 months before admission (figure). Pedal pulses were palpable on both sides and there were no signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Radiography of the soft tissue revealed diffuse calcified arterioles in a mesh-like pattern (figure). Histological examination of skin biopsy showed sclerosis and thrombosis of blood vessels (figure) and von Kossa stains were positive for calcium deposits (figure), confirming the diagnosis of calciphylaxis.Calciphylaxis is a syndrome of systemic medial calcification of the arteries leading to tissue necrosis. Skin biopsy and radiographic features are helpful in the diagnosis; but negative results do not necessarily exclude the diagnosis. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, several comorbid conditions are known to increase its development. Associated risk factors in our patient were: end-stage renal disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon. Recent reports indicate that low parathyroid hormone levels in association with adynamic bone diseases can also be associated with calciphylaxis. Unfortunately, there is still no standardised treatment for calciphylaxis. Based on previous reports, phenprocoumon was withdrawn in our patient and he was treated with cinacalcet, daily haemodialysis, sodium thiosulfate, and bisphosphonate. After 4 weeks, skin condition improved and the patient was discharged home.

A 46-year-old woman presented to our outpatient clinic in June, 2013, with frequent collapse, ischaemic scalp ulcerations, and hair loss (figure). She had undergone carotid endarterectomy in 2005, after a small right hemispheric stroke, and had no other medical history apart from hypercholesterolaemia. She had no previous dermatological or scalp problems. She took clopidogrel 75 mg, aspirin 80 mg, and simvastatin 40 mg daily.
Magnetic resonance angiography showed occlusion of both common carotid arteries, the innominate artery, and the right vertebral artery, and 80% stenosis of the orifice of the left subclavian artery. The circle of Willis was perfused by the left vertebral artery, and the right vertebral artery was filled retrograde from the left side. Blood supply to the head was maintained by the stenosed left subclavian artery (figure).
We inserted an 8?℅?24 mm balloon-expandable Express stent (Boston Scientific, Natick, MA, USA) to the stenosed left subclavian artery via the left groin (appendix). There were no complications. Postintervention transcranial Doppler showed an increase of 120% in the mean velocity of the left medial cerebral artery, from 40 cm/s to 88 cm/s after stenting.
At follow-up in December, 2013, the patient's dizziness and collapse had resolved. Her scalp lesions were almost healed, and hair growth had normalised (appendix).
Ischaemic scalp lesions due to insufficient tissue perfusion are rare. Most cases of scalp ischaemia are caused by giant cell arthritis, malignancy (angiosarcoma or melanoma), radiotherapy, or inflammation. In our case the cause was treatable with revascularisation of the extracranial arteries.
output: Ischaemic scalp ulceration due to subclavian artery stenosis with multiple extracranial artery occlusions

An 82-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-year history of progressive generalized weakness. Four months before presentation, a left adrenal mass had been identified incidentally on computed tomography (CT) that had been performed to evaluate an episode of chest pain. During the month preceding presentation, he had lost 8 kg of weight and had become unable to sit up in bed. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies were notable for a white-cell count of 2700 per cubic millimeter (reference range, 3700 to 10,500), a normal adrenal axis, and negative testing for HIV. Owing to concern for cancer, positron-emission tomography每CT of the whole body was performed and showed an adrenal mass on each side with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake (left image shows a coronal view), a 17-cm-long spleen without FDG uptake (asterisk in left image), and no other abnormal findings. Subsequent biopsy of the left adrenal mass showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with intracellular fungal organisms (middle, arrows; hematoxylin and eosin staining) that stained positive with Grocott＊s methenamine
silver (right). The organism causing this disease is predominantly found in what geographic regions?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and pathological findings, this is a case of **Histoplasmosis** with bilateral adrenal involvement.

The diagnosis is supported by:
- Bilateral adrenal masses with FDG uptake
- Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation
- Small intracellular yeast organisms (2-4 米m) within macrophages
- Positive Grocott's methenamine silver staining showing characteristic small oval yeasts

**Geographic regions where Histoplasma capsulatum is predominantly found:**

Ohio and Mississippi River Valleys in the United States (endemic regions including Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, and parts of the southeastern states), Central America, South America (particularly Brazil), parts of Africa, and Southeast Asia.
target: Central and mideastern United States & Central America

input: A 14-year-old girl presented with progressively growing bilateral painful axillary tumours (figure A). Histopathology showed slightly hyperplastic glandular tissue without cytological atypia within the reticular dermis and fatty tissue (figure B). The glandular epithelium stained positive for oestrogen and progesterone receptors (figure C), which led to the diagnosis of ectopic breast tissue. An MRI scan showed extensive axillary breast tissue without connection to the eutopic breasts (figure D). Ectopic breast tissue occurs in 2每6% of the general population, mainly after incomplete regression along the milk-line. Complete excision was done in our patient because she complained of pain and cosmetic disturbance, and because of the increased risk of primary ectopic breast carcinoma. Ectopic breast tissue should be considered in clinical differential diagnosis of tumours along the milk-line. Histological examination is required to rule out malignancy and in case of a wait-and-see approach, regular breast cancer screening is mandatory.

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs〞specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7﹞9 to 17﹞7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13﹞6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes〞although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements〞usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus〞which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

A 46-year-old woman presented to our outpatient clinic in June, 2013, with frequent collapse, ischaemic scalp ulcerations, and hair loss (figure). She had undergone carotid endarterectomy in 2005, after a small right hemispheric stroke, and had no other medical history apart from hypercholesterolaemia. She had no previous dermatological or scalp problems. She took clopidogrel 75 mg, aspirin 80 mg, and simvastatin 40 mg daily.
Magnetic resonance angiography showed occlusion of both common carotid arteries, the innominate artery, and the right vertebral artery, and 80% stenosis of the orifice of the left subclavian artery. The circle of Willis was perfused by the left vertebral artery, and the right vertebral artery was filled retrograde from the left side. Blood supply to the head was maintained by the stenosed left subclavian artery (figure).
We inserted an 8?℅?24 mm balloon-expandable Express stent (Boston Scientific, Natick, MA, USA) to the stenosed left subclavian artery via the left groin (appendix). There were no complications. Postintervention transcranial Doppler showed an increase of 120% in the mean velocity of the left medial cerebral artery, from 40 cm/s to 88 cm/s after stenting.
At follow-up in December, 2013, the patient's dizziness and collapse had resolved. Her scalp lesions were almost healed, and hair growth had normalised (appendix).
Ischaemic scalp lesions due to insufficient tissue perfusion are rare. Most cases of scalp ischaemia are caused by giant cell arthritis, malignancy (angiosarcoma or melanoma), radiotherapy, or inflammation. In our case the cause was treatable with revascularisation of the extracranial arteries.

An 81-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a 1-year history of shortness of breath on exertion. The patient also had a history of cryptogenic liver cirrhosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.On examination we found him to have a pan-systolic murmur, fine bilateral basal crackles on chest auscultation, heart rate 73 beats per min, and respiratory rate 17 breaths per min. A 75-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital with fatigue and vomiting. She also reported that for the previous 6 months she had muscle weakness, central obesity, and skin fragility. She had a history of dyslipidaemia and hypertension.On examination, we found the patient to be febrile with a temperature of 38～C, her blood pressure was 140/60 mm Hg, and her heart rate between 90 and 100 beats per min. She was cognitively impaired and lethargic.
Laboratory investigations showed an elevated white blood cell count of 11﹞17?℅?109 per L (normal range 4﹞5每11﹞5), a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 391﹞63 mg/L (normal <6), and profound hypokalaemia: serum potassium concentration 1﹞76 mmol/L (normal 3﹞5每5).
We started empirical antibiotic treatment with cefoxitin and metronidazole and began an intravenous infusion of potassium chloride. She continued to vomit; her serum potassium concentration remained low and her temperature remained around 38～C, and daily blood glucose levels showed a gradual increase requiring sliding scale insulin.
A CT scan of the patient's thorax and abdomen showed a large mass near the omental bursa (figure) and filling defects in the distal branches of the pulmonary artery, indicating a pancreatic neoplasm with a concurrent pulmonary embolism. Compression ultrasonography with doppler showed a deep venous thrombosis in the patient's left calf; we started her on enoxaparin.
A percutaneous, transgastric, ultrasound-guided biopsy was done and histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen showed a pancreatic adenocarcinoma of low differentiation and pleomorphic giant cells. Immunohistochemistry testing was positive for CK7, MUC1, AE1/AE3, and E-cadherin.
Despite continuous potassium repletion, daily laboratory examinations persistently showed severe hypokalaemia〞with average serum potassium concentrations of around 2 mmol/L.
Further exploration of the patient's hypokalaemia found a spot urine potassium concentration of 40﹞4 mmol/L and a spot urine sodium concentration of 90﹞9 mmol/L, indicating renal wasting.
Additional investigations found raised plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH; 121﹞6 pg/mL; normal 4﹞7每48﹞8), high cortisol level (51 米g/dL; normal 6﹞24每18﹞0), and low levels of thyroid stimulating hormone (0﹞02 mIU/L; normal 0﹞5每8﹞9) in the context of a metabolic alkalosis.
Taken together, the findings indicated a diagnosis of ectopic Cushing's syndrome consistent with an ACTH-secreting pancreatic tumour.
We started treatment with the steroid synthesis inhibitor ketoconazole orally at a dose of 200 mg twice a day. The patient's potassium level returned to normal after 1 month, she was then treated palliatively, and died 3 months later.
Neuroendocrine tumours of the bronchus, lung, thymus, and pancreas, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, and pheochromocytoma are the most frequent sites of ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions, but they can occur in almost every type of neoplasm. The resulting Cushing's syndrome〞also known as paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome〞usually develops rapidly and has features that are more pronounced: some patients present with purple striae, profound hypokalaemia〞as seen in our case〞and severe hypertension. The more typical features of Cushing's syndrome〞the rounding of the face, and weight gain in the recognised distribution〞are unusual in cases caused by ectopic ACTH-secreting lesions. Cushing's syndrome may cause a prothrombotic state and as such is a recognised risk factor for thromboembolic disease. Persistent electrolyte disturbances in combination with such tumours should always raise suspicion of ectopic Cushing's syndrome (video).
output: Ectopic Cushing's syndrome secondary to ACTH-secreting pancreatic adenocarcinoma

input: A 62-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital because she had been having involuntary movement of her right arm and leg for the previous month. In her medical history, she had developed type 2 diabetes approximately 10 years ago, which was treated with metformin and glimepiride. However, her blood glucose had been poorly controlled. A physical examination showed involuntary, unilateral, choreiform movements affecting only her right side (video). Further neurological examination showed her cranial nerves to be intact, ocular examination was normal, and there were no abnormal pyramidal signs〞specifically, muscle strength was normal, and tone and reflexes were normal. Sensory neurological examination also found no abnormalities. Laboratory examination showed an elevated fasting blood glucose, with values ranging from 7﹞9 to 17﹞7 mmol/L. Her serum glycosylated haemoglobin was 13﹞6%. She had no ketones in her urine, and an unenhanced cranial CT scan showed a mild hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia. A cranial MRI showed lesions of hyperintensity in both the putamen and caudate nucleus on the left side (figure). A T2-weighted MRI also showed mild hyperintensity in the left corpus striatum (figure), which led us to consider the possibility of an ischaemic infarct. However, hyperintensity was also shown in a T1-weighted MRI sequences, which reassured us that it was not ischaemic damage. The patient was diagnosed with hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia. Subcutaneous injections of insulin were added to the patient's diabetic medications in an effort to improve the control of her blood glucose. And haloperidol and clonazepam were prescribed to control the chorea. Within 2 weeks, the choreiform movements were much reduced.Neurological complications of diabetes are common; however, so-called diabetic striatopathy is relatively rare. When it does occur, it is usually in the context of non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and in patients with type 2 diabetes〞although it may occur in patients with type 1 disease. It was previously described only in Asian women, but nowadays it is known to also affect other populations as well. Patients with diabetic striatopathy have a characteristic T1 hyperintensity signal in basal ganglia with sparing of the internal capsule. Hyperglycaemic injury to the basal ganglia is thought to be responsible for the hyperkinetic movements〞usually manifesting as hemichorea or hemiballismus〞which mostly resolve after glycaemic control has been achieved.

A 58-year-old man was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of persistent fever and pancytopenia. Physical examination showed no other abnormal findings. However, a septic screen isolated Mycobacterium abscessus from his blood and bone marrow. An 18fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT scan showed an area of increased uptake in the patient's prostate (figure). Prostate specific antigen was 8﹞06 ng/mL〞previously, it had been measured and reported to be 0﹞8 ng/mL. A transrectal biopsy of his prostate showed granulomatous inflammation. Tissue cultures grew M abscessus. He said he had never had prostatic manipulation before. However, he had been previously diagnosed with benign prostatic enlargement and, 1 year before start of current symptoms, he had surgical resection of a neuroendocrine intestinal tumour.Recently, despite no evidence of residual disease, he had become worried about the possibility of recurrence. He decided to respond to an advertisement he had heard on the radio extolling the benefits of stem cell treatments〞including cancer prevention or recurrence. He said the clinic told him that the treatment was a type of ※immunotherapy§ that would allow his own stem cells to recognise any cancer cells as abnormal and destroy them. Further, he said they explained that the procedure entailed extracting his blood which would then be ※stimulated to produce abundant stem cells§ and these would then be injected into him intravenously.
A few hours after the infusion, the patient developed profuse vomiting and high-grade fever. He was given intravenous hydration and antibiotics, without resolution. He then attended our hospital.
Initially, we ruled out immunodeficiency〞a hallmark of disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacteria〞and only after repeat questioning of other possible risk factors did he disclose details of the ※stem cell treatment§. We believe the ※stem cells§ had been contaminated with mycobacteria prior to being transfused into the patient. The infusion〞into the blood stream〞enabled dissemination and seeding of the mycobacteria in the previously diseased prostate.
The field of stem cell therapy has grown substantially. However, unregulated, unscientifically proven, and irresponsible use has also increased worldwide leading to rising numbers of cases of patients being infected from products contaminated with a variety of different bacteria including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter cloacae, and Citrobacter freundii.
output: Disseminated Mycobacterium abscessus infection with prostatic involvement secondary to contaminated stem cell infusion

A 59-year-old man came to our hospital saying that he had been accidentally shot by a fellow hunter during an expedition to the local moorland. He was alone when he walked into the department. During physical examination he was found to be asymptomatic and all his vital signs were stable. His blood pressure was 125/75 mm Hg, and he did not complain of any dizziness or shortness of breath. Furthermore, no active bleeding was noted. An emergency whole-body CT (figure) was done and showed that shotgun pellets were evenly distributed in his body〞from his knees to his neck〞and that some had penetrated internally to affect several organs. A CT scan of his chest also showed that two of the pellets had reached the mediastinum: one had stopped a few millimetres from the floor of the aortic arch (figure), and the other one penetrated the pericardium, stopping between the pericardium and the lateral wall of the left ventricle (figure). A CT angiogram showed that no contrast agent was leaking from around the aorta or pericardium. We also did an echocardiogram, which, except for a small pericardial effusion, indicated that the patient was haemodynamically stable. The CT angiogram was repeated 24 h later, and, fortunately for the patient, nothing significantly had changed. At this stage, there were no indications for cardiac surgery to remove the pellets so〞with the patient's agreement〞we decided to take no further action after having weighed up the pros and cons of undertaking high-risk cardiac surgery or leaving the pellets where they were. After a few days of observation and antibiotic prophylaxis ceftriaxone (1 g a day for a week), the patient was discharged. He remained symptom free when seen again several months later.Hunting rifles and shotguns use cartridges that contain variable numbers of small pellets. Once the rifle or shotgun is discharged, these tiny projectiles spread out evenly and circumferentially from the barrel to increase the possibility of hitting a target. Judging by the distribution of the pellets on our patient's torso, we surmised that his fellow hunter had shot him from approximately 20 m. In the assessment of such patients, a key consideration is whether any pellets have penetrated vital organs. Furthermore, it is necessary to decide whether to surgically remove the pellets or simply leave them inside the body, where they will eventually be encapsulated in fibrous tissue.
output: Shotgun injury with pellet penetration of multiple organs including mediastinal structures (aortic arch and pericardium)

input: A 4-month-old boy who was exclusively breast-fed presented to the clinic with a 6-week history of a worsening rash. Physical examination revealed extensive erosive plaques throughout the body. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Based on the patient's age (4 months), diet (exclusively breast-fed), and the characteristic presentation of the rash (extensive, erythematous, erosive plaques with scaling/crusting, typically involving periorificial and acral areas, though generalized here), the clinical picture is pathognomonic for **Acrodermatitis enteropathica**.

While classic genetic Acrodermatitis enteropathica usually presents after weaning, this presentation in an exclusively breast-fed infant is characteristic of **Transient Neonatal Zinc Deficiency** (caused by a defect in the mother's ability to secrete zinc into breast milk). However, in the context of diagnostic terminology for this specific skin eruption, it is classified as Acrodermatitis enteropathica.

A 62-year-old man came to our outpatient clinic with purpura on his eyelids. 7 months before, periocular purpura appeared after a minimal trauma. These lesions did not resolve for months. Serum protein electrophoresis showed the presence of a monoclonal (M) protein. Immunofixation of both serum and urine determined its type: IgA-竹-type Bence-Jones protein. Bone-marrow examination was diagnostic for myeloma. Radiography showed small osteolysis of the head and cervical spine. Further investigations showed bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and cardiac involvement. The diagnosis of systemic AL-amyloidosis was made from the combination of clinical findings, the presence of amyloid deposits in skin biopsy sample, and the plasma cell dyscrasia. Treatment with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone was given. Autologous haemopoietic cell transplantation is planned.

This disease occurs in patients with plasma cell dyscrasia, in particular multiple myeloma. Amyloid is composed of a fibrillar component (immunoglobulin light chain material derived from the abnormal paraprotein) and a nonfibrillar protein termed amyloid P component. It deposits in extracellular tissue of several organs (skin, kidney, heart, liver, and peripheral nerve system). The prognosis depends on the number and severity of internal organ involvement and haematological response to treatment.

input: A 59-year-old man with end-stage renal disease and haemodialysis since 2008 was admitted with painful, non-healing ulcerations on his legs. The lesions developed without known trauma 2 months before admission (figure). Pedal pulses were palpable on both sides and there were no signs of chronic venous insufficiency. Skin biopsy and radiographic features are helpful in the diagnosis; but negative results do not necessarily exclude the diagnosis. Although the pathogenesis remains unclear, several comorbid conditions are known to increase its development. Associated risk factors in our patient were: end-stage renal disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and oral anticoagulation with phenprocoumon. Unfortunately, there is still no standardised treatment for calciphylaxis. Based on previous reports, phenprocoumon was withdrawn in our patient and he was treated with cinacalcet, daily haemodialysis, sodium thiosulfate, and bisphosphonate. After 4 weeks, skin condition improved and the patient was discharged home.

Five children〞whose ages ranged from 3 to 11 years〞attended our temporary medical camp complaining of variously sized protrusions in their abdomens pushing the umbilicus forward. The lesions had been present in all the patients since birth. All the children were spontaneous, normal vaginal deliveries, but none had been assessed by a doctor within the past 12 months. The aetiological abdominal wall defect under the protruding umbilicus was easily felt, so we made a diagnosis of an umbilical hernia in all the children. We referred all five patients to the nearest hospital for further assessment.
Umbilical hernia is a common condition found in children. The incidence ranges from 10 to 25% of newborn babies, and it appears to be more common among African populations for reasons that are not well understood. The condition is also associated with babies that are either premature or of low birthweight. In utero, the umbilical cord passes through the umbilical ring〞a defect in the linea alba〞to reach the fetal circulation. After birth, the umbilical ring usually closes spontaneously, with closure occurring within the first 5 years of life, but it may take up until the child reaches teenage years. Without closure, the small intestine can herniate through the umbilical ring; the extent of the fascial opening of the umbilical ring〞not the size of the herniation〞determines the likelihood of spontaneous closure. Often, the umbilical hernia is reducible〞as in our cases. The situation is most serious when the hernia is incarcerated and becomes irreducible: such patients will complain of tenderness and firmness, and erythema will be seen around the hernia. At this stage the umbilical hernia may become strangulated and even rupture.
Management of umbilical hernia begins with observation. If it is reducible and slowly decreasing in size, the recommendation is to watch and wait. Children with large umbilical hernias that do not appear to decrease within the first 2 years of life are candidates for surgical correction. Surgical intervention is certainly indicated in incarcerated umbilical hernia.

A 95-year-old woman attended our oral medicine department reporting a painful white plaque on the left margin of her tongue. input: A 24-year-old man presented with increasingly blurred vision in his right eye. Visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and less than 20/200 in the left eye. After pupil dilation, examination showed that the right lens had posterior subcapsular cataract and modest, inferior, subluxation. By contrast, the left crystalline lens was superiorly subluxated, by approximately 50%, with a dramatic view of the stretched lens zonules and areas of zonule deficiency (figure).
output: Lens subluxation (ectopia lentis) with zonular deficiency

Visual acuity was 20/40 in the right eye and less than 20/200 in the left eye. After pupil dilation, examination showed that the right lens had posterior subcapsular cataract and modest, inferior, subluxation. Five children〞whose ages ranged from 3 to 11 years〞attended our temporary medical camp complaining of variously sized protrusions in their abdomens pushing the umbilicus forward. The lesions had been present in all the patients since birth. All the children were spontaneous, normal vaginal deliveries, but none had been assessed by a doctor within the past 12 months. Interestingly, the remote village of Pataase, where we located our camp to provide basic medical care, in a rural area 25 km north of Cape Coast, the capital city of the Central Region of Ghana, was home to a total of 75 children〞including the five (figure) with the umbilical protrusions.The three older boys were aged 11 years, 8 years, and 5 years. The two younger boys, whose mother is pictured with them, were identical twins and 3 years old. On physical examination, the umbilical protrusions were all reducible and painless. The aetiological abdominal wall defect under the protruding umbilicus was easily felt, so we made a diagnosis of an umbilical hernia in all the children. We referred all five patients to the nearest hospital for further assessment.
Umbilical hernia is a common condition found in children. The incidence ranges from 10 to 25% of newborn babies, and it appears to be more common among African populations for reasons that are not well understood. The condition is also associated with babies that are either premature or of low birthweight. In utero, the umbilical cord passes through the umbilical ring〞a defect in the linea alba〞to reach the fetal circulation. After birth, the umbilical ring usually closes spontaneously, with closure occurring within the first 5 years of life, but it may take up until the child reaches teenage years. Without closure, the small intestine can herniate through the umbilical ring; the extent of the fascial opening of the umbilical ring〞not the size of the herniation〞determines the likelihood of spontaneous closure. Often, the umbilical hernia is reducible〞as in our cases. The situation is most serious when the hernia is incarcerated and becomes irreducible: such patients will complain of tenderness and firmness, and erythema will be seen around the hernia. At this stage the umbilical hernia may become strangulated and even rupture.
Management of umbilical hernia begins with observation. If it is reducible and slowly decreasing in size, the recommendation is to watch and wait. Children with large umbilical hernias that do not appear to decrease within the first 2 years of life are candidates for surgical correction. Surgical intervention is certainly indicated in incarcerated umbilical hernia.

A 75-year-old female patient with stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lungs with EGFR exon 21 Leu858Arg mutation presented to the Ophthalmology Department at the Prince of Wales Hospital in Hong Kong in March, 2017, with initial symptoms of bilateral severe dry eyes, followed by sequential ulcerations of the cornea and anterior uveitis causing reduced vision and pain. Blood tests were done and found a substantially raised anti-nuclear antibody titre, positive rheumatoid factor, and syphilis serology (TPPA++ EIA每 TP++). Corneal scrapings did not yield any organism growth. The patient denied previous history of syphilis infection but reported a positive drug history of erlotinib use (100 mg daily) for more than 1 year for her lung cancer. Syphilitic uveitis was an unlikely differential diagnosis because examination of her fundi did not reveal any inflammation of the vitreous humour, choroid, or retina, and pupil examination was normal.Slit-lamp photographs with diffuse and assisted illumination revealed an active roundish ulceration on the right inferonasal cornea with an overlying epithelial defect (figure, A). Her left eye showed a healed ulcer (figure, B). Bilateral curly and elongated lashes, upper lid purplish rashes, and nail dystrophy were observed. A clinical diagnosis of erlotinib-related ophthalmopathy was made.
Her ocular inflammation recurred despite the use of artificial tears, bandage contact lenses, treatment for syphilis (three weekly injections of intramuscular benzylpenicillin [2﹞4 million units]), and topical and systemic prednisolone. After discussion with her oncologists, her oncologists agreed to discontinue erlotinib and her right corneal ulcer healed within 2 weeks. Later, her oncologists suggested that she switch to gefitinib treatment in view of rising carcinoembryonic antigen levels; however, her corneal ulcer recurred within 1 week after starting gefitinib. Gefitinib was then stopped by the oncologists and the ulcer again healed within 2 weeks. The patient's eyes were stable while on artificial tears, but her carcinoembryonic antigen levels were rising, and the patient refused further chemotherapy as advised by her oncologists.
Ocular side-effects of tyrosine kinase inhibitors are not uncommon, but they usually happen within weeks of initiating treatment. Discontinuing the medication is the most definitive treatment. Severe corneal ulcerations would ultimately lead to perforation and loss of sight. A balance between ocular complications and oncological control should therefore be discussed carefully with the patient. Inter-disciplinary care for such patients is essential.

An 18-year old man presented to University College London Hospital (UCLH) in April, 2016, with stage IIIB classical Hodgkin lymphoma. He received chemotherapy and autologous haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT) for primary progressive disease (details of treatment regimens are presented on appendix p 1). In January, 2017, he had a first relapse, for which he received brentuximab vedotin and reduced intensity conditioning haploidentical, allogeneic HSCT. He had a second relapse in May, 2018. Salvage chemotherapy with eight cycles and graded regimen donor lymphocyte infusions did not induce remission. With few options for further treatment, we elected to give the licensed dose of 240 mg nivolumab on a 2-weekly schedule.4 days after the first dose of nivolumab, in February, 2020, he presented at UCLH with pyrexia, oral ulceration, an erythematous palmar rash, and multiple penile ulcers (figure A; appendix p 2). He received antibiotics and antivirals and 2 mg/kg intravenous methylprednisolone but continued to deteriorate with worsening skin features (widespread erythematous lesions, peri-orbital swelling, heliotrope rash, frank oral desquamation), reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale of 11 of 15), and complex partial seizures. On day 8, he was intubated with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8 of 15, upgoing plantars, clonus, decorticate posturing, and status epilepticus.
Investigations excluded infectious, autoimmune or vasculitic, and paraneoplastic syndromes. His cerebrospinal fluid was unremarkable, and MRI of the brain revealed diffuse cerebral oedema, which was attributed to CNS graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Skin biopsy confirmed GVHD, manifesting as erythema multiforme, with a lymphohistiocytic dermal infiltrate comprising PD-1-low, CD8+ T cells (figure B; appendix p 3).
The process appeared steroid-refractory, so we commenced a 5-day course of plasma exchange (without taper; 1﹞5 volumes; SpectraOptia) on day 8 to deplete circulating nivolumab (half-life 26﹞7 days), its presumed driver. On day 3 of plasma exchange, the patient was extubated with no residual neurological deficits and a clinically significant improvement in mucosal ulceration and rash. ELISA confirmed plasma clearance of nivolumab by day 2 of plasma exchange, ongoing at day 6, with a corresponding increase in soluble PD-1 concentration (appendix p 3). The patient continued on steroids beyond the 5-day course of plasma exchange and commenced tacrolimus, which was stopped 8 months later.
PET-CT confirmed remission at 1 month and 12 months after initiation of plasma exchange with the absence of chronic GVHD. A repeat head MRI at 6 months showed normal intracranial appearances (appendix p 4).
Nivolumab-mediated inhibition of PD-1 can deliver prolonged remission in relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma after allogeneic HSCT but can be complicated by GVHD. Acute GVHD affects more than half of patients with lymphoma who receive this treatment, with concerningly high mortality, but rare neurological involvement. Steroid refractoriness is common, and alternative immunosuppressants are often required.
This is the first report of use of plasma exchange for nivolumab depletion in acute, life-threatening multisystem GVHD after haploidentical, allogeneic HSCT. Our pharmacokinetic data support the hypothesis that PD-1 inhibitors can be swiftly depleted by plasma exchange and that this single intervention can lead to full clinical recovery, even in steroid-refractory disease.
This patient's complete, durable remission following one dose of nivolumab highlights its potency in relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma after allogeneic HSCT, but the risk of severe or life-threatening, steroid-refractory GVHD is substantial. In this setting, plasma exchange represents a novel, safe treatment that does not affect anti-tumour response and might benefit patients with severe toxicity. This case emphasises the need for evaluation of optimal nivolumab dosing after allogeneic HSCT in well designed clinical studies.

output: Acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) induced by nivolumab following allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation

A 26-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of dry, itchy eyes, and poor vision at night. She also reported dry, itchy skin, and brittle nails.She was a teetotaller and had no history of bowel surgery. On examination, we found no evidence of malabsorption, chronic liver disease, cholestasis, or pancreatic disease; a physical examination was unremarkable apart from abnormalities in her eyes. The patient's unaided visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes and she had symmetrical, triangular, foamy, keratinised patches over her bulbar conjunctiva, adjoining the temporal limbus of both eyes (figure). The cornea was normal and a fundoscopic examination found no abnormalities.
We concluded the lesions were Bitot's spots〞indicative of xerophthalmia stage X1B, according to the WHO classification.
Laboratory investigations〞including full blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests〞were normal. Microscopic examination of a sample of the patient's stool was negative for ova, parasites, and cysts for Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Giardia duodenalis (giardiasis), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebiasis), and Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm).
We prescribed oral vitamin A 10?000 U/day for 3 months and lubricating eye drops. The patient's symptoms and signs resolved within 1 month of starting therapy. As a woman of childbearing age, we advised her to try and maintain a varied, healthy diet〞specifically rich in fruits and vegetables. We also counselled her to seek medical advice if she was planning to have children in order to prevent recurrence of vitamin A deficiency (VAD) in her or its development in her offspring.
Keratin admixed with Corynebacterium xerosis from the stratum corneum of the conjunctiva along with metaplasia of conjunctival epithelium due to VAD may produce Bitot's spots. The foamy appearance may be due to gas produced by the bacteria. Histopathological examination normally shows keratinisation, inflammatory infiltrates, with the accumulation of Gram-positive bacilli. The prevalence of subclinical VAD in India is about 61%, which is one of the highest in the world. Bitot's spots represent the pathognomonic clinical finding which can be used to estimate the prevalence of VAD. In low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), primary VAD is usually attributed to malnourishment with an increased susceptibility occurring during pregnancy and lactation. Young children are also at increased risk because of high nutritional demands.
Globally, nearly 4﹞5 billion people are at risk of VAD due to intestinal parasite infections. Gender difference in access to eye care services may be responsible for the higher incidence of blindness in women in LMICs.
Bitot's spots respond rapidly to vitamin A supplements and indicate a level of VAD that can be reversed without the development of blindness; the finding should therefore prompt immediate treatment. If xerophthalmia and blindness ensue, then mortality can be as high as 40% within the first year of diagnosis (video).

Skin biopsy confirmed GVHD, manifesting as erythema multiforme, with a lymphohistiocytic dermal infiltrate comprising PD-1-low, CD8+ T cells (figure B; appendix p 3).
The process appeared steroid-refractory, so we commenced a 5-day course of plasma exchange (without taper; 1﹞5 volumes; SpectraOptia) on day 8 to deplete circulating nivolumab (half-life 26﹞7 days), its presumed driver. On day 3 of plasma exchange, the patient was extubated with no residual neurological deficits and a clinically significant improvement in mucosal ulceration and rash. ELISA confirmed plasma clearance of nivolumab by day 2 of plasma exchange, ongoing at day 6, with a corresponding increase in soluble PD-1 concentration (appendix p 3). The patient continued on steroids beyond the 5-day course of plasma exchange and commenced tacrolimus, which was stopped 8 months later.
PET-CT confirmed remission at 1 month and 12 months after initiation of plasma exchange with the absence of chronic GVHD. A repeat head MRI at 6 months showed normal intracranial appearances (appendix p 4).
Nivolumab-mediated inhibition of PD-1 can deliver prolonged remission in relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma after allogeneic HSCT but can be complicated by GVHD. Acute GVHD affects more than half of patients with lymphoma who receive this treatment, with concerningly high mortality, but rare neurological involvement. Steroid refractoriness is common, and alternative immunosuppressants are often required.
This is the first report of use of plasma exchange for nivolumab depletion in acute, life-threatening multisystem GVHD after haploidentical, allogeneic HSCT. Our pharmacokinetic data support the hypothesis that PD-1 inhibitors can be swiftly depleted by plasma exchange and that this single intervention can lead to full clinical recovery, even in steroid-refractory disease.
This patient's complete, durable remission following one dose of nivolumab highlights its potency in relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma after allogeneic HSCT, but the risk of severe or life-threatening, steroid-refractory GVHD is substantial. In this setting, plasma exchange represents a novel, safe treatment that does not affect anti-tumour response and might benefit patients with severe toxicity. This case emphasises the need for evaluation of optimal nivolumab dosing after allogeneic HSCT in well designed clinical studies.

A 75-year-old female patient with stage IV adenocarcinoma of the lungs with EGFR exon 21 Leu858Arg mutation presented to the Ophthalmology Department at the Prince of Wales Hospital in Hong Kong in March, 2017, with initial symptoms of bilateral severe dry eyes, followed by sequential ulcerations of the cornea and anterior uveitis causing reduced vision and pain. Blood tests were done and found a substantially raised anti-nuclear antibody titre, positive rheumatoid factor, and syphilis serology (TPPA++ EIA每 TP++). Corneal scrapings did not yield any organism growth. The patient denied previous history of syphilis infection but reported a positive drug history of erlotinib use (100 mg daily) for more than 1 year for her lung cancer. Syphilitic uveitis was an unlikely differential diagnosis because examination of her fundi did not reveal any inflammation of the vitreous humour, choroid, or retina, and pupil examination was normal.Slit-lamp photographs with diffuse and assisted illumination revealed an active roundish ulceration on the right inferonasal cornea with an overlying epithelial defect (figure, A). Her left eye showed a healed ulcer (figure, B). Bilateral curly and elongated lashes, upper lid purplish rashes, and nail dystrophy were observed. A clinical diagnosis of erlotinib-related ophthalmopathy was made.
Her ocular inflammation recurred despite the use of artificial tears, bandage contact lenses, treatment for syphilis (three weekly injections of intramuscular benzylpenicillin [2﹞4 million units]), and topical and systemic prednisolone. After discussion with her oncologists, her oncologists agreed to discontinue erlotinib and her right corneal ulcer healed within 2 weeks. Later, her oncologists suggested that she switch to gefitinib treatment in view of rising carcinoembryonic antigen levels; however, her corneal ulcer recurred within 1 week after starting gefitinib. Gefitinib was then stopped by the oncologists and the ulcer again healed within 2 weeks. Ocular side-effects of tyrosine kinase inhibitors are not uncommon, but they usually happen within weeks of initiating treatment. Discontinuing the medication is the most definitive treatment. Severe corneal ulcerations would ultimately lead to perforation and loss of sight. A balance between ocular complications and oncological control should therefore be discussed carefully with the patient. Inter-disciplinary care for such patients is essential.

A 26-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 6-month history of dry, itchy eyes, and poor vision at night. She also reported dry, itchy skin, and brittle nails.She was a teetotaller and had no history of bowel surgery. On examination, we found no evidence of malabsorption, chronic liver disease, cholestasis, or pancreatic disease; a physical examination was unremarkable apart from abnormalities in her eyes. The patient's unaided visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes and she had symmetrical, triangular, foamy, keratinised patches over her bulbar conjunctiva, adjoining the temporal limbus of both eyes (figure). The cornea was normal and a fundoscopic examination found no abnormalities.
We concluded the lesions were Bitot's spots〞indicative of xerophthalmia stage X1B, according to the WHO classification.
Laboratory investigations〞including full blood count, liver function tests, and renal function tests〞were normal. Microscopic examination of a sample of the patient's stool was negative for ova, parasites, and cysts for Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm), Giardia duodenalis (giardiasis), Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebiasis), and Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm).
We prescribed oral vitamin A 10?000 U/day for 3 months and lubricating eye drops. The patient's symptoms and signs resolved within 1 month of starting therapy. As a woman of childbearing age, we advised her to try and maintain a varied, healthy diet〞specifically rich in fruits and vegetables. We also counselled her to seek medical advice if she was planning to have children in order to prevent recurrence of vitamin A deficiency (VAD) in her or its development in her offspring.
Keratin admixed with Corynebacterium xerosis from the stratum corneum of the conjunctiva along with metaplasia of conjunctival epithelium due to VAD may produce Bitot's spots. The foamy appearance may be due to gas produced by the bacteria. Histopathological examination normally shows keratinisation, inflammatory infiltrates, with the accumulation of Gram-positive bacilli. The prevalence of subclinical VAD in India is about 61%, which is one of the highest in the world. Bitot's spots represent the pathognomonic clinical finding which can be used to estimate the prevalence of VAD. In low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs), primary VAD is usually attributed to malnourishment with an increased susceptibility occurring during pregnancy and lactation. Young children are also at increased risk because of high nutritional demands.
Globally, nearly 4﹞5 billion people are at risk of VAD due to intestinal parasite infections. Gender difference in access to eye care services may be responsible for the higher incidence of blindness in women in LMICs.
Bitot's spots respond rapidly to vitamin A supplements and indicate a level of VAD that can be reversed without the development of blindness; the finding should therefore prompt immediate treatment. If xerophthalmia and blindness ensue, then mortality can be as high as 40% within the first year of diagnosis (video).

A 65-year-old man attended our outpatient clinic for diagnostic evaluation of abnormal blood tests detected during a routine check requested by his cardiologist. The investigations showed a raised serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (406 U/L; normal <60) and a raised serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration of 99﹞20 米IU/mL (normal 0﹞27每4﹞20). The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0﹞67 ng/dL (normal 0﹞93每1﹞70) and 1﹞5 pg/mL (normal 2﹞0每4﹞4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies〞including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies〞were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism〞specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes〞without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative〞without detectable autoantibodies〞and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1﹞5 米g/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone〞posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges〞the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. An abdominal CT scan had shown rectosigmoid thickening, and a colonoscopy confirmed near complete bowel obstruction. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23﹞5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15﹞0 g/dL (normal 12﹞9每16﹞5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80每98), leukocyte count 9﹞0?℅?109 per L (normal 3﹞2每9﹞4), platelet count 301?℅?109 per L (normal 155每371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia〞reaching the level of the aortic arch〞containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without〞until recently〞any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ? weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.
Hiatal hernias are common with an estimated prevalence of 15每20% in western populations; large hiatal hernias〞often referred to as upside-down stomach〞are rare, and may cause heartburn, postprandial discomfort, dysphagia, and anaemia from chronic bleeding. They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic〞as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion〞as was the case in our patient〞risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.
