A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurological department of our institution in October, 2016, because of acute dysarthria. Her symptoms started 2 weeks ago at the same time as a severe cold that had developed immediately after she received an influenza vaccine.
The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.
output: Solitary basal skull metastasis from breast cancer causing hypoglossal nerve paresis

The patient's free thyroxine and free tri-iodothyronine were low at 0﹞67 ng/dL (normal 0﹞93每1﹞70) and 1﹞5 pg/mL (normal 2﹞0每4﹞4) respectively. Anti-thyroid antibodies〞including thyroid peroxidase antibodies and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies〞were not detected.The patient did not report any symptoms indicative of hypothyroidism〞specifically fatigue, constipation, or an increased sensitivity to cold. He had no history of thyroid disease.
On general physical examination, the patient did not have a goitre, and his cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes were not enlarged or tender.
Thyroid sonography showed a destructive thyroiditis with a heterogeneous, hypoechoic sonographic pattern and slightly increased vascularisation in both thyroid lobes〞without circumscribed nodules (figure; appendix).
In the absence of specific anti-thyroid antibodies, our considered differential diagnoses were: a subacute or infectious thyroiditis, a seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis, or a drug-induced thyroiditis.
Infectious thyroiditis is commonly associated with thyroid pain and elevated inflammatory markers; both of which were not present in our patient. Regarding autoimmune thyroiditis, approximately 5% of cases are seronegative〞without detectable autoantibodies〞and display a hypoechoic sonographic pattern akin to a destructive thyroiditis; biochemical abnormalities are mild with slight TSH elevation and minimally reduced concentrations of the peripheral hormones. We considered a diagnosis of seronegative autoimmune thyroiditis unlikely in our patient. That left us with the possibility of a drug-induced thyroiditis.
The patient reported that he had been started on amiodarone, because of symptomatic episodes of ventricular tachycardia, 5 months ago. We therefore immediately started oral levothyroxine at a dose of 1﹞5 米g/kg bodyweight per day, which led to the rapid normalisation of the patient's thyroid hormone levels.
The prevalence of amiodarone-induced overt hypothyroidism is reported to be approximately 5% of amiodarone-treated patients, with subclinical manifestations five times as frequent. In the absence of autoimmunity, the withdrawal of amiodarone can be considered in subclinical cases.
Even though thyrotoxicosis is the most feared endocrinological side-effect of amiodarone〞posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges〞the importance of hypothyroidism caused by the drug should not be underestimated, despite its relatively easy clinical management (video).

A 91-year-old man was referred to our cancer centre for assessment and treatment of pulmonary metastases from a previously diagnosed colorectal cancer. The patient had a 2-week history of occasional haemoptysis and mild dyspnoea.The diagnosis of colorectal cancer had been made 2 years earlier after the patient presented with a large persistent peri-anal abscess and obstructive symptoms. An abdominal CT scan had shown rectosigmoid thickening, and a colonoscopy confirmed near complete bowel obstruction. The patient had a Hartmann's resection with end colostomy, and the diagnosis was confirmed as Grade 2 adenocarcinoma of the rectum, stage pT3N1; he did not have an adjuvant treatment due to his advanced age and preference. 2 months later, the patient was found to have biopsy-proven recurrence of the malignancy after a colonoscopy. Restaging CT scans found new bilateral pulmonary nodules, considered to be metastases.
When we saw the patient, he was stable. He was breathing comfortably with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per min, blood pressure was 114/75 mm Hg, heart rate 89 beats per min, oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. He was not cyanotic, and his BMI was 23﹞5 kg/m2.
On chest auscultation, bowel sounds were audible in the mid and lower posterior thorax bilaterally, but not audible when auscultated from the anterior thorax. Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 15﹞0 g/dL (normal 12﹞9每16﹞5), mean corpuscular volume 104 fL (normal 80每98), leukocyte count 9﹞0?℅?109 per L (normal 3﹞2每9﹞4), platelet count 301?℅?109 per L (normal 155每371). A CT scan of the patient's chest showed two metastatic pulmonary deposits in the right and left lobes and a large hiatal hernia〞reaching the level of the aortic arch〞containing the stomach, and small and large intestines; importantly, a segment of bowel was adjacent to one of the metastatic deposits (figure).
Upon reviewing previous imaging, we found that the hiatal hernia had been present 17 years ago and that it had increased in size since that time. Additionally, the patient, on further questioning, did recall occasionally having regurgitation and dysphagia without〞until recently〞any bleeding, abdominal discomfort, or dyspnoea. Due to the radiation tolerance limit of the bowel adjacent to the metastatic lesions, we decided that it was unsafe for the patient to have ablative-dose stereotactic radiotherapy. Instead, we treated him with lower-dose palliative radiotherapy to control his haemoptysis. At follow-up 2 and ? weeks after the radiation, the patient reported resolution of the haemoptysis, and stability in terms of his dyspnoea and cough.
Hiatal hernias are common with an estimated prevalence of 15每20% in western populations; large hiatal hernias〞often referred to as upside-down stomach〞are rare, and may cause heartburn, postprandial discomfort, dysphagia, and anaemia from chronic bleeding. They are often surgically corrected on an elective basis due to perceived risks of unpredictable complications such as gastric volvulus, oesophageal and gastric obstruction, incarceration, strangulation, and infarction of the herniated organs. However, they can also be asymptomatic〞as was the case with our patient.
Stereotactic ablative radiotherapy delivers precise, high doses of radiation, and is often used in metastasis-directed treatment of oligometastatic colorectal cancer. The small bowel is one of the most radiosensitive organs, and the presence of a loop of bowel adjacent to a target lesion〞as was the case in our patient〞risks stereotactic ablative radiotherapy causing enteritis, perforation, stricture, and fistula. Lower-dose palliative radiation is effective for controlling haemoptysis from metastatic lesions and has a lower risk of toxicity to nearby organs, but it is inferior to stereotactic radiation in terms of tumour control and in producing a sustained response.

A 76-year-old female patient was admitted to the neurological department of our institution in October, 2016, because of acute dysarthria. Her symptoms started 2 weeks ago at the same time as a severe cold that had developed immediately after she received an influenza vaccine.
The patient was on anticoagulation therapy with dabigatran because of atrial fibrillation and had a history of a deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism 7 years ago. Additionally, the patient was also receiving treatment for hypertension (bisoprolol, amlodipine, and ramipril). As a consequence, a thromboembolic accident or a cerebral haemorrhage was initially discussed. Furthermore, a potential adverse event of the recent influenza vaccination was considered as a differential diagnosis.
Physical examination revealed hypoglossal paresis on the left side (figure, A). No other neurological abnormalities could be found. Blood pressure was 174/103 mmHg at admission. No abnormalities were recorded in routine cellular blood cell count and blood chemistry; in particular, no signs of infection or inflammation were noted. No specific cerebrovascular risk factors were apparent. An initial cranial CT scan ruled out any bleeding or infarction. Doppler sonography of the cranial vessels was unremarkable.However, a left-sided, stage I primary breast tumour was documented in the patient's medical history. This tumour had been diagnosed 9 years ago. At that time, the patient was treated with breast-conserving surgery, radiotherapy of the left breast, and adjuvant endocrine treatment with tamoxifen for 1 year. Tamoxifen therapy was stopped after 1 year as a consequence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
During further examination of the acute hypoglossal paresis, cerebral MRI detected a solitary tumoral lesion at the basal skull (figure, B), affecting the left hypoglossal nerve. Except for this solitary lesion, none of the other staging procedures used, including CT scan of the chest and abdomen and bone scan, found any additional metastatic lesions. Therefore, a secondary, solitary metastatic breast tumour at the basal skull was assumed. The patient was treated with locoregional radiotherapy, antiresorptive treatment with zoledronate, and first-line endocrine therapy with an aromatase inhibitor. Furthermore, the patient subsequently received speech therapy. As a result of all these therapeutic measures, the hypoglossal paresis soon regressed completely and the patient is currently without any symptoms 8 months after primary treatment.
Solitary breast cancer metastases are rare, but affected patients often have a good chance of achieving long-term remission. In our case, the work-up to investigate an acute, uncommon clinical finding led to the diagnosis.
output: Solitary skull base metastasis from breast carcinoma causing isolated hypoglossal nerve palsy

A 6-year-old boy with Ewing's sarcoma presented with generalised skin rash, low grade fever (38～C), and red eyes. Itchiness in the hands and feet preceded the rash. The child received chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide) and blood transfusion 1 week before the onset of symptoms. Examination revealed purplish discoloration of both palms and soles in a glove and socks pattern (figure, A每C). Lesions resembled petechiae over the trunk, hands and feet, and face. Oral mucosa was erythematous with the rash including both pinnae (figure, D). The boy was neutropenic (haemoglobin 11﹞5 g/dL, total leucocyte count 0﹞5?℅?106/L, and platelet count 20?℅?109/L).
The striking glove and socks distribution of the rash prompted the diagnosis of papular purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) related to parvoviral infection. Parvovirus serology showed immunoglobulin M positivity. Skin biopsy revealed lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate with red-blood-cell extravasation. The boy was initiated on antibiotics (cefoperazone每sulbactam and amikacin, as per unit guidelines for febrile neutropenia), which were stopped 2 days later because he was afebrile and the blood cultures were sterile. Rash resolved with desquamation over the next 2 weeks. Blood counts also normalised after 1 week.
In children, parvovirus B19 infection usually presents as erythema infectiosum. Although uncommon, infection can manifest itself as PPGSS, which is an acute self-limited dermatosis characterised by fever, acral pruritus, oedema, petechiae, and oral lesions. The distinguishing feature is the symmetric erythema of hands and feet, with sharp margins at wrists and ankles. Other causes of PPGSS include cytomegalovirus, Coxsackie virus, and measles virus. The disease is mostly self-limited with a benign prognosis.
Febrile neutropenia is an oncological emergency that needs prompt initiation of antibacterial treatment. Recognition of such a classic manifestation, especially in an immunocompromised host, is essential to avoid aggressive treatment. Unlike patients with erythema infectiosum, individuals with PPGSS are regarded as infectious and should be isolated. Further, immunocompromised children need to be monitored for red-cell aplasia as a manifestation of persistent parvovirus infection. The index child has been well since illness, and completed his chemotherapy in June 2013.

A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of 汐1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40每70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

A 39-year-old man was admitted to our department with a 1-day history of pain in his left flank and dizziness. His medical history included poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and a stone in the left upper ureter. On admission to the hospital, he appeared to be in septic shock. His temperature was 38﹞1～C and his blood pressure was 66/35 mm Hg. Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 16﹞58?℅?109 per L with 93﹞6% neutrophils. His renal function was abnormal: blood concentrations of creatinine and urea nitrogen were 0﹞499 mg/dL and 15﹞4 mmol/L, respectively. He was hyperglycaemic with a blood glucose concentration of 24﹞7 mmol/L.Escherichia coli were isolated in a blood culture but not in a urine culture. A CT scan of his abdomen was done immediately and showed a diffusely swollen left kidney (figure). Board-spectrum antibiotics were started empirically and 10 h later an enhanced CT scan showed that the left kidney had expanded because of gas in the parenchyma and para-renal space〞especially in the renal veins. Based on these findings, we made a diagnosis of an emphysematous pyelonephritis. Because of the risk of an air embolism, an open, exploratory operation was undertaken. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit after the surgery for further resuscitation and control of his electrolytes. Repeat CT scans done 4 days and 23 days after the operation showed reducing amounts of gas in the left kidney (figure). When we repeated laboratory investigations just before he was discharged, his routine blood tests and renal function had returned to within the normal ranges: his blood creatinine concentration was 0﹞198 mg/dL, his blood urea nitrogen concentration was 8﹞6 mmol/L, and his blood glucose concentration was 4﹞8 mmol/L.
E coli infections in patients with diabetes and urinary tract obstruction, either occurring alone or together, are the cornerstones in the development of emphysematous pyelonephritis. In patients with poorly controlled blood glucose concentrations, the situation is complicated further by possible impairment of tissue circulation. Additionally, the high levels of blood glucose provide microorganisms with a more favourable environment in which to form gas. Mixed acid fermentation of glucose by Enterobacteriaceae is the major pathway of gas formation〞carbon dioxide and hydrogen are the main components of the gas.

A 16-year-old girl attended our outpatient clinic complaining about a hard lump on the second toe of her left foot. She said it had been present for 6 years, but that in the past 3 months it had become moderately painful and that the pain was aggravated by walking. She said that the lump had not increased in size. She reported no history of trauma and no relevant medical history.On examination, the patient was fit and well, and all vital signs were within normal limits. The lump was firm and round and located on the proximal phalanx of her second toe of her left foot; there were no overlying skin changes. A man aged 42 years with alcohol use disorder and of no fixed abode was admitted to hospital for acute abdominal pain that started 12 h previously. Blood tests showed a high lipase concentration (745 IU/L), and an abdominal CT scan confirmed the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis with one acute necrotic collection, characterised as moderately severe acute pancreatitis according to the Atlanta classification.2 days later, the man presented with acute pain in both legs and local examination showed multiple purpuric erythematous macular lesions. On day 4, these lesions were characterised as subcutaneous erythematous nodules associated with inflammatory oedema of the left ankle although both legs were affected (figure, A).
A punch biopsy was performed and histology showed cytosteatonecrosis in the superficial part of the hypoderm (figure, B), characterised by lobular panniculitis with dense inflammation, and necrosis together with foaming macrophages and so-called ghost adipocytes (without nuclei). No lesions that would suggest vasculitis or T-cell lymphoma were reported. Blood tests ruled out autoimmune disease or vasculitis and the concentration of 汐1-antitrypsin was normal. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological cultures were negative. Skin lesions, oedema, and pain in the lower limbs resolved spontaneously after 7 days, confirming the diagnosis of pancreatic panniculitis.
Systemic panniculitis is caused by the release of pancreatic enzymes, leading to necrosis of hypodermic fat tissue and sometimes bone tissue. Systemic panniculitis mainly affects men aged 40每70 years who have a history of chronic alcohol use disorder. Lesions are typically dermo-hypodermic inflammatory nodules or plaques, predominantly on the lower limbs and fingers. In case of chronic pancreatitis or pancreatic carcinoma, dermatological lesions might precede the usual manifestations of underlying pancreatic disease by several weeks to several months. Systemic symptoms can occur, such as fever, arthralgia, or bone pain due to intraosseous fat necrosis. Histologically, a predominantly lobular pattern with fat necrosis and ghost adipocytes is pathognomonic. Treatment with glucocorticoids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is usually ineffective. Apart from the usual spontaneous resolution of skin lesions with the treatment of pancreatitis, octreotide has been proposed as an option due to an inhibitory effect on lipase activity, and tetracycline has also been proposed in the treatment of panniculitis.

A 68-year-old woman presented to our hospital with pain in her left hip. She said it had started 2 weeks previously and had gradually worsened. She gave no history of trauma; however, she did have a history of rheumatoid arthritis, which was well controlled with weekly injections of methotrexate. There was no history of corticosteroid use. She also had a history of squamous cell carcinoma of the anus, which had been treated with chemotherapy. The woman had finished a course of adjuvant external beam pelvic radiotherapy 6 months before seeing us. She did not smoke cigarettes and did not drink alcohol excessively. On examination, she was unable to weight bear due to pain, and had significant groin pain on passive hip flexion and internal and external rotation. An initial plain x-ray and MRI of the patient's pelvis was normal (figure) and provided no clues as to the cause of her symptoms. She was allowed home with simple analgesia; at an outpatient review 6 weeks later, her symptoms had improved.She re-attended 6 months later, reporting a sudden worsening of the pain over the previous 3 weeks. Her mobility was also significantly reduced. We repeated the x-ray of her pelvis, which showed striking avascular necrosis of her left hip, with resorption and proximal migration of the femoral head and erosion of the superior acetabulum (figure). We carried out cemented total hip arthroplasty with acetabular bone grafting because of the patient's severe pain, significantly reduced mobility, and progressive radiographic changes consistent with Association Research Circulation Osseous stage IV avascular necrosis (AVN). 1 year later, the patient required a revision total hip arthroplasty with acetabular reconstruction because of early failure of the acetabular component secondary to ongoing acetabular AVN (figure). We allowed her home 2 days after the operation and at her last follow-up appointment she had made good progress with her rehabilitation.
Hip AVN is a recognised complication of pelvic radiotherapy. Other important causes include trauma, excessive alcohol consumption, infiltrative diseases (such as Gaucher's disease), endogenous or exogenous steroid exposure, sickle cell disease, and viral infections. Symptoms can be vague and early findings of both x-ray and MRI can be subtle〞as in our patient. The final pathophysiological event is reduced blood supply to the femoral head, which leads to necrosis and collapse of the bone and articular cartilage, which is why MRI is now recognised as the most sensitive and specific method of diagnosing AVN.
Clinicians should maintain a low index of suspicion for this condition〞especially in patients with non-specific hip pain who have previously been treated with radiotherapy.

The skeleton of a human being buried over 1000 years ago, in the medieval archaeological site of Torre Velha, in north-eastern Portugal, was referred to us for analysis and investigation (appendix).On examination, we found the outstandingly well preserved skeleton of an adult who was likely to have been more than 25 years old at the time of death. The person was approximately 1﹞80 m tall. Notably, out of the six skeletons examined, where height could be ascertained, this individual was the tallest (appendix). Based on pelvic morphology and metric analysis of the skeleton, we concluded that the individual was a man. However, the bi-iliac width of our person was 289 mm, considerably larger than the average width previously reported for ancient Portuguese men (mean 261﹞8 mm; SD=13﹞4; Student's t test: t=22﹞6944; df=124; p<0﹞001). Additionally, the individual's teeth were worn asymmetrically, indicating probable malocclusion of the jaw and maxillary prognathism (figure; appendix). Bone densitometry analysis showed normal bone mineral density values (0﹞792每0﹞999 g/cm2).
Genetic analysis was undertaken using a variety of different methodologies〞including the calculation of X chromosome to Y chromosome autosome ratios (0﹞902 and 0﹞298, respectively), X chromosome and Y chromosome dosages (approximately 2 and 1, respectively), and X chromosome heterozygosity (approximately 0﹞2). We also determined the Y chromosome haplogroup to be R1b-P310 (R1b1a1b1a1), a frequent western-European and pan-European lineage, in accordance with the individual's Iberian genetic ancestry (appendix).
Furthermore, using a novel Bayesian method, allowing us to probabilistically assign individuals to karyotypes based on the number of sequencing reads〞or DNA fragments sequenced〞mapping to the X, Y, or autosomal chromosomes, we concluded our individual's karyotype to be 47,XXY, and rejected models of contamination of XXY and XX or XY (figure; appendix). The closeness of the observed position of the studied individual and theoretical position for an XXY karyotype (figure) strongly agrees with our posterior probability of approximately 1 for this individual having a Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype. Considering the morphological findings〞specifically the height, the bi-iliac width, the possible jaw malocclusion, and the maxillary prognathism〞the genetic findings〞indicating a karyotype of 47,XXY〞we concluded that the studied individual had Klinefelter's syndrome.
The prevalence of Klinefelter's syndrome in the general population has previously been reported to be 0﹞1每0﹞2%, but many patients remain undiagnosed.
Typically, people with Klinefelter's syndrome are tall, have broad hips, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynaecomastia; they may have mandibular prognathism. Obesity, low glucose tolerance, and diabetes are observed, as well as osteoporosis because of androgen deficiency. Notably, the absence of osteoporosis in our case does not preclude a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome; osteoporosis is only present in approximately 10每40% of cases. Genetically, about 80% of cases are 47,XXY.
DNA from osteological remains is often scarce, degraded, fragmented, and unsuitable for analysis using commonly available techniques for clinical diagnosis of chromosomal aneuploidies. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel Bayesian method, which, we believe, is a potentially efficient statistical way of analysing fragmented DNA from a variety of sources (eg, ancient DNA, cell-free DNA, and DNA from forensic cases).

PCR testing of a swab specimen from the lesion was positive for orthopoxvirus DNA and cowpox virus-specific oligonucleotides. Exposure to what animal is the likely route of transmission?
output:
Based on the clinical history and the positive PCR test for cowpox virus, the patient has a cowpox infection. Although the virus is named "cowpox," the natural reservoir lies in wild rodents. In modern cases, particularly involving children, transmission to humans most frequently occurs through contact with infected **domestic cats** (which acquire the virus from hunting rodents).

The skeleton of a human being buried over 1000 years ago, in the medieval archaeological site of Torre Velha, in north-eastern Portugal, was referred to us for analysis and investigation (appendix).On examination, we found the outstandingly well preserved skeleton of an adult who was likely to have been more than 25 years old at the time of death. The person was approximately 1﹞80 m tall. Notably, out of the six skeletons examined, where height could be ascertained, this individual was the tallest (appendix). Based on pelvic morphology and metric analysis of the skeleton, we concluded that the individual was a man. However, the bi-iliac width of our person was 289 mm, considerably larger than the average width previously reported for ancient Portuguese men (mean 261﹞8 mm; SD=13﹞4; Student's t test: t=22﹞6944; df=124; p<0﹞001). Additionally, the individual's teeth were worn asymmetrically, indicating probable malocclusion of the jaw and maxillary prognathism (figure; appendix). Bone densitometry analysis showed normal bone mineral density values (0﹞792每0﹞999 g/cm2).
Genetic analysis was undertaken using a variety of different methodologies〞including the calculation of X chromosome to Y chromosome autosome ratios (0﹞902 and 0﹞298, respectively), X chromosome and Y chromosome dosages (approximately 2 and 1, respectively), and X chromosome heterozygosity (approximately 0﹞2). We also determined the Y chromosome haplogroup to be R1b-P310 (R1b1a1b1a1), a frequent western-European and pan-European lineage, in accordance with the individual's Iberian genetic ancestry (appendix).
Furthermore, using a novel Bayesian method, allowing us to probabilistically assign individuals to karyotypes based on the number of sequencing reads〞or DNA fragments sequenced〞mapping to the X, Y, or autosomal chromosomes, we concluded our individual's karyotype to be 47,XXY, and rejected models of contamination of XXY and XX or XY (figure; appendix). The closeness of the observed position of the studied individual and theoretical position for an XXY karyotype (figure) strongly agrees with our posterior probability of approximately 1 for this individual having a Klinefelter's syndrome karyotype. Considering the morphological findings〞specifically the height, the bi-iliac width, the possible jaw malocclusion, and the maxillary prognathism〞the genetic findings〞indicating a karyotype of 47,XXY〞we concluded that the studied individual had Klinefelter's syndrome.
The prevalence of Klinefelter's syndrome in the general population has previously been reported to be 0﹞1每0﹞2%, but many patients remain undiagnosed.
Typically, people with Klinefelter's syndrome are tall, have broad hips, sparse body hair, small testes, and gynaecomastia; they may have mandibular prognathism. Obesity, low glucose tolerance, and diabetes are observed, as well as osteoporosis because of androgen deficiency. Notably, the absence of osteoporosis in our case does not preclude a diagnosis of Klinefelter's syndrome; osteoporosis is only present in approximately 10每40% of cases. Genetically, about 80% of cases are 47,XXY.
DNA from osteological remains is often scarce, degraded, fragmented, and unsuitable for analysis using commonly available techniques for clinical diagnosis of chromosomal aneuploidies. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel Bayesian method, which, we believe, is a potentially efficient statistical way of analysing fragmented DNA from a variety of sources (eg, ancient DNA, cell-free DNA, and DNA from forensic cases).

An 80-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of acute-onset severe polyarthralgia of the hands, feet, elbows, and shoulders with associated swelling of the dorsum of the hands and feet. The patient had a preceding history of anorexia and weight loss for 2 months associated with fatigue and prolonged morning stiffness. On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B每D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24每48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease〞especially a malignancy〞should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20每50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 6-week-old infant was seen in our emergency department with his family, who reported him to be lethargic and unwell; his abdomen was distended and he had not passed faeces for 4 days.
The patient had been born at full term weighing 3﹞3 kg (typical range 2﹞5每4﹞0) after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He had passed faeces 48 h after birth with a glycerine suppository; from that point on he had passed daily, watery stools, developed repeated vomiting, and had failed to gain weight.
On examination, the infant was emaciated〞weighing 3﹞5 kg (typical range at 6 weeks 2﹞3每4﹞9)〞with a significantly distended abdomen; he was febrile with a temperature of 38﹞5～C and tachycardic (heart rate 180 beats per min). The patient had no features of chromosomal abnormalities or suspicion of a neurodevelopmental disorder; he had no family history of gastrointestinal difficulties.
Laboratory investigations showed a leucocytosis of 28﹞0?℅?109 per L (typical range 6﹞0每17﹞5), and lactic acidosis with a venous lactate concentration of 3﹞3 mmol/L (typical range 0﹞5每2﹞2). An abdominal x-ray showed significant colonic distension; faeces were seen in the rectum but no air (figure).The patient was resuscitated in the neonatal intensive care unit and was given twice daily rectal irrigations with saline; he was also given intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole).
Further investigations included a suction rectal biopsy which found aganglionosis〞an absence of ganglion cells〞on three sections (section 1 at 1 cm, section 2 at 2 cm, and section 3 at 3 cm). Two transitions from dilated to narrowed colon were seen on contrast enema: one segment in the mid-sigmoid colon and the second in the descending colon (figure).
After a month of inpatient nutritional optimisation〞initially the patient had total parenteral nutrition, followed by a combination of oral and nasogastric lavage feeds with breastmilk and formula〞the patient had laparoscopic colonic biopsies taken and an end ileostomy. Histopathological examination of samples of the biopsies obtained during this operation confirmed Hirschsprung disease to the level of the distal splenic flexure. The patient was allowed home 7 weeks after the day of his initial admission.
At 11 months old, the patient had a planned laparotomy with Swenson pull-through of his distal transverse colon; this involved taking additional colonic biopsies to assess the location of the ganglion cells, resection of the aganglionic rectum, sigmoid, and descending colon, mobilisation of the splenic and hepatic flexures with takedown of the ligament for Treitz, and pull-through of the normal distal transverse colon to his anal canal with anastomosis 1 cm proximal to the dentate line.
At the age of 1 year and 1 month, the patient had an ileostomy reversal during a planned re-admission.
At his most recent follow-up, at 3 years of age, the patient had been doing well: he had been passing faeces regularly with no evidence of constipation; he was well-nourished and developing normally.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (HAEC) is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs in Hirschsprung disease. HAEC is characterised by abdominal distention, fever, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Other associated symptoms include colicky abdominal pain, lethargy, and passing blood-stained stools. The condition is caused by a large stool burden in an aganglionic segment of bowel leading to bacterial overgrowth and infection. Initial management requires prompt recognition, antibiotics, and rectal irrigations. Delayed diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease can result in life-threatening enterocolitis and severe malnutrition.

A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy〞with limited benefit〞for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised〞especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking〞as in our case〞despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.
output: Parkinson's disease with PRKN gene mutation (early-onset Parkinson's disease)

input: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1 year history of horns growing on the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right index and middle fingers. 3 years previously, the patient had undergone traumatic amputation of these fingers. The patient was not in an immunocompromised state. Physical examination showed opaque, yellowish, scabrous horny outgrowths on the amputated stumps of the proximal interphalangeal joints (figure A). The hyperkeratotic horns showed fungal hyphae on microscopy and grew?Trichophyton rubrum?in microbiological cultures. A diagnosis of ringworm of the finger was made. The lesions improved after treatment with oral itraconazole at 400 mg per day for 1 week and topical salicylic acid, without relapse (figure B).Ringworm species invade the stratum corneum of the skin, and damage keratinised tissues. T rubrum often induces the clinical feature of hyperkeratosis in tinea pedis. It is the main cause of onychomycosis and leads to thickened nail plates. Moreover, T rubrum can form cutaneous horns, as occurred in the present case.
output: Tinea manus (ringworm of the finger) with cutaneous horn formation caused by Trichophyton rubrum

On examination she had marked stiffness of the neck and shoulders and required high back support (figure A). The patient's hands and feet were swollen with pitting oedema giving a boxing glove appearance of the hands (figure B每D). There was tenderness in the wrists and hands over the metacarpophalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints with reduced range of motion. X-ray of the hands revealed soft tissue swelling with no joint erosions and x-ray of the spine revealed age related degenerative changes with no evidence of an axial spondyloarthopathy. Ultrasound of the shoulders and hands showed subdeltoid and subacromial bursitis with minimal fluid and extensor synovitis in both hands.The patient's blood results showed anaemia, markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (100 mm/hr) and C-reactive protein (50 mg/L); tests for rheumatoid factor, anticitrullinated protein antibody, antinuclear antibody, HLA B27, and multiple myeloma screen were all negative. Joint aspirate of the left wrist did not reveal any evidence of a crystal-related arthropathy. A diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica with remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis and pitting oedema (RS3PE) was made. The patient was started on 20 mg of prednisone per day; however, there was no appreciable response to treatment, and the patient's joint pains, stiffness, and swelling persisted.
The patient's 2-month history of anorexia and weight loss and, particularly, unresponsiveness to moderate dose steroids raised the possibility of a malignancy. On further evaluation and after doing an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and ultrasound of the abdomen, the patient was diagnosed with a metastatic, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the colon, indicating that her steroid resistant polymyalgia rheumatica with RS3PE was paraneoplastic in origin. Paraneoplastic RS3PE often does not respond to steroids alone and should be targeted by treating the underlying malignancy.
RS3PE is an uncommon condition that is characterised as an acute polysynovitis associated with pitting oedema that tends to affect individuals who are older than 50 years. This condition can occur in isolation or be associated with other connective tissue diseases, malignancies, or, more rarely, infections or drugs. Polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE is very sensitive to low-to-moderate doses of steroids, with a starting dose of prednisone of 15 to 20 mg/day typically showing a substantial response within 24每48 hours of treatment initiation. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine, medications that can be useful in patients with steroid resistance, have been studied in these patients; however, the response to steroids has been more pronounced and robust.
The absence of a response to moderate dose of steroids should call into question the diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica RS3PE or suggest a secondary cause of the disease. Before labelling a case as steroid resistant, a search for a secondary cause of the disease〞especially a malignancy〞should be made, because paraneoplastic RS3PE is not uncommon. In 20每50% of cases, RS3PE has been associated with a malignancy. 75% of cases of paraneoplastic RS3PE are due to solid tumours.

A 54-year-old man presented to our emergency department reporting several weeks of diffuse abdominal pain. He had no medical history of note.On physical examination we found his abdomen was soft with some slight tenderness and there were diffuse petechiae on his hands and feet. The patient was afebrile and his vital signs were stable.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised serum C-reactive protein concentration of 12﹞2 mg/dL (normal <0﹞6).
An abdominal CT scan showed signs of occult ileocecal perforation and segmented small bowel wall thickening. During an explorative laparotomy, we found multiple 5每10 cm haemorrhagic small bowel skip lesions (figure) without any perforations; we did not resect any of the affected segments because they showed active peristalsis.
Further laboratory testing showed the presence of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies against proteinase 3 of 241 IU/mL (normal <10), haematuria, proteinuria, urinary casts, and normal serum creatinine concentration. Urine output was unremarkable.
We made a diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting with intestinal manifestations; treatment with prednisolone significantly relieved the patient's abdominal pain and he was allowed home.
1 month later, the patient attended again with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis. A CT scan showed free intra-abdominal air. We undertook a further explorative laparotomy and found several ileal perforations; we carried out a small bowel resection and constructed an ileostomy.
Histopathological work-up of the excised bowel showed necrotic tissue with severe peritonitis and some small vessels with microthrombi and partially enhanced infiltrating granulocytes in the vessel walls; a renal biopsy sample confirmed granulomatosis with polyangiitis. At regular follow-up visits on treatment with prednisolone and cyclophosphamide, no new manifestations of systemic vasculitis were detected.
Skip lesions of the bowel are usually seen in inflammatory bowel disease, distal thromboembolic mesenteric ischaemia, and lupus enteritis.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small to medium vessel necrotising vasculitis whose exact aetiology is unclear; it mostly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys and there is a potential for multiorgan involvement. First intestinal manifestations leading to surgical complications are extremely rare and depending on the extent of involvement, granulomatosis with polyangiitis may be treated with immunosuppressive agents〞including glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, or rituximab〞the caveat being that such therapies might increase the risk of intestinal perforation (video).

A 41-year-old professional hockey referee was referred to our clinic with an 8-month history of walking difficulties; previously he had consulted several orthopaedic surgeons and had undergone physical therapy〞with limited benefit〞for a presumed knee injury. The patient had no notable medical history, but reported two maternal aunts with Parkinson's disease which had presented at over the age of 65 years; his parents and sister were healthy. On examination he appeared generally fit and well; however, a neurological examination found that he had hypomimia, mild rigidity, and bradykinesia on motor tasks in both legs, but predominantely in the right (video). The patient's gait showed dystonic posturing of the right foot with involuntary plantar flexion and inversion, and asymmetrically reduced arm swing; his walking difficulties improved by running and walking backwards (figure; video). Additionally, despite having difficulties walking, he reported no problems while riding his bicycle (video).Laboratory investigations showed no atypical findings, imaging likewise. Molecular genetic analysis showed compound heterozygous mutations of the parkin (PRKN) gene, confirming a diagnosis of early-onset Parkinson's disease. A levodopa and carbidopa combination, which was titrated up to 100 mg three times a day, provided sustained clinical benefit. At follow-up 6 months later, the patient reported feeling better, without fluctuations of motor function; the bradykinesia had improved and there was less dystonic posturing when walking. He had resumed his professional activities.
PRKN mutations are the commonest type of autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, accounting for between 14 and 25% of early-onset cases. A delay between symptom onset and diagnosis is often observed because dystonia and parkinsonism may be unrecognised〞especially in younger patients. Important clinical clues may be overlooked; for example, people with Parkinson's disease may find running or riding a bicycle easier than walking〞as in our case〞despite clear motor impairment, which is suggestive of dystonia.
The combination of parkinsonism with lower-limb dystonia in a young patient should alert clinicians to the possibility of Parkinson's disease with a genetic aetiology. Early-onset Parkinson's disease, caused by PRKN mutations, is a possibility, especially if hyper-reflexia, diurnal fluctuations, and levodopa-induced lower-limb dyskinesia are present.

input: A 56-year-old woman presented with a 1 year history of horns growing on the proximal interphalangeal joints of the right index and middle fingers. 3 years previously, the patient had undergone traumatic amputation of these fingers. A 69-year-old woman with axial and peripheral spondyloarthritis (diagnosed in 2016) was in remission on anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy (adalimumab 40 mg every other week). She presented to our rheumatology unit with a 3-month history of inflammatory back pain and polyarthralgia associated with morning stiffness lasting more than 1 h.These symptoms were associated with asthenia, cough, and a weight loss of 10 kg in the past 3 months. On examination, restricted movement of the lumbar and dorsal spine and tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment of the left wrist were noted. Both the Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Score (ASDAS) and the Bath Ankylosing Spondylitis Disease Activity Index (BASDAI) reflected active disease (ASDAS=4﹞7 and BASDAI=7). Her serum C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was unusually high (24 mg/L). Because the patient was immunocompromised, we performed chest and abdominal CT scans to rule out neoplasm or infection. The chest CT revealed an intracardiac, heterogeneous, obstructive mass in the left atrium, measuring 70 mm by 49 mm suggesting a myxoma, and this was confirmed on cardiac MRI (figure, A). The mass was not present on a CT scan performed in 2017. Considering the overproduction of interleukin (IL)-6 by cardiac myxomas, we measured serum IL-6 concentration, which was 23 pg/mL (normal range <7 pg/mL).
The patient underwent surgical excision (figure, B), and the histopathological assessment confirmed the diagnosis of myxoma, which was positive for calretinin. Adalimumab was discontinued because of the infection risk during surgery. Postoperative follow-up found normalisation of CRP concentration (<3 mg/L) and a decrease in arthralgia intensity. 1 month after surgery, the patient was in remission (ASDAS <1﹞3, BASDAI=2﹞4), with a normal serum IL-6 concentration (<7 pg/mL), without reintroduction of adalimumab. Adalimumab was reintroduced 4 months after the surgery to avoid the relapse of the spondyloarthritis. 1 year after the surgery, the patient is still in remission with normal CRP concentration. Cardiac myxoma is rare with an incidence rate of 0﹞5 per million people, but it is the most common primary benign neoplasm of the heart. Most myxomas are asymptomatic and found incidentally; however, some can mimic systemic diseases. Because of the embolic risk and the risk of cardiac arrest, standard treatment is surgical excision.
output: It is a frequent malignant neoplasm

input: A 63-year-old man with a history of follicular lymphoma presented with 2 weeks of fatigue and 3 days of dyspnea. On physical examination, he had decreased breath sounds at the base of both lungs. A chest radiograph revealed pleural effusions, which were greater on the right side than on the left. Thoracentesis of the right side resulted in the removal of 1 liter of milky, yellow fluid. A chylothorax was suspected. Which of the following pleural fluid tests is most commonly used to diagnose a chylothorax?
output:
Triglyceride level

The most commonly used pleural fluid test to diagnose a chylothorax is the **triglyceride level**. A pleural fluid triglyceride concentration >110 mg/dL (1.24 mmol/L) is diagnostic of chylothorax, while a level <50 mg/dL essentially excludes the diagnosis.

In this patient with follicular lymphoma, the chylothorax is likely due to lymphomatous obstruction or infiltration of the thoracic duct or lymphatic system.

input: A 64-year-old male farmer presented to our hospital in April, 2013, with a 3 month history of painless, progressive swelling of his chest wall and lower jaw, and 10 kg unintentional weight loss. On examination he had multiple lumps about 3?℅?1﹞5 cm around the angle of the mandible, and multiple 10?℅?8 cm lumps at the mid sternal region and of the left lower anterior chest wall (figure). These lumps were non-tender to palpation, hard, and tethered, with irregular contours, no tempertature changes or overlying skin changes. Blood tests were normal and HIV serology was negative. CT Chest showed a soft tissue mass 8?℅?10﹞6?℅?8 cm encasing and eroding the body of sternum with presternal and retrosternal soft tissue components (appendix), and whole-body PET CT fusion showed increased 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) uptake (appendix). Histological and immunohistochemical examination of a biopsy specimen from the chest wall swelling showed tightly-packed small round cells with high mitotic activity infiltrating fat and starry sky appearance (figure), positive for CD20, Bcl-2, Mum-1, and Bcl-6, and negative for CD10, CD3, Cyclin-D1, and TdT, with Ki-67 nearly 100%. Conventional cytogenetics showed complex structural and numerical abnormalities including characteristic t (8;14) (appendix). We diagnosed high risk group adult Burkitt lymphoma stage IV, and started treatment with modified Magrath regimen of four alternating cycles of R-CODOX-M and R-IMVAC chemotherapy. The patient achieved complete remission with disappearance of sternal swellings, normal peripheral blood counts, normal bone marrow aspirate, and no evidence of 18FDG uptake on repeat PET scan. He remained in remission at last 3 month follow-up in December, 2013.

An 85-year-old man was admitted to hospital with a 5-day history of fever and neck pain. He had a 12-year history of chronic kidney disease and gouty arthritis; however, the patient did not take urate lowering drugs. On admission to hospital, physical examination revealed neck pain and stiffness. He had a blood pressure of 140/102 mm Hg, pulse rate of 95 per min, respiration rate of 18 breaths per min, and body temperature of 38～C. Laboratory results revealed a white blood cell count of 11?200 cells per mm3 (reference 4?000每10?000) and C-reactive protein level of 12﹞26 mg/dL (reference 0﹞0每0﹞3). MRI findings suggested cervical osteomyelitis and meningitis (figure A). Cervical spine CT revealed curvilinear calcifications of the transverse ligament of the atlas (figure B). After assessing blood cultures, ceftriaxone (2 g every 12 h) and vancomycin (1750 mg loading, followed by 750 mg every 48 h) were administered intravenously as empirical antibiotic treatments. On the second day of admission, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis did not reveal meningitis (white blood cell count 8 cells per 米L, glucose concentration 79 mg/dL, and protein concentration 168 mg/dL), and CSF culture and molecular tests were negative for bacteria and mycobacteria. The patient was diagnosed with crowned dens syndrome and administered 20 mg prednisolone, and his symptoms dramatically improved. However, CSF examination under polarising microscopy revealed monosodium urate crystals (figure C). Dual-energy CT confirmed the calcifications to be monosodium urate crystals (figure D). The patient's uric acid concentration was 10﹞4 mg/dL (reference 0每7﹞0) and subcutaneous tophi were not apparent on physical examination 9 days after hospital admission. Crowned dens syndrome is a rare finding in calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease and could be clinically similar to meningitis, so it should be suspected when the evidence for infection is unclear. Our patient had a history of gout, and monosodium urate crystals were confirmed by CSF analysis and dual-energy CT, suggesting that the symptoms were caused by gout flare in the cervical spine. Thus, physicians should consider that intrathecal monosodium urate crystal formation can cause meningitis-like symptoms in patients with gout history.
output: Crowned dens syndrome caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition (spinal gout)

An 87-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. She had a history of chronic kidney disease, pulmonary embolism, and recent right-sided ischaemic stroke causing aphasia and hemiparesis. She was taking aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin.On examination we found the patient to be well and afebrile. Her blood pressure was 134/86 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 95% on room air, and she had bilateral rhonchi prominent in her lung bases.
Laboratory investigations found a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 11﹞4 g/dL; normal 12每16), serum creatinine concentration was 1﹞34 mg/dL (normal 0﹞6每1﹞5), and the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 36 mL/min per 1﹞73 m2. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with no signs of ischaemia and chest x-ray showed patchy multifocal airspace opacities in both lungs〞indicating possible pneumonia. A chest CT with intravenous contrast showed no abnormalities〞ruling out the possibility of a pulmonary embolus〞and the upper parts of the patient's kidneys, seen on the same image, also showed no obvious lesions, and notably no intraparenchymal contrast medium (figure). The lung windows of the CT showed ground glass changes.
Over the next 48 h, the patient became oliguric and her serum creatinine concentration increased to 2﹞4 mg/dL. A non-contrast CT of the patient's abdomen and pelvis (figure) showed renal parenchymal enhancement from retained intravenous contrast medium 53 h after administration. The patient's urine sodium concentration was 36 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium was 0﹞7%. Considering the findings, we made a diagnosis of contrast-associated acute kidney injury (AKI) in the context of a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
The patient was started on supportive AKI care〞including adjustment of medication doses, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and judicious administration of fluids〞and antitussives and paracetamol for the chest infection. Her dyspnoea improved and her serum creatinine concentration peaked at 3﹞7 mg/dL, with an eGFR of 10 mL/min per 1﹞73 m2, 4 days after the administration of the contrast. 7 days after the initial contrast CT, the serum creatinine concentration returned to the preadmission baseline of 1﹞3 mg/dL. The patient was then transferred to a nursing facility and seen again 3 weeks later; at that time her kidney function was stable.
Retained intravenous contrast can be seen on a plain radiograph or a non-contrasted CT study of the abdomen more than 24 h after the administration in situations of significant renal impairment〞including end stage renal disease or AKI〞when the glomerular filtration rate is 45 mL/min per 1﹞73 m2 or less. Retained contrast accompanied by an acute rise in the serum creatinine concentration〞in the absence of other causes of AKI〞is highly suggestive of contrast-associated nephropathy. Oliguria and a low fractional excretion of sodium are also typical features. Contrast may be retained in the kidneys for several days〞although is it usually cleared within 24每72 h after the injury.

A 17-year-old man reporting a 3-year history of an acneiform eruption and a 4-month history of worsening swelling of his face, was referred to our specialist joint haematology-dermatology clinic. The patient had been found to have a monocytopenia of 0﹞2?℅?109 per L (normal 0﹞2每1﹞0); he had no other past medical problems.On examination he was generally well and vital signs were within normal limits. He had inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones on both cheeks, forehead, and chin. He also had severe facial lymphoedema extending from the jawline to the anterior hairline with debilitating periorbital swelling that limited eye opening (figure). Additionally, numerous cutaneous viral warts were noted on his hands and knees.
Laboratory investigations showed mild macrocytosis and the monocytopenia: haemoglobin concentration was 150 g/L (normal 130每165), mean corpuscular volume 99﹞7 fL (normal 77每95), neutrophils 3﹞08?℅?109 per L (normal 2﹞2每6﹞3), platelets 180?℅?109 per L (normal 150每450). Thyroid function, anti-nuclear antibodies, immunoglobulins, and inflammatory markers were unremarkable.
Histopathological analysis of samples of skin biopsies from the chin and lower eyelid showed superficial and deep perifollicular and periadenexal lymphocytic inflammation as well as ectatic blood vessels in the superficial dermis: indicative of the clinical diagnosis of rosacea. No organisms were seen on periodic-acid-Schiff with diastase, Grocott, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains. Prolonged tissue culture did not isolate bacteria, mycobacterium, or fungi.
Notably, the patient had a family history of both myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML): his mother was diagnosed with MDS aged 27 years, AML aged 36 years, and she died aged 37 years; a maternal aunt was diagnosed with MDS aged 26 years and had an allogeneic transplant; his maternal grandmother was diagnosed with AML aged 24 and died one year later; and a maternal great aunt, who was diagnosed at an unknown age, with AML.
Putting the findings together〞monocytopenia, human papilloma viral infection, lymphoedema, and family history of myelodysplastic syndromes〞we suspected the patient had GATA2 deficiency.
Bone marrow studies confirmed MDS: refractory cytopenia of multilineage dysplasia and normal cytogenetics. Genetic testing showed a heterozygous pathogenic GATA2 variant (c.1061 C>T; p.Thr354Met).
The patient was started on low dose oral isotretinoin, vigilant monitoring of his full blood count, and regular manual lymphatic drainage of his face which after one year had significantly improved the rosacea and lymphoedema (figure). The response was sustained 2 years after completion of the therapy.
GATA2 is a zinc finger transcription factor required for haematopoiesis and lymphatic angiogenesis; several pathogenic mutations leading to GATA2 deficiency have been described. The syndrome segregates as an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous, and patients usually present in adolescence or early adulthood. Cutaneous infections, panniculitis, and lymphoedema in the setting of cytopenia, especially monocytopenia, should trigger suspicion of GATA2 deficiency. Lymphoedema associated with GATA2 deficiency is usually confined to the lower limbs and genitalia〞known as Emberger syndrome〞and marked facial lymphoedema, as seen in our patient, has not previously been reported. Most patients with GATA2 haploinsufficiency develop myeloid neoplasms before the age of 50 years and may require haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation which can be curative.

A 17-year-old man reporting a 3-year history of an acneiform eruption and a 4-month history of worsening swelling of his face, was referred to our specialist joint haematology-dermatology clinic. The patient had been found to have a monocytopenia of 0﹞2?℅?109 per L (normal 0﹞2每1﹞0); he had no other past medical problems.On examination he was generally well and vital signs were within normal limits. He had inflammatory papules and pustules without comedones on both cheeks, forehead, and chin. He also had severe facial lymphoedema extending from the jawline to the anterior hairline with debilitating periorbital swelling that limited eye opening (figure). Additionally, numerous cutaneous viral warts were noted on his hands and knees.
Laboratory investigations showed mild macrocytosis and the monocytopenia: haemoglobin concentration was 150 g/L (normal 130每165), mean corpuscular volume 99﹞7 fL (normal 77每95), neutrophils 3﹞08?℅?109 per L (normal 2﹞2每6﹞3), platelets 180?℅?109 per L (normal 150每450). Thyroid function, anti-nuclear antibodies, immunoglobulins, and inflammatory markers were unremarkable.
Histopathological analysis of samples of skin biopsies from the chin and lower eyelid showed superficial and deep perifollicular and periadenexal lymphocytic inflammation as well as ectatic blood vessels in the superficial dermis: indicative of the clinical diagnosis of rosacea. No organisms were seen on periodic-acid-Schiff with diastase, Grocott, and Ziehl-Neelsen stains. Prolonged tissue culture did not isolate bacteria, mycobacterium, or fungi.
Notably, the patient had a family history of both myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and acute myeloid leukaemia (AML): his mother was diagnosed with MDS aged 27 years, AML aged 36 years, and she died aged 37 years; a maternal aunt was diagnosed with MDS aged 26 years and had an allogeneic transplant; his maternal grandmother was diagnosed with AML aged 24 and died one year later; and a maternal great aunt, who was diagnosed at an unknown age, with AML.
Putting the findings together〞monocytopenia, human papilloma viral infection, lymphoedema, and family history of myelodysplastic syndromes〞we suspected the patient had GATA2 deficiency.
Bone marrow studies confirmed MDS: refractory cytopenia of multilineage dysplasia and normal cytogenetics. Genetic testing showed a heterozygous pathogenic GATA2 variant (c.1061 C>T; p.Thr354Met).
The patient was started on low dose oral isotretinoin, vigilant monitoring of his full blood count, and regular manual lymphatic drainage of his face which after one year had significantly improved the rosacea and lymphoedema (figure). The response was sustained 2 years after completion of the therapy.
GATA2 is a zinc finger transcription factor required for haematopoiesis and lymphatic angiogenesis; several pathogenic mutations leading to GATA2 deficiency have been described. The syndrome segregates as an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance. Clinical manifestations are heterogeneous, and patients usually present in adolescence or early adulthood. Cutaneous infections, panniculitis, and lymphoedema in the setting of cytopenia, especially monocytopenia, should trigger suspicion of GATA2 deficiency. Lymphoedema associated with GATA2 deficiency is usually confined to the lower limbs and genitalia〞known as Emberger syndrome〞and marked facial lymphoedema, as seen in our patient, has not previously been reported. Most patients with GATA2 haploinsufficiency develop myeloid neoplasms before the age of 50 years and may require haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation which can be curative.

A 74-year-old female patient presented in November, 2017, with a 3-month history of pain in the upper left thigh. X-ray revealed three osteolytic lesions of the left femur, one of which was breaking the cortical bone. No organomegaly was noted on physical examination. Blood counts and biochemical tests were normal except for mild hypergammaglobulinemia (16﹞9%) with positive immunofixation for monoclonal immunoglobulin A (0﹞2 g/dL in the serum, but urine negative).Multiple myeloma was suspected, and whole-body PET scan documented increased fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in several bone sites (SUVmax 4﹞9每10﹞9): at the head of humeri, sacrum, iliac wings, right acetabulum, and proximal femurs (figure, A), with extension into the soft tissues surrounding the broken cortex of the left femur.
A routine marrow biopsy from the iliac crest was unexpectedly normal on immunohistology for the plasma cell marker CD138 and the B-cell marker CD20. However, a core biopsy of the left femural neck documented a massive infiltration by mature lymphoid cells with ample cytoplasm and hairy projections positive for CD20, annexin-1 (figure, B), and BRAFV600E, thereby establishing a diagnosis of hairy cell leukaemia.
Morphological and flow-cytometric analyses of peripheral blood did not show any hairy cells, and a sensitive allele-specific PCR assay for BRAFV600E was also negative in both the blood and iliac marrow aspirate.
The patient received chemotherapy with cladribine (0﹞14 mg/kg per day for 5 consecutive days subcutaneously) and her pain gradually subsided. A PET scan 8 weeks later showed substantially decreased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose at multiple bone lesions.
Although skeletal involvement can occur in hairy cell leukaemia (in around 3% of cases), patients with hairy cell leukaemia, who are mostly males, usually also present with cytopenias, splenomegaly, circulating hairy cells, and diffuse leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Focal bone lesions accompanied by none of these characteristic features, but rather by a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance as occurred in this woman, represent a challenging differential diagnosis with more frequent neoplasms, especially multiple myeloma.
output: Hairy cell leukaemia with focal bone lesions

A 60-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-day history of mild, diffuse abdominal pain and discomfort in her abdomen. The patient's medical history was unremarkable apart from a cholelithiasis-related cholecystectomy which had been done 12 years earlier.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; her pulse was 75 beats per min and blood pressure 145/80 mm Hg. She was febrile with a temperature of 38﹞0～C; she had diffuse left-sided abdominal tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a mildly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 16 mg/dL (normal <6) and a raised white blood cell (WBC) count of 12﹞6?℅?109 per L (normal range 4每11); carcinoembryonic antigen concentration was within normal range (1﹞2 ng/mL; typical value for non-smoker or ex-smoker <3﹞8 and for smokers <5﹞5).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3﹞3 cm?℅?2﹞8 cm?℅?8﹞0 cm intramural peripherally enhancing hypodense lesion together with pericolic fat stranding and haziness which had caused mild upstream large bowel distention〞we presumed it was an abscess in the large bowel wall; features〞colonic wall outpouchings〞consistent with a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis were also seen (figure). Importantly, no extraluminal air was seen. Considering the patient's clinical condition, particularly the absence of signs of peritonitis, we decided to manage her conservatively; she was started on intravenous fluids and treated empirically with piperacillin and tazobactam. Over the next few days, the patient's symptoms improved; her temperature, WBC count, and CRP concentration reduced. A repeat CT scan 7 days after admission showed almost complete resolution of original findings〞indicating spontaneous resolution of the abscess and further confirming the initial diagnosis (figure). The patient was allowed home 8 days after admission and prescribed oral antimicrobial treatment (ciprofloxacin and metronidazole).
6 weeks later, an outpatient colonoscopy showed mild residual stenosis at the site of the previous intramural abscess with no other abnormalities; the patient reported no symptoms or difficulty passing faeces.
Abscesses complicate 15每30% of acute diverticulitis cases; intramural lesions are infrequently reported. Secondary partial intestinal obstruction may occur, but severe obstruction is rare. In most cases, abscesses spontaneously resolve. Conservative treatment is favoured in smaller-sized abscesses (<3每4 cm); further intervention may be needed for larger ones.
The treatment approach depends upon abscess location and the overall medical condition of the patient; conservative management is preferable. The differential diagnosis of such a lesion should include various types of colitis-related abscesses, inflammatory bowel disease, contained perforations, infected enteric duplication cysts, and, most significantly, colon cancer. Importantly, in patients with radiologically confirmed acute diverticulitis, colonic cancer has been found to have a 1-year incidence rate ranging from 1﹞6% to 2﹞7%. To exclude an underlying colonic malignancy, patients with acute diverticulitis are advised to undergo colonoscopy approximately 6每8 weeks following their episode.

A 30-year-old white man with no ocular history presented to eye casualty in Sidcup in October, 2012, with bilateral central visual loss, following inhalation of poppers. On examination his visual acuity was 6/12 on the right and 6/18 in the left eye. Slit lamp biomicroscopy showed subtle macular changes in the form of yellow foveal spots (figure). Spectral domain optical coherence tomography showed clear disruption of the foveal cone inner segment每outer segment layer (figure). At follow-up 6 months later, the patient's visual acuity and examination findings remained unchanged, despite cessation of poppers use.
Poppers (slang for various alkyl nitrite compounds) are commonly used in the gay community, for their ability to relax the anal sphincter and known psychoactive effects. Following changes to legislation in 2006, poppers' main ingredient, isobutyl nitrite, was substituted for isopropyl nitrite. Since then, there have been several reports of a new form of visual loss termed poppers maculopathy. The exact mechanism by which poppers cause damage to central photoreceptors is unknown, but there is a clear cause每effect relationship. Despite online warnings outlining the risks of poppers, the number of individuals presenting with associated visual loss is increasing. Fundoscopy findings can be very subtle, with more striking changes seen on optical coherence tomography. The relatively easy availability and widespread use of poppers is underestimated and concerning, given the propensity for permanent damage to the eyes. We would encourage both end-users and healthcare professionals to be aware of the potentially serious and irreversible damage poppers can have on vision.
