A 51-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 4-day history of fever, chills, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhoea.1 week before these problems began, the patient had a nevus removed from her right arm. The dermatologists were concerned it may have been a melanoma; she had a history of primary biliary cholangitis treated with ursodeoxycholic acid.
On examination, we found the patient to be unwell but responsive; her blood pressure was 85/59 mm Hg, her pulse was 107 beats per min, temperature was 39﹞0～C, respiratory rate 27 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 94%.
A CT scan of the patient's chest showed air space opacities with air bronchogram indicating a pneumonia in the left and right lower lobes (figure); a CT of the abdomen showed circumferential wall thickening of the right colon and surrounding fat stranding, indicating colitis. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pyogenes.
10 h after admission, the patient's condition deteriorated and she developed septic shock; she was given intravenous antibiotics, crystalloid fluid, and norepinephrine, and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU). 24 h after admission, she went into cardiogenic shock with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 25% with hypokinesis of the basal and midventricular segments〞typical of an inverted takotsubo cardiomyopathy (appendix); on admission her LVEF had been 50%.
Troponin blood concentration was 104?819 ng/L (normal <74). Coronary angiography showed no abnormalities. We made a diagnosis of septic cardiomyopathy, and the patient was treated with dobutamine. After some initial improvement her condition worsened and she was readmitted to the ICU because of pulmonary oedema and a persistent fever (temperature was 38﹞8～C): LVEF was still decreased at 25%. A whole-body CT scan showed diffuse myocardial calcifications of the left ventricle (figure) but no focus of secondary pulmonary or abdominal infection.
Histopathological examination of a sample obtained at endomyocardial biopsy confirmed myocardial calcifications (figure). Considering the findings in the round, we made a diagnosis of diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe streptococcal sepsis, and high-dose〞2 mg/kg〞corticosteroids were started. The fever abated and the patient's clinical status improved; she was allowed home 3 months after admission. Corticosteroids were decreased and stopped at 3 months and the patient was treated with dapagliflozin, ramipril, and a cardioverter-defibrillator was implanted. 10 months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic and her LVEF was 40%; the microcalcifications were still present (appendix).
Diffuse myocardial calcifications following severe sepsis are uncommon and associated with a poor prognosis. High-dose pulses of corticosteroids are recommended but evidence for effectiveness remains weak in the absence of prospective clinical trials (video).

The combination of multiple brain abscesses and branching Gram-positive filaments is pathognomonic for **Cerebral nocardiosis**.

A 26-year-old man came to our emergency department accompanied by coworkers, who said their colleague was having difficulties with his speech. They explained that the factory employee had first complained to them about visual problems on his right side before he stopped talking altogether. They said the whole episode had started 1 h before.On examination, the patient was globally aphasic〞he was unable to speak and could not follow verbal requests. He repeatedly held his left hand up against the left side of his forehead indicating to us that he had pain there. On examination he was afebrile and he had no signs of meningism, no cranial nerve abnormalities, no sensorimotor deficits, and no pyramidal signs. Routine laboratory tests were all normal〞including blood glucose concentration, full blood count, liver and renal functions, coagulations tests, electrolytes, and C-reactive protein concentration.
MRI of the brain 1 h after admission showed no parenchymal abnormalities on diffusion-weighted imaging or T2-fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences, but there was conspicuous cortical venous dilatation in the left hemisphere on susceptibility-weighted MRI (figure). Contrast-enhanced perfusion-weighted MRI showed hypoperfusion in large areas of the left hemisphere, which did not correspond to any specific arterial territory (figure). Magnetic resonance angiography excluded any intracranial or extracranial large vessel occlusions or constrictions (figure).
The patient's aphasia gradually resolved 2 h after he came to the emergency department, but he then reported a severe pulsating left-sided hemicrania. When he was able to speak again, the patient explained that he had first noticed impaired vision of the right side of both his eyes. He then felt tingling in the fingers of his right hand which spread up his arm and then to his face; a few minutes later he began having difficulty speaking.
Notably the patient had no medical history. Although there was a family history of migraine. 10 h later a repeat MRI showed no parenchymal abnormalities〞but at this stage temporal lobe hyperperfusion was apparent, further supporting our original presumed diagnosis of a migraine with a prolonged aura. The patient was discharged on the next day symptom free.
In the context of a clear history of a gradual evolution of neurological symptoms over minutes, starting with visual impairment, followed by spreading sensory deficits and speech impairment, and succeeded by pulsating headache〞especially in a young adult with a family history〞migraine aura should be suspected. MRI findings of hypoperfusion and cortical venous dilatation in multiple vessel territories without diffusion or parenchymal abnormalities and the absence of vessel occlusions support the diagnosis of migraine with aura and exclude the important differential diagnosis of ischaemic stroke (video).

A 50-year-old man presented to our emergency department complaining of sudden onset of shortness of breath and pain in the back of his right shoulder. Notably, he did not report any neck pain, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs; he had no abdominal pain or fever.In his medical history, he had C6每C7 radiculopathy treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 2 years earlier; he reported no previous cardiac problems, hypertension, or alcohol use.
On examination we found the patient to have a raised body-mass index (29 kg/m2). He was not acutely distressed: his respiratory rate was 17 breaths per min, his heart rate was 64 beats per min, and his blood pressure was 130/84 mm Hg. A neurological examination found him to have full strength in both arms and legs, with normal sensation; his reflexes were normal.
A chest x-ray showed an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm compared to one done 2 years earlier when the patient had the cervical radiculopathy (figure).
A cervical MRI showed herniation of the C3每C4 disc with severe right C4 nerve root compression; the MRI from 2 years earlier showed a normal C3每C4 disc without stenosis (figure). Electrodiagnostic testing found right carpal tunnel syndrome〞with no evidence of brachial plexopathy. ECG was normal. His vitamin B12 concentration was low at 194 pg/mL, as was his iron concentration at 40 米g/dL.
After discussion of the treatment options with the patient, he elected for surgical management〞alternatives explored included conservative treatment with physiotherapy and monitoring of the diaphragm function, or surgical excision of the herniated disc, which might have resulted in additional paralysis of the diaphragm. C3每C4 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were done, which resulted in the complete resolution of the patient's shoulder pain and shortness of breath. A follow-up x-ray showed that the problematic elevation of the right hemidiaphragm had resolved.
Shoulder pain and shortness of breath〞particularly as acute presentations〞are a combination of symptoms indicating a wide variety of pathologies affecting numerous organs including the heart, lungs, pancreas, gallbladder, and gastrointestinal tract. Regarding the shortness of breath, paralysis of the diaphragm can occur as a result of malignancies, cardiac surgery, cervical spine surgery, and trauma to the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which originates from the C3, C4, and C5 nerve roots. However, the C4 root is the predominant origin of most function in most people. Regarding the shoulder pain, patients with C4 radiculopathy can present with pain in the axial cervical spine which can extend into the trapezial and scapular regions of the back; there is also the possibility that the pain may involve the anterior part of the chest.
output: Right hemidiaphragm paralysis secondary to C3-C4 disc herniation with C4 nerve root compression

A 25-year-old man attended our department with persistent, severe abdominal pain, which had started suddenly 1 h before, located in the umbilical area. The pain was followed by a 20 min period when the patient passed fresh blood from his rectum. When he arrived at the hospital, he was in a state of shock. His peripheral pulses were weak, his heart rate was 130 beats per min, and he needed emergency supportive treatment〞including 10 units of red blood cells. After 30 min, his bleeding stopped spontaneously, and he became haemodynamically stable.On examination, we found the patient's conjunctiva and mucosa were pale, and he had cutaneous neurofibromas〞one on his left jaw and one on his right flank〞and caf谷-au-lait macules on his chest, neck, back, and arms (figure). He also had axillary freckling. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral Lisch nodules〞iris hamartomas. Notably, he said that his father had similar lesions on his body; this information was later confirmed by the patient's uncle. No other members of the family had similar lesions.
Laboratory investigations showed that the patient was anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL. We did a gastroscopy, a colonoscopy, mesenteric artery angiography, and technetium-labelled red blood cell scintigraphy but did not find any abnormalities. However, a CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3 cm diameter mass with soft tissue density in the proximal jejunum; a double balloon enteroscopy confirmed the presence of a tumour (figure). Histopathological examination of biopsy samples from the lesion indicated a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST). Considering the findings on physical examination and the patient's family history, we made a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1. We did a segmental small bowel resection and the tumour was successfully removed. Detailed histopathological examination of a sample of the excised tumour showed spindle cells with mitotic activity, and immunohistochemical staining showed the spindle cells were c-kit and CD34 positive.
We have been following up the patient in our outpatient department for the past 2 years, and he remains well with no further complaints.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominantly inherited disorder characterised by skin lesions and peripheral nerve sheath tumours. Diagnosis is primarily based on the US National Institutes of Health diagnostic criteria: caf谷-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules, and a positive family history of the disease. If patients only have caf谷-au-lait macules and skin fold freckling, then the diagnosis is Legius syndrome.
Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 tend to develop rare tumours, including GISTs, and neuroendocrine tumours that originate from endocrine cells within the gastrointestinal tract. GISTs occur at an earlier age in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, are frequently located in the small intestine, and present with abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding. The characteristic skin lesions of neurofibromatosis type 1〞although superficial〞may be profoundly important as a diagnostic aid (video).
output: Neurofibromatosis type 1 with gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)

A 30-year-old man presented to our department in Leiden, Netherlands, with a 6-year history of recurrent solitary swellings. On average, he had 15 episodes per year. The swellings had started on his abdomen and had gradually moved to his chest, neck, and, more recently, his face. The swellings varied in size, were painless, appeared spontaneously, and resolved after 5每7 days. Treatment with high-dose antihistamine had had no effect. There were no other symptoms. The patient was otherwise healthy and did not take any medication.Physical examination revealed a swelling of the right cheek and upper lip. Photos of previous episodes revealed similar swellings of the left cheek (figure, A). The differential diagnoses included angio-oedema, granulomatous cheilitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and Kimura's disease, but these could not be confirmed by laboratory examination, histopathology, or clinical examination by a dental surgeon. Laboratory examinations, including eosinophil count and C1 esterase inhibitor concentrations, were completely normal except for IgE concentrations, which were elevated (3736 IU/mL, normal range is 0每99). A biopsy of the buccal mucosa showed a dense eosinophilic infiltrate. Ultrasound examination and MRI scan revealed a non-specific infiltration and enhancement of the subcutis.
The elevated IgE concentration and eosinophil in-filtration in the biopsy suggested a parasitic infection. A further inquiry revealed that the patient had consumed raw fish in Taiwan before the first swelling episode. Western blot analysis of serum for reactivity against crude antigens of Gnathostoma spinigerum third-stage larvae (L3) showed the presence of a specific 24 kDa band that was diagnostic for gnathostomiasis. Gnathostomiasis is a helminthic zoonosis, endemic in southeast Asia, which is transmitted through ingestion of larvae of G spinigerum in raw or undercooked fresh water fish, eels, frogs, reptiles, or birds. After ingestion, larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal wall and migrate through the subcutaneous tissue, causing typical migratory swellings and eosinophilia that can recur for years.
A revision of the MRI scan identified a larva of approximately 4﹞0℅0﹞2 cm (figure, B). The patient was treated with ivermectin 0﹞2 mg/kg once per day on 2 consecutive days. This treatment was successful because it stimulated the outward migration of the larva (an impression of the head of the larva became visible in the lower lip; appendix), which caused a temporary increase of the swelling. Eosinophilia was now present (1﹞03℅109 cells per L, normal value is <0﹞50 ℅ 109 cells per L). Further treatment, aiming to preclude potential migration towards the eye socket, consisted of albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days. The symptoms resolved within a few days and the patient remains symptom free.

Notably, he did not report any neck pain, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs; he had no abdominal pain or fever.In his medical history, he had C6每C7 radiculopathy treated with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion 2 years earlier; he reported no previous cardiac problems, hypertension, or alcohol use.
On examination we found the patient to have a raised body-mass index (29 kg/m2). He was not acutely distressed: his respiratory rate was 17 breaths per min, his heart rate was 64 beats per min, and his blood pressure was 130/84 mm Hg. A neurological examination found him to have full strength in both arms and legs, with normal sensation; his reflexes were normal.
A chest x-ray showed an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm compared to one done 2 years earlier when the patient had the cervical radiculopathy (figure).
A cervical MRI showed herniation of the C3每C4 disc with severe right C4 nerve root compression; the MRI from 2 years earlier showed a normal C3每C4 disc without stenosis (figure). Electrodiagnostic testing found right carpal tunnel syndrome〞with no evidence of brachial plexopathy. ECG was normal. His vitamin B12 concentration was low at 194 pg/mL, as was his iron concentration at 40 米g/dL.
After discussion of the treatment options with the patient, he elected for surgical management〞alternatives explored included conservative treatment with physiotherapy and monitoring of the diaphragm function, or surgical excision of the herniated disc, which might have resulted in additional paralysis of the diaphragm. C3每C4 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion were done, which resulted in the complete resolution of the patient's shoulder pain and shortness of breath. A follow-up x-ray showed that the problematic elevation of the right hemidiaphragm had resolved.
Shoulder pain and shortness of breath〞particularly as acute presentations〞are a combination of symptoms indicating a wide variety of pathologies affecting numerous organs including the heart, lungs, pancreas, gallbladder, and gastrointestinal tract. Regarding the shortness of breath, paralysis of the diaphragm can occur as a result of malignancies, cardiac surgery, cervical spine surgery, and trauma to the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which originates from the C3, C4, and C5 nerve roots. However, the C4 root is the predominant origin of most function in most people. Regarding the shoulder pain, patients with C4 radiculopathy can present with pain in the axial cervical spine which can extend into the trapezial and scapular regions of the back; there is also the possibility that the pain may involve the anterior part of the chest.
output: Phrenic nerve palsy caused by cervical disc herniation

input: A 39-year-old man presented to the emergency department with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, oliguria, and diffuse deposits on his skin. The physical exam findings are associated with what underlying disease?
output: Uremic frost secondary to chronic kidney disease (end-stage renal disease/uremia)

A 25-year-old man attended our department with persistent, severe abdominal pain, which had started suddenly 1 h before, located in the umbilical area. The pain was followed by a 20 min period when the patient passed fresh blood from his rectum. When he arrived at the hospital, he was in a state of shock. His peripheral pulses were weak, his heart rate was 130 beats per min, and he needed emergency supportive treatment〞including 10 units of red blood cells. After 30 min, his bleeding stopped spontaneously, and he became haemodynamically stable.On examination, we found the patient's conjunctiva and mucosa were pale, and he had cutaneous neurofibromas〞one on his left jaw and one on his right flank〞and caf谷-au-lait macules on his chest, neck, back, and arms (figure). He also had axillary freckling. Slit-lamp examination showed bilateral Lisch nodules〞iris hamartomas. Notably, he said that his father had similar lesions on his body; this information was later confirmed by the patient's uncle. No other members of the family had similar lesions.
Laboratory investigations showed that the patient was anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL. We did a gastroscopy, a colonoscopy, mesenteric artery angiography, and technetium-labelled red blood cell scintigraphy but did not find any abnormalities. However, a CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a 3 cm diameter mass with soft tissue density in the proximal jejunum; a double balloon enteroscopy confirmed the presence of a tumour (figure). Histopathological examination of biopsy samples from the lesion indicated a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST). Considering the findings on physical examination and the patient's family history, we made a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1. We did a segmental small bowel resection and the tumour was successfully removed. Detailed histopathological examination of a sample of the excised tumour showed spindle cells with mitotic activity, and immunohistochemical staining showed the spindle cells were c-kit and CD34 positive.
We have been following up the patient in our outpatient department for the past 2 years, and he remains well with no further complaints.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominantly inherited disorder characterised by skin lesions and peripheral nerve sheath tumours. Diagnosis is primarily based on the US National Institutes of Health diagnostic criteria: caf谷-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and Lisch nodules, and a positive family history of the disease. If patients only have caf谷-au-lait macules and skin fold freckling, then the diagnosis is Legius syndrome.
Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 tend to develop rare tumours, including GISTs, and neuroendocrine tumours that originate from endocrine cells within the gastrointestinal tract. GISTs occur at an earlier age in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1, are frequently located in the small intestine, and present with abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding. The characteristic skin lesions of neurofibromatosis type 1〞although superficial〞may be profoundly important as a diagnostic aid (video).
output: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen disease) with associated small-intestinal gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) causing acute gastrointestinal bleeding

A 30-year-old man presented to our department in Leiden, Netherlands, with a 6-year history of recurrent solitary swellings. On average, he had 15 episodes per year. The swellings had started on his abdomen and had gradually moved to his chest, neck, and, more recently, his face. The swellings varied in size, were painless, appeared spontaneously, and resolved after 5每7 days. Treatment with high-dose antihistamine had had no effect. There were no other symptoms. The patient was otherwise healthy and did not take any medication.Physical examination revealed a swelling of the right cheek and upper lip. Photos of previous episodes revealed similar swellings of the left cheek (figure, A). The differential diagnoses included angio-oedema, granulomatous cheilitis, sialadenitis, sialolithiasis, and Kimura's disease, but these could not be confirmed by laboratory examination, histopathology, or clinical examination by a dental surgeon. Laboratory examinations, including eosinophil count and C1 esterase inhibitor concentrations, were completely normal except for IgE concentrations, which were elevated (3736 IU/mL, normal range is 0每99). A biopsy of the buccal mucosa showed a dense eosinophilic infiltrate. Ultrasound examination and MRI scan revealed a non-specific infiltration and enhancement of the subcutis.
The elevated IgE concentration and eosinophil in-filtration in the biopsy suggested a parasitic infection. A further inquiry revealed that the patient had consumed raw fish in Taiwan before the first swelling episode. Western blot analysis of serum for reactivity against crude antigens of Gnathostoma spinigerum third-stage larvae (L3) showed the presence of a specific 24 kDa band that was diagnostic for gnathostomiasis. Gnathostomiasis is a helminthic zoonosis, endemic in southeast Asia, which is transmitted through ingestion of larvae of G spinigerum in raw or undercooked fresh water fish, eels, frogs, reptiles, or birds. After ingestion, larvae penetrate the gastrointestinal wall and migrate through the subcutaneous tissue, causing typical migratory swellings and eosinophilia that can recur for years.
A revision of the MRI scan identified a larva of approximately 4﹞0℅0﹞2 cm (figure, B). The patient was treated with ivermectin 0﹞2 mg/kg once per day on 2 consecutive days. This treatment was successful because it stimulated the outward migration of the larva (an impression of the head of the larva became visible in the lower lip; appendix), which caused a temporary increase of the swelling. Eosinophilia was now present (1﹞03℅109 cells per L, normal value is <0﹞50 ℅ 109 cells per L). Further treatment, aiming to preclude potential migration towards the eye socket, consisted of albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 14 days. The symptoms resolved within a few days and the patient remains symptom free.

A 32-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic with a 5-year history of increasing skin folds on his scalp, excessive sweating, joint pain, and development of a deep voice. The patient's medical history was significant for acne keloidalis nuchae which had been treated with antibiotics, isotretinoin, and surgical excision with primary closure of the residual lesions, one year before we saw him.On examination, we found the patient to be generally well; he had thickening of the skin on his scalp with prominent ridges and furrows (figure). He had coarse facial features (figure), acanthosis nigricans of the skin in his neck, axillae, and knuckles. Notably, his feet, hands, and tongue were enlarged. We found no other abnormal signs, and on further questioning, he reported no headaches, seizures, or visual disturbances.
We made a working diagnosis of cutis verticis gyrate (CVG) due to acromegaly.
Laboratory investigations found a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) concentration of 634 米g/L (normal 64每243), a raised growth hormone (GH) concentration of 9﹞4 米g/L (normal <3), unsuppressed post-glucose GH of 8﹞92 ng/mL (normal <1), free thyroxine of 1﹞44 ng/dL (normal 0﹞93每1﹞7), thyroid-stimulating-hormone 1﹞44 米UI/mL (normal 0﹞27每4﹞2), HbA1c 5﹞8% (normal <5﹞6), and glucose of 110 mg/dL (normal <100).
MRI of the patient's head showed a pituitary macroadenoma measuring 14 mm?℅?13 mm?℅?13 mm (figure)〞establishing the diagnosis of acromegaly.
The patient was referred to our surgical department and had a transsphenoidal resection of the tumour. After surgery, a repeat MRI showed no residual tumour. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient reported improvement of the hyperhidrosis, amelioration of the joint pain, and decreased macroglossia; IGF1 and GH levels were normal.
Acromegaly commonly presents with facial and acral dysmorphic features; other features include a headache, fatigue, and hyperhidrosis. Hypertension occurs in 20每50% of people with the condition. CVG refers to the thickening of the skin on the scalp creating furrows and ridges; it may present as an isolated finding or secondary to conditions such as pachydermoperiostosis, cerebriform intradermal nevus, Noonan syndrome, myxoedema, or〞as in our patient〞acromegaly. CVG is observed in 14每30% of patients with acromegaly and can be the first clinical manifestation. Pathogenesis of CVG in acromegaly is thought, acting through GH and IGF1, mainly over dermal fibroblasts, to increase deposition of glycosaminoglycans by mesenchymal cells, which produces skin changes. Improvement of CVG after a surgical intervention or medication for acromegaly supports this hypothesis.
Patients presenting with CVG require a full investigation since it may be the superficial clue to a serious systemic disease like acromegaly.
target: Cutis verticis gyrata secondary to acromegaly

A 51-year-old man who had been receiving haemodialysis for 15 years was referred to the Toranomon Hospital (Tokyo, Japan) with progressive calcified nodules on his fingers. He had been undergoing haemodialysis three times per week, for a total of 12 h per week. The patient had been deemed to have end-stage renal disease of unknown cause. He had undergone a parathyroidectomy 2 years before the referral because he was believed to have progressive extraskeletal calcification caused by hyperparathyroidism with constant hypercalcaemia that was refractory to medical treatment; laboratory findings were compatible with secondary hyperparathyroidism. Since the parathyroidectomy, laboratory findings had returned to normal, but the nodules had progressed and made him unable to grip. A family history could not be obtained because the patient was an orphan, but through a careful interview we identified a past medical history of recurrent urolithiasis, which was judged to be the leading cause of the end-stage renal disease. Physical examination showed clubbed fingers with exposed calcified masses (figure A). Radiography showed prominent bilateral calcified deposits (figure B) and nephrocalcinosis. Gas chromatography每mass spectrometry-based plasma metabolomic assessment showed substantially increased concentrations of oxalate (316 米mol/L) and glycerate (50﹞2 米mol/L; normal is <10 米mol/L for both), but glycolate concentration was almost normal at 13﹞3 米mol/L (normal is <12 米mol/L), suggesting the possibility of primary hyperoxaluria type 2. Genetic analysis showed a missense mutation, 181G↙A (Asp61Asn), of?GRHPR?in exon 2. We therefore diagnosed the patient as having primary hyperoxaluria type 2 and started intensive haemodialysis (25 h per week, Monday to Friday, for 2 years so far) in preparation for renal transplantation. The patient is currently on a waiting list for renal transplantation.Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by mutation of GRHPR, the gene encoding the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, which results in hyperoxaluria, recurrent urolithiasis, progressive nephrocalcinosis, end-stage renal disease, and, eventually, systemic oxalate deposition. Primary hyperoxaluria type 2, especially when associated with renal failure and caused by plasma oxalate concentrations exceeding the supersaturation index of oxalate in plasma (30 米mol/L), should be identified early because severe manifestations, as seen in our patient, can be prevented with early diagnosis, intensive management of dialysis, and timely transplantation.

A 67-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 2-month history of a low-grade fever and progressive weakness in the muscles of his face. He also reported drooling and slurred speech.He had a 10-year history of hypertension that was treated with antihypertensives.
On examination we found that he could not close his eyes, wrinkle his forehead, or raise his eyebrows and that the nasolabial folds of his face were flattened〞indicating a bilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy (figure). We found no other abnormalities on physical examination.
Laboratory investigations showed a mild anaemia, with a haemoglobin concentration of 11﹞6 g/dL, a leucocytosis of 17﹞2?℅?109 per L, and a monocytosis of 2﹞14?℅?109 per L. The patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 22 mm/h and C-reactive protein concentration was 10 mg/L. Infectious diseases〞including Lyme disease, HIV, syphilis, and herpes zoster〞were excluded. Neoplasms〞particularly head and neck tumours〞were ruled out, and granulomatous diseases, like sarcoidosis, and metabolic and autoimmune diseases〞including Guillain每Barr谷 syndrome, systemic autoimmune diseases, and vasculitis were excluded.
A peripheral blood smear showed excessive monocytosis with left shift, dysplastic granulocytes, promonocytes, and blasts (figure). A bone marrow aspiration confirmed the diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML).
Cytogenetic analysis found trisomy of chromosome 8; DNA sequencing showed mutations in the RUNX1, SF3B1, and CBL genes. Nerve conduction studies found an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy〞affecting the facial nerves and the peripheral nerves in the patient's arms and legs. We decided to treat the patient using corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin. He remained afebrile with no improvement of his facial nerve palsy. We decided against using hypomethylating agents because in Europe azacitidine has been approved only for CMML patients with white blood cell counts of less than 13?℅?109 per L.
2 months later, while still on steroid therapy, the patient was admitted with a fever, aphthous stomatitis, and arthralgias. Physical examination found an aphthous ulceration on the right side of the tongue, synovitis of the wrists and right knee, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Soon after admission, the patient complained of an acute onset abdominal pain; he was hypotensive and tachycardic, and had tenderness and rigidity of the right upper quadrant. Multiphase CT scan of the abdomen showed a large haematoma of the right kidney with active bleeding; he also had multiple disseminated microaneurysms〞up to 1 cm in diameter〞of both interlobar arteries, indicative of a medium-vessel vasculitis (figure). We did not see the spleen when entering the peritoneal cavity. Mother and baby were allowed home 4 days after the delivery.
We prescribed the patient 40 mg once a day of enoxaparin for 6 weeks〞to prevent post-partum thrombosis after an endoscopy, on the day after the caesarean section, showed small varices.

In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Caf谷 au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple caf谷 au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.
output: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia

A 70-year-old man presented to our department reporting fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss of 18 kg over the previous 3 months. He said he had been taking numerous nutritional supplements and vitamins daily.On examination, the patient had large, painful lymph nodes in his neck and axilla, and splenomegaly. Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 916?000?℅?109 per L.
He was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and started on fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. After four courses, the patient's alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level increased to 326 U/L; he was asymptomatic with a normal bilirubin. After stopping the supplements and vitamins, the ALT normalised. Approximately 18 months later, the patient's ALT increased again to 290 U/L. Further investigations found the patient to be positive for HBsAg and anti-HBc, and his blood concentration of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA was greater than 170?000?000 IU/mL. Entecavir 0﹞5 mg daily was started; his HBV DNA and ALT levels rapidly improved (figure).
Immunosuppressive therapy can cause reactivation of HBV replication, manifesting as an increase in serum HBV DNA levels, with or without increase in ALT level. Severe cases may lead to liver failure and death. HBV reactivation is more common in patients who are HBsAg-positive〞chronic HBV〞but it can also occur in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive, indicating a past HBV infection. The latter usually occurs in the setting of potent immunosuppressive therapies such as rituximab and may be accompanied by reappearance of HBsAg. The presence of anti-HBs decreases but does not eliminate the risk of HBV reactivation.
The risk of HBV reactivation in patients who received rituximab without antiviral prophylaxis has been reported to be 33每65% in patients who are HBsAg-positive and 6每24% in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive. Prophylactic antiviral therapy has been shown to be 80每100% effective in preventing HBV reactivation; notably, it is more effective than starting antiviral therapy at or after the onset of HBV reactivation.
Current oncology and hepatology society guidelines recommend patients anticipating rituximab or other anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy should be screened for HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG〞which was not done in this patient who received rituximab years before the national recommendations. If either test is positive, then prophylactic antiviral therapy with entecavir or tenofovir should be started to prevent HBV reactivation (video).
HBV DNA testing prior to anticancer therapy can help stratify the risk of HBV reactivation, and HBV DNA monitoring may lead to earlier detection of HBV reactivation. Antiviral therapy should be continued for at least 12 months after the last dose of rituximab.
It is also important to bear in mind that elevated ALT levels in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia receiving treatment may also result from liver injury caused by the chemotherapeutic agents, some nutritional supplements, and other viral hepatitis〞including A, C, or E.

She had no abdominal tenderness, vaginal bleeding, lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, or signs of chronic liver disease including jaundice, clubbing, or ascites.
Abdominal ultrasound with colour Doppler showed a viable intrauterine pregnancy and splenomegaly〞measuring 23 cm in oblique craniocaudal length〞with peri splenic varices (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin concentration 7﹞4 g/dL; normal 11﹞4每14﹞7), a leukocyte count of 4﹞2?℅?109 per L (3﹞84每10﹞0), platelet count of 206?℅?109 per L (164每387), and a lactate dehydrogenase concentration of 547 U/L (250每580).
Liver function tests and investigations for thalassaemia, chronic viral and autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, and Wilson's disease were negative.
Peripheral blood film showed teardrop-shaped red cells without blasts. Bone marrow biopsy showed a hypercellular marrow with relative myeloid hyperplasia, megakaryocytic proliferation with atypia, and minimal fibrosis (WHO grade 1/3). DNA sequencing showed a JAK2-V617F mutation with a 31% median allele burden; no BCR-ABL1 fusion gene was found. Cytogenetic analyses showed a 46,XX karyotype. No features of malignancy, lymphoproliferative, or other chronic myeloid disorders were seen.
Taken together with the splenomegaly, we diagnosed pre-fibrotic primary myelofibrosis, using the revised WHO 2016, criteria and scored the patient 0 (indicating a good prognosis) on the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System plus.

Following endoscopic variceal ligation, we started propranolol 20 mg twice daily to prevent further bleeding; the patient was then monitored for fetal growth restriction.
From 26 weeks＊ gestation, we prescribed 45 米g weekly of pegylated interferon alfa-2a, increasing to 90 米g a week from 29 weeks＊ gestation, to reduce the size of the spleen.
At 34 weeks＊ gestation, ultrasound scans showed fetal growth restriction. The spleen was 17 cm and had regressed away from the pelvic brim, allowing us to deliver a baby girl, weighing 2080 g with normal Apgar scores, by a lower-segment caesarean section using a Pfannenstiel incision (figure). A 70-year-old man presented to our department reporting fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss of 18 kg over the previous 3 months. He said he had been taking numerous nutritional supplements and vitamins daily.On examination, the patient had large, painful lymph nodes in his neck and axilla, and splenomegaly. Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 916?000?℅?109 per L.
He was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and started on fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. After four courses, the patient's alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level increased to 326 U/L; he was asymptomatic with a normal bilirubin. After stopping the supplements and vitamins, the ALT normalised. Approximately 18 months later, the patient's ALT increased again to 290 U/L. Further investigations found the patient to be positive for HBsAg and anti-HBc, and his blood concentration of hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA was greater than 170?000?000 IU/mL. Entecavir 0﹞5 mg daily was started; his HBV DNA and ALT levels rapidly improved (figure).
Immunosuppressive therapy can cause reactivation of HBV replication, manifesting as an increase in serum HBV DNA levels, with or without increase in ALT level. Severe cases may lead to liver failure and death. HBV reactivation is more common in patients who are HBsAg-positive〞chronic HBV〞but it can also occur in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive, indicating a past HBV infection. The latter usually occurs in the setting of potent immunosuppressive therapies such as rituximab and may be accompanied by reappearance of HBsAg. The presence of anti-HBs decreases but does not eliminate the risk of HBV reactivation.
The risk of HBV reactivation in patients who received rituximab without antiviral prophylaxis has been reported to be 33每65% in patients who are HBsAg-positive and 6每24% in those who are HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc IgG positive. Prophylactic antiviral therapy has been shown to be 80每100% effective in preventing HBV reactivation; notably, it is more effective than starting antiviral therapy at or after the onset of HBV reactivation.
Current oncology and hepatology society guidelines recommend patients anticipating rituximab or other anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy should be screened for HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG〞which was not done in this patient who received rituximab years before the national recommendations. If either test is positive, then prophylactic antiviral therapy with entecavir or tenofovir should be started to prevent HBV reactivation (video).
HBV DNA testing prior to anticancer therapy can help stratify the risk of HBV reactivation, and HBV DNA monitoring may lead to earlier detection of HBV reactivation. Antiviral therapy should be continued for at least 12 months after the last dose of rituximab.
It is also important to bear in mind that elevated ALT levels in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia receiving treatment may also result from liver injury caused by the chemotherapeutic agents, some nutritional supplements, and other viral hepatitis〞including A, C, or E.

A 45-year-old man came to our emergency department in August because he experienced an abnormal, unpleasant sensation when his fingers and thumbs were touched; he also said that they were blue and felt weak. 4 h before, he had been paragliding and had flown into a tower of cumulonimbus clouds〞entering a summer thunderstorm〞where winds carried him rapidly upwards to more than 6000 m above sea level. At this height, the man encountered hail, rain, an air temperature of ?25～C, and wind speeds of up to 100 km/h for about 45 min. Because of the worsening dysaesthesia and the paresis of his fingers, the man had been unable to properly control and steer the paraglider and had landed on a rooftop after a further 15 min descent. Notably, the patient had worn thin gloves on his hands in contrast to thick clothing on his lower legs and face. When we first examined the man's fingers, they were cyanotic, swollen, numb, and paretic (figure). We decided to initially warm his hands and then started him on intravenous iloprost 20 米g once daily, oral aspirin 100 mg once daily, subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily, and topical betamethasone once daily. These treatments were continued for 10 days. 2 days after the paraglider's ordeal, blisters appeared on his fingers (figure) that were compatible with a diagnosis of grade 2 frostbite; these lesions were drained, and the dysaesthesia and paresis ameliorated. On the fifth day, erythema and desquamation of the lesions occurred (figure). The swelling reduced after 7 days〞although splinter haemorrhages were seen on the tenth day (figure). After 30 days, the fingers and thumbs had fully recovered without any residual tissue damage or sensorimotor deficits.Frostbite develops as a result of thermal injury to the skin and other tissues exposed to cold temperature; it is a recognised problem seen commonly in military personnel, homeless individuals, and winter sports enthusiasts. Grade 1 lesions are characterised by numbness and erythema of the affected skin, without blister formation; when blisters filled with clear fluid are seen, the lesions should be classified as grade 2. Grade 3 lesions are characterised by a blue-grey discolouration of the skin and haemorrhagic blisters resulting in black eschars. Grade 4 lesions involve muscles, joints, and bones and result in tissue necrosis and tissue loss. For grade 4 lesions, the recommendation is that the treating physician should adopt the principle of autoamputation〞whereby the damaged tissue spontaneously detaches from the body〞rather than carrying out early surgical amputation. Besides rewarming, which is primarily employed to stop vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, and thrombosis caused by the cold, several adjuvant treatments should be considered; aspirin, prostaglandins, and thrombolytic agents can be given because of their antiplatelet and vasodilatory effects. Additionally, damaged tissue should be protected against further insult to avoid it becoming infected. Fortunately, frostbite among paragliders is rare.

In December, 2015, an 18-month-old boy with an unremarkable medical history was admitted to the paediatric emergency room for left leg trauma following a fall. A clinical examination showed a leg deformity and total functional impairment of the limb. A radiograph of the leg (figure) revealed a diaphyseal tibial and fibular fracture, with condensed cortical bone and anterolateral bowing (Crawford type I). Caf谷 au lait spots were noticed on the child's trunk (figure). After 3 months of immobilisation in an above-knee cast, there were still no signs of bone healing. A clinical examination of the boy's mother revealed multiple caf谷 au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas, and confirmed the presence of a hitherto undiagnosed case of familial neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The course of the boy's disease confirmed that he was suffering from NF1-associated congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia (CPT). No cutaneous or visceral neurofibromas, Lisch nodules, or optic gliomas were observed. No other skeletal manifestations were noted. Surgical treatment (resection of the pseudarthrosis area and an induced membrane technique) was initiated 5 months after the fracture. 1 year after surgery, persistent non-union at the distal end of the tibia prompted surgical revision with a second induced membrane technique.Although up to 55% of cases of CPT are associated with NF1, only 3% of patients with NF1 have CPT. Young children often develop CPT long before the appearance of other signs. Most cases are unilateral. Cystic forms (as in the present case) show condensed cortical and thickened bone in the concavity of the deformity, together with a narrow medullary canal. Progression of the deformity can result in a transverse fracture. Crawford's classification is most frequently applied. Surgical treatment of CPT remains a challenge because of refracture, delayed union, non-union, and persistent lower limb disorders. Several surgical options have been described, such as resection and nailing, fibular vascularised grafting, and the induced membrane technique.
This case report demonstrates the importance of diagnosis of pathological fractures in children, since they can reveal NF1.

A previously well 79-year-old woman presented with the acute onset of coffee-ground emesis. She had no previous history of alcohol intake, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or ingestion of corrosive agents. Urgent oesophagogastroduodenoscopy was done. She was kept nil-orally and commenced on an intravenous proton-pump inhibitor, fluconazole, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a diffuse black appearance of the mucosa from the mid-oesophagus to the gastro-oesophageal junction (figure A), where there was a clearly demarcated boundary with normal mucosa (figure B)〞a finding consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis. This condition is also known as Gurvits' syndrome or black oesophagus. Acute oesophageal necrosis is a rare clinical entity that usually presents with either frank haematemesis or coffee-ground emesis. It has a characteristic endoscopic appearance of circumferential, friable, black-coloured mucosa in the distal oesophagus that ends clearly and abruptly at the gastro-oesophageal junction. It is thought to be caused by oesophageal ischaemia. Multiple factors might be involved, including haemodynamic compromise, malnutrition, drug ingestion, and underlying cardiovascular or renal disease. Although the oesophagus is largely protected from ischaemia by its complex and intricate anastomotic vascular network, there is a watershed area in the distal oesophagus that is more susceptible to ischaemic injury. Management of acute oesophageal necrosis generally involves resuscitation, supportive measures, and treatment of any coexisting illness. Antimicrobial therapy is usually unnecessary, except in the setting of oesophageal perforation, positive cultures, or suspected sepsis. Although complications of perforation and stricture formation are uncommon, acute oesophageal necrosis carries a high overall mortality risk due to its association with other comorbidities and critical illness. However, acute oesophageal necrosis in an otherwise healthy patient often resolves spontaneously and is associated with a more favourable outcome.Repeat oesophagogastroduodenoscopy of our patient 72 h later revealed complete resolution of the initial endoscopic findings (figure C). Our patient was subsequently discharged home following resolution of the injury and remains well at 6-month follow-up.

A 62-year-old man was referred to our clinic with a dark, atypical-looking lesion on his upper arm because the medical oncologists were concerned that it was possibly an early melanoma (appendix).The patient was otherwise fit and well; he had a malignant melanoma surgically removed from the middle of his back 18 months previously. He reported a history of renal cell carcinoma treated by a partial nephrectomy.
The lesion was examined using reflectance confocal microscopy (RCM) and showed a large, nucleated, solitary cell consistent with a Langerhans cell in the upper epidermis with a round or oval cell body, measuring approximately 20 米m, and highly refractile dendritic branches (figure).
Histology of the lesion confirmed a lentiginous junctional nevus with inflammation: a benign diagnosis.
RCM is an in vivo optical imaging technique used to visualise skin cells, appendages, and processes in real time; the technology allows for subcellular resolution in the horizonal or en face orientation of skin layers down to the papillary dermis showing superficial collagen. RCM uses a low-power, near-infrared, diode laser, emitting light of wavelength 820 nm.
Crucially, RCM cannot distinguish between activated Langerhans cells and dendritic melanocytes. Both have similar refractive indices and morphological features. However, their distribution is different and〞as in our patient〞a Langerhans cell might be suspected due to its location.
Since RCM is a newer diagnostic imaging approach being used more commonly now than ever before, it is useful to have some awareness of potential pitfalls when interpreting confocal images and identifying cells of interest.
Finally, Langerhans cells may become activated in the context of inflammatory immune response or trauma. While the transformation rate of a melanocytic nevus into cutaneous melanoma is thought to be extremely low〞about 1 in 33?000 for men older than 60 years〞it remains important to examine and remove suspicious lesions as rates of cutaneous melanoma continue to rise (video).

A 41-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 20-h history of progressively worsening sudden-onset, severe, left-sided neck pain. Additionally, he complained of a headache in the occipital region, odynophagia, and trismus. He reported no medical history of trauma or infection. A physical examination showed he had severely limited neck motion in all directions because of stiffness. Blood tests showed a leucocytosis (13﹞0?℅?109 per L), an elevated serum C-reactive protein concentration (124 mg/L), and a faster erythrocyte sedimentation rate (24 mm/h). A cervical spine x-ray showed swelling in both the retropharyngeal and prevertebral spaces and ill-defined calcifications anterior to the C2 (figure). A CT scan of the cervical spine showed calcifications in the longus colli muscle inferior to the anterior arch of the C1 and marked swelling and effusion in the retropharyngeal and prevertebral spaces (figure). Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli muscle was diagnosed, and an oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, loxoprofen, was prescribed for 5 days at a dose of 180 mg per day. The symptoms began to resolve within a few hours, and the range of the patient's neck movements recovered significantly within 2 days. And within 1 week, the patient was completely symptom-free.Acute calcific tendinitis of the longus colli muscle〞also known as retropharyngeal calcific tendinitis〞is a rare and benign condition caused by basic calcium phosphate deposition in the tendons of the longus colli muscle that is accompanied by an aseptic inflammatory process. The characteristic triad of symptoms is acute-onset neck pain, neck stiffness, and odynophagia. Other symptoms include occipital headaches, a limitation in the range of neck movements, trismus, sore throat, pharyngeal oedema, and a low-grade fever with elevated inflammatory markers. The key point in describing this case is to stress the importance of differentiating this benign condition from other serious or life-threatening conditions presenting in a similar way. The list of differential diagnoses is long but crucially includes retropharyngeal abscess, meningitis, infectious spondylitis, lymphadenitis, epiglottis, and oropharyngeal and spinal neoplasms. In this context, getting the diagnosis right will restrict the number of invasive investigations and possibly the prescription of unnecessary antibiotics or other treatments. The correct diagnosis is clinched by modern imaging methods〞a cervical CT being preferable to an x-ray. Antipyretic analgesics, with corticosteroids in severe cases, are effective treatments.

input: A 32-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 1-month history of continuous chest pain, which was worse with movement and on application of pressure to the anterior chest wall. Physical examination showed a pustule on the sole of his left foot (figure A) and multiple pustules on his palms (figure B). Blood analysis, chest radiography, and ECG results were normal. Microscopy and culture for bacteria of the pustules was negative, as was serology for Treponema pallidum and HIV. Immunological tests were done, but no abnormalities were found. A radioisotope scan showed intense activity at the sternoclavicular and first sternocostal joints (figure C). A diagnosis of synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome was made. Treatment with non-steroidal anti-inflammatories and methotrexate was started, resulting in clinical improvement. SAPHO syndrome is characterised by the variable association of osteoarticular manifestations, mainly on the anterior chest wall, and various dermatological conditions〞in particular palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne.

A 76-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis每myositis overlap being treated with mycophenolic acid and hydroxychloroquine was admitted for weight loss of 19 kg over 1 year, myositis relapse, new constellation of pancytopenia (haemoglobin 6﹞7 g/dL, white blood cell count 1﹞82?℅?109 per L, and platelet count 88?℅?109 per L), proteinuria (0﹞3 g per day), and low complement C3 concentrations (53 mg/dL [normal C3 range 83每193 mg/dL]). She was afebrile with stable blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation on room air. Extensive malignancy evaluation and infection screen were negative. She was treated for evolving systemic lupus erythematosus with oral prednisolone (0﹞5 mg/kg per day), intravenous immunoglobulin, and rituximab.
Baseline chest radiograph showed possible pneumatosis and dilated small bowels (figure A), which was confirmed on abdominal radiograph (figure B). The pneumatosis was initially managed conservatively, ie, the patient was allowed a normal diet and did not undergo further abdominal imaging or surgical procedures, as she was asymptomatic and moving her bowels. She then developed acute epigastric pain and tenderness without peritonism. She remained leukopenic with normal lactate concentrations and no acidosis. Abdominal CT showed extensive pneumatosis intestinalis (figure C, D), small bowel dilatation with no transition point, small bowel hypoenhancement, which was concerning for ischaemia, and free gas, suggestive of perforation (figure D). An urgent laparoscopy, however, showed a healthy bowel with segments of small bowel pneumatosis without perforation or dilatation. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis was diagnosed. Postoperatively, her abdominal pain resolved with esomeprazole. She cleared bowels and tolerated a soft diet 2 days later. Repeat CT 6 months later showed resolution of pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum. She was continued on hydroxychloroquine, monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, and tapered prednisolone for her overlapping connective tissue disease. Her weight, cytopenias, and complement concentrations improved.
With a reported prevalence of 0﹞03% in autopsy studies, pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis is a rare gastrointestinal manifestation of connective tissue disease characterised by submucosal, subserosal free gas-filled cysts, or both. Possible causes include increased luminal pressure, bacterial fermentation, and glucocorticoid-induced intestinal mucosa atrophy. Cyst rupture might cause pneumoperitoneum. Patients with pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis are often asymptomatic and respond well to conservative treatment. Surgery is indicated if there are concerns of bowel ischemia, perforation or peritonitis. Clinicians should have a heightened awareness of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis in patients with connective tissue disease.

Monozygotic twins, aged 2 years, were referred to our outpatient clinic because of a hairless area 2 cm?℅? 2 cm in a similar point on their occipital vertices (figure). The twin boys were born prematurely after 33 weeks and 3 days of gestation and it was initially thought that the hairless regions, which also had no skin cover, were caused by a fetal scalp electrode. The twins had otherwise developed normally, with no associated anomalies or syndromes, and the defects on their scalps had healed over with scar tissue. A detailed history was taken from the children's mother, who said that the pregnancy had been uncomplicated and that there was no history of skin conditions in the family. Notably, an ultrasound scan done at gestational week 8 showed an empty yolk sac which suggested that a third fetus had been present and was reabsorbed in utero.After considering the history and examining the lesions, we made a diagnosis of aplasia cutis congenita (ACC)〞simply a condition with a congenital absence of skin. Vanishing twin syndrome, which perhaps in our case ought to be described as vanishing triplet syndrome〞where usually twin fetuses convert to a singleton〞is a rare but well recognised phenomenon that is associated with widespread and predominantly truncal ACC. Non-syndromic ACC of the scalp has been associated with a mutation in the ribosome biogenesis factor (BMS1) gene. The suspected mechanism by which this mutation produces ACC is through an increase in the p21 level, which has been linked to an inhibition of cell proliferation and the formation of scar tissue. Scalp ACC in twins is very rare and we found only two other reported cases after a literature search.
At first glance, the scalp defect is easily confused with other conditions causing areas of hair loss, such as alopecia areata or naevoid conditions. The absence of skin poses a slight risk of CNS infection or of sagittal sinus haemorrhage before the healing occurs. Otherwise, ACC is considered benign once the scalp defect has healed and as such does not require further treatment. Therapeutic options include conservative management or surgery for aesthetic purposes, larger defects, or underlying bone defects. Since this condition is very rare, physicians outside of the dermatological arena should not be chastised for missing this spot diagnosis.

She was afebrile with stable blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation on room air. Extensive malignancy evaluation and infection screen were negative. She was treated for evolving systemic lupus erythematosus with oral prednisolone (0﹞5 mg/kg per day), intravenous immunoglobulin, and rituximab.
Baseline chest radiograph showed possible pneumatosis and dilated small bowels (figure A), which was confirmed on abdominal radiograph (figure B). The pneumatosis was initially managed conservatively, ie, the patient was allowed a normal diet and did not undergo further abdominal imaging or surgical procedures, as she was asymptomatic and moving her bowels. She then developed acute epigastric pain and tenderness without peritonism. She remained leukopenic with normal lactate concentrations and no acidosis. Abdominal CT showed extensive pneumatosis intestinalis (figure C, D), small bowel dilatation with no transition point, small bowel hypoenhancement, which was concerning for ischaemia, and free gas, suggestive of perforation (figure D). An urgent laparoscopy, however, showed a healthy bowel with segments of small bowel pneumatosis without perforation or dilatation. Pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis was diagnosed. Postoperatively, her abdominal pain resolved with esomeprazole. She cleared bowels and tolerated a soft diet 2 days later. Repeat CT 6 months later showed resolution of pneumatosis and pneumoperitoneum. She was continued on hydroxychloroquine, monthly intravenous immunoglobulin, and tapered prednisolone for her overlapping connective tissue disease. Her weight, cytopenias, and complement concentrations improved.
With a reported prevalence of 0﹞03% in autopsy studies, pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis is a rare gastrointestinal manifestation of connective tissue disease characterised by submucosal, subserosal free gas-filled cysts, or both. Possible causes include increased luminal pressure, bacterial fermentation, and glucocorticoid-induced intestinal mucosa atrophy. Cyst rupture might cause pneumoperitoneum. Patients with pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis are often asymptomatic and respond well to conservative treatment. Surgery is indicated if there are concerns of bowel ischemia, perforation or peritonitis. Clinicians should have a heightened awareness of pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis in patients with connective tissue disease.

Monozygotic twins, aged 2 years, were referred to our outpatient clinic because of a hairless area 2 cm?℅? 2 cm in a similar point on their occipital vertices (figure). The twin boys were born prematurely after 33 weeks and 3 days of gestation and it was initially thought that the hairless regions, which also had no skin cover, were caused by a fetal scalp electrode. The twins had otherwise developed normally, with no associated anomalies or syndromes, and the defects on their scalps had healed over with scar tissue. A detailed history was taken from the children's mother, who said that the pregnancy had been uncomplicated and that there was no history of skin conditions in the family. Notably, an ultrasound scan done at gestational week 8 showed an empty yolk sac which suggested that a third fetus had been present and was reabsorbed in utero.After considering the history and examining the lesions, we made a diagnosis of aplasia cutis congenita (ACC)〞simply a condition with a congenital absence of skin. Vanishing twin syndrome, which perhaps in our case ought to be described as vanishing triplet syndrome〞where usually twin fetuses convert to a singleton〞is a rare but well recognised phenomenon that is associated with widespread and predominantly truncal ACC. Non-syndromic ACC of the scalp has been associated with a mutation in the ribosome biogenesis factor (BMS1) gene. The suspected mechanism by which this mutation produces ACC is through an increase in the p21 level, which has been linked to an inhibition of cell proliferation and the formation of scar tissue. Scalp ACC in twins is very rare and we found only two other reported cases after a literature search.
At first glance, the scalp defect is easily confused with other conditions causing areas of hair loss, such as alopecia areata or naevoid conditions. The absence of skin poses a slight risk of CNS infection or of sagittal sinus haemorrhage before the healing occurs. Otherwise, ACC is considered benign once the scalp defect has healed and as such does not require further treatment. Therapeutic options include conservative management or surgery for aesthetic purposes, larger defects, or underlying bone defects. Since this condition is very rare, physicians outside of the dermatological arena should not be chastised for missing this spot diagnosis.

A 63-year-old man presented to our emergency department with a 1-year history of severe nocturia and straining to pass urine. Additionally, he reported having tenesmus and abdominal pain in the 2 weeks prior to attending. The patient had no significant medical history.On examination we found his abdomen to be moderately distended; it was soft and normal bowels sounds could be heard. A rectal examination showed a large pelvic mass with an irregular surface occupying the whole rectal ampulla.
Laboratory investigations found a haemoglobin concentration of 11﹞8 g/dL (normal 14﹞0每18﹞0) and a white blood cell count of 5﹞41?℅?109 per L (normal 4﹞0每10﹞0). The patient had a serum creatinine concentration of 1﹞37 mg/dL (normal 0﹞80每1﹞30), a blood sodium concentration of 139 mEq/L (normal 135每145) and a negative urinalysis; the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) serum concentration was 144 ng/mL (normal <4﹞0).
Multiparametric prostatic MRI showed an 18 cm?℅?13 cm lesion in the pelvis〞made up of numerous, pluri-lobulated cystic areas with a heterogeneous signal; with T2 hyperintensity in some loci〞indicating fluid, and T2 hypointensity in other parts〞suggestive of intracystic bleeding. The cystic lesions were in the basal and middle portions of the prostate gland, which were completely unstructured and recognisable, only in part, in the mid-apical and anterior portions. No significant lymphadenopathy was seen (figure). A bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic spread. Initially, we considered the mass to be a giant prostatic cystadenoma and a three-dimensional reconstruction model was obtained to choose the most appropriate surgical strategy (figure).
We carried out an open, radical prostatectomy using combined retrograde and anterograde approaches with limited pelvic lymph node dissection. The bladder was completely dislocated anteriorly and ended up in the right portion of the pelvis; it showed no signs of infiltration. Fluid obtained from aspiration of the cysts, sent for extemporaneous cytological analysis, had no neoplastic cells. The final histopathological examination showed a giant multilocular cystadenocarcinoma: ductal and acinar adenocarcinoma (Gleason score 4?+?4=8) mixed with the cystic tumour. Two 1 mm positive surgical margins〞one apical and one posterolateral on the right side〞were recorded on the prostate.
The tumour stage was pT3bN0 with nine lymph nodes, which when removed showed no tumour involvement. High-power microscopy showed nuclear stratifications, papillary structures, and Roman arch formations in the cystically dilated glands. The first postoperative PSA serum concentration was 0﹞12 ng/mL.
Because of the aggressive characteristics of the tumour and the adverse risk factors for early biochemical failure〞the tumour stage, histology, and high PSA level〞we decided to treat the prostate bed with adjuvant radiotherapy together with long-term androgen deprivation therapy.
At 6 month follow-up, the PSA serum concentration was undetectable and the patient had reached a satisfactory continence status using one pad per day.
Prostate cystadenocarcinoma is a very rare malignancy sometimes presenting as a large tumour that may be difficult to diagnose; its cystic nature means that it is not always possible to obtain a preoperative cytological or histopathological confirmation of the diagnosis that might then guide surgical management. Differentiating it from other pelvic cystic masses〞including its benign counterpart, prostatic cystadenoma〞is key. A particularly high PSA serum concentration〞as seen in our patient〞remains, we believe, the most valuable indicator of malignancy, even if preoperative imaging shows no metastatic spread and intraoperative cytological analysis does not indicate a tumour (video).
output: Prostate cystadenocarcinoma (ductal and acinar adenocarcinoma with multilocular cystic component)

A 29-year-old woman was referred to our renal clinic because of pain in her right flank and severe hypertension; her blood pressure was more than 180/110 mm Hg. She was diagnosed as having treatment-resistant-hypertension because her blood pressure remained high at 157/105 mm Hg despite being treated with three antihypertensive drugs, including a diuretic, at maximum doses. 24-h ambulatory monitoring showed increased daytime and nocturnal (non-dipper pattern) blood pressures. She had no history of previous medical difficulties. She was of normal weight and did not report having headaches or palpitations. On physical examination, she was not found to have oedema or any other relevant clinical findings.Considering the patient's young age, the absence of a family history or other risk factors for hypertension, and the high level and acute increase in her blood pressure, we commenced investigations for secondary causes of hypertension. The laboratory investigations we did included a full blood count, plasma-renin activity, blood concentrations of creatinine, cystatin C, potassium, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and aldosterone. We also requested a urinalysis and a 24-h urine test with levels of albuminuria, cortisol, catecholamines, and metanephrines. Finally, we completed the screening with a duplex ultrasound of the kidneys and echocardiography.
Renal parenchymal disease was ruled out because there was no albuminuria on urinalysis and serum creatinine and cystatin C concentrations were within normal range. Other causes〞such as obstructive sleep apnoea〞were discounted because of a low index of suspicion. A normal echocardiogram enabled us to rule out the possibility of coarctation of the aorta. A normal aldosterone-to-renin ratio allowed us to exclude primary aldosteronism; a normal TSH enabled us to eliminate thyroid disease; Cushing's syndrome was precluded because of a normal 24-h urinary cortisol and so was the possibility of a phaeochromocytoma because of normal concentrations of 24-h urinary catecholamines.
Interestingly, the only abnormal laboratory investigation was a low serum potassium concentration (3﹞3 mmol/L). However, the ultrasound of the right kidney showed a vascular malformation, raising the possibility of renal artery stenosis. A CT angiogram of the right kidney showed stenosis of the right renal artery, seven variously sized aneurysms〞coalescing into a mass of approximately 34?℅?27 mm in the right kidney〞and an arteriovenous fistula from one of the aneurysms near the right renal artery to the ipsilateral right ovarian vein (figure). The patient was diagnosed with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). FMD is a non-atherosclerotic and non-inflammatory vascular disease that can result in arterial stenosis, aneurysm formation, and dissection or occlusion, or both, of medium-sized arteries. It is usually diagnosed radiographically because histology is not typically available. There are two subtypes: multifocal FMD, the more common, has the appearance of a so-called string of beads, whereas focal FMD looks like a circumferential or tubular stenosis. Classic appearances can evolve with complicated aneurysm and fistula formation. Kidney-related diseases〞including diseases of the renal parenchyma and stenosis of the renal arteries〞are among the most common causes of secondary hypertension in non-obese patients with low indices of suspicion for obstructive sleep apnoea.

A 27-year-old woman attended our accident and emergency unit reporting fatigue and recurrent pain in the right side of her chest; the tiredness, which had been present for several years, had recently worsened.The patient had been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa (AN) at the age of 17 years; she severely restricted her diet, resulting in significant weight loss. She was prescribed antidepressants and hormone replacement therapy for previously disturbed periods.
On examination she was very unwell and markedly cachectic; her pulse was 98 beats per min, her blood pressure was 68/45 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 90% and BMI was 10 kg/m2. Laboratory investigations showed a pancytopenia with a white blood cell count of 2﹞07?℅?109 per L (normal 3﹞5每11﹞0), haemoglobin concentration of 10 g/dL (normal 12每16), and a platelet count of 78﹞0?℅?109 per L (normal 150每440). The patient's serum glucose concentration was 51 mg/dL (normal 70每100); liver function tests were as follows: alanine aminotransferase 347 units per L (normal <33), aspartate transaminase 173 units per L (normal <32), and lactate dehydrogenase 293 units per L (normal 135每214).
An initial CT scan of the patient's chest showed an apical condensation; on subsequent scans the lesion appeared with some excavation (figure). No signs of a pulmonary embolism were seen. Investigations for common viral, fungal, and bacterial causes of lung infections〞including tuberculosis〞were negative. A sample obtained from a lung biopsy, which we decided to do because the patient's chest pain was worsening, showed inflammatory changes surrounding an unknown material, indicating inhalation of a foreign body. No signs of malignancy were seen.
We prescribed amoxicillin and clavulanate and commenced enteral feeding. After 4 weeks in hospital the pancytopenia was still present, so we did a bone marrow aspirate which showed some hypocellular spicules with an increase in adipocytes surrounded by abundant extracellular pinkish material〞indicating gelatinous transformation (figure).
The patient was commenced on enteral nutrition with a progressive energetic regimen and concomitant correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalances; her weight increased from 32﹞5 kg to 39﹞5 kg and her BMI from 10 kg/m2 to 12 kg/m2. After 2 months of treatment the white cell count and platelet count had returned to normal levels. The patient then went to a specialised centre to continue with psychiatric and nutritional care.
The severity of AN is determined by the BMI: less than or equal to 17 kg/m2 is considered mild, 16 kg/m2 to 16﹞99 kg/m2 is moderate, 15 kg/m2 to 15﹞99 kg/m2 is severe, and less than 15 kg/m2 is extreme. Patients with a very low BMI〞as in our case〞are at high risk of developing the refeeding syndrome which occurs when rapid and inappropriate feeding is initiated after a long period of starvation. AN is also associated with an increased risk of gelatinous bone marrow transformation, which is reversible with treatment (video).
output: Gelatinous bone marrow transformation associated with anorexia nervosa
target: Nutritional refeeding should be optimized to reverse the bone marrow transformation and the potentially impaired immunity

A 3-year-old girl was referred to the dermatology department with blonde, straw-like, and unruly hair. The child's parents reported that since birth her hair had been sparse and slow growing. And from about one year of age, her parents had difficulty combing her hair.5 months earlier, the patient had a fever, dyspnoea, and chest pain; he had been seen in the community and a chest CT had shown bilateral dense sub-pleural infiltrates in both lower lobes of the lungs〞more on the left. Investigations had found a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 18﹞8 mg/dL (normal 0每0﹞5). The patient was initially diagnosed and treated for a community acquired pneumonia with oral cefuroxime and roxithromycin with limited clinical response; he was swapped on to oral levofloxacin for a further 14 days. The patient recovered and a CT scan, 1 months later showed almost complete disappearance of the infiltrates.
His medical history was unremarkable, he had no history of travelling abroad, no contact with animals, and he was employed in home renovation.
On examination, we found cyanosis in toes 1 and 5 of his left foot; arterial pulses were detected in the groin but they were absent in the popliteal fossae of both legs. He was afebrile.
CT-angiography showed filling defects the right kidney and spleen suggesting infarcts (appendix) and obstructions of the left femoral artery and right popliteal artery (figure). We started low-molecular-weight heparin.
Thrombi were extracted from the left iliac, common femoral and superficial femoral, and the right deep and superficial femoral arteries resulting in the restoration of blood flow to both legs.
Chest CT with angiography also showed large masses on the cusps of the aortic valve and trans-oesophageal echocardiography found a bicuspid aortic valve with masses attached to the aortic and ventricular surfaces of the valve.
Significant laboratory abnormalities included a raised CRP concentration 15﹞1mg/dL. Tests for anticardiolipin and anti-汕2 glycoprotein 1 antibodies were both strongly positive. Tests for anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Sm antibodies were negative; blood cultures were also negative.
At operation to replace the aortic valve, large vegetations were found over the left anterior-posterior commissure with destruction of the left aspect of both leaflets (figure). Cultures of samples of the values did not grow organisms but were positive on PCR for Coxiella burnetii; Q fever serology was also positive. We therefore made a diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome following Q fever.
