A 29-year-old woman was referred to our renal clinic because of pain in her right flank and severe hypertension; her blood pressure was more than 180/110 mm Hg. She was diagnosed as having treatment-resistant-hypertension because her blood pressure remained high at 157/105 mm Hg despite being treated with three antihypertensive drugs, including a diuretic, at maximum doses. 24-h ambulatory monitoring showed increased daytime and nocturnal (non-dipper pattern) blood pressures. She had no history of previous medical difficulties. She was of normal weight and did not report having headaches or palpitations. On physical examination, she was not found to have oedema or any other relevant clinical findings.Considering the patient's young age, the absence of a family history or other risk factors for hypertension, and the high level and acute increase in her blood pressure, we commenced investigations for secondary causes of hypertension. The laboratory investigations we did included a full blood count, plasma-renin activity, blood concentrations of creatinine, cystatin C, potassium, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and aldosterone. We also requested a urinalysis and a 24-h urine test with levels of albuminuria, cortisol, catecholamines, and metanephrines. Finally, we completed the screening with a duplex ultrasound of the kidneys and echocardiography.
Renal parenchymal disease was ruled out because there was no albuminuria on urinalysis and serum creatinine and cystatin C concentrations were within normal range. Other causes〞such as obstructive sleep apnoea〞were discounted because of a low index of suspicion. A normal echocardiogram enabled us to rule out the possibility of coarctation of the aorta. A normal aldosterone-to-renin ratio allowed us to exclude primary aldosteronism; a normal TSH enabled us to eliminate thyroid disease; Cushing's syndrome was precluded because of a normal 24-h urinary cortisol and so was the possibility of a phaeochromocytoma because of normal concentrations of 24-h urinary catecholamines.
Interestingly, the only abnormal laboratory investigation was a low serum potassium concentration (3﹞3 mmol/L). However, the ultrasound of the right kidney showed a vascular malformation, raising the possibility of renal artery stenosis. A CT angiogram of the right kidney showed stenosis of the right renal artery, seven variously sized aneurysms〞coalescing into a mass of approximately 34?℅?27 mm in the right kidney〞and an arteriovenous fistula from one of the aneurysms near the right renal artery to the ipsilateral right ovarian vein (figure). The patient was diagnosed with fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD). FMD is a non-atherosclerotic and non-inflammatory vascular disease that can result in arterial stenosis, aneurysm formation, and dissection or occlusion, or both, of medium-sized arteries. It is usually diagnosed radiographically because histology is not typically available. There are two subtypes: multifocal FMD, the more common, has the appearance of a so-called string of beads, whereas focal FMD looks like a circumferential or tubular stenosis. Classic appearances can evolve with complicated aneurysm and fistula formation. Kidney-related diseases〞including diseases of the renal parenchyma and stenosis of the renal arteries〞are among the most common causes of secondary hypertension in non-obese patients with low indices of suspicion for obstructive sleep apnoea.

input: A 35-year-old Libyan woman was referred to us from another institution with the diagnosis of massive pericardial effusion and pericardial tamponade. On admission to us, she was hypotensive, tachycardic and tachypnoeic. Electrocardiography showed unspecific low QRS voltage and ST-T segment flattening. Chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly. We did an emergency pericardial aspiration which yielded 1500 ml of yellow coloured fluid. A transthoracic echocardiogrm showed multiple cystic formations approximately 1﹞5每2 cm within the pericardial cavity (figure A), and confirmed the need for surgery. We did a standard median sternotomy and thoroughly irrigated the pericardium with hypertonic saline; multiple cysts were removed from the pericardium (figures B and C). Our patient was diagnosed with a ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst and pericardial tamponade. We established the diagnosis based on the gross appearance of the removed cysts, the echocardiogram results, and a high ESR. Hydatid disease is endemic in Libya, a southern Mediterranean country. Serological tests were not available. After surgery she was treated with oral albendazole for 12 days. She recovered well and was discharged 12 days after surgery. Pericardial tamponade due to hydatid disease is a rare condition that has been seldom reported in the literature.
output: Ruptured intrapericardial hydatid cyst with pericardial tamponade

Additionally, serum IgE specific for A simplex was increased. In view of the popularity of raw seafood consumption, clinicians should keep anisakidosis high on their list of differential diagnoses for a wide range of disorders, especially in patients known to have these dietary habits.

An 80-year-old man with a 6-month-history of shortness of breath on minimal exertion and fatigue was admitted to our unit for a planned operation to replace his stenotic aortic valve. The surgery was uneventful and a temporary ventricular epicardial pacing lead was placed on the free wall of the right ventricle. The patient remained haemodynamically stable in sinus rhythm post-surgery and was extubated 8 h later. The following day he was transferred from intensive care to our high dependency unit with the temporary epicardial pacemaker in VVI mode: stimulation amplitude 10 V, sensitivity 1 mV, and back-up pacing rate of 44 beats per min. A pacing check at that time showed no problems.2 days after the operation the patient had a cardiac arrest during mobilisation and physiotherapy; chest compressions were started, and the patient was re-intubated. The defibrillator showed ventricular fibrillation and he was shocked into sinus rhythm using 200 joules biphasic.
A telemetry review showed a spike on a T wave as a possible cause of the cardiac arrest: sinus rhythm was present during the first two cardiac cycles〞heart rate 76 beats per min〞followed by a premature pacing spike which produced a paced cardiac cycle. Another intrinsic cardiac cycle then followed. However, during the repolarisation phase of this cycle, a second pacing spike was seen falling on the T wave; this spike triggered polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that apparently degenerated into ventricular fibrillation (figure).
The patient was stabilised post-resuscitation and extubated 4 h later; he recovered well and was allowed home 12 days later. 1 month later he was well and asymptomatic when reviewed in our outpatient clinic.
Indications for temporary cardiac pacing include the management of bradyarrhythmias〞specifically atrioventricular block〞and both atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In cardiac surgery, insertion of temporary epicardial pacing wires is common practice; it both optimises myocardial function in patients, who postoperatively develop haemodynamically significant arrhythmias, and helps maintain a stable cardiac rhythm.
However, placement of epicardial pacing leads is not without risk. In the short term, function deteriorates mainly due to the inflammation around the surfaces of the myocardium and the leads. Daily checking of the pacemaker's pacing (the depolarisation of the atria or ventricles resulting from an impulse delivered from the generator down a lead to the heart) and sensing (the detection by the generator of intrinsic atrial or ventricular depolarisation signals) parameters after cardiac surgery is therefore paramount.
Pacemaker under-sensing occurs when the pacemaker fails to detect spontaneous myocardial depolarisation〞as probably happened in our patient〞and is a common reason for the appearance of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes. When the spikes fall on the T wave, then the patient may develop a tachyarrhythmia〞including polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. Increasing the pacemaker rate above that of the intrinsic heart rate may reduce the possibility of production of inappropriate ventricular pacing spikes.
output: Pacemaker-induced polymorphic ventricular tachycardia degenerating into ventricular fibrillation due to pacemaker under-sensing with R-on-T phenomenon

input: A 72-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of an itchy rash on his back. On physical examination, edematous, flagellate plaques and linear patches were present across the patient＊s entire back and upper buttocks. There was no adenopathy, dermographism, or mucosal involvement. What substance had the patient most likely handled and ingested before subsequently developing this rash?
output:
Shiitake mushrooms

The clinical presentation shows the characteristic flagellate dermatitis pattern - linear, whip-like erythematous streaks and plaques on the back. This distinctive pattern is pathognomonic for shiitake mushroom dermatitis (also known as shiitake flagellate dermatitis or toxicoderma).

This condition occurs after consumption of raw or undercooked shiitake mushrooms (Lentinula edodes). The causative agent is believed to be lentinan, a thermolabile polysaccharide that is inactivated by thorough cooking. The rash typically appears 24-48 hours after ingestion and is characterized by intensely pruritic, linear erythematous streaks that resemble whip marks, classically distributed on the trunk.

She also had white papules with ulcerations on the skin over her trunk, arms, and legs, but predominantly they were grouped around the large joints〞hips, knees, and elbows (figure). We noted a palpable tendon friction rub on the joints of the patient's hands; there was no swelling or tenderness.
Laboratory investigations found a raised C-reactive protein concentration of 33 mg/L (normal 0每5), anaemia with a haemoglobin concentration of 8﹞2 g/dL, and a moderately elevated creatine kinase of 480 U/L (normal <200).

Autoantibodies to rheumatoid factor (30 U/mL; normal <14) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies (19 U/mL; normal <5) were positive.

Ultrasound scans of the patient's joints〞specifically her hands and fingers〞showed polyarthritis.

Although calcinosis cutis is described in many diseases〞including metastatic diseases, lymphomas, and metabolic diseases〞it may occur secondary to medical treatments and trauma. Massive infiltrations〞as in our patient〞are rare and we were fortunate that our multimodal, disease-targeted pharmacological therapy combination was effective. Clinicians using such combined therapies for prolonged periods of time should remain mindful of the risk of infection (video).

A 55-year-old man attended our department for evaluation of cytopenias.The patient's difficulties began 5 years earlier when he presented with unexplained fevers, myalgia, arthralgia, recurrent auricular chondritis, and inflammatory skin lesions (appendix); 2 years after his initial presentation, he developed discomfort in his eyes, abdominal pain, and shortness of breath on exertion. He was found to have episcleritis, colitis, and an unclassified interstitial lung disease with features of organising pneumonia (appendix). Laboratory investigations at that time showed chronically elevated inflammatory markers〞including a raised C-reactive protein concentration of more than 50 mg/L (normal <3﹞1)〞and repeatedly mild cytopenias. The working diagnosis at that time was a relapsing polychondritis and the patient was treated with high dose oral prednisone with good response; however, he was unable to taper the dose to less than 20 mg daily. Numerous systemic therapies were tried as steroid-sparing agents〞including methotrexate, azathioprine, cytokine inhibitors (tocilizumab, sarilumab, anakinra, and infliximab), Janus kinase inhibitors (tofacitinib and baricitinib), and B-cell depletion (rituximab).
After 3 years of follow-up, repeated blood tests showed an increasing macrocytosis and persistent cytopenias: the patient's white blood cell count was 6?℅?109 per L (normal 4﹞0每11﹞0), neutrophils 4﹞2?℅?109 per L (normal 2﹞0每8﹞0), lymphocytes 0﹞6?℅?109 per L (normal 1﹞2每3﹞5), haemoglobin concentration 10﹞8 g/dL (normal 13﹞5每17﹞0), mean corpuscular volume 119 fL (82每98), and platelets 146?℅?109 per L (normal 150每400). A bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed normal cellularity with mild morphological dysplasia〞including prominent vacuolation of granulocytic and erythroid precursors (figure); cytogenetics showed a normal male karyotype. Serum copper concentration〞measured because deficiencies in both copper and zinc can cause cytopenias and produce vacuolated myeloid cells〞was low at 8﹞6 米mol/L (normal 11每26) and the patient was given oral copper supplements but to no avail.
Sanger sequencing of a peripheral blood sample from the patient showed a mutation affecting methionine-41 (c.122 T>C; p.Met41Thr) of the UBA1 gene and we made a diagnosis of the recently described X-linked inflammatory disease: vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic (VEXAS) syndrome (appendix). The patient continues to be treated with corticosteroids and has been referred for consideration for allogeneic stem-cell transplantation.
VEXAS syndrome〞first described in December, 2020, in 25 patients〞is a novel monogenic inflammatory syndrome affecting men. Key features include a treatment-refractory inflammatory syndrome, which develops in late adulthood, recurrent fevers, chondritis, vasculitis, and dysplastic bone marrow, and characteristic vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursor cells. Allogeneic stem-cell transplantation has been successful in a small number of patients and gene therapy is an area of active investigation (video).

A 26-year-old man reporting a 6-day history of fever, malaise, and a swollen cheek, was referred to our emergency room. The day before his attendance, he had been seen by his general practitioner and started on oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. However, his cheek continued to swell, and he developed a temperature of 39﹞4oC, prompting the referral.The patient had no medical history; he had all his childhood vaccinations. Additionally, he reported no sexual contacts other than with his male partner.
On examination, he did not appear acutely unwell; his vital signs were stable with his blood pressure 116/84 mm Hg, pulse 95 beats per min, and oxygen saturation 99%. The patient's left parotid gland was swollen and painful on palpitation (figure); he had no lymphadenopathy. An inspection of the oral cavity showed one ulcerative lesion on the ipsilateral lower lip (figure).
Laboratory investigations showed a mild lymphopenia (0﹞8?℅?109 per L; normal 1﹞0每3﹞5), an elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase concentration (91 IU/L; normal <38 IU/L), and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration (76 mg/L; normal <10 mg/L). Influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative.
The antibiotics were switched to oral levofloxacin to no avail, and the parotid swelling increased and fever persisted when the patient visited the outpatient clinic, 5 days after his initial presentation; the CRP concentration had decreased to 51 mg/L, but the parotid swelling and lip ulcer were still present. Serology for mumps, HIV, and syphilis and PCRs on a throat swab for mumps, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae all tested negative, besides mumps IgG〞confirming previous vaccination. However, PCRs on the throat and ulcer swabs were positive for human monkeypox (hMPX) virus: Ct-values of 18 and 22, respectively. Parotitis is mostly caused by a viral infection〞most often mumps. Other viral causes include HIV, enteroviruses, Epstein-Barr Virus, influenza, parainfluenza, and cytomegalovirus. Acute bacterial parotitis mostly occurs in neonates, or in elderly, or debilitated people. Non-infectious disorders associated with parotid swelling include collagen vascular disease, cystic fibrosis, sialolithiasis, diabetes, sarcoidosis, and tumours. Chronic parotitis may be confused with Sj?gren's syndrome. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of parotitis caused by hMPX virus.

A 64-year-old man with a history of atrial fibrillation with portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis was admitted to hospital with haematemesis. He was diagnosed with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension leading to variceal bleeding. He had two endoscopies with variceal banding and gastric variceal glue injection within 1 month that were unsuccessful; hence, he was referred to a tertiary unit for further management. Given his performance status and comorbidities, he was neither a candidate for surgery nor transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt; therefore, after careful counselling, glue embolisation of the culprit vein was performed via an endovascular approach. Post-procedure, the patient developed left homonymous hemianopia, which gradually worsened, leading to cortical blindness. The visual disturbance was further investigated with a CT scan (figure A). The CT images showed a right occipital infarct and multiple, scattered, high-density foci in subarachnoid space. Further MRI and MR angiogram (figures B每E) supported right distal posterior cerebral artery occlusion, probably due to glue embolisation.Unfortunately, our patient did not consent to further investigations to determine the mechanism, although a non-contrast echocardiogram did not show any cardiac sequelae of septal defects. After appropriate specialist consultation, his stroke has been managed with lifelong anticoagulation due to portal vein and superior mesenteric vein thrombosis and he had conservative management for the neurological symptoms, leading to partial improvement of his vision.
Glue embolisation acts as definitive treatment of gastric varices in selected cases, although complications do occur in 0﹞5每4﹞3% of patients. In a large retrospective case series (n=753), distant glue embolisation complications were reported in five patients (0﹞7%, one pulmonary, one brain, and three splenic). Embolisation to the right atrium and beyond has been reported in previous case studies, including systemic arterial embolisation due to septal defects. However, cerebral embolisation is uncommon but can present with cortical blindness, similarly to our case. Therefore, informed procedural consent must include glue embolisation and a high index of suspicion must be shown if a patient develops acute respiratory or neurological complications after the intervention.

A 10-year-old girl with an antenatal diagnosis of Klippel每Tr谷naunay syndrome was referred to our institution with a 1-day history of rectal bleeding. She had stools of normal consistency and frequency, had not been on any medication recently, and had no abdominal pain or other accompanying symptoms.Her physical examination revealed extensive red每purple masses on her right lower leg. These masses on the right lower quadrant felt like a paste when palpated. Laboratory tests revealed that her haemoglobin concentration was 10﹞6 g/dL, white blood cell count was 9000 cells per 米L, and platelet count was 221?000 cells per 米L; coagulation tests were normal. D-dimer was high and thromboelastogram results were normal.
An intravenous dose of tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg was started, and colonoscopy was done, which showed continuous submucosal involvement of the rectum and sigmoid, with areas of erythema and whitish zones suggestive of lymphatic lesions, without mucosal erosions (figure, A). Large varices were observed with extensive involvement through the descending, transverse colon, hepatic angle, and ascending colon (figure, B). They extended towards the lumen, in the shape of grape clusters, leaving only a small segment towards the caecum free of disease. The ileum could not be visualised. No mucosal lesions were evident. MRI enteroclysis showed concentric mural thickening of the rectum and proximal sigmoid of the right colon, especially at the level of the caecum and the proximal aspect of the ascending colon. Concentric thickening and hyperaemia of the adjacent rectum wall were also observed. Compared with an examination done 3 years previously, there was evidence of increased involvement of the intestinal wall and adjacent tissues. Given the impossibility of surgical resection, the patient has been treated with oral rapamycin 1﹞5 mg per day for the past 10 months. She has presented with two episodes of self-limiting rectal bleeding since she started rapamycin, and has been undergoing strict follow-up with a paediatric multidisciplinary team (including surgery, haematology, traumatology, and endocrinology).
Klippel每Tr谷naunay syndrome is a congenital vascular malformation, with a pathogenesis that is not completely understood. Alteration in the fetal mesoderm has been postulated, as a result of intrauterine damage causing dilation of the arteriovenous anastomosis, deep vein obstruction with varices, or hypertrophy of the lymphatic vessels. Gastrointestinal tract involvement is observed in up to 20% of cases, usually in the rectum and sigmoid, which can manifest as gastrointestinal bleeding, usually during the first decade of life. Since most of the time the bleeding is self-limiting and the involvement of the colon is distal, the patient should be followed up and treated for anaemia if necessary. Angiographic intervention such as embolisation of the bleeding vessel can sometimes be successful. Endoscopic therapy is usually preferred for localised lesions or postoperative residual disease. Endorectal resection extending to the transverse colon has been reported in cases of more extensive disease. Involvement of the ascending colon is very unusual, and the extensive involvement of the bowel makes this particular case unique and challenging.

A 23-year-old woman was referred to our hospital for a recurrent discharge of something resembling a white string from her anus. She explained that the problem had started 4 months ago and that she had no other symptoms. She said she had eaten raw fish as sashimi approximately 6 months earlier and that the discharge had started 2 months later. A physical examination found no abnormalities and the blood test results were all normal. However, based on her history, we suspected she had diphyllobothriasis and did a screening abdominal ultrasound scan, which showed a hyperechoic strand-like structure floating freely and moving autonomously in her intestinal tract (figure; videos 1 and 2). A subsequent capsule endoscopy showed a tapeworm (figure); a coprological examination was positive, confirming the diagnosis of diphyllobothriasis. We treated the patient with diatrizoate (Gastrografin, Bayer, Reading, UK) given through a duodenal tube to ensure that the scolex of the cestode was expelled: the complete, uninjured tapeworm measured 210 cm in length when we examined it outside the patient's body (figure). Mitochondrial DNA analysis of the COX-1 and NAD-3 gene sequences identified the causative cestode as Diphyllobothrium nihonkaiense〞based on comparisons with homologous sequences in GenBank.D nihonkaiense is the principal cestode causing diphyllobothriasis in Japan. It can infect anyone〞regardless of immune status〞who eats raw or undercooked fish harbouring infective larvae: once infected, the patient then becomes the worm's second intermediate host. Presenting symptoms include diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and bloating〞although up to 30% of patients report no problems.
Oral praziquantel remains the first-line treatment, with the introduction of the radio-opaque contrast medium Gastrografin into the duodenum via a tube the second choice: using Gastrografin ensures complete deworming〞ie, discharge of the whole organism, including the scolex〞as in our case. Diphyllobothriasis is typically diagnosed by detecting the cestode's ova or proglottids in the patient's faeces. However, the examination of stool samples for the ova is not routinely done in many clinics or hospitals; the detection is sometimes difficult and not definitive. Moreover, once a large part of the worm's body is excreted, the ova are undetectable for some time afterwards. Capsule endoscopy has been reported as a useful alternative for diagnosing diphyllobothriasis, but it is expensive and carries the risk of capsule retention〞occurring in approximately 2% of all patients undergoing small bowel capsule endoscopy. In our patient, the abdominal ultrasound vividly showed the tapeworm moving in the intestinal fluid in the gut. And although intestinal gas may sometimes prevent visualisation of the worm, we believe that an abdominal ultrasound scan offers a practical, real-time, non-invasive way of screening for diphyllobothriasis.

A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. Ophthalmologic examination revealed prominent bilateral corneal nerve fibres (figure A and B; white arrows) and multiple nodules along the eyelid margins (figure A and C; black arrows). She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3﹞2 ug/l; normal range <3﹞2 米g/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3﹞2 米g/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4﹞6 ng/l. One year later, the patient is healthy and taking daily L-thyroxine 112 ug, with no long-term surgical complications.
An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

A 24-year-old man presented to our clinic reporting severe anal pain and a pustular rash on his trunk, arms, penis, and fingers. The patient said the pain started 3 days after he had condomless penetrative and receptive anal intercourse with a man; he then developed a fever, chills, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. The skin lesions appeared approximately 8 days after the sexual activity: 2 days before he attended our clinic. The patient was previously fit and well with no medical history.On examination, we found him to be in obvious distress because of the anal pain; his temperature was 37﹞1～C, heart rate was 98 beats per min, and blood pressure was 140/98 mm Hg. He had approximately 10 vesicular lesions, without surrounding erythema, containing yellow fluid, and measuring between 2 mm and 3 mm on his trunk, arms, penis, and fingers; his penis was oedematous.
Laboratory investigations showed a C-reactive protein concentration of 16 mg/L, which increased to approximately 7 times this concentration on day 2 of his hospital stay. Anorectoscopy showed ulcerating lesions adjacent to the pectinate line of the anal canal (appendix). Anorectal and oropharyngeal swabs tested positive for monkeypox virus by PCR.
Histopathological analysis of tissue samples taken from the anal lesions (appendix) showed prominent inflammation and regional disruption of the crypt epithelium, specifically loss of columnar cell shape. Notably, balloon-like expansion of epithelial cells and regular eosinophilic plasma inclusions, typical of poxvirus infections of the skin, were absent. Immunohistochemistry for cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, and nucleic acid amplification tests for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoea were negative.
Paraffin-embedded biopsy samples were processed for thin-section electron microscopy (EM) to investigate whether cells are infected by monkeypox virus and whether they propagate the virus. Ultrathin sections of the samples were analysed by transmission EM. One section was entirely digitalised at high resolution by EM〞so called large-scale scanning-transmission EM〞to allow microscope-independent analysis by pan-and-zoom viewing at the computer screen. EM showed both mature and immature virus particles〞indicating virus replication〞organised in specific cytoplasmic areas of epithelial cells of colonic crypts and of interstitial cells (figure).
The patient was admitted to the infectious disease ward, because of anal pain, and prescribed a combination of morphine, metamizole, and gabapentin, which controlled his symptoms. He was allowed home, 8 days later, when his condition had improved. He had no antiviral treatment.

input: Various cases in professional sports have brought the matter of doping〞the use of performance-enhancing drugs〞to the attention of the broad public. Here, we present a case of doping in a 21-year-old amateur bodybuilder. The man presented to our clinic feeling generally unwell. He was subfebrile and had massive, deep ulcerations, abscesses, and pustules located on his chest and upper back (figure). Persistent questioning revealed a history of continuous abuse of anabolic-androgenic steroids (testosterone enantate 250 mg plus metandienona 30 mg twice weekly), which was consistent with the diagnosis of a severe acne conglobata that was anabolic-androgenic steroid induced. Additional investigations showed a substantial impairment in sperm concentration and reduced testicular volume. Skin lesions showed rapid improvement after discontinuation of anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse and with antiseptic and antibiotic therapy. However, the extensive scarring is likely to remain with the young man for the rest of his life.

A 10-year-old girl was referred to the Ophthalmology Department at Cantonal Hospital St Gallen, Switzerland, for intermittent divergent strabismus. She also had distinct facial features that included a narrow face, prominent chin, bulging lips, and nodules on the tongue and ears (appendix p 1). During planned strabismus surgery, a biopsy of one eyelid nodule was performed due to the unusual appearance of these lesions. Histological analysis revealed a neuroma, which prompted further systemic evaluation and led to the diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B), an autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndrome.
Urgent paediatric evaluation did not find biochemical evidence of phaeochromocytoma, but found elevated tumour markers calcitonin (129 ng/l; normal range <3 ng/l) and carcinoembryonic antigen (3﹞2 ug/l; normal range <3﹞2 米g/l) and a suspicious sonographic thyroid nodule (appendix p 2), which indicated a medullary thyroid carcinoma. The diagnosis of MEN2B was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, revealing the de novo, pathological, heterozygous RET proto-oncogene mutation Met918Thr. This is a high risk mutation that has an 100% incidence for aggressive early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma, and prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended after diagnosis. The patient did not show signs of dry eyes in infancy or throughout childhood, and did not have any dental, urinary, or skeletal atypicalities. Moreover, her growth variables and cognitive development (intelligent quotient) were within the normal range.
Our patient underwent a complete thyroidectomy with central lymphadenectomy, which would have been performed in the first year of life if the RET mutation had been known about. Histological analysis confirmed medullary thyroid carcinoma with lymphogenic metastasis and focal angioinvasion. After surgery, her carcinoembryonic antigen levels normalised (below 3﹞2 米g/l), but her calcitonin levels only dropped by 50% (63 ng/l). A cervicolateral lymphadenectomy was performed 3 months later, and incomplete biochemical control was reached with a minimum calcitonin level of 4﹞6 ng/l. An intestinal endoscopy was given due to long-standing flatulence and revealed ganglioneuromatosis, which will be observed clinically. Follow up also includes regular screening for phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma metastases.
Prominent corneal nerves and the development of multiple mucosal and cutaneous nodules in childhood should raise suspicion of MEN2B, warranting urgent investigation to manage early-onset medullary thyroid carcinoma.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of sore throat and progressive dysphagia. She had no history of any serious illness, chronic cough, or other chest symptoms. She had been taking various courses of antibiotics, including amoxicillin and a combination of amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, and paracetamol for sore throat without any relief.
General physical examination revealed normal findings, but oral examination found an enlarged right palatine tonsil with central ulceration (figure). Fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy did not identify any pharyngeal or laryngeal lesions, but a firm 3 cm right-upper cervical lymphadenopathy was detected during clinical examination. CT scan images showed a tumoural right tonsil infiltrating the base of the tongue and associated with necrotic cervical lymph nodes. A thoracic CT scan did not detect any pulmonary or nodal disease.A biopsy sample was taken from the ulcerated area of the right tonsil. Histopathological examination revealed granulomas and caseous necrosis consistent with tuberculosis. The culture from the tonsil biopsy sample and lymphadenopathy puncture was positive for acid-fast bacilli, suggesting the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serological tests for HIV and syphilis were negative. The tuberculin skin test was positive, with a 3 cm bulla.
The patient was started on a daily oral multidrug therapy consisting of 2 months of isoniazid (5 mg/kg), rifampicin (10 mg/kg), pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg), and ethambutol (15 mg/kg), followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin at the same doses. Treatment resulted in rapid resolution of the sore throat and progressive regression of the cervical lymph node.
Isolated tuberculosis of the tonsil in the absence of active pulmonary tuberculosis is an exceptional clinical entity and often mistaken for a malignancy. This infection is acquired by inhalation of tubercle bacilli, and commonly presents with sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Differential diagnosis of pharyngeal tuberculosis includes traumatic ulcers, haematological disorders, actinomycosis, syphilis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and cancer. Diagnosis is based on histopathological findings and on the identification of tubercle bacilli.

A 69-year-old woman was admitted to our ward with fever and respiratory failure. 3 weeks earlier she had been treated with ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection, caused by Escherichia coli; she had a history of diabetes.On examination she was oriented in time, place, and person; her blood pressure was 130/70 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per min, respiratory rate was 15 breaths per min, temperature 37﹞1～C, and oxygen saturation 94%. She had harsh vesicular breath sounds that were diffusely reduced with no added noises.

A CT angiogram showed bronchopneumonia and bilateral pulmonary nodules〞raising the suspicion of metastases (figure). A full-body CT, with contrast medium, showed thrombosis of the left renal vein and homolateral thickening of calyces＊ walls and renal pelvis. Urine cytology was negative for any urothelial malignancy. Our working diagnosis at this stage was septic emboli from a nephritic focus. However, despite 8 days of ceftazidime and clarithromycin, and enoxaparin, the patient's condition worsened. Given the working diagnosis, we did a transoesophageal echocardiography and broncho-alveolar lavage. The echocardiogram showed some thickening of the free margin of the aortic valve cusps with normal function; the mitral valve flaps showed some thickening with mild insufficiency. A set of blood and urine cultures were done which were negative for any infection and malignancy. At this stage, we suspected the patient had an autoimmune disease and we decided to start methylprednisolone empirically. The patient's condition improved, and she was able to go home 11 days later. At follow-up 1 month later, she reported rusty sputum, a persistent cough, and back pain; investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 16﹞76?℅?109 per L, neutrophils 90﹞5%, CRP concentration 15﹞2 mg/dL. An autoimmune screen showed no atypical results. An 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT of the chest showed three excavated lesions with hypermetabolic perimeters; we suspected either an inflammatory or an infectious process and the patient was readmitted.

Cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and a sample of a lung biopsy showed non-extended-spectrum 汕-lactamase-producing strain E coli, mucoid phenotype, characterised by a thick polysaccharide wall impervious to antibiotics. We started the patient on voriconazole and〞according to culture antibiogram〞ceftazidime and ampicillin combined with sulbactam. The methylprednisolone was gradually reduced over the next 8 weeks; the two largest chest lesions were drained. After 38 days of antibiotic treatment, the patient's symptoms had improved; she was no longer in respiratory failure and cultures of blood, urine, broncho-alveolar lavage fluid, and pleural fluid were negative. A chest CT scan showed a decrease in the size of the pulmonary lesions.
Although rare, an E coli urinary tract infection can spread to the lungs, causing a pneumonia. Mucoid phenotypes have been shown to be associated with advanced disease states〞specifically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii infections. A mucoid phenotype has never been shown to underlie the development of invasive disease after an E coli urinary tract infection, but such a possibility cannot be ruled out.

A 69-year-old man presented to our cardiology clinic troubled by breathlessness on exertion. He had a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. Physical examination showed jugular venous distension, bilateral ankle oedema, and a bunching of the right biceps when he flexed his arm〞so-called Popeye's sign〞indicating rupture of the proximal biceps tendon (figure and video); a rupture was confirmed by an ultrasound scan. Serum N-terminal-pro-B-type natriuretic peptide was 7088 pg/mL (normal range for patients aged 0每74 years is less than 125 pg/mL). A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed low voltage in the limb leads, as well as a pseudo-infarct pattern in the precordial ones (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy with a maximum wall thickness of 20 mm and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 40%. Cardiac MRI showed signs of myocardial infiltration. 99mTechnetium-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (99mTc-DPD) scintigraphy showed grade 3 myocardial uptake (figure). Serum and urine immunoelectrophoresis and free light chain assays ruled out a monoclonal component. Genetic sequencing analysis of the transthyretin gene found no mutations. Tying all the findings together, a diagnosis of heart failure secondary to wild-type transthyretin amyloid (ATTRwt) cardiomyopathy was made. The patient was treated with a combination of diuretics〞namely, furosemide 80 mg twice a day, hydrochlorothiazide 12﹞5 mg once a day, and spironolactone 100 mg once a day〞but he did not respond well. He remained symptomatic with advanced functional impairment and persistent signs of systemic venous congestion.ATTRwt, previously known as senile systemic amyloidosis, is a disease that typically affects the heart and tendons of elderly patients. A history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome or, less frequently, spontaneous tendon rupture in a patient with heart failure and preserved or mildly depressed LVEF should raise clinical suspicion of the condition. A definitive diagnosis of ATTRwt cardiomyopathy can be confirmed non-invasively with a positive finding on 99mTc-DPD scintigraphy, together with the absence of a monoclonal component in serum and urine samples, and a normal genetic sequencing analysis of the transthyretin gene. Current therapy for patients with ATTRwt cardiomyopathy is limited, with diuretics for relief of cardiac congestion being the mainstay of treatment. However, a recent randomised, placebo-controlled trial, published in September 2018, showed a significant reduction in the risk of death and hospitalisation from cardiovascular causes in patients with ATTRwt cardiomyopathy treated with tafamidis, a transthyretin stabilising agent. Tafamidis is expected to be available for clinical use in the near future.

A 66-year-old man attended our hospital reporting a 1-year history of progressively worsening difficulties with walking, falls, a tremor, and erectile dysfunction. Additionally, he believed he had become more impulsive, anxious, and he reported feeling resentment towards others. The patient had no notable medical or family history.On examination we found him to be generally well; neurological evaluation showed a mixed cerebellar and sensory ataxic gait with a positive Romberg sign. In addition, the patient had difficulty standing with both feet together, and walking during the tandem walk test (video).
Dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, as well as a bilateral postural and action tremor〞further cerebellar signs〞were noted. We also found the patient to have global areflexia and pallhypesthesia in both feet. Notably, during examination and interview, the patient made several out of place comments and jokes and laughed inappropriately. He scored 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment〞he had completed 11 years of full-time education〞but showed no impairment of daily functional activities.
MRI of his brain showed diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy with symmetrical middle cerebellar peduncle and periventricular hyperintensities, and diffuse corpus callosum thinning with hyperintensities (figure; appendix). Electrophysiological studies showed a sensory-motor polyneuropathy pattern with predominantly sensory involvement. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal.
Laboratory investigations〞including full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function tests, thyroid and parathyroid function tests, folate, vitamins B12 and E, cholesterol, ceruloplasmin, C-reactive protein concentration, and autoantibodies were all within typical range.
Considering the findings together, we proceeded to genetic testing for the fragile X syndrome, which showed 111 CGG trinucleotide repeats in the fragile X mental retardation 1 protein (FMR1) gene, confirming a diagnosis of fragile X-associated tremor or ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
We explained the diagnosis and symptoms of the condition to the patient and he was managed with physiotherapy focusing upon gait and balance training and on prevention of falls; he received advice from an occupational therapist and a clinical geneticist.
Fragile X syndrome and FXTAS are caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide in the FMR1 gene, which is also known as the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP) gene. A mutation in the FMR1 gene of more than 200 CGG trinucleotide repeats leads to the absence of the FMR1 mRNA protein and results in developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder〞a condition referred to as fragile X syndrome. A 47-year-old woman presented to our institution with a 1-month history of swelling and a painless skin plaque on her left breast. 6 years earlier, the patient had been treated for luminal A invasive ductal carcinoma in the superomedial quadrant of the left breast; she had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, breast-conserving surgery, radiation therapy〞a whole breast dose of 50 Gy plus a 10 Gy boost to the tumour bed〞and oral tamoxifen. The patient had been found to have no recurrence of the tumour at any subsequent follow-up appointments. She had no history of breast trauma or lymphoedema.

Diagnostic mammogram showed a developing asymmetry in the inferomedial quadrant of the left breast, as well as skin thickening and parenchymal oedema that were more pronounced compared with her previous mammograms (figure). Histological examination of a sample obtained by ultrasound-guided core biopsy showed solid epithelial proliferation with marked cellular atypia〞initially deemed suspicious for recurrence of the carcinoma (figure). Immunohistochemistry results were positive for CD31, ERG, and D2-40 on most target cells and for CD34 in subgroups of target cells (appendix), along with very high Ki67 expression (90% of target cells), findings compatible with post radiation angiosarcoma.
On post-biopsy follow-up〞54 days after the first ultrasound examination〞the previously 1 cm wide skin lesion had progressed to a 4 cm irregular violaceous plaque with subtle areas of yellowish discoloration on adjacent skin (figure). On ultrasound examination, the lesion appeared as an irregular, hypoechoic mass with thick echogenic rind; the high central vascularity on power Doppler remained visible (appendix).
The findings, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment options were discussed with the patient and together the decision was made to proceed to mastectomy of the affected breast.
On the day of mastectomy〞60 days after the first ultrasound examination〞additional satellite lesions and morphological changes in the nipple-areola complex were seen adjacent to the irregular violaceous plaque, with progression of the areas of yellowish skin discoloration (figure).

CT scans of the patient's head, chest, and abdomen showed no evidence of metastases.

At follow-up 3 months after the mastectomy, a new 1 cm violaceous skin lesion surrounded by a yellowish halo appeared in the mastectomy scar (appendix); recurrence of the post-radiation angiosarcoma was confirmed by histopathological analysis of a sample obtained from surgically excised tissue.
Post-radiation angiosarcoma is an uncommon aggressive complication of radiotherapy for breast cancer, with a median latency period of 5每6 years. A 36-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of sore throat and progressive dysphagia. She had no history of any serious illness, chronic cough, or other chest symptoms. She had been taking various courses of antibiotics, including amoxicillin and a combination of amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, and paracetamol for sore throat without any relief.
General physical examination revealed normal findings, but oral examination found an enlarged right palatine tonsil with central ulceration (figure). Fiberoptic nasopharyngoscopy did not identify any pharyngeal or laryngeal lesions, but a firm 3 cm right-upper cervical lymphadenopathy was detected during clinical examination. CT scan images showed a tumoural right tonsil infiltrating the base of the tongue and associated with necrotic cervical lymph nodes. A thoracic CT scan did not detect any pulmonary or nodal disease.A biopsy sample was taken from the ulcerated area of the right tonsil. Histopathological examination revealed granulomas and caseous necrosis consistent with tuberculosis. The culture from the tonsil biopsy sample and lymphadenopathy puncture was positive for acid-fast bacilli, suggesting the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serological tests for HIV and syphilis were negative. The tuberculin skin test was positive, with a 3 cm bulla.
The patient was started on a daily oral multidrug therapy consisting of 2 months of isoniazid (5 mg/kg), rifampicin (10 mg/kg), pyrazinamide (25 mg/kg), and ethambutol (15 mg/kg), followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin at the same doses. Treatment resulted in rapid resolution of the sore throat and progressive regression of the cervical lymph node.
Isolated tuberculosis of the tonsil in the absence of active pulmonary tuberculosis is an exceptional clinical entity and often mistaken for a malignancy. This infection is acquired by inhalation of tubercle bacilli, and commonly presents with sore throat and cervical lymphadenopathy.
Differential diagnosis of pharyngeal tuberculosis includes traumatic ulcers, haematological disorders, actinomycosis, syphilis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and cancer. Diagnosis is based on histopathological findings and on the identification of tubercle bacilli.

A 69-year-old man presented to our cardiology clinic troubled by breathlessness on exertion. He had a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. A 12-lead electrocardiogram showed low voltage in the limb leads, as well as a pseudo-infarct pattern in the precordial ones (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed left ventricular hypertrophy with a maximum wall thickness of 20 mm and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 40%. Tafamidis is expected to be available for clinical use in the near future.

A 32-year-old woman presented to our department for an evaluation of possible cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex.The patient had been diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex in her early childhood when she started having daily focal seizures. Genetic analysis when she was 16 years old confirmed a TSC1 (Q783X) de novo mutation. During adolescence, she had continued anticonvulsant medication〞a combination of carbamazepine and valproate〞and remained free from further seizures. However, after the initial diagnosis, regular follow-up imaging was not performed.
1 year before the assessment in our department, the patient was diagnosed with a papillary thyroid carcinoma for which she underwent a right hemi-thyroidectomy with lymphadenectomy. Following the operation, she reported an increase of the focal seizures〞thought to be provoked by stress. A neurological examination, at the time, was unremarkable and no dermatological signs specific to tuberous sclerosis complex were found〞such as hypomelanotic macules, or facial angiofibromas. Further, because of the lack of regular follow-up over the previous 17 years, extensive additional investigations were requested by the neurologist who saw her: brain MRI showed typical cortical tubers (figure) and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma adjacent to the foramen of Monro〞without any signs of obstruction (figure). Compared to an MRI from 17 years earlier, the giant cell astrocytoma showed no significant increase in size. Abdominal MRI showed cyst-like lesions in the patient's left kidney, which was thought to be a fat-poor angiomyolipoma (figure).
For completeness and because screening for the cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex had not been done previously, the patient was referred to our department: cardiac MRI showed myocardial fatty foci (figure) with no cardiac rhabdomyomas. We concluded that in the absence of cardiac rhabdomyomas no further follow-up cardiac imaging was indicated; cardiac magnetic resonance and an electrocardiogram were normal.
The patient was continued on anticonvulsant medication〞a combination of carbamazepine and lamotrigine〞and she remained seizure-free. Surgery and medical treatment with everolimus were considered for the subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, but because the lesion had remained stable, the neurologist decided to simply keep the patient under active surveillance. Diagnostic imaging of the patient's kidneys is also planned to be repeated regularly to monitor possible growth of the lesions.
Tuberous sclerosis complex is a protean disease. Regarding the heart, cardiac rhabdomyomas usually appear in the fetus and almost always regress in infancy. Although the presence of myocardial fatty foci〞as seen in our patient〞is not one of the clinical diagnostic criteria of tuberous sclerosis complex, they are strongly associated with the disease and can be useful in making the initial clinical diagnosis; the number of lesions correlates with the degree of extra cardiac involvement.
output: Tuberous sclerosis complex with myocardial fatty foci

A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 米mol/L; typical range 3﹞7每13﹞9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging〞including magnetic resonance angiography〞ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8〞indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting〞a provoking factor not previously reported〞and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.

input: A 25-year-old woman with severe obesity presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of blurred vision, headaches, and transient visual obscurations. Neurologic examination showed optic disk swelling and retinal hemorrhages in both eyes. An MRI and MRV of the head showed flattened posterior globes, an empty sella, and stenoses of the transverse sinuses without obstruction or thromboses. Which abnormality would most likely be notable from a lumbar puncture?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, this case is classic for:

**Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) / Pseudotumor Cerebri**

The lumbar puncture would most likely show:

**Elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H?O)**

The key features supporting this diagnosis include:
- Young woman with obesity (classic demographic)
- Symptoms: headaches, blurred vision, transient visual obscurations
- Bilateral papilledema with retinal hemorrhages (fundoscopy image)
- MRI findings: flattened posterior globes, empty sella, transverse sinus stenoses (all classic signs of elevated intracranial pressure)
- MRV showing no venous thrombosis (ruling out cerebral venous thrombosis)

The lumbar puncture in IIH typically reveals elevated opening pressure with normal CSF composition (normal protein, glucose, and cell count).

A 55-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department with a recurrence of chest pain, dyspnoea, cephalea, and pallor; he reported that he had been having repeated episodes of the symptoms for the past 24 h.
6 months before, the patient had a subacute ischaemic stroke of the left posterior circulation attributed to significant atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease; he had a medical history of type 2 diabetes and degenerative disease of the lumbar spine. He was prescribed low-dose aspirin, atorvastatin, and metformin.

A 32-year-old woman presented to our department for an evaluation of possible cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex.The patient had been diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex in her early childhood when she started having daily focal seizures. Genetic analysis when she was 16 years old confirmed a TSC1 (Q783X) de novo mutation. During adolescence, she had continued anticonvulsant medication〞a combination of carbamazepine and valproate〞and remained free from further seizures. However, after the initial diagnosis, regular follow-up imaging was not performed.
1 year before the assessment in our department, the patient was diagnosed with a papillary thyroid carcinoma for which she underwent a right hemi-thyroidectomy with lymphadenectomy. Following the operation, she reported an increase of the focal seizures〞thought to be provoked by stress. A neurological examination, at the time, was unremarkable and no dermatological signs specific to tuberous sclerosis complex were found〞such as hypomelanotic macules, or facial angiofibromas. Further, because of the lack of regular follow-up over the previous 17 years, extensive additional investigations were requested by the neurologist who saw her: brain MRI showed typical cortical tubers (figure) and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma adjacent to the foramen of Monro〞without any signs of obstruction (figure). Compared to an MRI from 17 years earlier, the giant cell astrocytoma showed no significant increase in size. Abdominal MRI showed cyst-like lesions in the patient's left kidney, which was thought to be a fat-poor angiomyolipoma (figure).
For completeness and because screening for the cardiac manifestations of tuberous sclerosis complex had not been done previously, the patient was referred to our department: cardiac MRI showed myocardial fatty foci (figure) with no cardiac rhabdomyomas. We concluded that in the absence of cardiac rhabdomyomas no further follow-up cardiac imaging was indicated; cardiac magnetic resonance and an electrocardiogram were normal.
The patient was continued on anticonvulsant medication〞a combination of carbamazepine and lamotrigine〞and she remained seizure-free. Surgery and medical treatment with everolimus were considered for the subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, but because the lesion had remained stable, the neurologist decided to simply keep the patient under active surveillance. Diagnostic imaging of the patient's kidneys is also planned to be repeated regularly to monitor possible growth of the lesions.
Tuberous sclerosis complex is a protean disease. Regarding the heart, cardiac rhabdomyomas usually appear in the fetus and almost always regress in infancy. Although the presence of myocardial fatty foci〞as seen in our patient〞is not one of the clinical diagnostic criteria of tuberous sclerosis complex, they are strongly associated with the disease and can be useful in making the initial clinical diagnosis; the number of lesions correlates with the degree of extra cardiac involvement.

A 43-year-old man who developed numbness and impaired fine motor skills in his left arm lasting approximately 10 min while chanting during a football match, attended our emergency room. The patient, who was visiting Germany for the UEFA European Football Championship, explained that the problems started at the end of the first half. He said he had been chanting continuously during the game. Despite complete resolution of the symptoms, he was concerned enough to seek help, and at half-time he came to our hospital by ambulance. We decided to admit him to our stroke unit for further investigations. He had no medical history; he said he had consumed a moderate amount of alcohol. He was a non-smoker.
On examination the patient was generally fit and well; his pulse was 92 beats per min, blood pressure was 140/90 mm Hg, and his oxygen saturation was 94%. Physical examination found no abnormalities.
Laboratory investigations showed a mildly elevated LDL cholesterol (142 mg/dL; normal range <115). A coagulopathy was excluded: clotting factors II and V were within normal range, tests for antiphospholipid syndrome were negative, antithrombin III activity was in normal range, and protein S and C levels were normal. The patient's homocysteine serum concentration was slightly elevated (15 米mol/L; typical range 3﹞7每13﹞9), genotyping found the wild-type variant of the MTHFR gene.
MRI showed a small acute embolic ischaemic lesion in the postcentral gyrus of the right hemisphere (figure 1); doppler and duplex sonography of extracranial and intracranial vessels and multimodal imaging〞including magnetic resonance angiography〞ruled out any atherosclerotic plaques, dissection, or vasculitis (figure 1). Electrocardiogram monitoring during more than 72 h of telemetry found no abnormalities.
Transoesophageal echocardiography showed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with spontaneous passage of bubbles and accentuation with Valsalva manoeuvre; no septal aneurysm was seen (figure 2). Atrial size and valvular structures were normal, and no intracardiac thrombi were seen. The Risk of Paradoxical Embolism score was 8〞indicating an 84% chance that a stroke is PFO-related. Venous ultrasound imaging showed no deep vein thromboses in the legs, pelvis, or vena cava. The patient left the hospital after 3 days with a prescription for an antithrombotic treatment. He took a flight back to his home country a day later.
The role of a PFO in young patients with acute ischaemic stroke has been the subject of much debate: several studies have shown PFO closure may reduce risk of recurrent strokes in young patients with cryptogenic stroke. A possible pathophysiologic mechanism is paradoxical embolism through the PFO facilitated by intrathoracic pressure elevation during pressing or coughing. We hypothesise that a paradoxical embolism in our patient was possibly provoked by continuous chanting〞a provoking factor not previously reported〞and we therefore advised him to avoid intensive chanting until interventional PFO closure.

A 26-year-old man with an 8-year history of breathlessness on exertion was referred to our hospital for assessment. Previously, he had been noted to have clubbing of his toes and a heart murmur.On examination, we found the patient to be peripherally and centrally cyanosed; he had grade 3 clubbing of his toes but not of his fingers (figure); his pulse was 82 beats per min, blood pressure was 110/72 mm Hg, and, notably, oxygen saturations were 98% in his hands and 86% in his toes while breathing room air, and he had grade 2 dyspnoea. He had a parasternal heave with a palpable second heart sound; on auscultation, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound was accentuated and closely split.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised haemoglobin concentration (20﹞0 g/dL; normal 13﹞2每16﹞6 in men) and haematocrit (52%; normal 38每48 for men).
An electrocardiogram showed right ventricular hypertrophy with right axis deviation; a chest x-ray showed a dilated main pulmonary artery with peripheral pruning (appendix). A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a 7 mm patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with right-to-left shunting (appendix).
Catheterisation showed an elevated pulmonary artery pressure of 120/68 mm Hg (normal 18/8每25/15) and a mean pressure of 108 mm Hg (normal 12每16) and an indexed pulmonary vascular resistance of 20﹞1 Wood units per m2 (normal 1每3; figure).
Because of the supra-systemic pulmonary artery pressures, we believed surgery was not feasible and therefore started the patient on oral sildenafil and bosentan.
During follow-up over the past 10 years, the patient presented on two occasions reporting blurred vision, tinnitus, and tingling in his hands and feet〞symptoms of hyperviscosity. He was treated with phlebotomy on both occasions and his symptoms improved. At his last follow-up, he remains on sildenafil and bosentan and continues to have grade 2 dyspnoea.
Clubbing usually involves both the upper and lower limbs in congenital heart diseases. Differential clubbing, characterised by the involvement of the toes with sparing of the fingers, is a distinctive feature of PDA with reversed shunt from right to left: Eisenmenger syndrome.
Cyanosis and clubbing may also involve the left upper limb if the left subclavian artery arises distal to the PDA. The treatment of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor, and bosentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist, has been shown to have some beneficial effects: offering hope to patients〞like ours〞whose PDAs are inoperable (video).

A 40-year-old woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease presented with fatigue, malaise, dizziness, difficulty ambulating, diarrhoea, easy bruising, and a diffuse rash involving her extremities and trunk that had been present for several days. She explained that she had limited her diet to consist mostly of bread, rice, dumplings, and the occasional egg white to reduce the symptoms she suffered from her gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin〞although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8﹞3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25﹞2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 米mol/L (normal range 23每50 米mol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

Neurologic examination showed optic disk swelling and retinal hemorrhages in both eyes. An MRI and MRV of the head showed flattened posterior globes, an empty sella, and stenoses of the transverse sinuses without obstruction or thromboses. Which abnormality would most likely be notable from a lumbar puncture?
output:
Based on the patient's presentation of obesity, headaches, transient visual obscurations, and the clinical findings of papilledema (optic disk swelling and hemorrhages shown in the fundus photo) and MRI signs of increased intracranial pressure (flattened posterior globes and empty sella shown in the MRI scans), the diagnosis is **Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension** (also known as pseudotumor cerebri).

A 71-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma with symptomatic bilateral lung metastases and multiple subpleural lesions started second-line cabozantinib (60 mg orally daily) after disease progression on pazopanib. After 3 months of therapy, in May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department and complained of a worsening of his dyspnoea, leading us to suppose that disease progression had occurred. However, a CT scan revealed an impressive volumetric reduction of the lung nodules but the onset of an apical grade 3 left pneumothorax (figure). The patient was admitted to hospital at the University Hospital of Verona (Verona, Italy) and was treated with thorax drainage with complete pneumothorax resolution and no further sequelae. Given this excellent response, cabozantinib treatment was continued. So far, the patient remains on cabozantinib treatment, with a treatment duration of 5 months. A second case of pneumothorax was observed in a 69-year-old woman with metastatic renal cell carcinoma 1 month after beginning second-line cabozantinib at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient had one subpleural lung lesion 5 cm in size. In May, 2018, the patient presented at the emergency department with a sudden worsening of dyspnoea, which led to a diagnosis of grade 3 pneumothorax, admission to the Oncological Department of the University Hospital of Verona, and treatment with drainage of the pneumothorax, which was ipsilateral to the pulmonary metastasis. Treatment with cabozantinib was continued, with a partial response recorded at subsequent disease evaluations. Cabozantinib therapy is still ongoing in this patient 6 months since the start of treatment.Tumour necrosis〞as a result of a rapid, dramatic response to cabozantinib〞of subpleural lung metastases might explain the pathogenesis of the pneumothorax in both these cases. Cabozantinib is the only approved tyrosine kinase inhibitor that has been shown to increase overall survival, progression-free survival, and overall responses compared with everolimus in previously treated patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Only two grade 3 and one grade 4 pneumothorax were reported with cabozantinib in the pivotal METEOR phase 3 trial. Pneumothorax, potentially related to the outstanding clinical activity of cabozantinib, is therefore an adverse event that must be considered in patients with peripheral lung or pleural metastases and unexpected onset of dyspnoea.

input: A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 1-month history of dizziness and episodes of hypotension during his outpatient haemodialysis sessions. In addition to end-stage renal disease, the patient had a history of a large anterior myocardial infarction and subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions with stent placement; this had resulted in an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, which had required the implantation of a left ventricular assist device 5 years before this admission. On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing〞with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation〞was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Despite treatment with intravenous ionotropes, the patient's right ventricular failure worsened and, sadly, he died in a hospice, 6 weeks after he first came to see us.Right ventricular failure after left ventricular assist device implantation is unfortunately common and results in significant morbidity and mortality. It is important to be able to recognise both the common features〞such as jugular vein distension and a pulsatile liver〞and the rare features, such as pulsation of the facial vein, in the diagnosis of right ventricular failure with concomitant tricuspid regurgitation. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system. However, incompetence〞and even complete absence〞of these valves has been reported in patients with longstanding tricuspid regurgitation and elevated central venous pressure.
output: Superior vena cava syndrome with severe tricuspid regurgitation secondary to right ventricular failure

Her diet was also devoid of red meat, fish, chicken, fruits, and vegetables.On physical examination, she had extensive, non-palpable, perifollicular haemorrhages involving her extremities (figure), ecchymosis (figure), and gingival bleeding. Corkscrew hairs, visible with the unaided eye, were seen all over her skin〞although they were much more apparent with dermoscopy (figure). Her laboratory results showed haemoglobin 8﹞3 mg/dL, haematocrit 25﹞2%, and a plasma vitamin C concentration of <5 米mol/L (normal range 23每50 米mol/L). Endoscopy of the upper gastrointestinal tract and colonoscopy of the lower bowel did not find a source of bleeding.
A biopsy of the skin from her right lower leg showed a corkscrew shaped profile of the hair follicle, and histopathological examination showed follicular hyperkeratosis and plugging (figure). Taken together, the clinical, laboratory, and histopathological findings were consistent with a diagnosis of scurvy. Vitamin C must be obtained from dietary sources and it is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues for the synthesis of collagen. It is also important for immune system function and iron absorption. Scurvy rarely affects adults but may be seen in some individuals with malnutrition or malabsorption. Signs and symptoms usually occur by the third month of inadequate consumption, and treatment is with vitamin C supplementation. Early diagnosis and treatment of scurvy can be life-saving, so recognition of the physical findings is important. This patient was given intravenous vitamin C followed by daily oral supplementation and her symptoms resolved within a few weeks.

A 53-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 1-month history of dizziness and episodes of hypotension during his outpatient haemodialysis sessions. In addition to end-stage renal disease, the patient had a history of a large anterior myocardial infarction and subsequent percutaneous coronary interventions with stent placement; this had resulted in an ischaemic cardiomyopathy, which had required the implantation of a left ventricular assist device 5 years before this admission. On examination, the patient had a distended jugular vein, a pulsatile liver, and prominent, pulsating facial veins (figure, video 1). An echocardiogram showed severe tricuspid regurgitation that was caused by annular dilatation and this, in turn, had resulted in malcoaptation of the valve leaflets (video 2). The patient was also noted to have significant enlargement and dysfunction of the right ventricle, as well as diastolic septal shift, indicating volume overload of the right ventricle (video 2). Ventricularisation of the right atrial pressure tracing〞with C-V waves that indicated severe tricuspid regurgitation〞was seen during cardiac catheterisation. Renowned Scottish cardiologist Sir James Mackenzie was one of the first physicians to publish a detailed description of pulsation of the facial vein associated with tricuspid regurgitation, in 1892, and the phenomenon has been the subject of much debate since then. Transmission of atrial pulsations to the facial vein are usually prevented by venous valves present around the lower border of the mandible and in the jugular venous system. However, incompetence〞and even complete absence〞of these valves has been reported in patients with longstanding tricuspid regurgitation and elevated central venous pressure.
