A 37-year-old woman with a 1-month history of fatigue, weight loss, palpitations, and dyspnoea, attended our clinic for investigation.
12 months earlier, the patient had embolisation of pelvic varicose veins, using glue and lipiodised oil, for pelvic venous disorder; she had reported a history of pelvic congestion syndrome with chronic pelvic pain beginning after a pregnancy 5 years earlier. The pain worsened just before the onset of menstruation. She also had symptomatic varicose veins in her legs. Venograms had confirmed abdominal-pelvic venous insufficiency with reflux in a dilated left ovarian vein, tortuous pelvic varicosities near the uterus, and bilateral dilated utero-vaginal venous plexuses.
The patient had no history of recent viral infection or neck pain; she was prescribed no medication.
On examination the patient was generally unwell; her blood pressure was 132/70 mm Hg, her pulse was 97 beats per min, and her BMI was 20﹞7 kg/m2. She had a firm, hard moderate-sized goitre but no signs of Graves＊ orbitopathy.
Laboratory investigations showed hyperthyroidism; the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration was biologically undetectable, the free thyroxine (FT4) concentration was above 100﹞0 pmol/L (typical range 12﹞0每22﹞0), and the free triiodothyroxine (FT3) concentration was 36﹞0 pmol/L (typical range 3﹞1每6﹞8). Tests for TSH-receptor antibodies were negative. Thyroglobulin concentration was 1143 ng/mL (typical range 3﹞5每77﹞0); C-reactive protein concentration was within typical range (<5 mg/L). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies were also within the normal range. Urinary iodine concentration was raised at 10﹞01 米mol/L (typical range 0﹞35每1﹞60).
123Iodine thyroid scintigraphy showed no significant uptake with a blunted measured value of 0﹞4% at 120 min (average value 12% at 120 min for a mean TSH of 1﹞2 mIU/L in France; appendix).
Considering the findings in the round, we ruled out thyrotoxicosis factitia because of the raised thyroglobulin concentration and concluded the most likely diagnosis was an iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis. As stated above, the patient was not prescribed amiodarone〞a recognised cause of iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis〞or any other drugs associated with thyroiditis and thyrotoxicosis, and she had no history of recent radiographic contrast exposure. However, an unenhanced abdominal CT scan showed lipiodised oil in the ovarian veins (figure 1); additionally, an unenhanced CT scan of the patient's neck, which we requested to give further weight to our conclusion that the patient had thyrotoxicosis secondary to the lipiodised oil, showed a very high density of the thyroid (147 Hounsfield units [HU]; typical range 80每100; figure 2).
The patient was commenced on oral prednisone at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day until laboratory investigations showed she was euthyroid; the corticosteroids were gradually reduced over 5 months.
At follow-up 18 months later, she was well with normal thyroid function.
Excessive intake of iodine can cause hyperthyroidism; mainly this occurs after exposure to iodinated radiographic material or treatment with amiodarone. Interestingly, a study proposed a cutoff level of 117 HU for the density of the thyroid seen on unenhanced CT scan to distinguish patients with amiodarone-induced hyperthyroidism from healthy controls and from euthyroid amiodarone-treated patients (appendix). With this in mind, we suggest that a hyperdense thyroid, seen on an unenhanced CT scan〞with a density level above 120 HU〞should raise the possibility of iodine overload and subsequent testing of the serum TSH concentration.

A 70-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital reporting puffy eyelids and swelling of both legs. She had a 7-year history of nephrotic syndrome and hypertension.On examination, she had swollen eyelids and oedema in both legs; her blood pressure was 172/81 mm Hg.

Cryoglobulinaemic glomerulonephritis〞which should be distinguished from ITG〞has deposits comprising short, curved microtubules or fibrillary substructures of diameters less than 30 nm.
ITG has IgG monoclonal and polyclonal variants: the monoclonal type has a higher incidence of haematological conditions〞including lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy. Monoclonal ITG is more commonly treated with clone-directed therapy and associated with frequent remissions and less end-stage kidney disease; it should therefore be subclassified into monoclonal and polyclonal variants. Recently〞as seen in our case〞improved prognosis in ITG may be possible due to rituximab-based therapy (video).
output: Immunotactoid glomerulopathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy

input: A 69-year-old woman with a 27-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the rheumatology clinic at Kochi Medical School hospital, Japan, with polyarthralgia of both hands and painless subcutaneous nodules on her right hand that had slowly grown over a year. Physical examination revealed arthritis mutilans with ulnar deviation and yellow masses on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers of the right hand (figure A). There were no abnormal findings in any part of the body other than the joints, such as the eyelids and trunk. Laboratory investigations revealed that the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor were 1﹞78 mg/dL (normal range <0﹞15 mg/dL) and 1?096﹞0 IU/mL (<15 IU/mL), respectively. Hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins were not detected. We performed a bone marrow biopsy, which was normocellular. An x-ray revealed severe erosion and deformities of the hand bones and punched-out bony radiolucencies associated with the subcutaneous nodular lesions (figure B). A skin biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous mass showed areas of cholesterol clefts and necrobiosis surrounded by foamy histiocytes, lymphocytes, Touton giant cells, and foreign body-type multinucleated giant cells (figure C每F). These findings confirmed a diagnosis of pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are an unusual form of rheumatoid nodule resembling tendon xanthomas, are often mistakenly diagnosed as xanthomatosis, and have been previously regarded by investigators as subcutaneous xanthogranuloma, observed in the juxta-articular sites of the hand, wrist, elbow, knee, foot, and acromioclavicular joints. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are distinguished from xanthomatosis by x-ray findings of demonstrable punched-out bony radiolucencies, which are not present in xanthomatosis. Cholesterol clefts surrounded by granulomatous reactions can also be observed in rheumatoid synovial fluid and bursitis, sometimes presenting as migrating chylous cysts. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule and xanthomatosis are easily misdiagnosed because their histopathological findings are similar. However, xanthomatosis is often associated with hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins, whereas pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule is not accompanied by these diseases and is found in the juxta-articular sites with punched-out bony radiolucencies. After initiating treatment with 6 mg oral methotrexate per week, the concentrations of CRP reduced to 0﹞63 mg/dL, polyarthralgia improved, and the pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules shrank.

input: A 34-year-old man with a history of intravenous drug use and hepatitis C infection presented to the ophthalmology clinic with a 1-week history of pain and decreased vision in his right eye. The visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Slit-lamp examination of the right eye showed conjunctival injection and inflammation in the anterior chamber. Indirect ophthalmoscopy showed vitreous haze with yellow-white lesions on the retina and optic nerve. Following workup, surgery was performed and a white mass measuring 4 mm by 3 mm by 1 mm was seen adherent to the optic nerve. What is the most likely diagnosis/etiology?
output: Endogenous endophthalmitis secondary to Candida infection (fungal endophthalmitis)

A 26-year-old woman presented at week 20 of pregnancy with a 3-month history of fever, cough, and breathlessness. She had hearing loss, epistaxis, nasal crusting, haemoptysis, and a purpuric rash over her legs. No significant weight loss was reported. Chest x-ray (with abdominal shield) showed bilateral cannonball opacities, and contrast-enhanced chest CT (with abdominal shield) revealed multiple nodules, without pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy (figure). Ultrasound of the patient's abdomen and pelvis showed a single live fetus and no abnormalities. Her haemoglobin concentration was 8﹞3 g/dL, total leucocyte count was 8﹞6?℅?109/L, platelet count was 600?℅?109/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 65 mm/h, and C-reactive protein concentration was 186 mg/L. The patient's serum anti-proteinase 3 antibody concentration was 102 U/mL. Sputum acid-fast bacilli and fungal smear, serum 汕-D-glucan and galactomannan, and Mantoux test results were all negative. A diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis was made.
The patient commenced remission induction therapy with intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g once daily for 3 days) and rituximab (1000 mg, two doses 2 weeks apart). She showed substantial improvement over the next 2每3 days and delivered a healthy baby girl at term. The patient commenced oral prednisolone immediately after induction therapy, starting at 60 mg/day for 1 month followed by taper every two weeks. She has received remission maintenance therapy with oral prednisolone (5 mg/day) and intravenous rituximab (500 mg every 6 months) for 1 year, and is planned to continue this treatment for at least 2 years total duration. A follow-up chest x-ray 6 months after the initial treatment showed complete resolution of lung nodules.
Cannonball opacities on chest x-ray usually suggest metastatic malignancies such as choriocarcinoma, lung carcinoma, renal cell cancer, or endometrial carcinoma, but, less frequently, can be due to other conditions, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, fungal infections, and tuberculosis. The most common chest radiological finding at presentation in patients with granulomatosis with polyangiitis is bilateral nodules or masses (reported in up to 90% of patients in case series). In the current case, hearing loss, purpuric rash, and upper respiratory symptoms led us to suspect granulomatosis with polyangiitis. The absence of pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy on chest radiology made a diagnosis of malignancy or infection less likely, the normal pelvic ultrasound helped to rule out choriocarcinoma, and the negative Mantoux test, sputum workup, and fungal serology helped to rule out infection. Elevated concentrations of anti-proteinase 3 antibodies and the patient's rapid response to immunosuppression contributed to confirmation of the diagnosis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis that can mimic malignancy and infections. This diagnosis should be suspected in patients with lung nodules when there are accompanying upper respiratory tract symptoms, rash, neuropathy, or eye, ear, or renal involvement.

A 45-year-old woman attended our dermatology outpatient clinic for her 3-monthly skin cancer surveillance appointment. Numerous actinic keratoses, in addition to two full thickness skin grafts were noted on examination of the dorsal hands (as illustrated by the graft on the right dorsal hand in the figure).Significantly in her medical history, the patient had two cadaveric-donor renal transplants because of renal failure secondary to chronic glomerulonephritis〞first aged 17 years, and then aged 41 years. She was prescribed immunosuppressive therapy, which included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone.
Aged 38 years, the patient was diagnosed with an invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the right dorsal hand which was treated with surgical resection and full thickness skin graft reconstruction. Histopathology confirmed a well-differentiated SCC; depth of invasion of 8 mm, with evidence of perineural invasion of nerves of <0﹞1 mm in diameter, but without lympho-vascular space invasion. The SCC was excised with adequate histopathologic margins; no evidence of locoregional nodal or distant metastatic disease was found.
Aged 39 years, the patient developed numerous actinic keratoses on her dorsal hands which were treated with conventional photodynamic therapy and 6-monthly topical 5-fluorouracil (which she continues to receive).
Aged 42 years, the patient developed a second invasive SCC of the left distal phalanx of the fifth finger which was again treated with surgical resection and full thickness skin graft reconstruction; histopathology again confirmed a moderately differentiated SCC, depth of invasion 1﹞5 mm, without evidence of perineural or lympho-vascular space invasion. The lesion was excised with adequate histopathologic margins; no evidence of locoregional nodal or distant metastatic disease was found.
The repeated development of malignancies and other skin lesions only on her hands caused us to review the case more circumspectly, and the absence of significant photodamage in other sun-exposed areas aroused our suspicion of an alternative aetiology.
The patient, who had skin phototype 1, had reliably informed us that she had adopted effective photoprotective measures, which included avoidance of sun exposure, use of sunscreen, and wearing photoprotective clothing, since the first transplantation.
However, upon closer questioning, she also said that, for more than 20 years, she had regular, monthly manicures which used unregulated ultraviolet radiation A (UVA) emitting lamps to set the nail polish.
Repeated exposure to UVA rays is well described in the setting of cutaneous carcinogenesis, acting via a direct DNA-damaging mechanism, to cause both photo-ageing and the development of keratinocyte malignancies. This effect is greatly amplified in immunosuppressed patients, particularly solid organ transplant recipients.
While it is difficult to conclude that manicure-associated UVA exposure was the sole driver of carcinogenesis in our patient, the absence of precancerous lesions and keratinocyte malignancies at sites other than the dorsal hands suggests it might have been a significant contributor.
A practical approach towards mitigating the risk of cutaneous carcinogenesis in the setting of unregulated UVA-emitting lamps might include advising patients to specifically request the use of a light-emitting diode lamp during manicures to minimise cumulative UVA exposure. We advocate for specific inquiry regarding such practices in patients attending transplant and dermatology clinics to inform at-risk populations about the need for photoprotection and risk of carcinogenesis.

A 44-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with diabetes at age 21 years presented with a three-day history of oligoarthritis involving both knees and wrists, and primary amenorrhea. Physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness in the affected joints. Pelvic examination showed a blind-ending vaginal pouch without the cervix. Radiographs of the knees and wrists showed calcification of the cartilage in both knees (figure A), both ulnocarpal joints, and right trapeziometacarpal joint (figure B), suggesting calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease.
Further laboratory investigations revealed hypomagnesemia (serum magnesium 1﹞15 mg/dL) with renal magnesium wasting (fractional excretion of magnesium 19﹞3%) and hypocalciuria. Serum calcium, urate, ferritin, alkaline phosphatase, rheumatoid factor, and intact parathyroid hormone concentrations were within normal limits. There were no clinical or historical features suggestive of alternative causes of arthritis, such as psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, palmoplantar lesions, or recent genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. Genetic testing was performed and a complete deletion of the HNF1B coding sequence was identified. This finding confirmed a diagnosis of HNF1B-related disease, characterised by maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 5, Mayer每Rokitansky每K邦ster每Hauser syndrome, and secondary CPPD disease due to hypomagnesaemia.
An abdominal CT scan was performed to look for structural atypicalities commonly associated with HNF1B mutations, including renal cysts, pancreatic atrophy, and uterine anomalies. Although none of these findings were present, the CT scan revealed calcification involving the pubic symphysis and bilateral hips (figure C). The diffuse distribution of calcifications in CPPD disease is often linked to genetic or metabolic disturbances. Although hypomagnesaemia is a recognised feature of HNF1B-related disease, the association between HNF1B-related disease and CPPD remains uncommon.
This case highlights the importance of thorough evaluation in patients presenting with extensive CPPD disease and multisystem involvement. HNF1B encodes a transcription factor that is crucial for pancreatic and genitourinary development and plays a key role in magnesium homoeostasis through the regulation of basolateral magnesium transport in the distal convoluted tubule. The triad of hypomagnesaemia, diabetes, and M邦llerian anomalies (associated with Mayer每Rokitansky每K邦ster每Hauser syndrome) should prompt consideration of HNF1B-related disease. The patient's arthritis was managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and magnesium supplementation was initiated. She was given a combination of glipizide and insulin for her diabetes, with the addition of empagliflozin for improved glycaemic control and to mitigate renal magnesium loss〞potentially by enhancing transcellular magnesium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule through upregulation of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 6, and increasing paracellular reabsorption in the loop of Henle.

A 69-year-old woman with a 27-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presented to the rheumatology clinic at Kochi Medical School hospital, Japan, with polyarthralgia of both hands and painless subcutaneous nodules on her right hand that had slowly grown over a year. Physical examination revealed arthritis mutilans with ulnar deviation and yellow masses on the metacarpophalangeal joints of the fingers of the right hand (figure A). There were no abnormal findings in any part of the body other than the joints, such as the eyelids and trunk. Laboratory investigations revealed that the levels of C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor were 1﹞78 mg/dL (normal range <0﹞15 mg/dL) and 1?096﹞0 IU/mL (<15 IU/mL), respectively. Hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins were not detected. We performed a bone marrow biopsy, which was normocellular. An x-ray revealed severe erosion and deformities of the hand bones and punched-out bony radiolucencies associated with the subcutaneous nodular lesions (figure B). A skin biopsy specimen of the subcutaneous mass showed areas of cholesterol clefts and necrobiosis surrounded by foamy histiocytes, lymphocytes, Touton giant cells, and foreign body-type multinucleated giant cells (figure C每F). These findings confirmed a diagnosis of pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are an unusual form of rheumatoid nodule resembling tendon xanthomas, are often mistakenly diagnosed as xanthomatosis, and have been previously regarded by investigators as subcutaneous xanthogranuloma, observed in the juxta-articular sites of the hand, wrist, elbow, knee, foot, and acromioclavicular joints. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules are distinguished from xanthomatosis by x-ray findings of demonstrable punched-out bony radiolucencies, which are not present in xanthomatosis. Cholesterol clefts surrounded by granulomatous reactions can also be observed in rheumatoid synovial fluid and bursitis, sometimes presenting as migrating chylous cysts. Pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule and xanthomatosis are easily misdiagnosed because their histopathological findings are similar. However, xanthomatosis is often associated with hyperlipidaemia, cryoglobulinemia, hypocomplementemia, and monoclonal paraproteins, whereas pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodule is not accompanied by these diseases and is found in the juxta-articular sites with punched-out bony radiolucencies. After initiating treatment with 6 mg oral methotrexate per week, the concentrations of CRP reduced to 0﹞63 mg/dL, polyarthralgia improved, and the pseudoxanthomatous rheumatoid nodules shrank.

A 56-year-old man was referred to our specialist unit after presenting to his primary care clinic with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion that were slowly worsening. He had been a smoker for 7 years but quit over a decade earlier. Also, he had worked for 8 years in underground coal mines, in Kentucky, USA. He left the profession when he was 26 years old following the collapse of a wall in the mine that left him disabled after a head injury and the development of seizures. During his time in the industry, he had worked exclusively at the coal face, primarily drilling and bolting into the ceiling of the mine to prevent collapses〞known in the trade as a roof bolter. He said he wore a dust mask inconsistently because it made breathing difficult.The patient's vital signs were within normal limits and a physical examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary function testing showed moderate obstruction without a bronchodilator response: forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio was low at 0﹞58 (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey III fifth percentile lower limit of normal [LLN] 0﹞67), with a low FEV1 of 1﹞97 L, 59% predicted (LLN 2﹞58 L), a normal FVC of 3﹞52 L, 81% predicted (LLN 3﹞41 L), a normal total lung capacity of 6﹞58 L, 107% predicted (LLN 5﹞06 L), and a normal diffusion of 25﹞3m L/mm Hg per min, 88% predicted (LLN 17﹞69 m L/mm Hg per min).
CT scan of the patient's chest showed numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules and an irregular right upper lobe mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (figure). A PET scan showed the lung mass and mediastinal lymph nodes with heterogeneous hypermetabolic uptake (appendix). Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of his mediastinal lymph nodes showed no infection, granuloma, or cancer. However, it did show anthracotic pigment laden macrophages. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (CWP) was suspected, but because of his relatively young age and short mining tenure, a transthoracic, CT-guided biopsy of his lung mass was done. Histopathological examination showed areas of focal collagenous fibrosis associated with anthracosis and polarised silicate particles; there was no evidence of cancer, granulomas, vasculitis, or infection (figure). We therefore made a definitive diagnosis of CWP and progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).
PET scans〞as our patient's imaging illustrates〞may fail to reliably distinguish PMF from malignancy as both are commonly hypermetabolic. Historically, CWP and PMF develop in miners with mining tenures of 25 years or more. However, in recent years, rates of severe disease have been increasing in younger miners with short mining tenures, despite improved health and safety regulations. Current mining practices〞including digging for thinner and harder to reach seams leading to increased cutting of rock and therefore higher exposure to silica〞may be a contributing factor. CWP and PMF should be considered in the differential diagnosis in both current and former coal miners presenting with respiratory problems regardless of age or the duration of coal mine employment. Early detection is crucial to prevent further dust exposure and delay progression of disease; effective treatments are lacking, and morbidity is irreversible (video).

output: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis with progressive massive fibrosis

A man aged 57 years, who had had herpes zoster 10 years previously, visited our emergency room with a tingling ache in his right lower back. Physical examination revealed neither eruption nor trauma on the body surface. However, an abdominal wall protrusion was observed on his right side, especially while he was standing (figure). Although pseudohernia should be suspected when a patient develops abdominal paresis coincident with or after a herpetic rash, abdominal paresis can also very rarely precede a rash. Awareness of this clinical condition might help physicians anticipate herpes zoster, allowing prompt treatment.
output: Disseminated herpes zoster with post-herpetic abdominal pseudohernia

On March 11, 2017, a 59-year-old woman came to our hospital's emergency department. She had been unwell for 7 days, with recurrent epigastric pain of acute onset that radiated into her right hemithorax, intensified during respiratory movements, and was accompanied by mild dyspnoea. Vomiting and dysphagia were absent. She had presented to our hospital because of the same symptoms 4 days before admission, but she was discharged after examination and investigations had shown no notable abnormalities: chest radiograph and electrocardiogram (ECG) were normal, as were C-reactive protein and troponin concentrations. She smoked 20 cigarettes daily, did not drink alcohol, and took atorvastatin.On admission, a chest radiograph revealed a right pleural effusion (figure, A). Considering her symptoms and her increased concentrations of serum D-dimer, a CT of the chest was done to rule out a pulmonary embolism, within 3 h of her arrival at the hospital. A 44-year-old woman〞35 weeks pregnant with dichorionic, diamniotic twins〞was admitted to our hospital with 7-day history of fever, weakness, and shortness of breath.Notably in the week before, the patient had been seen twice by her obstetrician and found to have normal or low blood pressure along with a fever. She had no other unusual medical history. On examination, the patient was pale and breathless; her temperature was 38﹞8～C, blood pressure was 110/60 mm Hg, and she had petechiae scattered about her body with oedema of both legs.
Laboratory investigations showed a haematocrit of 31﹞3% (normal >35), an elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) concentration of 110 units per L (normal <40), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was normal, total bilirubin concentration of 1﹞7 mg/dL (normal <1﹞2), a platelet count of 17?℅?109 (normal >150), and a 3+ proteinuria. A transvaginal ultrasound scan showed vertex twins and a marginal placenta praevia. A peripheral blood smear showed intraerythrocytic parasites〞Babesia microti〞with a 19﹞3% parasitaemia (figure).
The patient was transfused platelets and packed red blood cells and treated for babesiosis with a combination of intravenous clindamycin and oral quinine, which notably cross the placenta. An emergency caesarean was performed the next day; she delivered healthy twin boys who were monitored with daily B microti PCRs and blood smears.
On day 4 of the admission, a single B microti ring-form was identified in twin A's smear (figure) and on the same day his B microti PCR became positive. Twin B's B microti smear and PCR remained negative. To prevent symptomatic disease, the twins were treated with oral azithromycin and oral atovaquone.
After the delivery of her twins, the patient had a complicated course of severe babesiosis and eventually after 12 days in hospital she was able to go home; the twins never became symptomatic.
Initially, we considered that our patient might have had a diagnosis of HELLP〞Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets〞syndrome. However, the low to normal blood pressure and normal ALT, which indicated no liver injury, made us think again. Additionally, HELLP is usually preceded by hypertension without fever. Furthermore, blood smears in HELLP may show schistocytes and burr cells, but in this case, we found intraerythrocytic parasites.
The differential diagnosis for HELLP syndrome includes fatty liver of pregnancy, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, immune thrombocytopenia, and systemic lupus flare-up〞none of these fitted in this case.
Babesiosis is endemic in the New England region of the USA, including Connecticut. Most cases are asymptomatic; asplenic and immunosuppressed individuals, pregnant patients, and the very young (<2 months) and very old (>80 years) are prone to develop symptoms and may have severe disease. Vertically acquired babesiosis, as occurred in twin A, is very rare. In endemic areas, babesiosis should be considered in the list of differential diagnoses of a HELLP-like presentation. The peripheral blood smear should lead to the diagnosis.
output: Babesiosis with vertical transmission (congenital babesiosis in twin A)

A 79-year-old woman was referred to our department with a sudden onset of dyspnoea. She had end-stage kidney disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and, 6 months earlier, had started peritoneal dialysis. The patient did not report a cough, fever, or chills.On examination, her blood pressure was 154/93 mm Hg, heart rate 58 beats per min, oxygen saturation 91% room air, temperature 36﹞8～C. She had no oedema, nor any symptoms of right-sided heart failure. She had no abdominal pain. On chest auscultation, we found no breath sounds on the right side. Her weight had been stable.
A chest x-ray showed a new large right pleural effusion〞a previous x-ray, done 11 months earlier, had been reported as clear.
Analysis of a sample of pleural fluid showed a clear yellow liquid with a cell count of 113 cells per mm3, composed of 2% neutrophils and 45% lymphocytes. The protein concentration of the pleural fluid was 5 g/L, glucose concentration was 7﹞9 mmol/L, and creatinine concentration was 498 米mol/L, indicating a likely transudate.
Blood tests showed a white blood count of 8﹞67?℅?109 per L (normal 4﹞5每11﹞0), a C-reactive protein concentration of 0﹞8 mg/L (normal <5), glucose concentration of 5﹞4 mmol/L (normal 4﹞1每6﹞0), plasma protein concentration of 69 g/L (normal 66每87), albumin concentration of 32 g/L (normal 36每44), and a creatinine concentration of 512 米mol/L (normal range 45每84). Electrolytes and liver function tests were unremarkable.
The peritoneal dialysis fluid was clear and showed a glucose concentration of 7﹞8 g/L and creatinine of 484 米mol/L.
Peritoneal scintigraphy, combined with a single-photon-emission CT and CT (SPECT/CT) scan, showed radioactive tracer in the pleural cavity after infusion into the peritoneal cavity, confirming pleuro-peritoneal communication (figure, video). The patient's symptoms completely resolved on cessation of peritoneal dialysis. The recurrence of a pleural effusion, immediately on recommencing peritoneal dialysis, led us to decide on a definitive transfer to haemodialysis. After 8 months of follow-up, she remains asymptomatic, without any recurrence of a pleural effusion.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication is an uncommon complication of peritoneal dialysis, occurring in 1每2% of patients. The communication usually appears less than 3 months after initiating dialysis, but may also occur months to years later.
In 88% of cases, the pleural effusion is on the right side of the chest; left-sided defects are often covered by the heart and pericardium, making leakage on the left side less likely.
Pleuro-peritoneal communication takes place via congenital or acquired diaphragmatic defects and occurs when intra-abdominal pressure is increased by the administration of the peritoneal dialysis fluid.
A rapidly developed transudative unilateral pleural efffusion, with a high glucose concentration〞dextrose being the most commonly used osmotic agent in peritoneal dialysis〞accompanied by a high creatinine level, close to the dialysate composition, is highly suggestive of a leak of dialysate into the pleural cavity.
Dynamic imaging, such as SPECT/CT, shows the transfer of the radioactive tracer from the peritoneal to the pleural cavity and facilitates location of the site of the leak. Conservative treatment〞temporary interruption of the peritoneal dialysis for 2每6 weeks〞is effective in half of cases. Chemical pleurodesis or surgical interventions should be considered as second-line treatments, and the pros and cons of an invasive treatment should be weighed up against a definitive transfer to haemodialysis.
output: Pleuro-peritoneal communication secondary to peritoneal dialysis

A 28-year-old man was transferred to our hospital after he suddenly lost consciousness in the street. He had an initial diagnosis of opioid overdose. A 20-year-old woman presented with a 1-month history of swollen gums. Her medical history included seizures for the past 19 years and a macular patch on the right side of her face since birth. On the basis of her history and clinical presentation she was diagnosed with Sturge-Weber angiomatosis and drug-induced gingival enlargement. Extraoral skull radiographs showed tramline calcification because of angiomas affecting the leptomeninges. The patient was given meticulous oral treatment and her antiepileptic medication was changed. The angiomas present in our patient are malformations of blood vessels in the pia mater causing the calcification and loss of nerve cells in the cerebral cortex. These sequelae of the malformations give rise to the clinical symptom of seizures and radiological sign of tramline calcification.
output: Sturge每Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) with phenytoin-induced gingival enlargement

A 71-year-old woman with no medical history of note presented to the Department of Internal Medicine of the Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in August, 2013, with 1 month of joint pain. She also had cutaneous oedema with subcutaneous hardening that started in her legs, then spread to the trunk and arms, affecting the distal region of the limbs. On examination she had mild erythema and mild pitting leg oedema, and hardening of the subcutaneous tissue of the limb, lumbar, and breast areas. Both forearms showed a linear depression in the skin parallel to the course of the superficial veins, more obvious on raising the arm, that was consistent with the groove sign (figure). Blood tests showed a remarkable eosinophilia of 5﹞2?℅?109/L (normal range <0﹞7?℅?109/L). Skin and muscle biopsy showed macrophage infiltration of the fascia with scarce eosinophils, perimisial inflammation, and a dense eosinophilic infiltrate of the vessels, suggestive of eosinophilic fasciitis.
We started the patient on oral prednisone 1 mg/kg per day, that was tapered by 10 mg every 2 weeks to 10 mg daily, starting methotrexate after 3 months as a second-line agent, with rapid resolution of the eosinophilia and the cutaneous oedema, but slow and incomplete recovery of the subcutaneous hardening. 10 months after onset of the disease the hardening of the subcutaneous tissue has started to improve, mainly in the upper limbs, the last area to be affected by the disease. The patient is still taking methotrexate and steroids.
Eosinophilic fasciitis is an uncommon scleroderma-like disorder, first described by Shulman in 1974, characterised by induration of the skin, peripheral eosinophilia, hypergammaglobulinaemia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Groove sign is a characteristic finding of eosinophilic fasciitis, consisting of a depression along the course of the superficial veins, more marked on elevation of the affected limb. Because the upper dermis and epidermis are spared by the fibrotic process, and the connective tissue around the veins is relatively immobile, the superficial layers of skin can bow inward as the peripheral venous pressure falls.

input: A man aged 65 years presented to the otorhinolaryngology outpatient clinic at All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi (India), in January, 2018, with a 1-year history of progressive dysphagia to solids, cervical borborygmi (see video appendix 1), sensation of lump in throat, occasional regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. He denied any history of weight loss, recurrent cough, hoarseness, or pain. On physical examination a gurgling sound was elicited on pressing the neck (see video appendix 1). Video fluoroscopy revealed stasis of barium in the dilated upper oesophagus extending from C6 to T1 vertebrae (figure and video appendix 2). Trans-nasal oesophagoscopy revealed a large Zenker's diverticulum containing food residue (video appendix 3). The patient underwent endoscopic diverticulectomy. On the day after surgery, the dysphagia and gurgling sounds to liquids disappeared; the patient remained asymptomatic at 12-month follow-up visit.Zenker's diverticulum is an acquired pulsion pseudo-diverticulum originating in Killian's dehiscence, an area bounded by the oblique fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the transverse fibres of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It occurs because of increased intraluminal pressure in the hypopharynx during swallowing, caused by an inadequately relaxed cricopharyngeal upper oesophageal sphincter. Boyce's sign, a gurgling sound due to noise of splashing fluid accumulated in a large Zenker's diverticulum, can be heard on palpation. Although small diverticula might not cause symptoms, larger diverticula are usually symptomatic and surgery could be warranted.

A 19-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 7-year history of periodic lower abdominal and pelvic pain without fever, chills, or dysuria. She had not had menses nor vaginal intercourse. Physical exam revealed lower abdominal distention and a firm and tender suprapubic mass extending from the pelvis to the umbilicus. Perineal exam is seen in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?
output:
Imperforate hymen with hematocolpos

The image shows a bulging, bluish-tinged membrane at the vaginal introitus, which is characteristic of an imperforate hymen with accumulated menstrual blood behind it (hematocolpos/hematometrocolpos).

Key clinical features supporting this diagnosis:
- 19-year-old female with primary amenorrhea (never had menses)
- 7-year history of cyclic lower abdominal/pelvic pain (corresponding to menstrual cycles since menarche)
- Large suprapubic mass extending to umbilicus (accumulated menstrual blood)
- Bulging membrane at the introitus with bluish discoloration (blood behind the membrane)
- No vaginal intercourse (hymen intact)

A 52-year-old man attended our hospital reporting breathlessness on exertion that had been worsening over the past 2 weeks. He had smoked 20 cigarettes a day for the past 40 years. He had no other symptoms〞specifically no systemic or gastrointestinal complaints. The patient had tried to quit smoking 4 months earlier and had started vaping: he had been using commercially available e-cigarettes which did not have any 忖9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) added.The symptoms started some days after the patient had added a new flavour〞blueberry〞to the vaping fluid.
On examination, we found the patient to be apyrexial, with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg, a heart rate of 70 beats per min, and in sinus rhythm. Auscultation of his chest found no heart murmurs, but we heard vesicular breath sounds with discrete bilateral crepitations over the lung bases.
A high-resolution CT scan of the patient's chest (figure) showed lower lobe predominant, bilateral consolidations in a peribronchovascular distribution〞the pattern of organising pneumonia. Extensive diagnostic work-up did not provide any evidence for an infectious or rheumatological aetiology: C-reactive protein concentration and leucocyte count were normal. Antibody screening for hypersensitivity pneumonitis and collagen vascular disease was negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for any pathogenic agents; however, it showed a lymphocytic alveolitis with 70% lymphocytes.
Histopathological examination of a transbronchial lung biopsy confirmed an organising pneumonia, with interspersed pigment-containing macrophages indicating foreign body inhalation.
The patient stopped vaping e-cigarettes and was prescribed systemic steroid therapy, starting with 40 mg of oral prednisolone per day for 4 weeks, reducing by 10 mg per day every 4 weeks〞he is currently on 10 mg per day. After 4 months there was no improvement in the patient's symptoms and the imaging findings remained unchanged. 6 months after he first presented, we repeated the bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and cryobiopsy: we found no signs of lymphocytic alveolitis, but histopathology reported a diagnosis of non-specific interstitial pneumonia. Most cases of EVALI reported in the literature have involved patients using e-cigarettes with THC or cannabidiol added to the vaping liquid, where vitamin E is thought to be important in causing the lung damage; however, concerns about the effects of the constituents of the flavourings have also been raised. A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of progressive vision loss and headaches. MRI revealed a large sellar tumour with suprasellar extension, which was deemed a probable pituitary macroadenoma (figure A, B). The patient underwent transsphenoidal surgery because of visual field defects and headaches. Histological analysis after surgery revealed a giant cell tumour of bone (GCTB) and symptoms improved; however, 2 months later the large sellar每clival remnant compressing the optic chiasm (figure C, D) motivated a second surgery by pterional craniotomy. After surgery, tumour regrowth occurred (figure E, F), causing diplopia and blurred vision. A third decompressing operation aiming for maximal debulking before denosumab commencement was done endoscopically; however, only partial tumour removal was achieved (figure G, H). Denosumab (120 mg subcutaneously every 28 days) was initiated, and a marked response was noted after 6 months of treatment (figure I, J). After 14 months of denosumab, the patient remained symptom-free without needing further operations (figure K, L).GCTB represent 5每10% of bone tumours, classically affect long bones (<1% of all GCTB have a cranial location) and, although benign, can be locally aggressive. GCTB are histologically characterised by large multinucleated giant cells, but the clinical or radiological differential diagnosis can be challenging. Denosumab, an inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), can be used to treat GCTB, because RANKL is overexpressed by mononuclear neoplastic stromal cells. As shown here, denosumab should also be considered in the early management of sellar每clival GCTB. This case also highlights the sustained reduction in tumour mass achieved by denosumab, sparing the patient from further operations. If feasible, surgical resection is still preferable as the definitive treatment, because the effect of denosumab wears off after stopping treatment and tumour regrowth can occur. Lifelong denosumab treatment will thus be likely required in this case; however, increasing the intervals between denosumab administration can be attempted to prevent or minimise adverse events, such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fractures. Although GCTB is usually managed by rheumatologists, oncologists, or orthopaedics, sellar or parasellar GCTB might be first seen by endocrinologists, ophthalmologists, or neurosurgeons, who should be aware of this entity and the potential role of denosumab in its management.

She had an effusion on her left knee.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8﹞1 g/dL, platelet count of 90?℅?109 per L and white blood cell count was 5﹞1?℅?109 per L, but with 6% blasts〞confirmed on blood smear. 7 months earlier the patient's blood tests had been normal. Analysis of fluid obtained from arthrocentesis was consistent with pseudogout. An infection screen was negative. However, given the fever with functional neutropenia, we decided to commence her on broad spectrum antibiotics.
Bone marrow examination showed 20每25% blasts and morphology consistent with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related changes (figure). Flow cytometry dot plots of the marrow aspirate showed approximately 21% CD34+ and CD117+ myeloblasts (figure). The patient's karyotype was complex〞among several abnormalities it included monosomy of chromosome 17 (appendix). Additionally, a pathogenic mutation of the TP53 gene with a variable allele frequency of 64% was detected by next generation DNA sequencing using a 49 gene panel.
Given the patient's comorbidities, her unfit physical state, the complex karyotype, and the TP53 mutation, it was decided, after discussion with her, to try a combination of the hypomethylating agent〞azacitidine〞and the oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax. The patient developed multiple life-threatening events over subsequent weeks including atrial fibrillation, confusion, and renal failure without tumour lysis. After discussion of options, the family opted for comfort measures and the patient was transferred for care in a hospice and died 6 days later.
Among older patients〞especially those with adverse genetic findings〞AML is often resistant to chemotherapy and long-term survival rates remain low at 10%. Traditionally, treatment involves intensive chemotherapy followed by allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for fit patients. However, most older AML patients are unfit for curative-intent therapy and receive palliative lower intensity regimens. Oral inhibitors of mutant IDH1, IDH2, and FLT3 proteins〞found in approximately half of AML patients〞are now approved treatments in some countries. In addition to azacitidine with venetoclax, various other combinations have shown improved survival in subpopulations of older AML patients; none of these strategies, however, have been particularly successful in patients with TP53 mutations (appendix; video).

A 60-year old woman presented to the emergency department with a 2-day history of a painful, swollen left knee and a fever. She had a medical history of osteoarthritis, hypertension, and hyperlipidaemia.On examination she looked unwell; she was tachycardic (heart rate 104 beats per min) and febrile (temperature 39﹞1～C). She had an effusion on her left knee.
Laboratory investigations showed a haemoglobin concentration of 8﹞1 g/dL, platelet count of 90?℅?109 per L and white blood cell count was 5﹞1?℅?109 per L, but with 6% blasts〞confirmed on blood smear. 7 months earlier the patient's blood tests had been normal. Analysis of fluid obtained from arthrocentesis was consistent with pseudogout. An infection screen was negative. However, given the fever with functional neutropenia, we decided to commence her on broad spectrum antibiotics.
Bone marrow examination showed 20每25% blasts and morphology consistent with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related changes (figure). Flow cytometry dot plots of the marrow aspirate showed approximately 21% CD34+ and CD117+ myeloblasts (figure). The patient's karyotype was complex〞among several abnormalities it included monosomy of chromosome 17 (appendix). Additionally, a pathogenic mutation of the TP53 gene with a variable allele frequency of 64% was detected by next generation DNA sequencing using a 49 gene panel.
Given the patient's comorbidities, her unfit physical state, the complex karyotype, and the TP53 mutation, it was decided, after discussion with her, to try a combination of the hypomethylating agent〞azacitidine〞and the oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax. The patient developed multiple life-threatening events over subsequent weeks including atrial fibrillation, confusion, and renal failure without tumour lysis. After discussion of options, the family opted for comfort measures and the patient was transferred for care in a hospice and died 6 days later.
Among older patients〞especially those with adverse genetic findings〞AML is often resistant to chemotherapy and long-term survival rates remain low at 10%. Traditionally, treatment involves intensive chemotherapy followed by allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for fit patients. However, most older AML patients are unfit for curative-intent therapy and receive palliative lower intensity regimens. Oral inhibitors of mutant IDH1, IDH2, and FLT3 proteins〞found in approximately half of AML patients〞are now approved treatments in some countries. In addition to azacitidine with venetoclax, various other combinations have shown improved survival in subpopulations of older AML patients; none of these strategies, however, have been particularly successful in patients with TP53 mutations (appendix; video).

A 35-year-old woman presented to our emergency room with a 3-day history of dizziness, nausea, and fatigue. The patient said she had been diagnosed with a brain tumour 2 years earlier; at that time, she reported having diplopia as well as dizziness and fatigue. A stereotactic tumour biopsy was considered, but not done because she made a full recovery with high-dose steroid treatment.On examination, we found no neurological abnormalities, but she had a low blood pressure of 83/39 mm Hg.
Laboratory investigations showed severe hyponatraemia: sodium concentration was 109 mmol/L (normal 135每145). Urine osmolality was 336 mmol/kg (normal 200每1200)〞suggesting impaired water excretion〞and the urine sodium excretion was 44 mmol/L (normal 60每140)〞indicating syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion.
Further endocrine testing confirmed impaired production of corticotropin-releasing hormone: the patient's basal cortisol concentration was 52 nmol/L (normal 166每507) and her adrenocorticotropic hormone concentration was inadequately low 8﹞2 ng/L (normal <46﹞0).
A brain MRI showed a contrast-enhancing subthalamic tumefactive lesion, several periventricular lesions, and a lesion adjacent to the midbrain tectum (figure; video); the MRI of the spinal cord was normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed eight leukocytes per 米L (normal <5) and a CSF:serum albumin ratio of 6﹞5 (normal <6﹞3) with no oligoclonal bands. Further testing showed serum anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies (titre 1:32; normal <1:10), indicating neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). After 3% saline bolus, fluid restriction, and high-dose steroid treatment, the patient recovered and a further brain MRI, 1 month later, showed marked regression of the subthalamic lesion (figure; video). Off-label rituximab treatment was started 2 months after the patient presented initially, and she remained asymptomatic over the following 6 months while having continuous hydrocortisone replacement.
Retrospective chart analyses reported a SIADH secretion prevalence of about 15% in NMOSD; tertiary adrenal insufficiency due to inflammatory and demyelinating processes affecting the hypothalamus is rare and has mostly been described in multiple sclerosis. The brain circumventricular organs have osmoregulatory functions and are enriched with aquaporin-4 water channels; every patient with SIADH secretion and lesions affecting these organs should be tested for NMOSD. Notably, routine CSF analysis in NMOSD can be normal (video).

A 17-year-old boy was referred to the ophthalmology service at St Thomas' Hospital (London, UK) with bilateral red eyes, bilateral eye pain independent of eye movement that disturbed his sleep, photophobia, and mild, subjective blurring of vision. He had become infected with SARS-CoV-2 5 weeks before referral and had been diagnosed with paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 (PIMS-TS) and associated myocarditis.His Snellen visual acuity was excellent: 6/4 unaided in both eyes. He had bilateral, diffuse episcleral and deep scleral injection (vasodilatation with hyperaemia) that did not blanch with topical 10% phenylephrine; a bilateral anterior chamber grading of 2+ (16每25 cells in a 1 mm?℅?1 mm field); no vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis; and an otherwise unremarkable fundal examination (figure A, B). A B-scan ultrasound did not show any posterior scleritis. He was diagnosed with bilateral, diffuse, anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis.
Before his ophthalmology referral, the patient had been treated for PIMS-TS with a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (950 mg/day). He subsequently developed fever, had a rising C-reactive protein concentration 1 week post-admission (from 47 mg/L to 94 mg/L over the course of 1 day), and received 800 mg of intravenous tocilizumab on the day of his referral. After attending the ophthalmology service, he started a course of oral prednisolone (starting dose 40 mg/day for 17 days), guttae 0﹞1% dexamethasone (eye drops to both eyes at an initial schedule of once every 2 h for 3 days), and a 1-week course of guttae 1% cyclopentolate (eye drops to both eyes twice daily). Treatment (prednisolone and guttae 0﹞1% dexamethasone) was tapered over a 6-week period. 7 days after ophthalmology referral and review, the patient's symptoms had resolved and he had normal vision and no ongoing inflammation.
10 days after referral, the patient presented with a right facial (VIIth) nerve palsy and his prescribed regimen of prednisolone (40 mg/day, before tapering) was not changed. Neuroimaging showed mild inflammation of the right tympanic facial nerve (figure 1C). Prompt resolution of facial weakness occurred within 4 weeks.
It is imperative not to misdiagnose the potentially sight-threatening conditions of scleritis and uveitis as conjunctivitis, which is the commonly known ophthalmic association in PIMS-TS.
output: Bilateral diffuse anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis associated with PIMS-TS (Paediatric Inflammatory Multisystem Syndrome Temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2)

A 57-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of shortness of breath and dizziness. The physical examination was notable for pallor. Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin of 4.4 g per deciliter (reference range, 11.6 to 15.5), an elevated reticulocyte count, an elevated lactate dehydrogenase level, and a low haptoglobin level. The results of hemoglobin electrophoresis and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing were normal, and methemoglobin and direct antiglobulin tests were negative. A peripheral blood smear (left, Giemsa staining) showed poikilocytosis, nucleated red cells (black arrows), and polychromatic cells (white arrows). The peripheral blood smear also showed bite cells (left, red arrows), blister cells (left, asterisks), and erythrocyte inclusions (middle, Giemsa staining). The erythrocyte inclusions were identified as Heinz bodies on the basis of positive staining with methyl violet (right). Which of the following is the most likely etiology of this patient＊s hemolytic anemia?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation and laboratory findings, the diagnosis is:

**Oxidative hemolytic anemia (drug-induced or toxic oxidant exposure)**

The key diagnostic features include:
- Bite cells (caused by splenic removal of Heinz bodies)
- Blister cells
- Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin inclusions confirmed by methyl violet staining)
- Evidence of hemolysis (low hemoglobin, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocytes)
- Normal G6PD testing and hemoglobin electrophoresis

This pattern is characteristic of oxidative hemolytic anemia, most commonly caused by oxidant drugs (such as dapsone, sulfonamides, or nitrofurantoin) or toxic exposures in patients with normal G6PD levels when the oxidant stress is severe enough to overwhelm normal antioxidant defenses.

A 17-year-old boy was referred to the ophthalmology service at St Thomas' Hospital (London, UK) with bilateral red eyes, bilateral eye pain independent of eye movement that disturbed his sleep, photophobia, and mild, subjective blurring of vision. He had become infected with SARS-CoV-2 5 weeks before referral and had been diagnosed with paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome temporally associated with COVID-19 (PIMS-TS) and associated myocarditis.His Snellen visual acuity was excellent: 6/4 unaided in both eyes. He had bilateral, diffuse episcleral and deep scleral injection (vasodilatation with hyperaemia) that did not blanch with topical 10% phenylephrine; a bilateral anterior chamber grading of 2+ (16每25 cells in a 1 mm?℅?1 mm field); no vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis; and an otherwise unremarkable fundal examination (figure A, B). A B-scan ultrasound did not show any posterior scleritis. He was diagnosed with bilateral, diffuse, anterior non-necrotising scleritis with anterior uveitis.
Before his ophthalmology referral, the patient had been treated for PIMS-TS with a 3-day course of intravenous methylprednisolone (950 mg/day). He subsequently developed fever, had a rising C-reactive protein concentration 1 week post-admission (from 47 mg/L to 94 mg/L over the course of 1 day), and received 800 mg of intravenous tocilizumab on the day of his referral. After attending the ophthalmology service, he started a course of oral prednisolone (starting dose 40 mg/day for 17 days), guttae 0﹞1% dexamethasone (eye drops to both eyes at an initial schedule of once every 2 h for 3 days), and a 1-week course of guttae 1% cyclopentolate (eye drops to both eyes twice daily). Treatment (prednisolone and guttae 0﹞1% dexamethasone) was tapered over a 6-week period. 7 days after ophthalmology referral and review, the patient's symptoms had resolved and he had normal vision and no ongoing inflammation.
10 days after referral, the patient presented with a right facial (VIIth) nerve palsy and his prescribed regimen of prednisolone (40 mg/day, before tapering) was not changed. Neuroimaging showed mild inflammation of the right tympanic facial nerve (figure 1C). Prompt resolution of facial weakness occurred within 4 weeks.
It is imperative not to misdiagnose the potentially sight-threatening conditions of scleritis and uveitis as conjunctivitis, which is the commonly known ophthalmic association in PIMS-TS.
output: Scleritis and facial nerve palsy associated with PIMS-TS

output:
Based on the clinical presentation and the specific images provided, the patient is suffering from oxidative hemolysis. The peripheral blood smear displays classic signs of oxidative damage to red blood cells, including **bite cells** (degmacytes), **blister cells**, and **Heinz bodies** (precipitated denatured hemoglobin visualized with methyl violet stain).

While these findings are commonly associated with Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, the patient's G6PD level was normal (though levels can be falsely normal during an acute attack, the explicit mention of normal results along with normal hemoglobin electrophoresis often points towards an exogenous cause in a diagnostic vignette). The combination of severe oxidative hemolysis, negative Coombs test, and normal G6PD/electrophoresis in a 57-year-old woman is highly characteristic of toxicity from an oxidative drug. This specific case and set of images correspond to a documented case of **phenazopyridine toxicity**. Phenazopyridine is a urinary analgesic that can cause oxidative hemolysis even in individuals with normal G6PD enzyme levels.

**Phenazopyridine-induced hemolytic anemia**

A 9-year-old girl was admitted to our hospital with status epilepticus. Earlier in the day, she had complained of a headache and started vomiting. She then lost consciousness and began having a fit; the status epilepticus lasted 30 min and was stopped by phenobarbital. She had a congenital heart defect〞truncus arteriosus with interventricular communication〞which was surgically corrected a few days after birth. The girl was on long-term treatment with low-dose aspirin as the antiaggregant. She had no features of Marfan's or Ehlers每Danlos syndromes. Laboratory investigations showed leucopenia, low platelet count, and anaemia. Her C-reactive protein (CRP) was 45 mg/L and her erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 50 mm/h. Her liver enzymes were also slightly raised. A CT scan of her brain showed an intraparenchymal haematoma and intraventricular haemorrhage. Three-vessel arteriography showed a right Sylvian artery aneurysm (figure). Successive blood cultures and broad-range 16S recombinant DNA PCR〞as well as PCR for herpes simplex viruses 1每5〞were all negative. At this stage, our working diagnosis was endocarditis leading to the mycotic cerebral aneurysm, despite no signs of a fever. We drained the haematoma and commenced treatment with antibiotics; 2 days later, we embolised the aneurysm. The patient recovered and had a mild, left-sided hemiparesis when she left hospital after 4 weeks.1 month later, the girl was brought to the hospital again: weary and malnourished. She was admitted to the paediatric rheumatology unit, where she stayed for 6 weeks for investigation of non-infectious vasculitides associated with autoimmune diseases such as Sj?gren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, or juvenille idiopathic arthritis. Investigations showed hyperglycaemia, transaminitis, and raised inflammatory markers〞CRP concentration was 10 mg/L and ESR was 50 mm/h. All specific autoantibody tests were negative; however, a liver biopsy specimen showed features of a non-specific, subacute hepatitis without fibrosis or granuloma, and the concentration of peripheral naive T cells was low. Diagnoses under consideration at this stage were an autoimmune vasculitis with or without acquired and congenital immunodeficiencies〞a thymectomy had been done at the time of her original operation just after her birth.
At 3-month follow-up, a further cerebral aneurysm was detected, this time involving the contralateral left Sylvian artery (figure). The patient remained tired and benefited from enteral tube feeding. Her liver enzymes were raised to three times the upper limit of normal and her CRP was 15 mg/L. The aneurysm was again embolised and the right ventricle to pulmonary artery conduit was changed; culture of the explanted material did not show anything. We repeated an infectious screen〞including Q fever serology, which was positive. A PCR test of liver biopsy material, obtained 3 months earlier, for Q fever was also positive. The girl was treated for 12 months with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine and made a complete recovery.
Strokes in children are very uncommon. Beware of blood culture-negative and broad-range recombinant DNA PCR-negative results: the diagnosis might be Coxiella burnetii or Q fever.

A previously well 54-year-old woman with no history of trauma presented to Kimitsu Chuo Hospital (Kisarazu, Japan) in February, 2017, with a 1-year history of coccydynia during sitting. Digital rectal examination revealed a hard mass in the retrorectal area. Pelvic radiograph indicated disseminated calcification in front of the coccyx (figure, A) and pelvic CT scan showed a large retrorectal solid tumour containing calcific particles without destruction of the coccyx. Lumbosacral spine MRI showed that the retrorectal tumour was multilocular (figure, B). Colonoscopy was normal. Percutaneous biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, abdominal and vaginal ultrasonography, whole-body CT scat, pelvic MRI, and PET/CT detected no primary tumour. A diagnosis of isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer was made.
In compliance with the patient's wishes, radiotherapy〞not chemotherapy〞was initiated while surgical resection was considered. However, at 6 months after her first visit, radiotherapy resulted in no improvement and a repeat CT scan detected a tumour in the pancreatic head. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma, which was considered to be the primary lesion.
Retrorectal tumours are rare and many cases are asymptomatic and are only found incidentally because of their subtle clinical symptoms (eg, rectal discomfort, change in bowel habit, and chronic pain in the perineum). They are broadly categorised as benign versus malignant and congenital versus acquired. Most of them are benign developmental cysts resulting from abnormal closure of the ectodermal tube, such as epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, enteric cysts, or neurenteric cysts. Other benign retrorectal masses include teratomas, meningoceles, and neurilemmomas. Malignant retrotectal tumours that have been reported are chordoma, chondrosarcoma, and osteosarcoma. Although sacral metastases might be observed in patients with various malignancies, isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer is a very rare phenomenon.
Intratumoural calcification in malignancies derives from three factors: metastatic calcification caused by hypercalcaemia, dystrophic calcification occurring as a reaction to tissue necrosis, or ontogenic calcification in which cancer-producing mucin glycoproteins accelerate bonding of calcium and phosphorus. In this case, we believe that the low degree of differentiation and the mucin formation of mucinous adenocarcinoma, which is rare in pancreatic cancers, led to dystrophic and ontogenic calcification of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, respectively, since the patient did not have hypercalcaemia.
Although the patient was scheduled to receive pancreaticoduodenectomy and resection of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, liver metastases were subsequently found on pre-operative CT scan and the surgery was cancelled. She opted not to receive chemotherapy and was transferred to a hospice for end-of-life care.
output: Isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult pancreatic mucinous adenocarcinoma

A previously well 54-year-old woman with no history of trauma presented to Kimitsu Chuo Hospital (Kisarazu, Japan) in February, 2017, with a 1-year history of coccydynia during sitting. Digital rectal examination revealed a hard mass in the retrorectal area. Pelvic radiograph indicated disseminated calcification in front of the coccyx (figure, A) and pelvic CT scan showed a large retrorectal solid tumour containing calcific particles without destruction of the coccyx. Lumbosacral spine MRI showed that the retrorectal tumour was multilocular (figure, B). Colonoscopy was normal. Percutaneous biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, abdominal and vaginal ultrasonography, whole-body CT scat, pelvic MRI, and PET/CT detected no primary tumour. A diagnosis of isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer was made.
In compliance with the patient's wishes, radiotherapy〞not chemotherapy〞was initiated while surgical resection was considered. However, at 6 months after her first visit, radiotherapy resulted in no improvement and a repeat CT scan detected a tumour in the pancreatic head. Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the tumour identified a low-grade mucinous adenocarcinoma, which was considered to be the primary lesion.
Retrorectal tumours are rare and many cases are asymptomatic and are only found incidentally because of their subtle clinical symptoms (eg, rectal discomfort, change in bowel habit, and chronic pain in the perineum). They are broadly categorised as benign versus malignant and congenital versus acquired. Most of them are benign developmental cysts resulting from abnormal closure of the ectodermal tube, such as epidermoid cysts, dermoid cysts, enteric cysts, or neurenteric cysts. Other benign retrorectal masses include teratomas, meningoceles, and neurilemmomas. Malignant retrotectal tumours that have been reported are chordoma, chondrosarcoma, and osteosarcoma. Although sacral metastases might be observed in patients with various malignancies, isolated retrorectal metastasis from occult cancer is a very rare phenomenon.
Intratumoural calcification in malignancies derives from three factors: metastatic calcification caused by hypercalcaemia, dystrophic calcification occurring as a reaction to tissue necrosis, or ontogenic calcification in which cancer-producing mucin glycoproteins accelerate bonding of calcium and phosphorus. In this case, we believe that the low degree of differentiation and the mucin formation of mucinous adenocarcinoma, which is rare in pancreatic cancers, led to dystrophic and ontogenic calcification of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, respectively, since the patient did not have hypercalcaemia.
Although the patient was scheduled to receive pancreaticoduodenectomy and resection of the isolated retrorectal metastasis, liver metastases were subsequently found on pre-operative CT scan and the surgery was cancelled. She opted not to receive chemotherapy and was transferred to a hospice for end-of-life care.
output: Pancreatic mucinous adenocarcinoma with isolated retrorectal metastasis

A 42-year-old man with a history of an intermittent disorder of speech fluency beginning around the age of 4 years without any obvious triggers attended our unit for further investigation; he had agreed to participate in our MRI study on speech production.
The patient had no medical history and on clinical examination we found him to be fit and well.
However, he had moments when his speech fluency was lost; these were episodic, brief〞rarely lasting longer than 30 secs〞and occurring mostly, but not exclusively, at the beginning of words, and usually, but not always, with consonants rather than vowels. The episodes were markedly exacerbated by environmental stressors and were attenuated by cueing and external rhythms. Previously, several attempts had been made to treat and improve speech fluency with no lasting effect; the speech difficulty remained.
Notably, in his personal history, the patient had left school early to take up a technical apprenticeship. He had avoided professions which were more language-related and obtained an academic degree in engineering after 4 years of evening school.
More recently, he had just participated in speech therapy focusing on different kinds of block releasing techniques, combined with anti-anxiety training. An uncle and his daughter〞the patient's cousin〞had shown similar speech dysfluencies since they were children.
For our study, we used real-time MRI to non-invasively visualise the movements of the tongue and the oropharynx while the patient read a specially selected piece of text from a screen positioned in his field of vision as he was in the scanner.
The video clip, with 55 MRI images per second, showed a midsagittal cross-sectional plane covering the mouth, mandibular nasal cavities, pharynx, and larynx (figure; video). The intermittent repetitions of syllables and sounds, prolongations of sounds, and audible or silent blockings were visible as spasms and repetitive movements in parts of the tongue, lips, and velum. The video also showed fluent sounding segments of speech, thereby ruling out permanent speech disorders. A speech-language pathologist confirmed the diagnosis of stuttering and categorised it as moderate.
The patient was reassured that the visualisation had delineated his condition clearly and it enabled him to gain a greater understanding into its mechanics.
Stuttering affects about 1% of the adult population, mostly males, and has a high heritability. Relapse after therapy〞which includes fluency shaping and block modification techniques〞is frequent and often results in the condition continuing for many years. Stuttering can impair social development. Attempts to stop or to avoid stuttering may result in verbal, visual, or situational avoidance, and not speaking in circumstances where the patient would be expected to may be misinterpreted as inappropriate behaviour. Anxiety disorders〞including social anxiety disorder and generalised anxiety disorder〞are present in about half of the affected individuals and addressing them improves therapy outcomes.
The real-time MRI, which demonstrated the mechanical pathogenesis of the primary symptoms, has improved our understanding of and updates our thinking about stuttering; it gives a better understanding of what the inner articulators do wrong during this type of dysfluent speech.
Additionally, in clinical practice the method may be useful in identifying dysfunctional motor behaviour in speech production disorders. Further, it could potentially be used in visual biofeedback settings to aid in the acquisition and reinforcement of new speech patterns. We acknowledge that the use of a single slice MRI is a limitation that may possibly be overcome with future advances in MRI technology.
output: Females and males are equally affected

input: A 51-year-old woman with a diagnosis of scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome presented to our rheumatology department with widespread subcutaneous skin lesions. On examination, widespread subcutaneous calcification was noted, affecting the elbows, shoulders, hips, knees, buttocks, and ankles. She was positive for anti-nuclear antibodies, anti-La, anti-Ro, and anti-PM-SCL-75 antibodies. Tests for parathyroid hormone, renal function, calcium, and vitamin D were normal. Extensive investigation including PET-CT and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT excluded malignancy. A biopsy sample of the right thigh showed extensive calcification of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue in association with acute inflammation and necrosis. We found no evidence of calcification of the walls of the dermal and subcutaneous small vessels to suggest calciphylaxis. The appearance of the biopsy sample was consistent with dystrophic calcinosis cutis (figure). The x-ray images showed widespread subcutaneous calcification at the elbows, knees, ankle (including the Achilles tendon), and pelvis. Given the severity of the presentation, we obtained a CT scan of her pelvis to further characterise the extent of disease and to monitor the response to treatment (figure). The widespread distribution of the disease, with long bands of symmetrical subcutaneous calcification, was consistent with a diagnosis of calcinosis universalis. This condition is a more diffuse form of dystrophic calcinosis cutis than calcinosis cutis circumscripta, which is localised to a small area or joint. Calcinosis cutis is extremely rare in overlap connective tissue disease syndromes, with only few reported cases in the scientific literature.The patient is being treated with prednisolone, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and minocycline. Previous treatments have included rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate, intravenous immunoglobulin, and cyclophosphamide. A temporary improvement was seen in her condition with intravenous thiosulphate. She has had recurrent hospital admissions requiring treatment with intravenous antibiotics for skin and soft tissue infections at the site of calcinosis. Despite these interventions, her calcinosis remains severe and progressive and she is being considered for further intravenous sodium thiosulphate therapy.
output: Calcinosis universalis associated with scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome

A 42-year-old woman with a sudden onset of abdominal pain requested to see us urgently. 5 years earlier she had been diagnosed with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) and had missed multiple follow-up appointments. Despite having a large PNH clone〞greater than 50% of PNH granulocytes〞the patient had been asymptomatic with only mildly elevated haemolytic parameters and treatment with eculizumab had been deferred.On examination, she was afebrile and she had slight scleral icterus; vital signs were stable. The patient's liver was palpable with soft edges and there was right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs. The spleen was also palpable approximately 3 cm below the left costal margin.
Laboratory investigations showed elevated liver enzymes: aspartate aminotransferase 164 U/L (normal 13每35), alanine aminotransferase 116 U/L (normal 7每38), total bilirubin concentration 2﹞9 mg/dL (normal 0﹞2每1﹞3). D-dimer concentration was raised at 11?420 ng/mL (normal <500), lactate dehydrogenase was 1?111 U/L (normal 135每214), and her haemoglobin concentration was low at 9﹞2 g/dL (normal 11﹞5每15﹞5).
A CT scan and MRI of the patient's abdomen showed splenomegaly with a heterogeneous appearance of the liver with hypointensity along the vascular territory, tapering occlusion of the hepatic veins, and focal narrowing at the level of the confluence (figure): findings consistent with chronic Budd每Chiari syndrome.
After consultation with the hepatology service, no acute interventions were recommended. The patient was started on apixaban 5 mg twice a day and the anti-complement factor 5 inhibitor, ravulizumab〞starting with a loading dose of 3000 mg intravenously (weight-based dose), followed 2 weeks later with a maintenance dose of 3600 mg every 8 weeks.
Notably, deep sequencing of the PIGA gene showed five mutations: two frameshift (p.F150fs, p.E120fs), two missense (p.C81Y, p.S155Y), and one splice site (c.981+1G>A) at a mean total variant allele frequency of 16%.
The patient showed significant clinical improvement with resolution of her abdominal pain after 2 weeks of treatment.
PNH is a non-malignant disorder genetically defined by somatic loss-of-function mutations of the PIGA gene in haematopoietic stem cells. The mutations result in impaired biosynthesis of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI), a glycolipid structure that attaches specific proteins to the cell membrane. Impaired GPI-anchoring results in a deficiency of all GPI-linked proteins on the membranes of blood cells derived from the mutant clone. Among the GPI-linked proteins affected, deficiency of CD55 and CD59 on erythrocytes is responsible for increased sensitivity to complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis〞the cardinal symptom of PNH.
In addition to haemolysis, PNH causes bone marrow failure and thrombophilia〞the commonest cause of death. While thrombosis may occur at any site, unusual locations are typical of PNH-related hypercoagulability〞including hepatic vein thrombosis or Budd每Chiari syndrome which is seen in 10每25% of patients. Thrombosis can be either the initial presentation or can occur in the course of the disease; it is likely to be related to haemolysis as shown by the preventive effects of complement blockade treatment on the rate of this complication (video).
output: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) complicated by Budd-Chiari syndrome
