A 43-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic for 汐1 antitrypsin deficiency; CT scans showed basal predominant bullae, suggestive of the disease. On review in the clinic, he had no respiratory symptoms. He was a lifelong non-smoker, without any environmental or occupational exposures of note. He reported a history of recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces in his twenties that required bilateral pleurectomies. There was no family history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or emphysema. However, his daughter had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 14 years and his younger sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 31 years. Spirometry and the diffusion capacity of the patient's lungs for carbon monoxide were normal. His serum concentration of 汐1 antitrypsin was normal (concentrations of less than 11 米mol/L are considered abnormal and put the patient at high risk for the development of emphysema). A high-resolution CT scan of his chest (figure) showed numerous, thin-walled cysts in both lungs〞predominantly in the bases and sub-pleural areas. These cysts were surrounded by normal lung tissue without evidence of emphysema. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest of his sister, undertaken after she had a spontaneous pneumothorax, showed two small, thin-walled cysts in the left lower lobe (appendix). Given the imaging findings and his family history, genetic testing was done. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a deletion at position 469_471 in the Folliculin (FLCN) gene〞confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dub谷 (BHD) syndrome. Family screening was also done (figure) and all affected family members〞the patient's father, two elder sisters, and the patient's son〞had high-resolution CT scans of the thorax and MRIs of the kidneys.BHD syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, caused by germline mutations in the FLCN gene. It is characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal cancer. The cysts in BHD syndrome have several characteristics that may help distinguish them from other causes of diffuse cystic lung disease: they are basal predominant, thin-walled cysts, lentiform in shape and with a predilection for the subpleural region. The most serious complication of BHD syndrome is renal cancer, which has a prevalence of 24每37% in these patients. Once the diagnosis is made, all patients with BHD syndrome should undergo renal imaging at yearly intervals. Pneumothorax occurs in up to 25% of patients and the recurrence rate approaches 75%.
Lung cysts are commonly found on CT scans of the chest and have a wide range of aetiologies including smoking and rare genetic causes such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Lung cysts often have distinct characteristics that help to narrow down the diagnosis. In all patients presenting with a pneumothorax, it is crucial to ask about family history and consider doing a high-resolution CT scan of the thorax.

input: A 51-year-old woman with a diagnosis of scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome presented to our rheumatology department with widespread subcutaneous skin lesions. A 24-week pregnant 18-year-old woman was seen at her local health-care centre where she was found to have a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per min, a blood pressure of 250/90 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 39 beats per min. She collapsed and required intubation and ventilation. A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates〞pulmonary oedema〞and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel〞a progestagen only〞contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5〞indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient〞the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).
output: Pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) with mammary hamartomas

A 43-year-old man was referred to our specialist clinic for 汐1 antitrypsin deficiency; CT scans showed basal predominant bullae, suggestive of the disease. On review in the clinic, he had no respiratory symptoms. He was a lifelong non-smoker, without any environmental or occupational exposures of note. He reported a history of recurrent bilateral pneumothoraces in his twenties that required bilateral pleurectomies. There was no family history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or emphysema. However, his daughter had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 14 years and his younger sister had a spontaneous pneumothorax at the age of 31 years. Spirometry and the diffusion capacity of the patient's lungs for carbon monoxide were normal. His serum concentration of 汐1 antitrypsin was normal (concentrations of less than 11 米mol/L are considered abnormal and put the patient at high risk for the development of emphysema). A high-resolution CT scan of his chest (figure) showed numerous, thin-walled cysts in both lungs〞predominantly in the bases and sub-pleural areas. These cysts were surrounded by normal lung tissue without evidence of emphysema. A high-resolution CT scan of the chest of his sister, undertaken after she had a spontaneous pneumothorax, showed two small, thin-walled cysts in the left lower lobe (appendix). Given the imaging findings and his family history, genetic testing was done. The patient was found to be heterozygous for a deletion at position 469_471 in the Folliculin (FLCN) gene〞confirming a diagnosis of Birt-Hogg-Dub谷 (BHD) syndrome. Family screening was also done (figure) and all affected family members〞the patient's father, two elder sisters, and the patient's son〞had high-resolution CT scans of the thorax and MRIs of the kidneys.BHD syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition, caused by germline mutations in the FLCN gene. It is characterised by skin fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax, and renal cancer. The cysts in BHD syndrome have several characteristics that may help distinguish them from other causes of diffuse cystic lung disease: they are basal predominant, thin-walled cysts, lentiform in shape and with a predilection for the subpleural region. The most serious complication of BHD syndrome is renal cancer, which has a prevalence of 24每37% in these patients. Once the diagnosis is made, all patients with BHD syndrome should undergo renal imaging at yearly intervals. Pneumothorax occurs in up to 25% of patients and the recurrence rate approaches 75%.
Lung cysts are commonly found on CT scans of the chest and have a wide range of aetiologies including smoking and rare genetic causes such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Lung cysts often have distinct characteristics that help to narrow down the diagnosis. In all patients presenting with a pneumothorax, it is crucial to ask about family history and consider doing a high-resolution CT scan of the thorax.

A 45-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with a 4-h history of diplopia and vertigo.
The patient had been found to have a bicuspid aortic valve without any significant dysfunction; the bicuspid valve had been diagnosed when she was aged 25 years by transthoracic echocardiography when investigated for a systolic murmur. The patient was a non-smoker; she had previously been fit and well, and she was taking no medications.
On examination after admission, she was well and alert; her temperature was 36﹞7～C, blood pressure 186/105 mm Hg, and pulse rate 83 beats per min. She had ataxia in her arms.
An electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm. Laboratory investigations showed a mildly increased C-reactive protein concentration of 18 mg/L (normal <5); leukocytes and procalcitonin concentration were in normal range.
A brain MRI showed cerebellar bilateral ischaemic lesions; and transoesophageal echocardiography showed findings consistent with a marked thickening of the aortic leaflets with hypoechogenic masses, which was causing mild aortic regurgitation (figure; video).The hospital endocarditis team assessed the patient; empirical treatment with antibiotics〞amoxicillin and ceftriaxone〞was started after collection of four samples for blood cultures. Additionally, serological testing for bacteria〞including Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp, Aspergillus spp, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Brucella spp, and Legionellla pneumophilia〞causing blood culture-negative endocarditis, was carried out.
Antibiotics were stopped after 3 weeks〞given from day 1 of the admission to day 21〞after all microbiological results came back negative. Assays for antiphospholipid, rheumatic factor, and antinuclear antibodies were also negative; moreover, a workup for disseminated intravascular coagulation was also negative.
To investigate for possible peripheral emboli, a thoracic CT scan was done which showed a left inferior lung mass with mediastinal and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy (figure). An 18fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) PET/CT showed intense metabolic fixation of all tumour targets (figure). After lymphadenomectomy puncture, histopathological analysis of samples of a transthoracic needle biopsy of the lesion showed a solid architecture invasive adenocarcinoma; mucin-secreting cells were strongly positive for tumour marker thyroid transcription factor-1 and intensely positive (3+ in 100% of cells) for ALK-EML4 on immunohistochemical analysis. Fluorescence in situ hybridisation analysis found an ALK gene rearrangement in 93% of the nuclei, characterised by supernumerary red signals.
A diagnosis of marantic endocarditis was made and tyrosine kinase inhibitor treatment with crizotinib〞an ALK inhibitor〞was initiated on day 19. The patient described a transient visual disturbance 48 h later. Brain MRI showed additional small ischaemic lesions; owing to the perceived risk of intracranial bleeding due to recent brain infarcts, anticoagulation was not initiated. No subsequent neurological events were noted.
2 months after crizotinib initiation, the heart valve lesions had disappeared with no perforation or deterioration of function (figure; video). An 18F-FDG PET/CT confirmed a complete metabolic response (figure).
At 7-year follow-up, the patient is alive and well without cancer or evidence of marantic endocarditis.
Advanced malignancy is associated with marantic endocarditis, although it may be found with autoimmune diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. Treatment of the underlying cause〞in our case the malignancy〞may lead to resolution of the valvular lesions.
output: Marantic endocarditis secondary to ALK-rearranged lung adenocarcinoma

A 24-week pregnant 18-year-old woman was seen at her local health-care centre where she was found to have a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per min, a blood pressure of 250/90 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 39 beats per min. She collapsed and required intubation and ventilation. A chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates〞pulmonary oedema〞and she was treated with furosemide and nitroglycerin and transferred to our intensive care unit.She was not taking any medication, but she did have an etonogestrel〞a progestagen only〞contraceptive implant put in 6 months earlier. Around the time the implant was put in, she also had a lump in her right breast; a biopsy found it to be benign proliferative breast tissue. She had no significant medical or social history and there was no history of breast or ovarian cancer in her family.
On examination, we found the patient's breasts were asymmetrical; both were erythematous, tender, and had focal, palpable, mobile masses (figure). The skin of both breasts had a peau d'orange pattern. We found no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy. At this initial assessment, we were concerned for possible inflammatory breast cancer; a diagnostic mammogram and an ultrasound (figure) showed large bilateral masses. Given the skin findings, the rapid growth, and the large, irregular, and heterogeneous nature of the masses, our radiologist assigned a Breast Imaging-Reporting and Data System category of 5〞indicating that we considered the lesion highly suspicious of malignancy.
Histopathological examination of samples taken from both breasts, using core-needle biopsies, showed prominent pseudoangiomatous stromal hyperplasia (PASH) and mammary hamartomas.
We then removed the implant, and 1 week later, the patient reported significant reduction in breast size, pain, pressure, and erythema. We advised her against future use of exogenous hormonal therapies with the aim of reducing the likelihood of recurrence. She is planning to have both masses excised and oncoplastic reconstructive surgery carried out.
PASH masses can resemble breast cancer both on examination and at imaging, and tissue sampling is imperative for diagnosis. PASH is a hormone-sensitive process and rapid progression can occur with sudden hormonal changes, which given the timeline we believe was the case with our patient〞the contraceptive implant being the source of the excess hormone. PASH should be considered as an important differential diagnosis of breast hypertrophy in a premenopausal patient, particularly in the context of changes to the hormonal milieu.
The risk of developing breast cancer is not increased with PASH, and so follow-up using standard mammographic screening is recommended (video).

A 40-year-old woman was referred to our clinic by her optometrist because she had lesions on her retina suggestive of age-related macular degeneration (AMD). She was otherwise well: with no systemic or visual symptoms.In her medical history, the patient had no previous problems with her eyesight. However, at the age of 10 years, she had developed end-stage renal disease〞initially diagnosed as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis〞which eventually resulted in her having a right kidney transplant when she was 22 years old. 6 years later, aged 28 years, she developed signs of rejection and required hospitalisation. At that stage, a kidney biopsy led to a diagnosis of dense deposit disease (DDD). She received a second kidney transplant at age 39 years.
She had been prescribed a combination of immunosuppressive drugs〞prednisolone, mycophenolate, and tacrolimus〞for the past 2 years, and her blood pressure had remained stable without pharmacotherapy.
On examination, we found her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Fundus examination showed drusen-like deposits in the macula and numerous lesions in the peripheral retina of both eyes (figure). Optical coherence tomography showed subretinal dome-shaped deposits〞known as drusen〞in the peripheral retina, with some encroaching in the macular region of both eyes (figure). Drusen is the plural form of druse, a German word meaning node or geode.
Considering the situation in the round, including the patient's age and medical history, and the appearance and distribution of the fundus lesions, we concluded that the drusen were a feature of DDD rather than AMD. The patient continues to be followed up by both her nephrologist and ophthalmologist.
DDD, which was previously known as type II membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, is classified as either complement or immune complex mediated; DDD is considered a subtype of complement C3-mediated glomerulopathy. Patients with DDD have diffuse, dense deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, and unlike other forms of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, they also typically have drusen deposits in Bruch's membrane of the eye. It is a rare disease that usually presents in children aged 5每15 years old and eventually leads to end-stage renal disease.
Drusen in patients with DDD typically develop after more than 20 years, and although the retinal lesions do not directly cause visual impairment, vision can deteriorate, most commonly due to macular detachment, central serous chorioretinopathy, or choroidal neovascularisation similar to patients with AMD.
Anyone under the age of 50 years found to have retinal drusen should therefore be assessed for renal disease at the time of presentation, and should have regular ophthalmic examinations to monitor for the development of potential vision-threatening changes (video).
output: Retinal drusen associated with dense deposit disease (DDD)

A 2-year-old boy presented for severe frostbite after being outside on a cold day (mean temperature 每18～C). The child had reportedly spent 20每30 minutes outside and was found without gloves. Eight fingers (1每5 on the right hand, and 1, 2, and 5 on the left hand) first appeared pale, then developed severe blisters. He was admitted for wound care, surgical debridement of necrotic skin, and pain control. At first, radiographs of the hands were typical (appendix). The patient was discharged home after 2 weeks, following a favourable evolution. 1 year later, he presented with widened interphalangeal joints in the eight fingers affected by frostbite. On x-ray, there was substantial damage to the metaphyses and epiphyses (figure A). Conservative treatment (occupational therapy and splinting) was started. During follow up, joint damage progressed to deformity and growth restrictions in the affected fingers (appendix). At the age of 17 years, there is substantial joint and bone damage, finger shortening, and nail dystrophy in the eight fingers affected by frostbite (figure B and C). The patient does not report any joint pain or stiffness and has a near-typical functional status.
Frostbite is cold-induced tissue damage, with lack of supervision and alcohol and drug use as common risk factors in children and adolescents. Short-term complications include severe pain, infections, and tissue necrosis (ranging from skin blisters to extensive gangrene). Long-term sequelae include neuropathic pain, vasospasm, nails dystrophy, and risk for squamous cell-carcinoma. Additionally, frostbite arthropathy can appear months to years after the acute episode. In an immature skeleton, frostbite arthropathy can exceptionally result in physeal, growth plate, and epiphyseal destruction of affected phalanges. The frequency of this complication is unknown, with only a few historical cases published. Physicians should be aware of this rare complication of severe paediatric frostbite, which can occur even after an initially favourable evolution. In the absence of curative treatment, prevention of cold-induced injuries (especially in at-risk familial and environmental contexts) remains crucial.

A 43-year-old Australian-born, white man was referred to our unit because of increasing pain in both his ankles. The pain had developed approximately 7 days earlier. 3 days before the pain started, he had been admitted to hospital with cellulitis of his upper arm; he had been treated for septicaemia and acute kidney injury caused by an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes.In his medical history, the patient had been diagnosed with X-linked phosphataemia as a child; he had a family history of the disease, an Arnold-Chiari I malformation, and been treated with 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) and phosphate supplements, which he stopped taking from early adulthood. The patient had also been previously treated successfully with interferon for a hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection when he was 35 years old.
On examination we found moderate, bilateral ankle effusions, pain on both active and passive movement of the joints and marked bone deformity of his feet〞he had pes planus and hypertrophic growth of the midfoot region. He also had tenderness at the plantar fascial insertions but no gouty tophi.
x-rays of his feet showed significant heterotrophic ossification of the entheses of all hind and midfoot bones (figure) and fluid analysis from an ankle joint aspirate showed monosodium urate crystals.
We therefore attributed his symptoms to a gout flare precipitated by acute kidney injury and septicaemia. We treated him with colchicine and the pain reduced; we later confirmed that the gout flare had resolved with a dual-energy CT scan that showed no urate crystals. Despite the negative finding on the dual-energy CT scan, the patient continued to experience arthralgia in his ankles. We carried out further investigations to clarify the additional, underlying aetiology〞namely, the X-linked hypophosphataemia. The serum phosphate concentration was low (0﹞63 mmol/L; normal 0﹞75每1﹞50) and the calcitriol concentration was also low (19 pmol/L; normal 48每190); additional investigations were normal (appendix). CT scans of the patient's feet, ankles, and pelvis showed extensive enthesopathy (figure).
X-linked hypophosphataemia is a rare disorder often identified in childhood. Problems arise from inactivating mutations of the phosphate regulating endopeptidase homolog, X-linked (PHEX) gene. Hypophosphataemia is caused by poor absorption of phosphate in the intestine and impaired renal tubular reabsorption, with normal serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. The calcitriol is often low or normal in X-linked hypophosphataemia: findings that would be unexpected in cases where there is an increased level of calcitriol.
Patients have a range of medical problems depending on age. In children, problems include delayed and disproportionate growth, craniosynostosis, and rickets. In adults, problems include inappropriate mineralisation of fibrocartilage〞tendons insert into bone leading to the development of spurs or enthesophytes, which results in joint stiffness and pain or enthesopathy〞as in our patient. Adult patients mainly complain of arthralgia of the knees, hip, and back. Traditional treatment with oral phosphate and calcitriol may improve the rate of growth and mineralisation in childhood but fails to stop the progressive enthesopathy and arthropathy found in adulthood. Arthralgia may develop because of degenerative arthropathy which is a consequence of the progressive enthesopathy altering the architecture and mechanics of the foot.
Enthesopathy can occur in psoriatic arthritis, heavy metal exposure, skeletal fluorosis, hyperparathyroidism, and other heritable forms of hypophosphataemia. HCV-related osteosclerosis〞which was included in the differential diagnoses in this case〞can cause bone pain; however, it is not associated with enthesopathy and is characterised by accelerated bone turnover (video).

A 52-year-old right-handed woman was referred to our clinic reporting a 4-year history of spontaneous unpredictable episodes of dizziness. The patient was seen remotely due to restrictions imposed because of the COVID-19 pandemic. She described the episodes as a sudden sensation of feeling like the room was spinning for 5每40 s; they were happening approximately three times a day and she could identify no triggers. Occasionally, the episodes were associated with nausea and vomiting; they had also caused her to fall but did not result in any impairment of consciousness. The patient reported no visual symptoms, tinnitus, or headache. She was otherwise in good health and took no regular medication.The referral, from the otorhinolaryngology clinic via the family doctor, reported a negative Dix-Hallpike test and failure to improve the patient's symptoms with the Epley manoeuvre. The referrer diagnosed M谷ni豕re's disease〞a triad of tinnitus, vertigo, and hearing loss〞and prescribed the patient a trial of betahistine, bendroflumethiazide, and prochlorperazine with no benefit.
On remote examination the patient appeared well, although further examination was limited as there was no opportunity to test for nystagmus.
Laboratory investigations, previously arranged by the family doctor, had shown no atypical findings〞full blood count, renal profile, and liver function were all within normal range. A brain MRI, which had been done 1 year before our consultation, as part of the initial work-up, showed normal brain parenchyma and ventricular system. We requested a further MRI to include high-resolution axial T2-weighted sequences of the posterior fossa; this showed a prominent left-sided vascular loop extending into the internal auditory meatus and causing compression of the left eighth cranial nerve〞consistent with our suspected diagnosis of vestibular paroxysmia (figure). We prescribed the patient carbamazepine and she reported that her symptoms had resolved completely soon after commencing the treatment.
Vestibular paroxysmia is a rare cause of spontaneous, brief, and recurrent attacks of vertigo; episodes can be significantly disabling. The diagnosis〞as in our patient〞often goes unrecognised for many years. The key features differentiating vestibular paroxysmia from more common causes of vertigo are the spontaneity, the brevity, and the frequency. Regarding spontaneity, attacks are not typically triggered by head movement; syndromes to consider if attacks are triggered by head movement include benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, central positional nystagmus (caused by cerebellar and brainstem lesions), and bow hunter syndrome (vertebrobasilar insufficiency resulting from vertebral artery occlusion during neck rotation, usually from cervical spondylosis). Regarding brevity, attacks are usually < 1min; syndromes to consider if episodes are longer include M谷ni豕re's disease (typically attacks last 20 min to 12 h) and vestibular migraine (5 min to 72 h). And finally, regarding frequency, attacks occur up to 30 or more times per day; syndromes where episodes are less frequently include vertebrobasilar transient ischaemic attacks and epileptic vertigo.
Although infrequently encountered, vestibular paroxysmia is a condition to be aware of since it is an eminently treatable cause of dizziness and could very easily be mistaken for more common causes. MRIs typically show neurovascular compression of the eighth cranial nerve〞radiologists should be asked to specifically look for this.

A 68-year-old woman undergoing a routine surveillance endoscopy〞part of her follow-up for a Barrett's oesophagus〞was found to have a solitary, black lesion, approximately 4 mm in diameter, in the gastric body (figure). Biopsy samples were taken and microscopic examination showed gastric body mucosa with heavily pigmented cells in the lamina propria that infiltrated the crypts without destroying them (figure). Immunohistochemical examination of the biopsied tissue section showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using antibodies. Her medical history included the enucleation of her left eye 13 years earlier to remove a primary uveal melanoma; she had been discharged from routine follow-up. We then decided to carry out another gastroscopy to take deeper gastric biopsy samples. These showed infiltration of the muscularis mucosae by melanocytes with mild atypia. A full-body CT scan showed multiple lesions in her liver, which on subsequent MRI were confirmed to be melanin-laden metastases (figure). Gene mutation panel testing of the gastric biopsy specimens and of the ocular specimens taken at the time of the eye operation 13 years earlier showed the same oncogenic mutation: Gln209Leu in GNA11. Tests for the common cutaneous melanoma mutations in BRAF, NRAS, and KIT genes were negative. The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial testing a combination of selumetinib and paclitaxel chemotherapy for metastatic uveal melanoma. Uveal melanoma is a rare cancer representing less than 5% of all melanomas; it has a nearly 50-fold lower incidence rate than that of cutaneous melanomas. It is an aggressive disease, predominantly spreading to the liver in up to 50% of patients. Median survival with liver metastases is less than 6 months. Currently, there are no effective non-surgical treatments for metastatic uveal melanoma. Surveillance and monitoring of the liver〞after treatment of the primary lesion〞are recommended so that patients can receive early locoregional treatments. The length of time patients should be followed up is not established in current clinical guidelines. Uveal melanoma is associated with an almost linear continuation of recurrence over time and beyond 10 years without a plateau in risk of recurrence. Thus, late recurrences are not uncommon: 5 and 10 year cumulative metastasis rates are 25% and 34%, respectively. Cutaneous and uveal melanomas are biologically distinct. Uveal melanomas lack the typical cutaneous melanoma-associated mutations in the BRAF, NRAS, and NF1 genes, but have somatic mutations in the GNA11 and QNAQ genes in around 90% of cases; in cutaneous melanomas mutations in these genes are found in less than 10% of cases. Mutations in these genes activate the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase oncogenic pathway, providing a rationale for using MEK1/2 inhibitors, selumetinib for example, as agents in clinical trials results〞although to date the results have been disappointing. Functionally activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11, as well as in CYSLTR2 and PLCB4, leads to the subsequent activation of pathways〞which include the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase and Yap/Hippo pathways〞downstream beyond the MAP kinase pathway. These may offer potential novel therapeutic targets. Genetic profiling of primary uveal melanomas has some prognostic value. For example, inactivating mutations in the BAP1 gene〞found in approximately 50% of cases〞are highly likely to metastasise, whereas mutations in the SF3B1 and EIF1AX genes, occurring in approximately 19% and 24% of uveal melanoma cases, respectively, are less likely to metastasise.

A 46-year-old man presented with left lower quadrant pain, tenderness, and rebound tenderness on examination. He was afebrile and did not have leucocytosis. The abdominal CT showed a hypodense pericolonic oval mass of 2﹞5 cm with adjacent fat stranding: a classic picture of epiploic appendagitis (figure). Epiploic appendages are roughly 50每100 pedunculated adipose structures protruding from the serosal surface of the colon from the caecum to the rectosigmoid junction. Torsion of the pedicle or central venous thrombosis could cause epiploic appendagitis, which can simulate diverticulitis, appendicitis, and cholecystitis. Fever, chills, and leucocytosis are usually absent. In addition to the CT indicating this diagnosis, a non-compressible hyperechoic mass connected to the adjacent colon at the point of maximum tenderness on ultrasonography is indicative of epiploic appendages. Epiploic appendagitis needs only conservative management and pain control; however, failure to recognise this diagnosis could lead to unnecessary intervention.

An 80-year-old man with a 1-week history of a red, swollen, and painful right leg presented to our emergency department. Additionally, he had reported long-term fatigue. A deep vein thrombosis was excluded after an ultrasound of his leg and he was found to have an infected ulcer caused by chronic venous insufficiency and an iron deficiency anaemia. The patient was referred to our clinic for further exploration of his anaemia and painful leg.He had previously had a coronary artery bypass graft; he had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; atherosclerosis with peripheral arterial occlusive disease and coronary artery disease; recurrent deep venous thromboses; and alcohol misuse.
Laboratory investigations had previously found a low haemoglobin concentration of 9﹞8 g/dL (typical range 13﹞7每17﹞7), a mean corpuscular volume of 91 fL (typical range 80每100), and a serum ferritin concentration of 17 米g/L (typical range 22每320).
On examination we found the patient to be pale but not acute unwell. He had ulcers and pitting oedema of both shins and soft respiratory sounds in both lung bases.
Ordinarily, we would have done a routine colonoscopy to investigate possible causes of the patient's anaemia. However, considering the patient's general health and the likelihood of proceeding to surgery being low, we decided to manage the case conservatively.
An abdominal CT showed an unexplained lesion about 6﹞1 cm in length, located near the xiphoid, ventral to the liver (figure). No other atypical findings were seen. On review of a previous scan, done 4 years earlier, we found that the lesion had been present for some time and that it had increased in size.
Histopathological examination of a sample from a biopsy of the lesion showed lipocytes, megakaryocytes, erythroid precursors, and myeloid precursors: indicative of extramedullary haematopoiesis (EMH; figure).
Additional laboratory investigations ruled out monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells〞no M-protein was detectable and no JAK2 gene mutation was found. We did not do a bone marrow aspiration, for the reason stated above regarding the colonoscopy.
After 2 weeks of treating his ulcers with clindamycin and 2 months of ferrous fumarate, his haemoglobin concentration was 17﹞7 g/dL and his shins had improved.
Considering all the patient's pathologies, we believe that the cause of the EMH was likely to be multifactorial: the chronic ulcers and atherosclerosis, and the iron deficiency anaemia.
EMH is the expansion and differentiation of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells outside the bone marrow as a compensatory mechanism for ineffective haematopoiesis. In adults, EMH typically occurs in the presence of myeloproliferative malignancies. That it is also associated with other conditions〞including thalassemia〞is well appreciated.
Sites commonly affected are the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes; paravertebral areas, heart, chest, thymus, kidney, adrenal gland, prostate, pleura, nerves in the skin and spinal canal may be involved, but less frequently. On discovering a site of EMH, extensive investigations should be made to find the cause; appropriate treatment can then be started.
EMH in unusual locations〞as seen in our patient〞needs regular monitoring, and in selected cases where the lesion is causing local symptoms, surgical resection might be considered; not a realistic possibility in this case.

A 28-year-old Egyptian woman was referred to our specialised gestational trophoblastic disease clinic for treatment. She explained that 2 years earlier, her menstrual cycle had changed and become irregular with prolonged heavy bleeding lasting between 15 and 20 days; before this, her periods had been regular, lasting 30 days with 5 days of bleeding. The woman had two children and no history of contraceptive use, hormonal therapy, or any other medications. 3 months after the irregular bleeding started, the patient visited her local gynaecologist, who reported no uterine or cervical disease and prescribed diosmin tablets. At this stage, the patient's haemoglobin concentration was 10 g/dL〞importantly, her urine and serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels were not measured. The bleeding did not improve, and she had dilation and curettage of the uterus, during which a biopsy specimen was taken from the endometrium: histology showed a disordered proliferative endometrium. input: A 68-year-old woman undergoing a routine surveillance endoscopy〞part of her follow-up for a Barrett's oesophagus〞was found to have a solitary, black lesion, approximately 4 mm in diameter, in the gastric body (figure). Biopsy samples were taken and microscopic examination showed gastric body mucosa with heavily pigmented cells in the lamina propria that infiltrated the crypts without destroying them (figure). Immunohistochemical examination of the biopsied tissue section showed positive staining for melanoma associated antigens using antibodies. Her medical history included the enucleation of her left eye 13 years earlier to remove a primary uveal melanoma; she had been discharged from routine follow-up. We then decided to carry out another gastroscopy to take deeper gastric biopsy samples. These showed infiltration of the muscularis mucosae by melanocytes with mild atypia. A full-body CT scan showed multiple lesions in her liver, which on subsequent MRI were confirmed to be melanin-laden metastases (figure). Gene mutation panel testing of the gastric biopsy specimens and of the ocular specimens taken at the time of the eye operation 13 years earlier showed the same oncogenic mutation: Gln209Leu in GNA11. Tests for the common cutaneous melanoma mutations in BRAF, NRAS, and KIT genes were negative. The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial testing a combination of selumetinib and paclitaxel chemotherapy for metastatic uveal melanoma. Uveal melanoma is a rare cancer representing less than 5% of all melanomas; it has a nearly 50-fold lower incidence rate than that of cutaneous melanomas. It is an aggressive disease, predominantly spreading to the liver in up to 50% of patients. Median survival with liver metastases is less than 6 months. Currently, there are no effective non-surgical treatments for metastatic uveal melanoma. Surveillance and monitoring of the liver〞after treatment of the primary lesion〞are recommended so that patients can receive early locoregional treatments. The length of time patients should be followed up is not established in current clinical guidelines. Uveal melanoma is associated with an almost linear continuation of recurrence over time and beyond 10 years without a plateau in risk of recurrence. Thus, late recurrences are not uncommon: 5 and 10 year cumulative metastasis rates are 25% and 34%, respectively. Cutaneous and uveal melanomas are biologically distinct. Uveal melanomas lack the typical cutaneous melanoma-associated mutations in the BRAF, NRAS, and NF1 genes, but have somatic mutations in the GNA11 and QNAQ genes in around 90% of cases; in cutaneous melanomas mutations in these genes are found in less than 10% of cases. Mutations in these genes activate the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase oncogenic pathway, providing a rationale for using MEK1/2 inhibitors, selumetinib for example, as agents in clinical trials results〞although to date the results have been disappointing. Functionally activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11, as well as in CYSLTR2 and PLCB4, leads to the subsequent activation of pathways〞which include the phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase and Yap/Hippo pathways〞downstream beyond the MAP kinase pathway. These may offer potential novel therapeutic targets. Genetic profiling of primary uveal melanomas has some prognostic value. For example, inactivating mutations in the BAP1 gene〞found in approximately 50% of cases〞are highly likely to metastasise, whereas mutations in the SF3B1 and EIF1AX genes, occurring in approximately 19% and 24% of uveal melanoma cases, respectively, are less likely to metastasise.

An 80-year-old man with a 1-week history of a red, swollen, and painful right leg presented to our emergency department. Additionally, he had reported long-term fatigue. A deep vein thrombosis was excluded after an ultrasound of his leg and he was found to have an infected ulcer caused by chronic venous insufficiency and an iron deficiency anaemia. The patient was referred to our clinic for further exploration of his anaemia and painful leg.He had previously had a coronary artery bypass graft; he had a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; atherosclerosis with peripheral arterial occlusive disease and coronary artery disease; recurrent deep venous thromboses; and alcohol misuse.
Laboratory investigations had previously found a low haemoglobin concentration of 9﹞8 g/dL (typical range 13﹞7每17﹞7), a mean corpuscular volume of 91 fL (typical range 80每100), and a serum ferritin concentration of 17 米g/L (typical range 22每320).
On examination we found the patient to be pale but not acute unwell. He had ulcers and pitting oedema of both shins and soft respiratory sounds in both lung bases.
Ordinarily, we would have done a routine colonoscopy to investigate possible causes of the patient's anaemia. However, considering the patient's general health and the likelihood of proceeding to surgery being low, we decided to manage the case conservatively.
An abdominal CT showed an unexplained lesion about 6﹞1 cm in length, located near the xiphoid, ventral to the liver (figure). No other atypical findings were seen. On review of a previous scan, done 4 years earlier, we found that the lesion had been present for some time and that it had increased in size.
Histopathological examination of a sample from a biopsy of the lesion showed lipocytes, megakaryocytes, erythroid precursors, and myeloid precursors: indicative of extramedullary haematopoiesis (EMH; figure).
Additional laboratory investigations ruled out monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells〞no M-protein was detectable and no JAK2 gene mutation was found. We did not do a bone marrow aspiration, for the reason stated above regarding the colonoscopy.
After 2 weeks of treating his ulcers with clindamycin and 2 months of ferrous fumarate, his haemoglobin concentration was 17﹞7 g/dL and his shins had improved.
Considering all the patient's pathologies, we believe that the cause of the EMH was likely to be multifactorial: the chronic ulcers and atherosclerosis, and the iron deficiency anaemia.
EMH is the expansion and differentiation of haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells outside the bone marrow as a compensatory mechanism for ineffective haematopoiesis. In adults, EMH typically occurs in the presence of myeloproliferative malignancies. That it is also associated with other conditions〞including thalassemia〞is well appreciated.
Sites commonly affected are the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes; paravertebral areas, heart, chest, thymus, kidney, adrenal gland, prostate, pleura, nerves in the skin and spinal canal may be involved, but less frequently. On discovering a site of EMH, extensive investigations should be made to find the cause; appropriate treatment can then be started.
EMH in unusual locations〞as seen in our patient〞needs regular monitoring, and in selected cases where the lesion is causing local symptoms, surgical resection might be considered; not a realistic possibility in this case.

A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ℅100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called ※demodicidosis gravis§. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

A 28-year-old man presented to our rheumatology department with a 10-year history of progressive facial and truncal rash and mild muscle weakness. He had previously presented with these symptoms at a local dermatology clinic at age 18 years. After this initial examination, the patient was diagnosed with dermatomyositis and given combined treatment with prednisone, methotrexate, and hydroxychloroquine. This treatment resulted in improved muscle weakness after a few months; however, the patient had mild hepatotoxicity and so methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine were discontinued. He also reported recurrence of cutaneous involvement, which prompted re-referral and re-evaluation at our department 10 years later.
On re-examination, physical examination revealed a violaceous heliotrope rash on the eyelids and malar area, accompanied by a striking reticular erythematous eruption on the neck and back (figure 1A). Muscle involvement was assessed by use of the Manual Muscle Testing-8 scale, yielding a score of 150 (ie, normal muscle strength).
Histopathological evaluation of the reticular rash biopsy sample revealed interface dermatitis on haematoxylin and eosin staining (figure 1B), along with basement membrane thickening highlighted by periodic acid-Schiff staining (figure 1C). Laboratory investigations showed creatine kinase concentrations within the normal range (64 U/L; reference range 50每310 U/L) and exclusive anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-污 (anti-TIF1-污) antibody positivity, detected by immunoblot, with negative results for other myositis-specific autoantibodies. In China, there are currently no commercially available ELISA kits for anti-TIF1-污 antibody detection that have been approved by the China Food and Drug Administration. Muscle MRI showed no inflammation or oedema, and high-resolution pulmonary CT revealed no interstitial lung disease. Extensive malignancy screening, including whole-body PET每CT and gastrointestinal endoscopy, showed no occult neoplasms. Peripheral blood PCR revealed elevated interferon-stimulated genes (MX1 and IFI44), confirming a type I interferon signature. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analysis revealed MX1 expression in the basal epidermis and perivascular regions.
When the patient was first diagnosed at his local dermatology clinic at age 18 years, his clinical manifestations were characterised by prominent cutaneous features without evidence of calcinosis, which is suggestive of cancer-associated adult dermatomyositis. However, detection of myositis-specific autoantibodies, including anti-TIF1-污, was unavailable at the time. Upon re-evaluation 10 years later, and taking into account the patient's history, symptoms, laboratory examination, and cutaneous biopsy findings, the diagnosis of dermatomyositis was confirmed. Baricitinib (4 mg per day) combined with prednisone (0﹞8 mg/kg per day) were initiated. At 24 weeks follow-up at our department, Cutaneous Disease Area and Severity Index scores improved by 60% (scores reduced from 25 to 10), with reduced erythema intensity and extent of rash. As there was no progression of muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, or malignancy after 24 weeks, prednisone was tapered to 7﹞5 mg per day.
Anti-TIF1-污 antibodies are strongly associated with malignancy, with peak risk 3每5 years before and after disease onset. Characteristic cutaneous findings of anti-TIF1-污 positive dermatomyositis, including facial rash, V-neck and back rash, periungual telangiectasias, heliotrope rash, Gottron's sign, palatal patch, and diffuse photoerythema, are well documented. However, reticular rash, a rare manifestation as seen in this patient, expands the spectrum of cutaneous manifestations. Emerging evidence implicates type I interferon dysregulation in pathogenesis, and Janus kinase inhibitors might be of benefit to patients with refractory cutaneous dermatomyositis.

A 64-year-old woman presented with multiple asymptomatic, erythematosus papulopustular facial lesions (figure, A). The patient had been diagnosed with rosacea, and received oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice daily for 3 weeks as first-line therapy by her family doctor. Because of the poor response to therapy, she had been referred to our dermatology clinic for further evaluation. On clinical examination, the eruptions, which were practically asymptomatic, had a rosacea-like appearance. They had emerged and gradually worsened over a period of 5 weeks. There were no pathological findings on physical examination and routine laboratory test results were normal. Microscopic examination of specimens collected from the patient's skin by epidermal scraping showed many Demodex folliculorum mites (figure, B, magnification ℅100). The patient showed substantial improvement after treatment with oral metronidazole (250 mg three times daily for 2 weeks) and subsequent weekly topical permethrin (cream 5%).
Demodex spp are common saprophytic vermiform mites, which asymptomatically parasitise the hair follicles and the pilosebaceous glands of mammals. In human beings, two species of acarid mite have been identified: Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis. Sites favoured by Demodex spp mites include the scalp, forehead, and chin, and areas around the orbit, nose, and mouth. Demodex spp have been implicated in the development of various facial conditions, including pityriasis folliculorum, rosacea-like demodicidosis (also known as demodicosis), pustular folliculitis, demodectic blepharitis, and so-called ※demodicidosis gravis§. Clinical features of Demodex spp infestation include erythematopapulous and pustulous skin lesions together with erythematodesquamative changes of the face. Furthermore, demodicidosis should also be considered in any patient with rosacea-like dermatitis resistant to conventional rosacea therapies.
Although there is no consensus to how and what degree infestation with Demodex spp mites contributes to skin pathology, there is evidence that demodicidosis is a condition distinct from common rosacea. The prevalence of Demodex spp carriers increases with age. It is possible that large numbers of demodex mites can stimulate inflammatory or allergic reactions by mechanical blockage of follicles, or by acting as vectors for microorganisms, which ultimately results in connective tissue damage and telangiectasia. Another interesting hypothesis is that inflammatory response may be stimulated by antigenic proteins related to a bacterium (Bacillus oleronius) isolated from D folliculorum.

A 62-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-h history of abrupt-onset of right flank pain and vomiting.
The patient had a history of vertigo and recent unintentional weight loss with migrating lymphadenopathy. She was prescribed meclizine and loratadine. She reported no history of trauma.
On examination the patient was distressed and pale; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure 96/53 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 95%; her temperature was 36﹞6oC. She had tenderness in the right periumbilical region of her abdomen, with no rebound or guarding. Urine analysis showed 1+ protein, positive leukocyte esterase; microscopic examination showed 12 white blood cells, and 8 red blood cells.
Laboratory investigations found the patient to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 6﹞8 g/dL (reference range 11﹞7每15﹞7); she was given an emergency transfusion of packed red blood cells. Further tests showed a white blood cell count of 49?℅?103 per 米L (reference range 4﹞0每11﹞0), platelets 380?℅?103 per 米L (reference range 150每450), and serum creatinine concentration of 0﹞9 mg/dL (reference range 0﹞51每0﹞95).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a large right perinephric haematoma. A renal angiogram showed no signs of active bleeding.
The patient was stabilised with further medical management involving intravenous crystalloid fluid and an additional transfusion of packed red blood cells. Given the profound leukocytosis and absence of signs of infection, oncology colleagues were consulted, and an outpatient bone marrow biopsy was planned.
However, 2 days later, the patient presented to our hospital again with acute onset pain in the flank, but this time on the left side; her haemoglobin concentration was 6﹞0 g/dL and she was thrombocytopenic〞nadir of the platelet count was 7?℅?103 per 米L. She received a transfusion of platelets and further packed red blood cells.
An abdominal CT scan showed a new left perinephric haematoma; the right sided haematoma appeared stable (figure 1). A renal angiogram showed active bleeding from a left upper pole segmental arterial branch and a right upper pole peripheral arterial branch; these were then both successfully embolised. The patient then became oliguric and showed signs of acute kidney injury〞peak serum creatinine concentration was 3﹞6 mg/dL.The patient required intermittent haemodialysis while her renal function recovered over the next 2 weeks. During this time, analysis of a sample obtained by bone marrow biopsy (figure 3) showed monocytosis〞including atypical monocytes and slight dysgranulopoiesis〞indicative of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML); G-banded chromosomal analysis showed a 46, XX karyotype and genetic sequencing for common myeloid neoplasm-associated gene mutations showed CBL R420*, CBL C382S, IDH2 R140Q, and SRSF2 P95R mutations. Treatment with hydroxyurea was initiated and the patient was allowed home with oncology follow-up.Over the next few weeks, the leukocytosis, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia essentially resolved; treatment with hydroxyurea continued and correlated with improvement in her energy and strength. Repeat renal imaging〞both ultrasound and MRI〞showed resolution of both perinephric haematomas and no obvious underlying renal masses. Renal function subsequently improved and creatinine returned to typical range.
The patient stayed on 500 mg of hydroxyurea daily for 10 months after her initial hospitalisation with no major complications from the CMML. She had a mild anaemia, a normal creatinine, and returned to her previous functional status〞including returning to work.
Spontaneous renal or perinephric haemorrhage〞known as Wunderlich syndrome〞without any trauma〞is rare. Causes include renal neoplasm, vascular disease, coagulation abnormalities, and infections. While CMML can result in acute kidney injury through a variety of mechanisms〞including tumour lysis syndrome, renal thrombosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis, lysozyme induced nephropathy, and rarely renal infiltration〞to our knowledge, no cases have been reported of an association with Wunderlich syndrome. Notably, in this case, contrast nephropathy, ischaemia following the embolisation and acute blood loss, compression of the kidneys, and possibly leukaemic infiltration, may have contributed to the patient's acute kidney injury. Finally, we suspect leukaemic infiltration of both kidneys predisposed to the development of the spontaneous bilateral perinephric haematomas.

A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4﹞5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21﹞4 mmol/L (normal level <1﹞7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5﹞5 mmol/L (normal level <5﹞2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0﹞7 mmol/L (normal level <2﹞6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0﹞5 mmol/L (normal level >1﹞0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet〞less than 10% of total calories〞with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)〞the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

A 58-year-old man with a 31-month history of seeing peoples＊ faces as distorted and, in his words, appearing ※demonic§ visited our laboratory for assessment. The patient stated that the distortions〞severely stretched features of the face, with deep grooves on the forehead, cheeks, and chin〞were present on every person's face he encountered, but he reported no distortions when looking at objects, such as houses or cars. The patient said that even though faces were distorted, he was still able to recognise who they were. Notably, he reported no distortions when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper. The distortions were not accompanied by delusional beliefs about the identities of the people he encountered〞such as his family or friends.
The patient had a history of bipolar affective disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Additionally, he had a significant head injury at the age of 43 years that led to hospitalisation. He also had possible carbon monoxide poisoning at the age of 55 years, which occurred 4 months prior to the onset of his distortion symptoms. He was not prescribed any medications. He reported no use of illicit substances.
On initial assessment, the patient was well and not distressed; he had some mild low back discomfort. The distortions were very distressing to him initially, he said, but he had become habituated to them. Neuropsychological testing indicated no obvious abnormal general cognitive function; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. He had no deficits of visual acuity (10/10 in both eyes) or colour vision (Ishira plates: 25/25; Farnsworth每Munsell 100-hue test: average discrimination). Computer-based face perception tests indicated mild impairment in recognition of facial identity but normal recognition of facial expression. No laboratory investigations were done at this stage.
Whole-brain T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans showed a round lesion〞T1 dark and T2 bright〞measuring approximately 1 cm, located on the superior aspect of the head of the left hippocampus, displacing it inferiorly about 3 mm; despite this, the internal anatomy of the left hippocampus was preserved. The impression from the neurologist was that the lesion was probably an arachnoid cyst in the left hippocampal head; other observations included normal ventricle size, unremarkable midline structures, clear paranasal sinuses, and mild cerebral atrophy.
At 1-year follow-up, a repeated MRI showed no change in the size of the cyst.
As the patient reported no distortion when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper, we asked him to compare an in-person face to a photograph of the face taken in the same room under identical lighting conditions. By alternating between observing the in-person face〞perceived as distorted〞and the photo on a computer screen〞perceived as undistorted〞he provided real-time feedback on the perceived differences. We then used image-editing software to modify each photo until it matched his in-person perception (figure).Based on the patient's description of his visual perception, the neuropsychological assessment, and the distortion visualisations, we concluded that he had prosopometamorphopsia.
Prosopometamorphopsia is a rare neurological disorder of visual perception in which faces appear distorted in shape, texture, position, or colour. In most cases, the distortions occur all the time, whether the patient sees the face in person, on a screen, or on paper, thus making it difficult for patients to assess the accuracy of illustrations depicting their perceptual abnormalities because the illustration itself will appear distorted.
Prosopometamorphopsia's aetiology is varied and can occur in the context of head trauma, cerebral infarction, epilepsy, migraine, and hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder. The disorder can also manifest without detectable structural brain changes.
Our patient's unusual phenomenology, combined with computer software, enabled us to generate photorealistic visualisations of the distortions he experienced. Such images, we believe, have not been generated before (video).

A 73-year-old man with a history of hypertension and diverticulosis presented to our emergency department with a 1-day history of severe, lower abdominal pain, on his left side, associated with nausea. He did not report any other symptoms: dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, haematuria, fever, or diarrhoea.His vital signs were all normal except that he was hypertensive with a blood pressure of 187/104 mm Hg. A physical examination〞including a cardiac examination〞found no abnormalities. His white blood cell count was 9?℅?109 per L. His blood creatinine concentration was 0﹞8 mg/dL, and his liver function tests were normal: aspartate aminotransaminase was 28 IU/L and alanine aminotransaminase was 20 IU/L. A urinalysis showed 1+ protein, one white blood cell, and four red blood cells〞 thus within normal limits. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm with premature supraventricular complexes and variable P wave morphology in lead II with a mean duration of 133 ms and an amplitude of less than 0﹞25 mV. A non-contrast abdominal CT showed no calculi in the urinary tract. An urgent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT was done because of concerns about acute diverticulitis and intestinal ischaemia; this showed acute infarctions in the left kidney and spleen. Although the admission ECG was non-specific, the patient was started on anticoagulant medication, enoxaparin sodium injection 120 mg/day, because of a high index of suspicion that the infarctions were probably caused by cardioembolic events. Subsequently, continuous cardiac telemetry showed that the patient had paroxysmal atrial fibrillation〞confirmed with an ECG the next morning. An echocardiogram showed that all 4 chambers of the heart were of normal sizes with a left atrium dimension of 3﹞8 cm. There were no signs of valvular disease, the left ventricular ejection fraction was 60%, and a bubble study was negative. Interestingly, the patient's CHA2DS2-VASc score was four based on his age, hypertension, and thromboembolic events: 1 point for age 65每74 years, 1 point for a history of hypertension, and 2 points for the current embolic event. The patient's symptoms quickly improved, and he was discharged 3 days later in normal sinus rhythm on anticoagulants enoxaparin sodium 120 mg/day injection and warfarin 7﹞5 mg/day. Acute renal and splenic infarctions are rare and atrial fibrillation should be suspected as the cause even in the absence of arrhythmia on ECG. Other less frequent causes of renal and splenic infarctions include cancer and subacute bacterial endocarditis. Our case demonstrates that acute renal and splenic infarctions can manifest as the first and only presentation of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation even in the absence of arrhythmia on the ECG. For patients presenting with acute renal and splenic infarction, a work-up should include exploration for underlying paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, subacute bacterial endocarditis, and an underlying malignancy.

A 34-year-old man presented to our department with a 4-month history of constant, progressive epigastric abdominal pain. input: A 5-year-old boy presented to our department with a 2-day history of acute febrile illness. During evaluation, his blood samples were found to be so lipaemic (figure) that it caused interference in analyte measurements. The child was born of a non-consanguineous marriage, there was no history of failure to thrive or developmental delay, and there were no reports of any previous episodes of acute pancreatitis. Neither xanthomata nor hepatosplenomegaly was found at clinical examination. Laboratory test results found a normal fasting blood glucose concentration (4﹞5 mmol/L). However, triglycerides were found to be very high at 21﹞4 mmol/L (normal level <1﹞7 mmol/L). Total serum cholesterol was 5﹞5 mmol/L (normal level <5﹞2 mmol/L), LDL cholesterol by direct measurement was 0﹞7 mmol/L (normal level <2﹞6 mmol/L), and HDL cholesterol was 0﹞5 mmol/L (normal level >1﹞0 mmol/L). Investigations for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia were negative. Dilated fundus examination showed creamy white discolouration of retinal blood vessels (figure) suggestive of lipaemia retinalis; no retinal haemorrhages or exudates were seen. Fasting lipid profiles of other family members were normal. Taking into account the young age of the patient, the lipaemic plasma, the hypertriglyceridaemia, the lipaemia retinalis, and the lack of indications that his difficulties were secondary to any other diseases causing hypertriglyceridaemia, the boy was diagnosed with familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS). As treatment is mainly dietary fat restriction, the child was started on a low-fat diet〞less than 10% of total calories〞with medium-chain triglyceride supplements.FCS is characterised by impaired or absent activity of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)〞the key enzyme in catabolism of triglyceride rich lipoproteins, particularly chylomicrons. LPL is also involved in the accumulation of chylomicrons which give the milky appearance of the plasma. Bi-allelic mutations in the LPL gene account for around 80% of cases of FCS; the remainder are caused by mutations in one of four genes encoding proteins that interact with LPL. Early recognition and treatment of hyperlipidaemia are crucial to prevent systemic complications like acute pancreatitis. Many patients with elevated triglycerides do not have lipaemia retinalis for reasons that are unclear. The lipaemic appearance of the retinal blood vessels may persist after normalisation of the triglycerides on laboratory testing. Most systemic diseases have eye signs. The importance of an ophthalmological examination as a crucial component of a thorough medical examination cannot be overlooked.

A 58-year-old man with a 31-month history of seeing peoples＊ faces as distorted and, in his words, appearing ※demonic§ visited our laboratory for assessment. The patient stated that the distortions〞severely stretched features of the face, with deep grooves on the forehead, cheeks, and chin〞were present on every person's face he encountered, but he reported no distortions when looking at objects, such as houses or cars. The patient said that even though faces were distorted, he was still able to recognise who they were. Notably, he reported no distortions when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper. The distortions were not accompanied by delusional beliefs about the identities of the people he encountered〞such as his family or friends.
The patient had a history of bipolar affective disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Additionally, he had a significant head injury at the age of 43 years that led to hospitalisation. He also had possible carbon monoxide poisoning at the age of 55 years, which occurred 4 months prior to the onset of his distortion symptoms. He was not prescribed any medications. He reported no use of illicit substances.
On initial assessment, the patient was well and not distressed; he had some mild low back discomfort. The distortions were very distressing to him initially, he said, but he had become habituated to them. Neuropsychological testing indicated no obvious abnormal general cognitive function; Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. He had no deficits of visual acuity (10/10 in both eyes) or colour vision (Ishira plates: 25/25; Farnsworth每Munsell 100-hue test: average discrimination). Computer-based face perception tests indicated mild impairment in recognition of facial identity but normal recognition of facial expression. No laboratory investigations were done at this stage.
Whole-brain T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI scans showed a round lesion〞T1 dark and T2 bright〞measuring approximately 1 cm, located on the superior aspect of the head of the left hippocampus, displacing it inferiorly about 3 mm; despite this, the internal anatomy of the left hippocampus was preserved. The impression from the neurologist was that the lesion was probably an arachnoid cyst in the left hippocampal head; other observations included normal ventricle size, unremarkable midline structures, clear paranasal sinuses, and mild cerebral atrophy.
At 1-year follow-up, a repeated MRI showed no change in the size of the cyst.
As the patient reported no distortion when viewing facial images on a screen or on paper, we asked him to compare an in-person face to a photograph of the face taken in the same room under identical lighting conditions. By alternating between observing the in-person face〞perceived as distorted〞and the photo on a computer screen〞perceived as undistorted〞he provided real-time feedback on the perceived differences. We then used image-editing software to modify each photo until it matched his in-person perception (figure).Based on the patient's description of his visual perception, the neuropsychological assessment, and the distortion visualisations, we concluded that he had prosopometamorphopsia.
Prosopometamorphopsia is a rare neurological disorder of visual perception in which faces appear distorted in shape, texture, position, or colour. In most cases, the distortions occur all the time, whether the patient sees the face in person, on a screen, or on paper, thus making it difficult for patients to assess the accuracy of illustrations depicting their perceptual abnormalities because the illustration itself will appear distorted.
Prosopometamorphopsia's aetiology is varied and can occur in the context of head trauma, cerebral infarction, epilepsy, migraine, and hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder. The disorder can also manifest without detectable structural brain changes.
Our patient's unusual phenomenology, combined with computer software, enabled us to generate photorealistic visualisations of the distortions he experienced. Such images, we believe, have not been generated before (video).

A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third〞consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis〞also known as black oesophagus〞is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration〞especially among patients with underlying comorbidities〞awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.
