A 62-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a 2-h history of abrupt-onset of right flank pain and vomiting.
The patient had a history of vertigo and recent unintentional weight loss with migrating lymphadenopathy. She was prescribed meclizine and loratadine. She reported no history of trauma.
On examination the patient was distressed and pale; pulse was 75 beats per min, blood pressure 96/53 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation was 95%; her temperature was 36﹞6oC. She had tenderness in the right periumbilical region of her abdomen, with no rebound or guarding. Urine analysis showed 1+ protein, positive leukocyte esterase; microscopic examination showed 12 white blood cells, and 8 red blood cells.
Laboratory investigations found the patient to be anaemic with a haemoglobin concentration of 6﹞8 g/dL (reference range 11﹞7每15﹞7); she was given an emergency transfusion of packed red blood cells. Further tests showed a white blood cell count of 49?℅?103 per 米L (reference range 4﹞0每11﹞0), platelets 380?℅?103 per 米L (reference range 150每450), and serum creatinine concentration of 0﹞9 mg/dL (reference range 0﹞51每0﹞95).
A CT scan of the patient's abdomen showed a large right perinephric haematoma. A renal angiogram showed no signs of active bleeding.
The patient was stabilised with further medical management involving intravenous crystalloid fluid and an additional transfusion of packed red blood cells. Given the profound leukocytosis and absence of signs of infection, oncology colleagues were consulted, and an outpatient bone marrow biopsy was planned.
However, 2 days later, the patient presented to our hospital again with acute onset pain in the flank, but this time on the left side; her haemoglobin concentration was 6﹞0 g/dL and she was thrombocytopenic〞nadir of the platelet count was 7?℅?103 per 米L. She received a transfusion of platelets and further packed red blood cells.
An abdominal CT scan showed a new left perinephric haematoma; the right sided haematoma appeared stable (figure 1). A renal angiogram showed active bleeding from a left upper pole segmental arterial branch and a right upper pole peripheral arterial branch; these were then both successfully embolised. The patient then became oliguric and showed signs of acute kidney injury〞peak serum creatinine concentration was 3﹞6 mg/dL.The patient required intermittent haemodialysis while her renal function recovered over the next 2 weeks. During this time, analysis of a sample obtained by bone marrow biopsy (figure 3) showed monocytosis〞including atypical monocytes and slight dysgranulopoiesis〞indicative of chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia (CMML); G-banded chromosomal analysis showed a 46, XX karyotype and genetic sequencing for common myeloid neoplasm-associated gene mutations showed CBL R420*, CBL C382S, IDH2 R140Q, and SRSF2 P95R mutations. Treatment with hydroxyurea was initiated and the patient was allowed home with oncology follow-up.Over the next few weeks, the leukocytosis, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia essentially resolved; treatment with hydroxyurea continued and correlated with improvement in her energy and strength. Repeat renal imaging〞both ultrasound and MRI〞showed resolution of both perinephric haematomas and no obvious underlying renal masses. Renal function subsequently improved and creatinine returned to typical range.
The patient stayed on 500 mg of hydroxyurea daily for 10 months after her initial hospitalisation with no major complications from the CMML. She had a mild anaemia, a normal creatinine, and returned to her previous functional status〞including returning to work.
Spontaneous renal or perinephric haemorrhage〞known as Wunderlich syndrome〞without any trauma〞is rare. Causes include renal neoplasm, vascular disease, coagulation abnormalities, and infections. While CMML can result in acute kidney injury through a variety of mechanisms〞including tumour lysis syndrome, renal thrombosis, extramedullary haematopoiesis, lysozyme induced nephropathy, and rarely renal infiltration〞to our knowledge, no cases have been reported of an association with Wunderlich syndrome. Notably, in this case, contrast nephropathy, ischaemia following the embolisation and acute blood loss, compression of the kidneys, and possibly leukaemic infiltration, may have contributed to the patient's acute kidney injury. Finally, we suspect leukaemic infiltration of both kidneys predisposed to the development of the spontaneous bilateral perinephric haematomas.

An 8-year-old boy was referred to our centre for haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. 2 years earlier he had been diagnosed with X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.The unrelated donor was 10 out of 10 HLA-matched; bone marrow was chosen as the graft source. The patient was given a conditioning regimen of busulfan, fludarabine, and thiotepa along with graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis based upon standard recommendations: ciclosporin, anti-T-lymphocyte globulin, and short-term methotrexate.
Neutrophil engraftment was achieved on day +14. However, the early post-haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation period was complicated by the development of peri-engraftment syndrome: the patient had a non-infectious fever, non-productive cough, and respiratory distress with moderate hypoxia that required oxygen support via a nasal cannula. Additionally, interstitial infiltrates were seen on a chest CT scan. He was treated with methylprednisolone, initially at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day and progressively tapering down over 2 weeks, with good response.
On day +39, the patient reported abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea〞his stool output increased from 500 mL per day to a maximum of 2900 mL per day. Investigations for Clostridioides difficile, parasites, stool cultures, and viral DNA testing of samples of the patient's stool and blood〞for cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, and rotavirus〞were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound examination showed a thickened bowel wall in the jejunal and ileal region and free abdominal fluid; colour doppler imaging of the arterial blood flow in the superior mesenteric artery showed increased perfusion (figure).
Notably, endoscopic evaluation was contraindicated because of the patient's clinical state〞he was febrile and physically moribund〞with a severe thrombocytopenia of 5?℅?109 platelets (normal 140每440).
We diagnosed the patient as having grade IV GVHD〞skin 0, liver 0, and gut 4. Methylprednisolone was restarted at a dose of 2 mg/kg per day, but to no avail. We then moved to second-line therapy which included ruxolitinib and oral beclomethasone dipropionate. The patient's diarrhoea and abdominal pain gradually improved and by day +100 both had completely resolved; the abnormal ultrasound findings also resolved (figure). The patient was allowed home after 2 months; at follow-up he was fit and well.
Intestinal GVHD〞along with opportunistic infections〞remains a major cause of death in patients undergoing allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; timely diagnosis is of crucial importance since any delay in the commencement of immunosuppressants may have dramatic consequences for the patient.
Even though endoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing GVHD, it is associated with the risk of major life-threatening complications when undertaken in such clinically vulnerable patients. Therefore, alternative radiological investigations〞including a CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast, magnetic resonance enterography, PET-CT, and both standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography〞need to be considered for diagnosing and assessing GVHD.
Notably, standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography combined with colour-coded and power doppler〞as shown in this case〞are valuable, time-saving, non-invasive and non-ionising, readily repeatable, and well tolerated investigations for the diagnosis, assessment, and follow-up of patients with intestinal GVHD (video).
target: Standard and contrast enhanced transabdominal ultrasonography, along with color-coded and power doppler emerged are not a valuable option for diagnosing GVHD.

The patient was given a conditioning regimen of busulfan, fludarabine, and thiotepa along with graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis based upon standard recommendations: ciclosporin, anti-T-lymphocyte globulin, and short-term methotrexate.
Neutrophil engraftment was achieved on day +14. However, the early post-haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation period was complicated by the development of peri-engraftment syndrome: the patient had a non-infectious fever, non-productive cough, and respiratory distress with moderate hypoxia that required oxygen support via a nasal cannula. Additionally, interstitial infiltrates were seen on a chest CT scan. He was treated with methylprednisolone, initially at a dose of 1 mg/kg per day and progressively tapering down over 2 weeks, with good response.
On day +39, the patient reported abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea〞his stool output increased from 500 mL per day to a maximum of 2900 mL per day. Investigations for Clostridioides difficile, parasites, stool cultures, and viral DNA testing of samples of the patient's stool and blood〞for cytomegalovirus, adenovirus, and rotavirus〞were negative.
Abdominal ultrasound examination showed a thickened bowel wall in the jejunal and ileal region and free abdominal fluid; colour doppler imaging of the arterial blood flow in the superior mesenteric artery showed increased perfusion (figure).
Notably, endoscopic evaluation was contraindicated because of the patient's clinical state〞he was febrile and physically moribund〞with a severe thrombocytopenia of 5?℅?109 platelets (normal 140每440).
We diagnosed the patient as having grade IV GVHD〞skin 0, liver 0, and gut 4. Methylprednisolone was restarted at a dose of 2 mg/kg per day, but to no avail. We then moved to second-line therapy which included ruxolitinib and oral beclomethasone dipropionate. The patient's diarrhoea and abdominal pain gradually improved and by day +100 both had completely resolved; the abnormal ultrasound findings also resolved (figure). The patient was allowed home after 2 months; at follow-up he was fit and well.
Intestinal GVHD〞along with opportunistic infections〞remains a major cause of death in patients undergoing allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation; timely diagnosis is of crucial importance since any delay in the commencement of immunosuppressants may have dramatic consequences for the patient.
Even though endoscopy remains the gold standard for diagnosing GVHD, it is associated with the risk of major life-threatening complications when undertaken in such clinically vulnerable patients. Therefore, alternative radiological investigations〞including a CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast, magnetic resonance enterography, PET-CT, and both standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography〞need to be considered for diagnosing and assessing GVHD.
Notably, standard and contrast-enhanced ultrasonography combined with colour-coded and power doppler〞as shown in this case〞are valuable, time-saving, non-invasive and non-ionising, readily repeatable, and well tolerated investigations for the diagnosis, assessment, and follow-up of patients with intestinal GVHD (video).
target: Standard and contrast enhanced transabdominal ultrasonography, along with color-coded and power doppler emerged are not a valuable option for diagnosing GVHD.

A 69-year-old woman who was obese presented to our emergency department with breathlessness after episodic vomiting and diarrhoea that had started the night before. She also reported right-sided pleuritic chest pain radiating to the back. She had a medical history of hyperlipidaemia and recurrent urinary tract infections.On examination she was anxious, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, and hypoxic, initially requiring supplemental oxygen, which was given through a nasal cannula. Her lungs were clear on auscultation. Arterial blood gas showed combined metabolic and respiratory acidosis. A chest x-ray was initially read as clear except for bilateral pleural effusion (figure). We decided to intubate her because she had acute hypoxic hypercarbic respiratory failure. CT of her chest showed pneumomediastinum from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragmatic hiatus, right pneumothorax, large right pleural effusion, right subcutaneous emphysema, and complete collapse of the lower lobe of the right lung (figure). On closer retrospective review of the chest x-ray, the pneumomediastinum and right subcutaneous emphysema were visible (figure). Interestingly, the subcutaneous emphysema was not palpable on physical examination.
Oesophagoscopy with minimal air inflation showed severe oesophagitis with diffuse, circumferential, black, friable mucosa that spontaneously bled from the middle to the distal third〞consistent with a diagnosis of acute oesophageal necrosis (figure). We also found a slit-like perforation measuring 20 mm in the distal third of the oesophagus and put in a stent; using video-assisted thoracoscopy, we explored and washed out the mediastinum. 30 days later, when the oesophageal stent was removed, the mucosa was pink and healed. After 3 months in hospital, the patient went home.
Acute oesophageal necrosis〞also known as black oesophagus〞is a rare but important finding. It is associated with a high mortality and perforation is a serious complication that may lead to mediastinitis and empyema. Because of rapid clinical deterioration〞especially among patients with underlying comorbidities〞awareness and prompt recognition of this condition are essential for timely intervention. Vigilant chest x-ray review for any hints of pneumomediastinum or pneumothorax in any patient with significant vomiting and chest pain is essential as, initially, such findings can be subtle even to the trained eye.

output: Acute oesophageal necrosis (black oesophagus) with distal oesophageal perforation (Boerhaave syndrome)

An 83-year-old man was admitted to our hospital reporting a 3-week history of cough and exertional dyspnoea. At the time of admission, the patient was 4 weeks into a 6-week course of daptomycin and rifampicin because he had an infected prosthetic knee joint; he also had a history of pituitary hypoplasia and had not been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2.On examination, he was afebrile, his vital signs were normal, and there was no sign of active infection in the prosthetic knee joint.
Laboratory investigations showed a long-standing lymphopenia of 0﹞7?℅?109 cells per L (normal 1﹞5每4﹞0) and a raised C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration of 186﹞5mg/L (normal 0每5). The patient's eosinophil cell count was 0﹞3?℅?109 per L (normal 0每0﹞4), haemoglobin concentration 97 g/L (normal 130每170), and platelet cell count was 322?℅?109 per L (normal 150每400). RT-PCR of four consecutive nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 were negative; routine sputum culture and sensitivity, tuberculosis work-up, respiratory viral screen, and HIV serology were all negative.
Chest imaging〞both x-ray and CT〞showed bilateral, predominantly peripheral pulmonary infiltrates (figure).
The patient was initially treated as presumed PCR-negative COVID-19 and the antibiotics were replaced with ceftriaxone; dexamethasone was not indicated because he was not hypoxic.
On day 7, due to persisting cough, a bronchoscopy was done; examination of the washings showed an eosinophilic infiltrate. A diagnosis of acute eosinophilic pneumonitis (AEP) was established through the modified Philit criteria: a respiratory illness of less than 1 month duration, pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging, an eosinophilia of at least 25% in bronchoscopic washings, and the exclusion of other pulmonary eosinophilic diseases such as allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis and vasculitis. We thought parasitic infections were unlikely to be the cause〞given the absence of a peripheral blood eosinophilia or any history of travel to a country where such infections are endemic. Additionally, the patient had no occupational or lifestyle exposure risk factors. And finally, x-ray and CT findings were not suggestive of fungal infections or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody test was negative. The patient responded rapidly to high dose prednisolone and was allowed home 14 days after he was admitted. At follow-up 3 months later, the patient's chest x-ray was normal.
Common causes of AEP include inhaled toxins〞such as smoking, inhalational drugs, and dust〞medications, and parasitic and fungal infections. Daptomycin therapy is a well recognised cause of eosinophilic pneumonitis, and we believe this was the most likely cause in our case.
Notably, the patient's symptoms, biochemical, and radiological findings〞including lymphopenia, raised CRP, and bilateral peripheral pulmonary infiltrates〞pointed towards a diagnosis of PCR-negative COVID-19. Clinicians need to be on the look out for those subtle nuances that might indicate alternative diagnoses.

A 51-year-old woman with a 2-month history of exertional dyspnoea, fatigue, and low-grade fever presented to our rheumatology clinic. She had a medical history of well controlled hypertension, and had mechanic's hands (scaly, hyperkeratoic rash) and 3 out of 5 according to the Oxford scale for strength in deltoids and biceps.
Laboratory investigations found a creatine kinase concentration of 3193 IU/L (normal range 26每200 IU/L) and creatinine concentration of 90﹞2 米mol/L (normal range 35每106 米mol/L). Antinuclear antibodies were positive with a 1:160 titre (normal range <1:80) in a cytoplasmic pattern, anti-EJ antibody was positive (identified through immunoblotting), and a chest CT showed a fibrotic non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern (figure A).
Considering the patient's presentation and laboratory findings, a diagnosis of anti-synthetase syndrome was made. She was treated with methylprednisolone (40 mg per day) and cyclosporine (50 mg twice per day) for five days, and monitored at regular intervals as an inpatient. Over 2 weeks after the initial treatment the patient's creatine kinase concentration decreased gradually; however, she began to show decreased urine output, her creatinine concentration increased to 600﹞3 米mol/L, her haemoglobin concentration dropped from 87 g/L to 73 g/L, and her platelet count gradually decreased from 266?℅?109 per L to 78?℅?109 per L. Furthermore, the patient developed abdominal pain with bloody stools 3 weeks after the initial treatment. Abdominal enhanced CT showed swelling of the small intestine wall, suggesting ischemic bowel disease (figure B). The patient had percutaneous renal biopsy, and the pathological results showed microthrombus formation in the glomerular capillary lumen, disintegration and shedding of tubular epithelial cells, and renal tubular cast formation (figure C每F), indicating thrombotic microangiopathy with acute renal tubular injury.
The patient continued glucocorticoid therapy but stopped cyclosporine (due to deteriorating kidney function and the risk of kidney damage caused by cyclosporine itself). Meanwhile, continuous renal replacement therapy, plasma exchange, and immunoglobulin infusion were performed, and rituximab was tried (2?℅?500 mg intravenous infusions, each separated by 15 days) to treat both thrombotic microangiopathy and anti-synthetase syndrome. The patient's symptoms of ischemic bowel disease and changes in the blood system were improved; however, her impaired renal function did not recover and regular haemodialysis was performed during follow-up for 3 months.
Anti-synthetase syndrome is a subtype of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, and has clinical features including interstitial lung disease, myositis, Raynaud's phenomenon, arthritis, mechanic's hands, and fever. Thrombotic microangiopathy rarely accompanies anti-synthetase syndrome; only about six cases of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy have been reported, of which two cases had no or only mild kidney injury. However, the pathogenetic mechanisms that link anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy remain obscure. One hypothesis is that activation of the complement system might play a role in promoting anti-synthetase syndrome and thrombotic microangiopathy simultaneously. Other studies have suggested that, under certain circumstances, circulating autoantibodies in patients with autoimmune inflammatory muscle diseases (including anti-synthetase syndrome) might inhibit plasma von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity, which is another pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy. Patients could need combination therapy to treat anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy, including plasma exchange, glucocorticoids, and immunosuppressive drugs. However, the combination of anti-synthetase syndrome with thrombotic microangiopathy is still difficult to treat and as such is associated with a poor survival rate.

A 78-year-old man with primary central nervous system lymphoma was transferred to our cancer centre for further treatment. The patient had been diagnosed 3 months earlier after he presented to another hospital with back pain, numbness, and tingling in all extremities; he had two cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate, which had produced a partial response. The patient had also been given dexamethasone for cerebral oedema; his medical history included type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease. He was originally from a country with a high prevalence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.
The patient's Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status score ranged from 3 to 4 due to the aggressive cancer; we planned to give him two additional cycles of rituximab and high-dose methotrexate and continue dexamethasone.
2 months after admission〞the patient had completed one rituximab combined with methotrexate cycle and started the second〞treatment was discontinued due to worsening cognitive function and chemotherapy-related leukoencephalopathy; whole brain radiotherapy was then started. A week later the patient was allowed home to continue treatment as an outpatient.
4 weeks later, the patient was readmitted with nausea, anorexia, increased daytime somnolence, and elevated liver transaminase levels (figure). On examination he was lethargic, but we found no clinical findings〞including scleral icterus or ascites〞compatible with cirrhosis. Notably, baseline HBV serology tests using an ADVIA Centaur XP immunoassay system (Siemens Diagnostics, Tarrytown, NY, USA) had been done 2 months before chemotherapy was initiated at the previous hospital, with non-reactive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) total results. He was not tested for hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs). However, on re-testing at our centre using an ARCHITECT analyser (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL, USA) we found reactive HBsAg and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) results but with a persistently non-reactive HBcAb total result; non-reactive anti-HBs; and the HBV-DNA level was 14?100?000 IU/mL, log10 7﹞15 IU/mL (COBAS HBV assay, Roche Molecular Systems), indicating HBV reactivation with hepatitis flare but without liver failure. FibroTest (Mayo Clinic Laboratories) findings were compatible with F4 fibrosis〞but liver ultrasonography with elastography showed normal echogenicity. Tests for total and IgM antibody to hepatitis B core antigen (IgM anti-HBc), HBeAg, hepatitis D total antibody, hepatitis E RNA, herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 DNA, and cytomegalovirus DNA in blood were negative. The HBV genotype was B. No HBV polymerase, precore, or basal core promoter mutations were detected.Entecavir, 0﹞5 mg orally daily, was started, which produced a good virologic response (figure).

An 86-year-old man was seen at home by an ambulance crew after a fall associated with sudden severe lower back pain and weakness in his legs. The paramedics reported that they found the patient alert and haemodynamically stable; his legs appeared pale〞although the colour returned during the journey to the hospital〞and he had weak pedal pulses.On arrival at the emergency department, we also found him to be alert and comfortable. He did not report any breathlessness or chest pain either ongoing or pre-admission.
In his medical history, he had hypertension, diabetes mellitus, prostatic hypertrophy, and atrial fibrillation (AF) and was prescribed amlodipine, tamsulosin, ramipril, and warfarin.
On examination, the patient's vital signs were normal, but he had bilateral flaccid weakness and paraesthesia of his legs, and his right femoral pulse was weaker compared to the left.
Laboratory investigations〞apart from a raised blood lactate concentration of 5﹞5 mmol/L (normal <1﹞0)〞were unremarkable. His electrocardiogram showed rate-controlled AF with no acute changes.
However, a contrast CT scan〞examining for traumatic injuries〞showed dilatation of the ascending aorta and an extensive Stanford type A aortic dissection with sparing of the coronary ostia and with no pericardial or pleural effusions (appendix). An echocardiogram showed a clear dissection flap, a dilated aortic root, and mild to moderate aortic regurgitation (figure). While we were doing the echocardiogram, fluid started accumulating rapidly in the pericardial space; there were no warning signs or preceding symptoms. The fluid accumulation led to right ventricular and then left ventricular compression and cardiac tamponade resulting in a brief period of a so-called ※swinging heart§ appearance in the blood-filled, pericardial sac (video). The patient became unresponsive and then had a cardiac arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was unsuccessful.
Ascending aortic dissection presenting solely with the features of spinal cord ischaemia with no chest symptoms is extremely rare: occurring in less than 1% of cases. If unrecognised and untreated, it is invariably catastrophic due to proximal extension of the dissection which can either affect blood flow in the left main stem coronary artery or〞as in our patient〞result in lethal cardiac tamponade due to aortic rupture. The lower limb weakness resulting from the spinal cord ischaemia is caused by restricted blood flow to the spinal arteries.
Evolving cardiac tamponade〞which we believe has not been recorded on transthoracic echocardiogram previously〞is a life-threatening emergency that even in a surgical centre has a high mortality. With type A aortic dissection emergency surgery can reduce the 1-month mortality from 90% to 30%. Stringent control of the blood pressure〞using intravenous agents such as labetalol〞and adequate analgesia are essential while awaiting surgery (video).
output: Stanford type B aortic dissection with retrograde expansion.

An 18-year-old woman with recurrent epigastric discomfort and diarrhea is diagnosed with Giardia lamblia infection, and subsequently undergoes gastroduodenoscopy with the findings in this image. What is the diagnosis?
output:
Nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the duodenum

The endoscopic image shows numerous small, whitish, rounded nodules throughout the duodenal mucosa, giving it a characteristic "cobblestone" or polypoid appearance. This pattern is classic for nodular lymphoid hyperplasia (NLH).

The association with Giardia lamblia infection is clinically significant, as nodular lymphoid hyperplasia of the small intestine is commonly associated with:
- Giardia lamblia infection
- Immunodeficiency states (particularly common variable immunodeficiency/CVID)
- IgA deficiency

The combination of recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms, Giardia infection, and this endoscopic finding should prompt evaluation for an underlying immunodeficiency, as patients with NLH and giardiasis often have hypogammaglobulinemia.

A 14-year-old boy came to our clinic with lumps in his oral cavity. His mother informed us that the lesions had appeared spontaneously 13 years before. The boy had taken numerous drugs for the condition without effect. Another 8-year-old son had similar lesions. The patient was of North American Indian descent. Oral examination showed several papulonodular lesions on the cheek mucosa, lip mucosa, and tongue (figure). The lesions were painless to palpation, soft, of different diameter, and similar in colour to normal mucosa. The clinical diagnosis was focal epithelial hyperplasia (FEH), a rare benign condition caused by human papillomavirus subtype 13 or 32. An incisional biopsy was done. Microscopic analysis showed parakeratosis, acanthosis, epithelial hyperplasia, and koilocytic cells (figure), which confirmed FEH. The patient had therapy with CO2 laser ablation; however, it is not possible to predict when FEH lesions will recur or where new lesions will be seen.

A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm〞between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38﹞9～C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze〞known as the sun-setting sign〞and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12℅109per 米 per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery〞the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention〞including drainage if possible, as in our case〞followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome〞the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

Computed tomography of the abdomen showed herniation of a loop of ileum on the left side inferior to the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle, and medial to the common femoral vessels with compression the femoral vein. Small bowel loops were dilated proximal to the herniation and collapsed distal to it. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
output:
Based on the clinical presentation of an elderly female with signs of small bowel obstruction (abdominal pain, vomiting, distension) and the specific anatomical findings on CT, the diagnosis is clear.

The CT scan and description reveal a hernia sac containing a loop of ileum located:
1.  **Inferior to the inguinal ligament**: This distinguishes it from inguinal hernias, which are superior to the ligament.
2.  **Medial to the common femoral vessels**: The femoral canal is the anatomical space medial to the femoral vein. The images show the hernia sac compressing the femoral vein laterally.
3.  **Lateral to the pubic tubercle**: The femoral ring is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament and is situated inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.

This constellation of anatomical findings is pathognomonic for a **femoral hernia**. The presence of dilated proximal bowel loops and collapsed distal loops indicates incarceration with small bowel obstruction.

Femoral hernia

An 85-year-old Gujarati woman with a 1-day history of confusion, left-sided weakness, and slurred speech attended our hospital. She had a history of headaches, which had been extensively investigated for 2 years from 2013. She also had hypertension. She had no history of recent travel.On examination, she was afebrile. She had a dense left hemiparesis; cranial nerves, visual fields, and fundoscopy examinations were normal. She was also in atrial fibrillation.
A CT scan of the patient's brain showed multiple cortical and subcortical, hypodense lesions; an MRI showed the lesions to be ring-enhancing, with surrounding vasogenic oedema (figure). A CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis found no abnormalities and a transthoracic echo was normal.
Blood investigations found her haemoglobin concentration was 12﹞4 g/dL (normal range 12﹞0每15﹞5); her white cell count was 9﹞4?℅?109 per L (normal range 4﹞3?℅?109每10﹞8?℅?109); neutrophil count was 7﹞9?℅?109 per L (normal range 1﹞5?℅?109每8?℅?109); lymphocyte count was 0﹞7?℅?109 per L (normal range 1﹞0?℅?109每4﹞8?℅?109); C-reactive protein concentration was 4﹞6 mg/L (normal range <3); and eosinophil count was 0﹞1?℅?109 per L (normal range <0﹞45?℅?109). Blood cultures were negative. HIV, syphilis, and Brucella spp serology were negative. An autoimmune screen was negative and serum immunoglobulins were not raised.
A lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 22 cm water (normal range 10每25), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear, with 98% lymphocytes (60 cells per 米L; normal range 0每5), a normal glucose concentration (3﹞1 mg/L; normal range 2﹞8每4﹞2), and a total protein concentration of 0﹞66 g/L (normal 0﹞15每0﹞45). GeneXpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra; Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) of the CSF〞for diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis〞was negative. However, we still suspected the diagnosis to be tuberculous meningoencephalitis because of the patient's ethnicity, and we started empirical treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, and prednisolone.
The patient's condition deteriorated and on day 3 of the admission, she had tonic每clonic seizures, which were initially controlled with lorazepam and levetiracetam. However, her Glasgow Coma Scale steadily dropped to 4 by the afternoon; she had an extensor response to pain stimuli, tachypnoea, pinpoint pupils, and absent doll's head and corneal reflexes. An urgent meeting between the family and clinicians was held; a consensus was made to stop active treatment〞including a decision not to carry out a brain biopsy〞and to keep the patient comfortable. She died 11 days after admission. A post-mortem examination found multiple haemorrhagic lesions in the brain (figure). Histopathology showed large amoebic cysts in the perivascular spaces and blood vessel lumens (figure). PCR for brain amoebae〞Acanthamoeba spp, Naegleria fowleri, and Balamuthia mandrillaris〞on formalin-fixed paraffin embedded tissue was negative. However, colleagues with expertise in parasitology from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, USA, using both real-time PCR and conventional genotyping PCR of the samples, were able to make a positive diagnosis for B mandrillaris (appendix). The family was informed.
Amoebic encephalitis is a difficult diagnosis to confirm and may need both diagnostic real-time PCR and conventional genotyping PCR. Often a definitive diagnosis can only be made by brain biopsy or post-mortem examination. B mandrillaris was first isolated in 1986 from the brain tissue of a mandrill. It causes serious cutaneous infections and encephalitis and is fatal in more than 98% of patients (video).

input: A 65-year-old man presented with a recent history of weight loss, early satiety, mild flank pain, and this rash on his legs. CT scan revealed a mass in the head of the pancreas. Which neuroendocrine tumor is associated with this characteristic rash?
output:
Glucagonoma

The image shows necrolytic migratory erythema (NME), which is the characteristic rash associated with **glucagonoma** - a rare neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreatic alpha cells that secretes excess glucagon.

Key features supporting this diagnosis:
- **Necrolytic migratory erythema**: The erythematous, erosive rash with a migratory pattern, blistering, and crusting typically affects the lower extremities, perineum, and perioral areas
- **Weight loss and early satiety**: Common symptoms of glucagonoma syndrome
- **Pancreatic mass**: Glucagonomas typically arise in the pancreatic body or tail, though can occur in the head

The glucagonoma syndrome (4D syndrome) includes:
- **D**ermatitis (necrolytic migratory erythema)
- **D**iabetes mellitus
- **D**eep vein thrombosis
- **D**epression

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3﹞5 cm?℅?3﹞0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm?℅?9﹞5 cm?℅?26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavall谷e lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavall谷e lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially〞as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavall谷e lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures〞although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavall谷e lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

A 34-year-old man was brought to our Emergency Department after a truck ran over the right side of his body while he was out walking. He had no medical history.On examination, the patient's vital signs were stable; he had tenderness over his right shoulder, mild tenderness and bruising over the right hip, and abrasions over the right side of his arm, chest, abdomen, and right flank. His pelvis was stable, and movements of the right hip joint were unaffected.
Laboratory investigations were within normal range. No fractures were seen on x-rays of the patient's chest, pelvis, right shoulder, and right femur. A whole-body CT scan showed subcutaneous haematomas about 3﹞5 cm?℅?3﹞0 cm in the right infra-axillary region, right lateral abdominal wall, and pelvis.
We admitted the patient under the trauma service; an MRI of his right shoulder showed an acute contusion of the right supraspinatus muscle and right acromioclavicular joint. The patient was allowed home after an orthopaedic review with a plan of conservative treatment: analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy.
At follow-up with his general practitioner, 3 weeks later, the patient had an ill-defined soft, fluctuant swelling over his right flank and a fluctuant, non-tender swelling around the right hip with no abnormalities of the overlying skin.
At further assessment, 5 weeks after the accident, the swelling over the patient's right flank had resolved, but the one over his right hip area had grown larger. An MRI of the right hip showed a large 14 cm?℅?9﹞5 cm?℅?26 cm fluid signal collection with multiple fat locules within the deep subcutaneous tissue of the right posterolateral proximal thigh and hip, immediately superficial to the intact deep fascia (figure). The findings were consistent with a diagnosis of a Morel-Lavall谷e lesion.
The patient underwent open debridement; a mixture of blood and serous fluid was drained from the lesion and multiple pseudo-polyps, that had formed as a result of fat necrosis, were excised along with the capsule of the cavity. The cavity was washed out and the incision was closed.
The patient was allowed home. At postoperative follow-up in the trauma clinic, 4 weeks later, the lesion had completely resolved.
A Morel-Lavall谷e lesion is a rare, closed, internal degloving soft-tissue injury usually resulting from trauma. Lesions can present acutely after the trauma or they can develop a few days or weeks after the injury; they are often missed initially〞as in our case. They develop by shearing forces which lead to separation of the skin and subcutaneous tissues from the underlying fascia, leading to fluid accumulation in the perifascial space.
In approximately 8% of cases, Morel-Lavall谷e lesions are associated with underlying pelvic or acetabular fractures〞although the true incidence may be higher in such patients. When the lesion is small, it may be overlooked. Additionally, Morel-Lavall谷e lesions are sometimes misdiagnosed as a post-traumatic muscle contusion, haematomas, or myositis ossificans. Early recognition of the condition prevents the development of complications such as infections or skin necrosis. MRI is the investigation of choice, aiding diagnosis, and guiding management.

On examination we found her to be unwell, with a respiratory rate of 20 breaths per min, pulse rate of 103 beats per min, a temperature of 38﹞11～C, blood oxygen saturation of 95%, and a blood pressure of 136/93 mm Hg.
A chest CT showed inflammation in both lungs and the patient was then intubated using an endotracheal tube.
Laboratory investigations showed a raised white blood cell count of 14﹞20?℅?109 per L (normal 4﹞5每11﹞0); absolute neutrophil count was 13﹞83?℅?109 per L (normal 1﹞8每7﹞5) with a percentage of 97﹞3%.
Sequencing of a strain isolated from the patient's sputum showed that she had a lung infection caused by the Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase (KPC)-producing KPC-2 strain.
We commenced treatment with antibacterial drugs: polymyxin B plus the cefoperazone-sulbactam combination for 8 days, followed by tigecycline plus fosfomycin for 2 days, and then ceftazidime-avibactam for 21 days. However, 3 days after stopping the ceftazidime-avibactam combination and replacing it with fosfomycin monotherapy, the patient's temperature increased again. Further laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 10﹞46?℅?109 per L, with an absolute neutrophil count of 8﹞63?℅?109 per L; neutrophils were 82﹞4%.
Carbapenem-resistant K pneumoniae was still cultured from a sample of the patient's sputum.
We then re-sequenced the bacteria which showed that one of the genes encoding carbapenemases〞the KPC-2 genotype〞had evolved, in vivo, from blaKPC-2 to blaKPC-76 through a 7-amino acid tandem repeat, between amino acids 262 and 268 (262V-268N dup), and a D179Y substitution mutation. We presumed the change had resulted in the treatment failure.
Additionally, antimicrobial susceptibility testing indicated that the K pneumoniae had changed its antimicrobial susceptibility profile: initially it had the characteristic growth of classic KPC-2 (figure), which is susceptible to the ceftazidime-avibactam and aztreonam-avibactam combinations; and after 3 weeks, the profile had changed to the New Delhi metallo-汕-lactamase-producing K pneumoniae, which is resistant to the ceftazidime-avibactam combination but susceptible to aztreonam-avibactam (figure).
The patient was then given the ceftazidime-avibactam combination plus amikacin, and then was switched to tigecycline plus meropenem; her symptoms improved, and her vital signs stabilised. She was then transferred to a rehabilitation facility for further treatment.
At the molecular level, nucleotide deletions, mutations, insertions, and tandem repeats are the mechanisms most commonly responsible for bacterial resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam.
The newer antibiotic combinations, such as carbapenem, meropenem, and the cyclic boronic acid 汕-lactamase inhibitor, vaborbactam, can be considered as salvage therapies for the treatment of infections caused by emerging strains with novel KPC-variants〞although these agents have not yet been marketed for clinical use in many countries.

A 27-year-old man presented to our hospital with a 4-month history of bilateral frontal headache, irritability, frontal lobe signs, bilateral proptosis, and nasal obstruction. He had no other signs or symptoms of a systemic illness. Rhinoscopy showed a soft tissue mass obstructing both nasal airways. A CT scan of his head showed hyperdense lesions involving both the paranasal sinuses (figure), with expansions into the frontal interdiplo? spaces, and some calcification (figure). An MRI scan of the brain showed a soft tissue mass extending along the anterior cranial fossa floor up to the sellar and parasellar regions (figure). Endoscopic biopsy was inconclusive; however, because of raised intracranial pressure, the patient was taken to surgery for craniotomy and excision of the lesion.During the operation, an extradural grey-coloured, foul smelling, soft tissue mass was seen carpeting the cranial fossa floor over both frontal lobes and extending up into the air sinuses. The intracranial pressure was reduced on completion of the operation.

Systemic antifungal chemotherapy should be started prior to any surgical intervention. A 6-month-old infant was brought to our hospital by his parents because they were concerned that the child's head had been getting progressively larger and that he had been refusing feeds. The parents also said that their child had a fever and was vomiting; his problems had been getting worse over the previous 2 months. The infant had no history suggestive of congenital heart disease or immunosuppression, and he had not received any vaccinations. He was born by normal vaginal delivery, and the pregnancy was uncomplicated. The child had reached all the normal developmental milestones for age until the current problems began. On examination he was conscious but moderately malnourished and healed boils were seen over his scalp. His anterior fontanelle was tense and full, and his occipitofrontal circumference was 47 cm〞between the 98th and the 99th percentiles. He was febrile with an axillary temperature of 38﹞9～C. Examination of his eyes found them to have a persistent downward gaze〞known as the sun-setting sign〞and his pupils were 4 mm in diameter and sluggishly reactive to light (figure). He had muscle weakness in his left arm and left leg, with power recorded as 1/5.A full blood count found a haemoglobin concentration of 8 g/dL and a leucocytosis (12℅109per 米 per L). Serum concentrations of electrolytes, urea, and creatine were normal. HIV testing with rapid diagnostic kits was negative. A CT of the infant's brain showed a huge right frontoparietal lesion and a smaller right parieto-occipital lesion: a ring around the outside of both hypodense lesions was enhanced by contrast. There was substantial midline shift and effacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle, and compensatory dilatation of the contralateral occipital horn (figure).
We made a diagnosis of cerebral abscesses causing macrocephaly; the anaemia was corrected by a blood transfusion and the child's haemoglobin concentration was 12 g/dL when he went to the theatre.
During the operation we made burr holes in the right frontoparietal and parieto-occipital regions and drained 250 mL of purulent, yellowish fluid from both lesions; we irrigated the brain with normal saline and did intraoperative barbotage with ceftriaxone solution.
Microbiological cultures of the fluid grew Staphylococcus aureus that was sensitive to ceftriaxone: the infant was therefore commenced on ceftriaxone at a dose of 100 mg/kg per day, divided into two and given intravenously every 12 h for 6 weeks. We then changed the antibiotic to oral cefuroxime, which was given for a further 2 weeks. The infant remained in hospital during the entire time, firstly, to ensure compliance and, secondly, to reduce the possibility of recurrence. He made a very good recovery〞the left hemiparesis resolved completely and all the features of raised intracranial pressure resolved. An ultrasound scan of the brain showed no residual abscess collection.
Brain abscesses in children are rare. Bacteria causing the infection include Klebsiella pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and group A S aureus: the relative frequencies of the different causative organisms vary by geographical location. Predisposing factors for a child developing a brain abscess include malnutrition, low socioeconomic class, HIV infection, congenital heart disease, and being immunocompromised. Early detection and appropriate surgical intervention〞including drainage if possible, as in our case〞followed by long-term antibiotic treatment can lead to a successful outcome. Importantly, children who have been treated for the initial infection need long-term follow-up to monitor for sequelae such as hearing and visual loss, epilepsy, and motor and behavioural problems. Age remains an important factor in predicting outcome〞the younger the patient, the more likely a successful result.

A 74-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. A plain-film radiograph of the abdomen showed marked dilatation of bowel loops and abrupt termination of gas within the descending colon, referred to as a colon cutoff sign. The colon cutoff sign is classically described in association with which disease process?
output:
Acute pancreatitis

The colon cutoff sign is classically associated with **acute pancreatitis**. This radiographic finding refers to the abrupt termination of colonic gas at the splenic flexure region, with gaseous distension of the transverse colon proximally and relative absence of gas distally in the descending colon.

The mechanism relates to the spread of pancreatic inflammation to the phrenicocolic ligament, which causes localized ileus and spasm at the splenic flexure, resulting in this characteristic appearance on plain abdominal radiographs.

A 53-year-old man was referred to the dermatology clinic with a 20-year history of a generalised, pruritic rash〞with features of both psoriasis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis〞and an 8-year history of progressive arthritis, diagnosed as polyarticular gout, that had recently affected his ability to walk.The patient had been prescribed topical steroids and allopurinol with little improvement to his skin or joint disease.
On examination he was generally well but confined to a gurney because of his arthritis. He had ill-defined facial erythema and erythematous scaly plaques involving approximately 30% of the body surface area of his trunk and extremities (figure; appendix). He also had tophaceous nodules and flexion deformities bilaterally in both his metacarpophalangeal and proximal inter-phalangeal joints.
While the patient's thin, scaly lesions resembled an eczematous dermatitis, the moderate demarcation of some plaques suggested psoriatic skin disease, so he was initiated on the tumour necrosis factor-汐 (TNF汐) inhibitor adalimumab; no improvement was noted at 5 months and it was stopped (appendix).
Histopathological examination of a sample of a skin biopsy〞with the hope of clarifying the diagnosis〞showed the spongiotic pattern of an eczematous dermatitis (appendix). The anti-interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) 汐 antibody, dupilumab〞approved for eczema in the form of atopic dermatitis〞was prescribed which, after 5 months, failed to show any clinical improvement.

Significant clearance of the patient's skin plaques was noted after 16 weeks, which was sustained at follow-up 9 months later (figure; appendix). The patient also reported substantial improvement in joint mobility and regained his ability to walk independently and to type on a keyboard. Therefore, we believe that in addition to gout, the patient had long-standing, undiagnosed psoriatic joint disease, which was improved by IL-23 blockade. Further, since the two forms of joint disease are known to co-occur, they may have arisen from a common pathway abnormality.
Overactivity of the IL-23 signalling pathway is involved in a range of skin diseases, including psoriasis vulgaris, some cases of pityriasis rubra pilaris, and hidradenitis suppurativa. In eczematous rashes with psoriasiform features, it is important to consider the possibility of IL-23-driven diatheses, which may cause both cutaneous and joint disease. Using high-resolution transcriptomic analysis may〞as in this case with indistinct clinical features〞enable more precise targeting of treatments in patients with a broad range of chronic inflammatory conditions.

A 21-year-old woman presented to our hospital for the first time with a history of seizures. The patient's mother had witnessed the fits and described them as lasting approximately 10 min, causing a loss of consciousness, and incontinence of urine〞compatible with a tonic-clonic seizure.She had no significant medical or family history and was not taking any medication.
On examination the patient was afebrile, her blood pressure was 201/127 mm Hg, and she was drowsy. Direct fundoscopy showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations showed serum potassium concentration was 2﹞2 mmol/L (normal 3﹞5每5﹞1) and bicarbonate was 35 mmol/L (normal 21每31); serum creatinine concentration was normal. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
Chest-x ray, brain MRI, electroencephalogram, and doppler examination of the patient's renal arteries were all normal. The patient was admitted, and during her 4 day stay no further seizures were seen. Her blood pressure was slowly lowered using intravenous labetalol given at a dose of 1 mg per min; she was later started on oral amlodipine 10 mg, clonidine 0﹞2 mg daily, and carvedilol 12﹞5 mg twice a day. She continued with these medications and oral potassium chloride after leaving the hospital.
Further investigations for causes of secondary hypertension showed normal concentrations of free plasma metanephrines, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, and 24 h urine cortisol and creatinine. Plasma renin activity ranged from 24﹞48 to 30﹞86 米g/L per h (reference range 0﹞25每5﹞82), and serum aldosterone ranged from 1﹞02 to 1﹞39 nmol/L (reference range 0﹞03每0﹞89). An abdominal CT scan showed a solitary 11 mm central kidney mass measuring 88 Hounsfield units〞arterial and venous phases〞which was too dense to be a benign cyst (figure). Selective renal venous sampling demonstrated a left to right renin ratio of 1﹞3.
The patient underwent a partial left nephrectomy and examination after removal showed a well circumscribed, variegated, and orange to red nodule, measuring 1﹞6 cm?℅?1﹞5 cm?℅?1﹞3 cm surrounded by normal renal parenchyma (figure). Histological examination of a sample of the nodule showed sheets of round to oval uniform cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (figure) and immunostaining for renin was strongly positive (figure). The diagnosis was a juxtaglomerular tumour〞also known as a reninoma.
Postoperatively, the patient's blood pressure was 132/93 mm Hg, plasma renin activity ranged between 2﹞9 and 0﹞57, and serum aldosterone was 0﹞44 and 0﹞11 at 1 and 6 h, respectively. 1 h after surgery, blood pressure remained at 132/93 mm Hg without any medications. 4 weeks postoperatively, the blood pressure was 113/76 mm Hg off all medications; 16 months later, blood pressure and electrolytes remained normal. Renal cell carcinomas may present with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and raised plasma renin concentrations〞similarly to the presentation of the benign nodule found in our patient〞and therefore need to be excluded by looking specifically for radiographic features of metastasis on imaging.
An extensive and timely work-up of secondary causes of hypertension in young people is paramount〞particularly those with severe rises in blood pressure; the diagnosis and removal of a reninoma〞as in this case〞may save patients from a lifetime of antihypertensive medication.

output:
Based on the images and the clinical presentation, the diagnosis is **Butterfly vertebra**.

**Analysis:**
1.  **Imaging:** The frontal chest radiograph (left) shows a distinct vertical radiolucent cleft in the middle of a mid-thoracic vertebral body (arrows), creating two lateral wedge-shaped halves that resemble the wings of a butterfly. The coronal CT scan (right) confirms this finding, showing a sagittal cleft through the vertebral body. The adjacent vertebral endplates (from the vertebrae above and below) are depressed toward the center to fill the gap.
2.  **Clinical Context:** The patient is a 21-year-old woman with no history of back pain. The finding was incidental. This is characteristic of butterfly vertebra, which is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.
3.  **Etiology:** A butterfly vertebra is a congenital anomaly resulting from the **failure of fusion of the lateral chondrification centers** of the vertebral body during embryological development, caused by the persistence of the notochord in the sagittal plane. The term "Butterfly vertebra" is the standard diagnostic name for this anomaly.

The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness〞persisting for several minutes〞followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8每12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11每18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation〞related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.
output: Retinal vasospasm with transient choroidal ischemia

The differential diagnosis of transient monocular vision loss (TMVL), based on clinical history alone, is a common clinical problem. A 66-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of recurrent right TMVL. He had more than 15 episodes without provocation. He described multiple islands of visual loss that coalesced to complete monocular blindness〞persisting for several minutes〞followed by recovery in a reverse manner. While venous access was being obtained for fluorescein angiography (FA), the patient reported onset of an attack. The examination was thus fortuitously done during vision loss.Normally, following intravenous injection, the dye passes through the short posterior ciliary arteries and appears in the optic disc and choroid within 8每12 s, depending on the age, cardiovascular status of the patient, and speed of dye injection. The arterial retinal circulation appears 11每18 s after injection. However, in our patient, FA of the right eye showed slightly delayed filling of the central retinal artery and severely delayed filling of the nasal choroid and prelaminar region of the optic disc (figure). The circulation of the left eye was normal. Examination 1 week later confirmed retinal circulation was normal between attacks (figure). A diagnosis of vasospasm was made and after treatment with nifedipine 5 mg twice a day, the attacks ceased. The patient remained attack free at 8 months' follow-up.
Many attempts have been made to classify TMVL from patients' descriptions to distinguish embolic from non-embolic attacks. Further, it has been speculated that the reticulated, patchy pattern of TMVL corresponds to interruption of the choroidal circulation〞related to its lobular arrangement. This will very rarely occur due to thromboembolism because of the extensive anastomoses between the posterior ciliary arteries supplying the choroid. However, whereas vasospasm of the central retinal artery has been directly observed, choroidal perfusion abnormalities can usually only be identified by FA, and no photographic evidence for this assertion has been published. Our Clinical Picture provides the first direct confirmation for the proposed theory that the reticulated pattern of TMVL is a signature of transient ischaemia of the choroidal lobular circulation. Clearly, such cases should be managed as vasospasm.

A 21-year-old woman presented to our hospital for the first time with a history of seizures. The patient's mother had witnessed the fits and described them as lasting approximately 10 min, causing a loss of consciousness, and incontinence of urine〞compatible with a tonic-clonic seizure.She had no significant medical or family history and was not taking any medication.
On examination the patient was afebrile, her blood pressure was 201/127 mm Hg, and she was drowsy. Direct fundoscopy showed no abnormal findings.
Laboratory investigations showed serum potassium concentration was 2﹞2 mmol/L (normal 3﹞5每5﹞1) and bicarbonate was 35 mmol/L (normal 21每31); serum creatinine concentration was normal. A screen for drugs of abuse was negative.
Chest-x ray, brain MRI, electroencephalogram, and doppler examination of the patient's renal arteries were all normal. The patient was admitted, and during her 4 day stay no further seizures were seen. Her blood pressure was slowly lowered using intravenous labetalol given at a dose of 1 mg per min; she was later started on oral amlodipine 10 mg, clonidine 0﹞2 mg daily, and carvedilol 12﹞5 mg twice a day. She continued with these medications and oral potassium chloride after leaving the hospital.
Further investigations for causes of secondary hypertension showed normal concentrations of free plasma metanephrines, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, dehydroepiandrosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate, and 24 h urine cortisol and creatinine. Plasma renin activity ranged from 24﹞48 to 30﹞86 米g/L per h (reference range 0﹞25每5﹞82), and serum aldosterone ranged from 1﹞02 to 1﹞39 nmol/L (reference range 0﹞03每0﹞89). An abdominal CT scan showed a solitary 11 mm central kidney mass measuring 88 Hounsfield units〞arterial and venous phases〞which was too dense to be a benign cyst (figure). Selective renal venous sampling demonstrated a left to right renin ratio of 1﹞3.
The patient underwent a partial left nephrectomy and examination after removal showed a well circumscribed, variegated, and orange to red nodule, measuring 1﹞6 cm?℅?1﹞5 cm?℅?1﹞3 cm surrounded by normal renal parenchyma (figure). Histological examination of a sample of the nodule showed sheets of round to oval uniform cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm (figure) and immunostaining for renin was strongly positive (figure). The diagnosis was a juxtaglomerular tumour〞also known as a reninoma.
Postoperatively, the patient's blood pressure was 132/93 mm Hg, plasma renin activity ranged between 2﹞9 and 0﹞57, and serum aldosterone was 0﹞44 and 0﹞11 at 1 and 6 h, respectively. 1 h after surgery, blood pressure remained at 132/93 mm Hg without any medications. 4 weeks postoperatively, the blood pressure was 113/76 mm Hg off all medications; 16 months later, blood pressure and electrolytes remained normal. The patient was urged to check her blood pressure at regular intervals in the future and to report any persistent elevations.
Renal cell carcinomas may present with hypertension, hypokalaemia, and raised plasma renin concentrations〞similarly to the presentation of the benign nodule found in our patient〞and therefore need to be excluded by looking specifically for radiographic features of metastasis on imaging.
An extensive and timely work-up of secondary causes of hypertension in young people is paramount〞particularly those with severe rises in blood pressure; the diagnosis and removal of a reninoma〞as in this case〞may save patients from a lifetime of antihypertensive medication.
